title: Programming and software engineering
text:
The coding round and the general system-design round as they are run for senior ML candidates: algorithmic patterns, Python depth, the systems languages behind inference stacks, SQL, backend and distributed-systems fundamentals, testing and profiling of ML code, and working with AI coding agents. Almost every posting names something in this area (Python alone is in about 60%), because a senior ML engineer is hired to ship and operate software, and a model that cannot be tested, profiled or served reliably is not a product.
Coding (algorithms and data structures)Practical coding (ML or backend task, often AI-assisted)System design (general)Debugging and performance roundCode review roundReview these cards →

title: Programming and software engineering
text:
The senior bar
What separates a senior answer from a mid-level one in this area.

States the invariant and the complexity before writing code, then tests the edge cases unprompted (empty input, ties, duplicates, overflow of memory rather than of integers)
Explains performance from the mechanism (GIL, copies, cache misses, queueing, network round trips) and measures before changing anything
Designs for failure by default, so every remote call has a timeout, a retry policy, an idempotency story and a backpressure path
Gives numbers in system design (QPS, bytes, p99 budget, cost) and picks the simplest design that meets them, then says what breaks at 10x
Treats ML code as software with unit tests on transforms and losses, golden tests on a frozen checkpoint, a tiny end-to-end run in CI, and tolerance bands instead of exact equality
Uses coding agents with a verification loop and stays accountable for the diff, and can say where generated code typically fails

title: Programming and software engineering
text:
Skills, checklists and questions
Tick an item when you can explain it without notes; ticks are saved in this browser. Open a question to see the answer.

Python 66% of postings

 Can explain what the GIL blocks and what it does not, and why DataLoader uses processes
 Can explain reference counting, the cyclic GC and why RSS stays high after objects are freed
 Can turn an eager pipeline into a generator pipeline and name the single-pass pitfall
 Can vectorise a nested loop with broadcasting or einsum and estimate the size of every temporary
 Can say where the per-object overhead of Python containers comes from and what to use instead (NumPy, Arrow, slots)



coreconceptMLE AI RE What is the GIL, and what does it mean concretely for a PyTorch data loader and for a Python model server?

The GIL is a lock in CPython that lets only one thread execute Python bytecode at a time. Threads still help when the work releases the lock: blocking I/O, and C extensions that drop it during long calls (NumPy on large arrays, PyTorch operators, most compression and many image-decoding libraries). Pure-Python CPU work (per-sample augmentation logic, JSON parsing, a tokenizer written in Python) gets no speed-up from threads.
Data loading. DataLoader(num_workers=N) uses worker processes for this reason. The costs are those of processes:

Batches cross a process boundary (pickled, tensors through shared memory).
Each worker holds the dataset object. With fork the pages start shared, but reference-count updates write to them, so a large Python list of objects is gradually copied into every worker. Store samples in NumPy or Arrow buffers instead.
Worker start-up is paid every epoch unless persistent_workers=True.

Serving. One Python process runs Python code on one core. The usual designs:

Several worker processes behind a load balancer; each loads its own copy of the model, which multiplies GPU memory.
One model process with dynamic batching, where the forward pass runs in C++/CUDA with the GIL released, and Python only orchestrates.
Move CPU-heavy pre-processing out of Python: Rust tokenizers, a C++ or dedicated inference server.

CPU-bound code inside an async handler is worse than slow: it blocks the event loop for every request.
Version note: CPython 3.13 added an experimental free-threaded build (PEP 703) and 3.14 made it officially supported but still optional. Single-thread overhead and extension support are the practical limits, so check each library before relying on it.
Follow-ups

Why does a thread pool speed up downloading images but not resizing them in pure Python?
Why can the memory of DataLoader workers grow during an epoch even when nothing leaks?




seniordebuggingMLE AI RE A preprocessing job over a 200 GB JSONL file is killed for running out of memory. Explain enough of Python’s memory behaviour to find the cause and fix it.

Something is materialising the data. Look for readlines(), list(...), sorted(...), json.load of the whole file, a list that accumulates results, or a DataFrame built from Python objects.
Why Python objects are expensive. Everything is a heap object with a header. On 64-bit CPython an int is 28 bytes, a float 24, an empty str about 50, an empty dict 64, and a list stores 8-byte pointers to its elements. A list of \(10^8\) floats costs about \((8 + 24) \times 10^8 = 3.2\) GB against 0.8 GB as a float64 array. A list of dicts per record is the worst case.
How memory is released. Reference counting frees an object when its count reaches zero; the cyclic garbage collector handles reference cycles later. Freed memory goes back to CPython’s allocator and not necessarily to the OS, so RSS can stay near its peak. Hidden references keep objects alive: a global cache, a closure, a stored traceback, a list of losses that still hold a graph.
Fixes.

Stream with generators: for line in f reads lazily; a generator pipeline (parse(filter(read(f)))) holds one record at a time. Generators are single-pass, and their exceptions surface at iteration time, not at creation.
Process in bounded chunks (itertools.islice, or itertools.batched from 3.12) and write each chunk out, for example to partitioned Parquet.
Columnar storage for what must stay in memory: NumPy, Arrow, __slots__ or dataclass(slots=True) for small records.
Shard the file and run one process per shard; np.memmap or Arrow memory mapping for random access.
Know which operations copy: NumPy basic slicing returns a view, boolean and fancy indexing copy, and so does most pandas filtering.

Measure with tracemalloc or memray, and peak RSS with /usr/bin/time -v. sys.getsizeof is shallow and undercounts containers.
Follow-ups

What is the difference between a generator expression and a list comprehension at run time?
RSS does not drop after del big_list. Is that a leak?




corecodingMLE AI RE Compute all pairwise squared Euclidean distances between X of shape (n, d) and Y of shape (m, d) without Python loops. What are the memory and numerical pitfalls?

import numpy as np

def pairwise_sq_dists(X: np.ndarray, Y: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    # ||x - y||^2 = ||x||^2 + ||y||^2 - 2 x.y   -> (n, m)
    x2 = np.einsum("ij,ij->i", X, X)[:, None]     # (n, 1)
    y2 = np.einsum("ij,ij->i", Y, Y)[None, :]     # (1, m)
    d2 = x2 + y2 - 2.0 * (X @ Y.T)                # one BLAS matmul
    np.maximum(d2, 0.0, out=d2)                   # clamp rounding error
    return d2
Why not plain broadcasting: ((X[:, None, :] - Y[None, :, :]) ** 2).sum(-1) builds an \((n, m, d)\) temporary. With \(n = m = 10^4\), \(d = 768\) in float32 that is \(10^8 \times 768 \times 4\) bytes, about 307 GB. The expanded form needs only the \((n, m)\) output, 400 MB.
Pitfalls:

Cancellation: for near-identical points the three terms nearly cancel and the result can be slightly negative, which becomes NaN under sqrt. Clamp at zero, and use float64 if small distances matter.
Even \((n, m)\) may not fit: chunk over rows of X and reduce each chunk (top-k, min) before moving on.
For top-k per row use np.argpartition(d2, k, axis=1)[:, :k], \(O(m)\) per row, and sort only those \(k\).
Shape discipline: keep [:, None] and [None, :] explicit and assert the output shape.

Why vectorised code is fast: the loop runs in compiled code over contiguous typed memory, with SIMD and multi-threaded BLAS, and without creating a Python object per element. The gain over a Python loop is typically one to two orders of magnitude. It stops paying when the expression creates many large temporaries, since memory bandwidth then dominates; use in-place operations, numexpr, Numba, or move to the GPU (torch.cdist).
Follow-ups

Rewrite it for cosine similarity. What must be true of the inputs?
When is a Python loop over chunks faster than a single vectorised expression?




Engineering practices (testing, review, CI) 53% of postings

 Can list the test layers for ML code (unit, numerical, tiny end-to-end, golden, data)
 Can make a training run reproducible and say what remains non-deterministic
 Can describe the release gates of a model pipeline and the stages of a rollout
 Can review an ML pull request for leakage and eval validity, not only style



seniordesignMLE AI RE How do you test ML code, given that training has no obvious expected output?

Split the code into parts that do have an expected output, and test stochastic parts through invariants and tolerances.

Unit tests on deterministic pieces. Transforms, tokenisation, collation, masks, metrics, and losses against a hand-computed case or a slow reference implementation. Assert shapes and dtypes.
Invariance tests. Padding a sequence, or batching it with others, must not change its output. With a causal mask, changing token \(t+1\) must not change the output at \(t\). Permuting set-valued inputs must not matter.
Numerical tests. torch.autograd.gradcheck in float64 for custom autograd code. Compare with torch.testing.assert_close and a tolerance, never with exact equality.
Tiny end-to-end run (seconds, on CPU, in CI). Overfit one batch to near-zero loss. Initial loss is about \(\ln C\) for a \(C\)-class softmax. One optimiser step changes every trainable parameter and no frozen one. Save, load and get the same outputs. Resuming from a checkpoint matches an uninterrupted run.
Golden tests. A frozen checkpoint and fixed inputs produce stored outputs within tolerance. This catches silent changes in preprocessing, tokenizer versions and post-processing. Updating a golden file is a reviewed change with a stated reason.
Data tests. Schema, ranges, null rates, label distribution, no id overlap between train and test, and a parity test that sends the same raw record through the offline and online feature paths.
LLM applications. Stub the model in unit tests (record and replay), and run a fixed evaluation set with pass thresholds as a slower gate.

Determinism. Seed Python, NumPy and PyTorch, seed DataLoader workers and pass a generator, and use torch.use_deterministic_algorithms(True). Results still differ across GPU models, library versions and thread counts, so regression tests use bands, not bit equality.
What not to do: assert a metric from a stochastic training run to three decimals, or put hour-long tests on every pull request.
Follow-ups

Which bug does the “overfit one batch” test catch that unit tests miss?
A golden test fails after a dependency upgrade with differences of 1e-4. What do you do?




staffdesignMLE AI What does CI/CD look like for a model, as opposed to a stateless service? What gates a model release?

A service release is determined by code. A model release is determined by code, data, configuration, random seed and environment, and its quality is statistical. So the pipeline versions more things and the gates are comparisons with noise bands.
Identity. A model artifact is traceable to a code commit, a data snapshot id, a config, a seed and a container image. If any is missing, the model cannot be reproduced or audited.
On every pull request (minutes). Lint and type check, unit tests, the tiny training smoke test, golden inference test, image build.
On merge or nightly (hours). Train (full or reduced), then evaluate on frozen sets and compare with the production baseline.
Release gates.

Primary offline metric not worse than baseline beyond the noise floor. Measure the floor by re-running the baseline with different seeds.
No regression on protected slices; calibration within bounds.
p99 latency, memory and cost per request measured on the target hardware.
Interface compatibility with serving: feature list, tokenizer hash, pre- and post-processing versions.
For LLM systems: safety and regression suites. Prompts and configuration go through the same gates, because a prompt change is a model change.

Delivery. A registry with stages; shadow traffic, then a canary of a few percent, then an A/B test, then full rollout. Automatic rollback on SLO or guardrail breach, with the previous model kept deployable.
Hard parts.

Flaky evaluations: a gate inside the noise blocks good changes and passes bad ones.
Evaluation sets go stale and get overfitted by repeated use; refresh them and keep a held-back set.
GPU cost of CI: tier the tests, and cache data and checkpoints.
CI cannot see drift; that is monitoring’s job.

Review norms. Reviewers of ML changes check split hygiene, leakage, metric code and whether the comparison is fair, not only style. Experiment configs are committed, so results can be re-run.
Follow-ups

How do you set the tolerance of a metric gate?
Who owns the evaluation set, and how do you stop the team overfitting to it?




System design and architecture 45% of postings

 Can run a 45-minute design in a fixed order (requirements with numbers, estimates, API and data model, diagram, deep dive, failures)
 Can do back-of-envelope estimates for QPS, storage and fleet size
 Can design a durable execution service with leases, heartbeats, idempotent steps and replay



coreconceptMLE AI RE Give me your structure for a 45-minute system design interview. Where do senior candidates lose points?

A fixed order, with rough timings:

Requirements (5 min). The two or three core flows, what is out of scope, and non-functional targets as numbers: QPS, p99 latency, data volume, availability, consistency, cost.
Estimates (3 min). A day has about \(10^5\) seconds, so \(10^9\) requests per day is roughly 12,000 QPS on average; plan for a peak of two to three times that. Storage is records x size x retention. The estimates decide whether one machine, one database or a sharded fleet is needed.
API and data model (5 min). Endpoints, entities, keys and access patterns; the access patterns choose the store.
High-level design (10 min). Client, load balancer, stateless services, storage, cache, queue. Trace one read and one write through the diagram.
Deep dive (15 min). One or two hard parts: the hot path, the consistency problem, the scaling bottleneck. Offer candidates and let the interviewer pick.
Failure and operations (5 min). What happens when each component dies, overload behaviour, monitoring, rollout, cost.
Wrap-up. Trade-offs taken, and what changes at 10x.

Where points are lost:

Drawing boxes before asking for numbers.
Naming technologies instead of requirements (“Kafka” instead of “a durable log, because two consumers need replay”).
Presenting one design with no alternative and no stated trade-off.
Waiting to be led. At senior level the candidate drives and checks in.
Designing for scale the requirements do not ask for.
No write path, no data model, no failure story.
For ML candidates: all model and no system, or the reverse.

Useful magnitudes: a main-memory reference is about 100 ns, an SSD random read about 100 microseconds, a round trip inside a datacentre about 0.5 ms, across continents 100 to 150 ms.
Follow-ups

How do you decide how deep to go on a component the interviewer has not asked about?
Estimate the storage for one year of request logs for the system you just described.




staffdesignMLE AI Design a durable execution service for long-running agent or batch-inference jobs: steps take minutes to hours, workers crash, and steps call external tools with side effects.

Requirements. Submit, cancel and inspect jobs; a job survives worker and orchestrator crashes and resumes without redoing completed steps; every step runs at least once with an idempotent effect; timeouts and retries per step. Assume tens of thousands of concurrent jobs.
Core idea. Persist progress as an append-only event history per job (step scheduled, started, completed with its result). Workers are stateless; the orchestrator’s state can always be rebuilt by replaying the history. Workflow engines such as Temporal follow this model.
Components.

API and a transactional metadata store (jobs, steps, history).
Task queues with leases: a worker claims a step, heartbeats to extend the lease, and the step is redelivered if the lease expires.
Timer service for retries, timeouts and scheduled wake-ups.
Blob store for large inputs and outputs; the history holds references.

Semantics.

Lease expiry means redelivery, so steps are at-least-once. Each step passes a stable idempotency key (job id plus step id) to external tools.
Completing a step and enqueueing the next one must be atomic: write both in one transaction and publish from an outbox table, otherwise a crash between them strands the job.
A worker that lost its lease may still be running. Give each claim a fencing token and reject completions that carry a stale one.
On replay, orchestration code must take the same decisions. Model calls, tool results, clock reads and random numbers are recorded as step results and read back, never re-executed.

Long steps. Heartbeats carry a progress checkpoint (for example the batch offset), so a retry resumes mid-step. GPU pre-emption is handled the same way.
Failure policy. Per-step backoff and attempt limits, non-retryable error classes, a dead-letter state for human intervention, and compensation steps (a saga) to undo earlier side effects.
Scale and fairness. Partition history by job id; separate queues per tenant and priority; admission control at submit.
Operations. A per-job timeline, detection of jobs with no heartbeat, cost per job.
Trade-offs. Adopting an existing engine is usually right. Histories grow without bound for very long jobs, so snapshot and truncate. A DAG scheduler such as Airflow recovers at task granularity and suits batch pipelines, not interactive agents.
Follow-ups

A step charged a customer and the worker died before recording completion. What happens next?
Why must LLM calls be recorded rather than re-run on replay?




Debugging and performance profiling 42% of postings

 Can choose between py-spy, cProfile, line_profiler and torch.profiler and read a flame graph
 Can time GPU code correctly (warm-up, synchronize)
 Can prove or rule out a GPU-starved input pipeline with two experiments
 Can investigate a p99 regression where p50 is unchanged



coreconceptMLE AI RE A Python training or serving process is slow. Which profilers do you reach for, in what order, and what does each one tell you?

Measure coarse to fine, and change one thing at a time.

Stage timing and system view. Wall-clock per stage (data, forward, backward, optimiser; or queue wait, preprocessing, model, post-processing). nvidia-smi for GPU utilisation and memory, htop for per-core CPU, iostat for disks. This usually identifies which stage to profile.
py-spy. A sampling profiler that attaches to a running process with no code change: py-spy dump --pid prints every thread’s stack (the tool for a hung job), py-spy top is a live view, py-spy record -o out.svg --pid writes a flame graph. --native includes C-extension frames and --subprocesses follows workers. Overhead is low enough for production.
cProfile. Deterministic tracing with call counts and cumulative time per function. Its overhead is large and uneven (it inflates code that makes many small calls), so use it offline. line_profiler gives line-level detail in one hot function.
torch.profiler. Per-operator CPU and CUDA time, memory and input shapes, with a trace export. Sort by CUDA time to find the expensive operators, and look for unexpected CPU-GPU copies.
System level. perf for native code, strace -c for system calls, tracemalloc or memray for Python memory, torch.cuda.memory_summary() for GPU memory.

Reading a flame graph. Width is the share of samples, not time order; height is stack depth. Look for wide plateaus. An on-CPU profile hides waiting (I/O, locks, a starved GPU); use a wall-clock mode when the process is slow but not busy.
GPU timing. CUDA calls are asynchronous, so a timer around a GPU operation measures only the launch. Call torch.cuda.synchronize() before reading the clock, and discard warm-up iterations (lazy initialisation, cuDNN algorithm search, compilation).
Expectation. Amdahl’s law bounds the gain: speeding a fraction \(p\) of the run time by a factor \(s\) gives \(1 / ((1 - p) + p/s)\) overall.
Follow-ups

py-spy shows most samples in a queue.get call. What does that mean?
Why can cProfile point you at the wrong function?




seniordebuggingMLE RE GPU utilisation during training sits at 30 to 40% and fluctuates. How do you confirm that the input pipeline is the bottleneck, and how do you fix it?

Confirm with two experiments.

Train on one cached batch in a loop, with no loader. If throughput jumps and utilisation goes to nearly 100%, the GPU was starved.
Iterate the loader alone, with no model, and measure samples per second. Compare with the model’s maximum from the first experiment. The lower number is the bottleneck.

Also split each step into data-wait time and compute time (synchronise before reading the clock). A large data-wait share means starvation.
Rule out other causes of low utilisation. A .item(), .cpu() or print every step forcing a sync; logging or checkpointing in the loop; metrics computed on the CPU; a model or batch so small that Python and kernel-launch overhead dominate; in distributed training, ranks waiting for the slowest one.
Locate the cause inside the loader.

All worker cores at 100%: CPU-bound (decode, augmentation, tokenisation). py-spy dump on a worker shows where.
Cores idle with high I/O wait: storage- or network-bound.
The main process busy while workers are idle: collation or inter-process transfer.

Fix by cause.

CPU-bound: more num_workers up to the physical cores (watch RAM), persistent_workers=True, a larger prefetch_factor; move work offline (pre-tokenise, pre-resize, store decoded arrays); decode or augment on the GPU in batches.
I/O-bound: pack millions of small files into shards (tar/WebDataset, Parquet, LMDB) for sequential reads; cache on local NVMe; read in parallel.
Transfer: pin_memory=True with .to(device, non_blocking=True); return tensors or arrays from workers, not Python objects.
Variable-length data: bucket by length so batches are not padded to the longest sample.

Sizing. The loader must match the model’s throughput. If the GPUs consume 2,000 images per second and one core decodes and augments on the order of 100 to 200 per second (measure it), the job needs 10 to 20 cores for data alone.
Re-profile after each fix; the bottleneck moves.
Follow-ups

Utilisation is 100% but throughput is still low. What now?
Why can increasing num_workers make things slower?




seniordebuggingMLE AI After a deploy, the p99 latency of a Python inference service doubled while p50 is unchanged. How do you investigate?

If the SLO is breached, roll back first and investigate on a canary or in staging. Then: p50 unchanged with a worse p99 means the slowdown is intermittent, or tied to load or to a subset of requests, not a uniformly slower code path.
Narrow it down with data.

Which replicas, endpoints, tenants, request sizes? One bad node looks very different from a fleet-wide shift.
Diff the deploy: code, dependencies, model, config, base image, resource limits, replica count.
Break latency into stages with tracing: queue wait, preprocessing, model, post-processing, downstream calls. Find which stage owns the tail.

Usual suspects, by signature.

Tail tracks input length. A new model or a batching change (padding to the longest sequence in the batch).
Tail in queue wait. Fewer replicas, a lower concurrency limit, a changed batching window, or throughput per replica dropped slightly and pushed utilisation toward saturation.
Spikes at a round number (exactly 1 s, 5 s). A downstream timeout followed by a retry.
Unrelated requests slow at the same moment. Something blocks the event loop (a synchronous call in an async handler) or a thread pool is saturated.
Periodic spikes. Garbage collection, a background job, cache expiry, a metrics flush.
CPU throttling. The container’s CPU quota is lower than the threads it runs; check the cgroup nr_throttled counter.
Only new replicas. Cold start: lazy model load, first-call compilation, cold caches.
Shape-dependent recompilation or algorithm search on input shapes not seen during warm-up.

Tools. Per-stage latency histograms, a latency heat map over time, per-replica comparison, py-spy dump during a slow period, an event-loop-lag metric.
Verify. Reproduce with a load test at a constant arrival rate (open loop). A closed-loop generator that waits for each response slows down with the server and under-reports the tail (coordinated omission).
Follow-ups

Throughput per replica dropped 5%. How can that double p99?
How do you detect that the event loop is being blocked in production?




Distributed systems 35% of postings

 Can explain why exactly-once delivery is not achievable and how idempotent processing replaces it
 Can write a retry policy with exponential backoff, jitter and a retry budget
 Can compare linearizable, causal and eventual consistency and pick one per use case
 Can explain consistent hashing, hot keys and tail-latency amplification under fan-out
 Can explain why an unbounded queue does not fix overload and what to do instead



coreconceptMLE AI RE Explain at-most-once, at-least-once and exactly-once. How do you make a retried request or a redelivered message safe?

A sender that gets no reply cannot tell whether the request was lost or the reply was. It has two choices: do not retry (at-most-once, work may be lost) or retry (at-least-once, work may be duplicated). Exactly-once delivery is not achievable under failures. What systems provide is exactly-once effect: at-least-once delivery plus processing that is idempotent or transactional.
Idempotency. An operation whose effect is the same applied once or many times.

Naturally idempotent: set a value, delete by id, upsert keyed by event id, overwrite a partition.
Made idempotent: the client generates a unique key per logical operation; the server records the key and the result in the same transaction as the effect, and replays the stored result on a repeat.
Consumers: a dedup table keyed by message id, or committing the input offset atomically with the output. Kafka transactions make consume-process-produce atomic inside Kafka; an email, a payment or a launched GPU job outside it is still at-least-once.

Retry policy.

Retry only errors that can succeed later (timeouts, 503, 429), never validation errors.
Exponential backoff with jitter: sleep a random time in \([0, \min(\text{cap}, \text{base}\cdot 2^{n})]\). Without jitter, clients that failed together retry together.
Bound attempts and add a retry budget (for example, retries at most 10% of requests), so an outage is not amplified into a retry storm.
Retries multiply across layers: three layers with three attempts each can produce 27 calls. Retry at one layer and propagate deadlines.

ML examples: a replayed event stream double-counts clicks in training data; an agent tool sends the same email twice after a timeout; a re-run batch-inference job appends duplicate rows instead of overwriting its date partition.
Follow-ups

Where exactly must the idempotency key be stored for the guarantee to hold?
Is an LLM generation call idempotent? Does it matter?




seniortrade-offMLE AI RE What consistency guarantees can a replicated store offer, and which would you pick for an online feature store, a model registry and a rate-limit counter?

The models, strongest first.

Linearizable. The store behaves like a single copy: once a write completes, every later read sees it. Needs consensus (Raft, Paxos): a majority must acknowledge, so \(2f+1\) nodes tolerate \(f\) failures, writes cost a quorum round trip, and a minority partition cannot serve.
Causal and session guarantees. Read-your-writes, monotonic reads: weaker, but enough for most user-facing flows.
Eventual. Replicas converge once writes stop. Concurrent writes need a resolution rule: last-writer-wins (silently drops writes under clock skew), version vectors, or CRDTs.

Quorum replication with \(N\) replicas, \(W\) write acknowledgements and \(R\) read replicas makes a read overlap the latest write when \(R + W > N\) (for example \(N=3\), \(W=2\), \(R=2\)). That alone is not linearizability.
CAP says that during a partition you choose consistency or availability; PACELC adds that without a partition you still trade latency against consistency. Isolation levels (serializable, snapshot) are a separate axis about concurrent transactions.
Choices.

Online feature store. Eventual with bounded staleness. Features are already seconds to hours old, and availability and p99 matter more. Monitor replication lag as a feature-freshness metric.
Model registry and deployment config (“which version is production”). Linearizable or transactional: small data, few writes, and two servers disagreeing about the live model is a correctness bug. Use a relational database or etcd.
Rate-limit counter. Approximate: local counters synchronised periodically; slight over-admission is acceptable.
Usage and billing ledger. Transactional and idempotent.

The classic failure is assuming read-after-write on an asynchronous replica: the user updates a setting, the next request reads a lagging replica and sees the old value. Route those reads to the leader or carry a version token.

seniortrade-offMLE AI RE How do you partition data or traffic across nodes, and how do you handle rebalancing, hot keys and queries that must touch every shard?

Schemes.

Hash, hash(key) mod N. Even load, but changing \(N\) remaps almost every key.
Consistent hashing. Keys and nodes are hashed onto a ring; a key belongs to the next node clockwise. Adding or removing a node moves about \(K/N\) of \(K\) keys. Virtual nodes (many ring positions per machine) even out the load. Rendezvous hashing, or a fixed number of logical partitions assigned to nodes (Redis Cluster uses 16,384 slots), achieve the same.
Range. Supports ordered scans, but sequential keys such as timestamps all land on the last partition. Prefix the key with a hash bucket.

Rebalancing. Move whole partitions, not individual keys; throttle the copy; serve reads from both the old and new owner during the move.
Hot keys. A celebrity account, a NULL key, one very popular prompt. Hashing does not help, because one key is one partition. Options: cache in front, split the key with a suffix and aggregate on read, isolate it on dedicated capacity, or limit it.
Scatter-gather. A query that fans out to \(n\) shards waits for the slowest one. If each shard exceeds its p99 with probability 0.01, at least one does with probability \(1 - 0.99^{n}\): 63% for \(n = 100\). Mitigate with hedged requests, per-shard deadlines with partial results, and fewer, larger shards.
In ML systems.

A sharded vector index queries every shard for its top \(k\) and merges, so tail latency grows with the shard count.
Routing by conversation or user id with consistent hashing keeps a session on the same replica, so prefix caches stay warm.
In Kafka the partition key decides ordering (guaranteed only within a partition) and the unit of parallelism.
Sharded embedding tables: skewed id frequency makes some shards much hotter than others.

Follow-ups

staffdesignMLE AI Requests arrive faster than your GPU fleet can serve them. Walk through queues, backpressure, rate limiting and load shedding, and say what you would build first.

A queue absorbs bursts; it does not fix sustained overload. With arrival rate \(\lambda\) and service rate \(\mu\), the M/M/1 mean time in system is \(1/(\mu - \lambda)\): it grows without bound as utilisation \(\rho = \lambda/\mu\) approaches 1, and for \(\lambda > \mu\) the queue grows forever. So queues must be bounded and the system must be able to say no.
Layers, in the order I would build them.

Bounded queue with deadlines. Reject when full (429 or 503 with Retry-After): that is backpressure to the caller. Drop requests whose deadline has already passed instead of computing answers nobody is waiting for.
Concurrency limits per replica. For LLMs, limit in-flight requests or in-flight tokens rather than requests per second, because the cost of one request varies by two orders of magnitude.
Per-tenant rate limits and fairness. A token bucket per key, charged in tokens (estimate before, reconcile after), separate queues per tenant or priority class so one tenant cannot starve the rest, and interactive traffic ahead of batch.
Degradation. A smaller model, a lower output cap, a cached or stale answer, skipping the reranker.
Retry control. Retry budgets and circuit breakers. Without them the system can stay overloaded after the original spike has passed, because retries keep the load up.
Autoscaling. Necessary, but a GPU node plus model load takes minutes, so shedding has to cover the gap.

import time

class TokenBucket:
    def __init__(self, rate: float, burst: float):
        self.rate, self.burst = rate, burst
        self.tokens, self.t = burst, time.monotonic()

    def allow(self, cost: float = 1.0) -> bool:
        now = time.monotonic()
        self.tokens = min(self.burst, self.tokens + (now - self.t) * self.rate)
        self.t = now
        if self.tokens >= cost:
            self.tokens -= cost
            return True
        return False
Across many gateway instances, keep the bucket in a shared store with an atomic update, or use local buckets with periodic synchronisation and accept approximate limits.
Metrics to alert on: queue depth, time spent queued, rejection rate by tenant, and goodput (requests completed within their deadline), which is the number that falls in an overload while throughput looks healthy.

Satisfying the check instead of the intent. Editing or deleting a failing test, special-casing the test input, swallowing exceptions, adding a silent fallback, mocking the thing under test.
Local fix, global damage. Patching the symptom at the call site, duplicating a helper that already exists, breaking a convention or invariant that was not in its context, ignoring concurrency and failure paths.

Long-task drift. Early constraints are forgotten as the context fills; the final summary claims more than the diff contains or than was actually run.
Silent ML bugs. Wrong axis, unintended broadcasting, leakage between splits, an off-by-one in shifted labels, a wrong mask. Nothing crashes and the loss still decreases.

Review the diff, not the description. Read the tests first: do they assert behaviour, and could they fail?

Keep diffs small enough to read properly; split large ones.

Shape.

What a senior design specifies.

Idempotency. POST accepts an Idempotency-Key; the server stores key to response for a retention period (for example 24 h) and replays it. Same key with a different body is an error.
Errors. One envelope (code, message, request id), with status codes that tell the client what to do: 400/422 fix the request, 401/403, 404, 409, 429 with Retry-After, 503 overloaded, 504 deadline exceeded. State which are retryable.
Deadlines and cancellation. The client sends a deadline; it propagates to downstream calls, and a cancelled request frees its GPU slot.
Limits. Payload size, batch size, rate limits per key in requests and in tokens, returned in headers.
Versioning. Additive changes only within /v1. The model version is separate from the API version: the client can pin a model id, and every response reports which model produced it.
Pagination. Opaque cursors, not offsets.
Observability. Request id, trace context, and usage (tokens, latency) in the response.
Security. Authentication, per-tenant isolation, and a stated policy on logging request content.

REST or gRPC. gRPC (HTTP/2, protobuf, generated clients, deadlines and streaming built in) for internal service-to-service calls; JSON over HTTP with SSE for public and browser clients. With protobuf, never reuse or renumber fields; add new optional fields only.

seniortrade-offMLE AI Where would you put caches in an ML serving path, and what goes wrong with each?

What is cacheable.

Feature lookups per user or item, with a TTL of seconds to minutes.
Embeddings, keyed by content hash and model version.
Whole responses for deterministic requests, keyed by a hash of model version, normalised input and parameters.
Retrieval results and, for LLMs, the computed state of a shared prompt prefix.

Whether it pays depends on the request distribution: head-heavy traffic caches well, a long tail does not. Expected latency is \(h\,t_{\text{hit}} + (1-h)\,t_{\text{miss}}\), but the tail does not improve unless the hit rate \(h\) exceeds the percentile: with 90% hits, p99 is still a miss.
Patterns. Cache-aside (read cache, on miss read the source and populate) is the default; write-through keeps the cache current at the cost of write latency. Invalidate by TTL or, better, by versioned keys: put the model or feature version in the key so a deploy invalidates naturally.
Failure modes.

Stampede. A hot key expires and many requests recompute it at once. Use single-flight (one loader per key), jittered TTLs, or serve stale while refreshing.
Cold start. After a deploy or restart the cache is empty, latency jumps and the backends take full load. Warm it, or ramp traffic gradually. If the system cannot survive an empty cache, the cache is a hard dependency and its failure is an outage.
Staleness. Acceptable for a slowly changing embedding, not for a price or an account balance.
Wrong key. A personalised response stored under a shared key leaks data between users; a key without the experiment arm or model version contaminates A/B tests.
Nondeterminism. Caching a sampled generation changes product behaviour: the same question always gets the same answer.
Write races. Updating the database and the cache separately can leave them inconsistent; delete the cache entry after the write commits and rely on TTL as the backstop.

Monitor hit rate, latency by hit and miss, eviction rate and entry age.
Follow-ups

How does single-flight work across several server instances?
Hit rate is 95% but p99 did not move. Why?

seniorconceptMLE RE As an ML engineer, what should you be able to explain about C++ ownership (RAII, smart pointers, move semantics), and why are inference runtimes written in C++?

RAII. A resource’s lifetime is tied to an object’s scope: the constructor acquires, the destructor releases, and the destructor runs deterministically at scope exit, including when an exception unwinds the stack. It covers memory, file handles, mutexes (std::lock_guard) and GPU buffers. There is no garbage collector, so there are no collector pauses.
Ownership in the type.

std::unique_ptr<T>: single owner, no overhead, move-only.
std::shared_ptr<T>: shared ownership through an atomic reference count; copying it costs an atomic increment. std::weak_ptr breaks cycles.
Raw pointers and references mean “not the owner”.
Rule of zero: let members manage resources. If you write one of destructor, copy or move operations, you probably need all five.

Move semantics. std::move is a cast to an rvalue reference. The move constructor then takes over the source’s buffer in \(O(1)\) instead of deep-copying in \(O(n)\); the source stays valid but unspecified. Mark move constructors noexcept, otherwise std::vector copies elements when it reallocates. Returning by value is cheap through copy elision. Pass large read-only objects by const& or std::span.
Typical bugs. Dangling references, use-after-free, iterator invalidation after push_back, data races, undefined behaviour. Tools: AddressSanitizer, ThreadSanitizer, UBSan.
Why inference stacks use it.

Real multi-threading with no GIL.
Control over memory layout and allocation (arenas, pinned memory, zero-copy between stages).
Direct access to CUDA, TensorRT, SIMD intrinsics.
No interpreter overhead per operation, which matters for small models at high QPS.
Predictable tail latency, and it embeds in non-Python hosts (mobile, vehicles, trading systems).

PyTorch is a Python front end over a C++ core; ONNX Runtime, TensorRT, Triton and llama.cpp are C++.

Every DataLoader worker gradually copies the dataset’s Python objects (reference-count writes defeat copy-on-write).
A list that accumulates tensors still attached to the graph (append loss.item(), not loss).
Unbounded prefetch queues, or loading the whole dataset into RAM.

(139 is 128 + 11, a segmentation fault, usually in native code.)
Bus error (SIGBUS) in workers means shared memory is exhausted. PyTorch passes tensors between processes through /dev/shm, and Docker’s default size for it is 64 MB. Raise --shm-size, or mount a memory-backed volume in Kubernetes.

fork copies the address space lazily; spawn starts a fresh interpreter, is slower, needs picklable arguments, and is required when workers use CUDA.
Kubernetes sends SIGTERM, waits a grace period, then sends SIGKILL. Handle SIGTERM to write a checkpoint when a job is pre-empted.
A crashed parent can leave worker processes holding GPU memory; find them with nvidia-smi and kill the PIDs.
The page cache explains why a second epoch reads faster; “available” memory, not “free”, is the number to read.
os.cpu_count() reports host cores, not the container’s CPU quota, so thread pools and worker counts oversubscribe unless set explicitly (OMP_NUM_THREADS).

seniorconceptMLE AI Walk through what happens on the network when a client calls a streaming inference endpoint over HTTPS. Where do latency and failures come from?

Connection setup. DNS lookup (cached for its TTL), TCP three-way handshake (one round trip), TLS 1.3 handshake (one more; two with TLS 1.2), then the request. A new connection therefore costs two or more round trips before the server sees the request, which is 200 ms or more across continents. Connection pooling and keep-alive remove that cost; a client that opens a connection per request pays it every time.
HTTP versions.

HTTP/1.1: one request at a time per connection.
HTTP/2: many streams multiplexed over one TCP connection; gRPC runs on it. A lost packet stalls every stream on that connection (TCP head-of-line blocking).
HTTP/3: QUIC over UDP, per-stream loss recovery.

Load balancing. L4 balances connections, L7 balances requests. Long-lived HTTP/2 and gRPC connections pin a client to one backend behind an L4 balancer: load is uneven, and newly added replicas receive nothing until connections recycle. Use an L7 proxy or client-side balancing.
Streaming specifics.

Proxies that buffer responses must be configured to pass chunks through.
Idle timeouts (often around 60 s by default) cut a stream that pauses, for example during a long tool call; send heartbeats.
TCP flow control is the backpressure: a slow reader fills its receive window and the server’s writes block.
The server learns of a disconnect only when a write fails or a keep-alive probe times out; cancel generation then.

Latency and failure sources.

Nagle’s algorithm interacting with delayed ACKs adds tens of milliseconds to small writes; set TCP_NODELAY.
Retransmission after loss: Linux’s minimum retransmission timeout is 200 ms, so a little loss creates a visible tail.
Missing timeouts. Connect, read and total deadlines are separate, and a missing read timeout hangs forever on a half-open connection.
Port or connection-table exhaustion under high connection churn.

Tools. curl -v with its -w timing variables for DNS, connect, TLS and first byte; dig; ss; tcpdump; mtr.

Bytecode is JIT-compiled as it gets hot, so a fresh instance is slow for its first requests. Benchmark after warm-up and warm new instances before they take traffic.

Executor failures come in two kinds: JVM heap exhaustion, and the Python worker exceeding the memory overhead allowance.

corecodingMLE AI Given events(user_id, ts), assign session ids where a session ends after 30 minutes of inactivity, then return each user’s session count and median session length. Which window functions do you need?

Gaps and islands: LAG flags the rows that start a session, and a running SUM of the flags numbers the sessions.
WITH flagged AS (
  SELECT
    user_id,
    ts,
    CASE
      WHEN LAG(ts) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY ts) IS NULL
        OR ts - LAG(ts) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY ts) > INTERVAL '30 minutes'
      THEN 1 ELSE 0
    END AS is_new_session
  FROM events
),
sessionized AS (
  SELECT
    user_id,
    ts,
    SUM(is_new_session) OVER (
      PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY ts
      ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
    ) AS session_seq
  FROM flagged
),
sessions AS (
  SELECT user_id, session_seq,
         MIN(ts) AS started_at, MAX(ts) AS ended_at, COUNT(*) AS n_events
  FROM sessionized
  GROUP BY user_id, session_seq
)
SELECT
  user_id,
  COUNT(*) AS n_sessions,
  PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (
    ORDER BY EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM ended_at - started_at)
  ) AS median_session_seconds
FROM sessions
GROUP BY user_id;
This is PostgreSQL syntax; interval arithmetic and the median function differ by engine.
Points to state:

Window functions are evaluated after WHERE, GROUP BY and HAVING, so they cannot be filtered in WHERE: use a CTE, or QUALIFY where the engine has it.
With ORDER BY and no frame, the default frame is RANGE ... CURRENT ROW, which includes all rows tied on the ordering key. Write ROWS explicitly for running totals.
ROW_NUMBER is unique, RANK leaves gaps after ties, DENSE_RANK does not. Latest row per key is ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY id ORDER BY updated_at DESC) = 1.
Data issues: duplicate events, time zones, one-event sessions of length zero, and a bot with millions of events making one partition very expensive to sort.
Incremental daily runs need a look-back, because a session can cross midnight.

Follow-ups

seniordebuggingMLE AI A revenue number doubled after someone joined the orders table to a new table. Which join pitfalls do you check, including the ones specific to building training sets?

Start with row counts: compare COUNT(*) and COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) before and after the join. If they differ, the join key is not unique on the other side.
General pitfalls.

Fan-out. Joining to a table with several rows per key multiplies rows, and SUM double-counts. Aggregate the many-side to the join grain first, or dedupe it with ROW_NUMBER.
LEFT JOIN turned inner. A WHERE predicate on the right table removes the NULL-extended rows. Put the predicate in the ON clause.
NULL semantics. NULL = NULL is not true, so NULL keys never match. x NOT IN (subquery) returns no rows if the subquery yields any NULL; use NOT EXISTS. COUNT(col) and AVG(col) skip NULLs.
Type and format mismatches. String '007' against integer 7, trailing spaces, case, timestamps in different time zones.
Upstream duplicates. Replayed or late events; make the key unique before joining.
Skew. One key value (NULL, 0, a default id) carries a large share of rows, and one task of the distributed join runs for hours. Filter it or salt the key.

Training-set pitfalls.

Point-in-time correctness. Join each label row to the feature values as of the event time (latest row with feature_ts <= event_ts), not to today’s snapshot. Otherwise the features contain information from after the label, which is leakage that inflates offline metrics. Implement it with ROW_NUMBER over the eligible feature rows, or with ASOF JOIN where the engine has one.
Window overlap. A 7-day aggregate that includes the label period.
Survivorship. An inner join to a table that exists only for converted or retained users silently drops the negatives.

Habits that prevent all of these: assert key uniqueness, log row counts at each step, and reconcile one total against a trusted source.

seniorcodingAI MLE Write a Go HTTP handler that relays a streaming LLM response to the client as Server-Sent Events. How do cancellation and backpressure work in your code?

func streamHandler(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
    flusher, ok := w.(http.Flusher)
    if !ok {
        http.Error(w, "streaming unsupported", http.StatusInternalServerError)
        return
    }
    w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "text/event-stream")
    w.Header().Set("Cache-Control", "no-cache")

    ctx := r.Context()               // cancelled when the client disconnects
    tokens, errc := generate(ctx, r) // unbuffered <-chan string, buffered <-chan error

    heartbeat := time.NewTicker(15 * time.Second)
    defer heartbeat.Stop()
    for {
        select {
        case <-ctx.Done():
            return // generate sees the same ctx and stops
        case tok, open := <-tokens:
            if !open {
                if err := <-errc; err != nil {
                    fmt.Fprintf(w, "event: error\ndata: %q\n\n", err.Error())
                } else {
                    fmt.Fprint(w, "data: [DONE]\n\n")
                }
                flusher.Flush()
                return
            }
            payload, _ := json.Marshal(map[string]string{"delta": tok})
            fmt.Fprintf(w, "data: %s\n\n", payload)
            flusher.Flush()
        case <-heartbeat.C:
            fmt.Fprint(w, ": ping\n\n")
            flusher.Flush()
        }
    }
}

Framing. An SSE event is data: lines ended by a blank line. Tokens are JSON-encoded because a raw newline in a token would break the framing. Lines starting with : are comments, used as heartbeats so idle proxies do not close the connection.
Flush. Without Flush the response is buffered and the client sees nothing until the end. Reverse proxies may buffer too and must be configured not to.
Cancellation. r.Context() is cancelled on disconnect and must be passed to the upstream call, so the GPU stops generating for a client that left. The producer goroutine must also select on ctx.Done() when sending, or it blocks forever on the channel: a goroutine leak.
Backpressure. The channel is unbuffered, so the producer blocks until the handler has written the previous token; the write blocks when the client’s TCP window is full. A slow client therefore holds an upstream slot, so set a write deadline (http.ResponseController) and a total deadline.
Errors after the 200. The status line is already sent, so errors travel in-band as an event.

SSE fits one-way token streams over plain HTTP; WebSocket is for bidirectional sessions such as voice. Go suits gateways because goroutines are cheap, the scheduler uses all cores and deployment is one static binary.

Where exactly would a goroutine leak in this design, and how do you test for it?
How do you resume a stream after the connection drops halfway?

import asyncio
import random

class Retryable(Exception):
    """Raised by `call` for 429, 5xx and connection errors."""

async def run_all(prompts, call, max_concurrency=32, max_attempts=5, timeout_s=60.0):
    sem = asyncio.Semaphore(max_concurrency)

    async def one(prompt):
        async with sem:
            for attempt in range(max_attempts):
                try:
                    return await asyncio.wait_for(call(prompt), timeout_s)
                except (Retryable, asyncio.TimeoutError):
                    if attempt == max_attempts - 1:
                        raise
                    cap = min(30.0, 0.5 * 2 ** attempt)
                    await asyncio.sleep(random.uniform(0, cap))   # full jitter

    return await asyncio.gather(*(one(p) for p in prompts), return_exceptions=True)

gather returns results in input order regardless of completion order. return_exceptions=True keeps one failure from discarding every other result.
The semaphore bounds in-flight requests. It is held during backoff on purpose, so errors reduce the request rate.
Retry only retryable errors, with exponential backoff and jitter, and honour Retry-After when the server sends it.
Never swallow asyncio.CancelledError; cancellation must propagate.
A timeout per attempt. Without one, a hung connection holds a slot forever.

At 100,000 prompts:

All results live in memory and a crash loses them. Write each result to disk as it completes, keyed by a stable id, and skip finished ids on restart.
100,000 tasks are created up front. Use a bounded asyncio.Queue with a fixed set of worker tasks so the producer is slowed down.
Provider limits are usually on tokens per minute as well as requests; add a token bucket in front of the call.
Retrying is safe for pure generation but not for calls with side effects; those need an idempotency key.
Check the HTTP client’s connection-pool limit, which can cap concurrency below the semaphore.

On Python 3.11+ asyncio.TaskGroup and asyncio.timeout give cleaner cancellation.

    role: "tool", toolCallId: call.id, content: JSON.stringify(body),

  if (!parsed.success) return reply({ error: parsed.error.issues });

  history: Message[],
  llm: (h: Message[], s: AbortSignal) => Promise<Message>,
  signal: AbortSignal,
  maxSteps = 8,
): Promise<Message> {

    const msg = await llm(history, signal);
    history.push(msg);
    if (!("toolCalls" in msg)) return msg;
    history.push(...(await Promise.all(msg.toolCalls.map((c) => execute(c, signal)))));

from collections import defaultdict

def longest_k_distinct(s: str, k: int) -> int:
    count = defaultdict(int)
    best = left = 0
    for right, ch in enumerate(s):
        count[ch] += 1
        while len(count) > k:          # shrink until the window is valid again
            c = s[left]
            count[c] -= 1
            if count[c] == 0:
                del count[c]
            left += 1
        best = max(best, right - left + 1)
    return best

Deleting keys whose count reaches zero, otherwise len(count) is wrong.
k = 0 and the empty string (both return 0 here).
“Exactly k” is not monotone; compute at_most(k) - at_most(k - 1).
For a fixed-size window, add the new element and remove the one that leaves; do not recompute the window.

def top_k_frequent(items, k):

    heap = []                               # min-heap of (count, seq, item), size <= k

def min_largest_sum(nums: list[int], m: int) -> int:
    def feasible(cap: int) -> bool:
        parts, cur = 1, 0
        for x in nums:
            if cur + x > cap:
                parts += 1
                cur = x
            else:
                cur += x
        return parts <= m

    lo, hi = max(nums), sum(nums)      # the answer lies in [lo, hi]
    while lo < hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if feasible(mid):
            hi = mid                    # mid works: keep it
        else:
            lo = mid + 1                # mid fails: discard it
    return lo
Invariant: feasible(hi) is true and every value below lo is infeasible. The interval shrinks every iteration because mid < hi. Cost: \(O(n \log(\text{sum} - \text{max}))\).
Pitfalls:

lo must start at max(nums); below that the greedy check is meaningless because one element alone exceeds the cap.
For “largest \(x\) that works” use mid = (lo + hi + 1) // 2 with lo = mid, or the loop never ends.
For a real-valued answer, run a fixed number of iterations (about 50 halvings) instead of comparing floats.
Say why the predicate is monotone; that is the whole correctness argument.

from collections import deque

def topo_order(n: int, edges: list[tuple[int, int]]) -> list[int] | None:
    """Edge (u, v) means u must run before v. Returns None if there is a cycle."""
    adj = [[] for _ in range(n)]
    indeg = [0] * n
    for u, v in edges:
        adj[u].append(v)
        indeg[v] += 1
    queue = deque(i for i in range(n) if indeg[i] == 0)
    order = []
    while queue:
        u = queue.popleft()
        order.append(u)
        for v in adj[u]:
            indeg[v] -= 1
            if indeg[v] == 0:
                queue.append(v)
    return order if len(order) == n else None


class DSU:
    def __init__(self, n: int):
        self.parent = list(range(n))
        self.size = [1] * n

    def find(self, x: int) -> int:
        while self.parent[x] != x:
            self.parent[x] = self.parent[self.parent[x]]   # path halving
            x = self.parent[x]
        return x

    def union(self, a: int, b: int) -> bool:
        ra, rb = self.find(a), self.find(b)
        if ra == rb:
            return False                                   # already connected
        if self.size[ra] < self.size[rb]:
            ra, rb = rb, ra
        self.parent[rb] = ra
        self.size[ra] += self.size[rb]
        return True
Kahn’s algorithm is \(O(V+E)\); nodes on a cycle never reach in-degree zero, so a short order means a cycle. The DFS alternative uses three colours and reports a cycle on a back edge; in Python write it iteratively, because the default recursion limit is 1000.
Union-find with path compression and union by size costs \(O(\alpha(n))\) amortised per operation, effectively constant. It cannot delete edges and does not give paths; for those use BFS or DFS.
Topological order is what a DAG scheduler, a build system and reverse-mode autodiff all compute.

def reservoir(stream, k):

        if i < k:

        else:

    """stream yields (item, weight > 0). Efraimidis-Spirakis A-Res."""
    heap = []                                  # min-heap of (key, seq, item)
    for seq, (x, w) in enumerate(stream):
        u = 1.0 - random.random()              # in (0, 1], so log is defined
        key = math.log(u) / w                  # log of u ** (1 / w)

\[\frac{k}{n}\cdot\frac{n}{n+1}\cdots\frac{N-1}{N} = \frac{k}{N}.\]

A DP is value propagation over a graph of states whose dependency order is known in advance. The derivation is mechanical:

Brute force as decisions. Align the last characters of \(a[1..i]\) and \(b[1..j]\): match or substitute, delete from \(a\), or insert into \(a\).
State. What must the remaining problem know? Only the two prefix lengths. Say it in one sentence: \(d[i][j]\) is the minimum number of edits turning \(a[1..i]\) into \(b[1..j]\).
Recurrence from the last decision. \[d[i][j] = \min\big(d[i-1][j] + 1,\; d[i][j-1] + 1,\; d[i-1][j-1] + [a_i \ne b_j]\big)\]
Base cases. \(d[i][0] = i\), \(d[0][j] = j\).
Order. Each state depends on smaller \(i\) or \(j\), so row by row is a valid topological order.
Cost. \(O(mn)\) time; \(O(\min(m, n))\) memory with two rolling rows, unless the alignment itself must be recovered.

Common state families: one prefix index (house robber, LIS), two indices (LCS, edit distance), interval \([i, j]\) (matrix chain), index plus capacity (knapsack, pseudo-polynomial), bitmask for \(n \le 20\) (TSP in \(O(n^2 2^n)\)), tree DP, and (node, resource used) for constrained shortest paths.
A table works only when the state graph is acyclic. If states can be revisited (moves in four directions on a grid, cyclic graph), the order must be discovered: BFS for unit costs, 0-1 BFS for costs in \(\{0, 1\}\), Dijkstra for non-negative costs, Bellman-Ford with negative edges.
ML instances: word error rate is edit distance over words; Viterbi and the CTC forward pass are DPs over (time, state); beam search is an approximation, not a DP.
Follow-ups

Recover the actual edit script. What memory does that need?
Why does Dijkstra fail with negative edges, in terms of the order in which states are finalised?




corecodingMLE AI REasked at Anthropic Implement an LRU cache with O(1) get and put. Then a staged follow-up, as in a timed assessment: build an in-memory key-value store with fields, add a prefix scan, add per-field TTL where every call carries a timestamp, and finally add backup and restore.

LRU cache. A hash map from key to node, plus a doubly linked list ordered by recency. The map gives O(1) lookup; the list gives O(1) move-to-front and O(1) eviction from the tail. Two sentinel nodes remove every empty-list branch.
class Node:
    __slots__ = ("key", "val", "prev", "next")
    def __init__(self, key=None, val=None):
        self.key, self.val, self.prev, self.next = key, val, None, None

class LRUCache:
    def __init__(self, capacity):
        self.cap, self.map = capacity, {}
        self.head, self.tail = Node(), Node()      # head.next is most recent
        self.head.next, self.tail.prev = self.tail, self.head

    def _unlink(self, n):
        n.prev.next, n.next.prev = n.next, n.prev

    def _push_front(self, n):
        n.prev, n.next = self.head, self.head.next
        self.head.next.prev = n
        self.head.next = n

    def get(self, key):
        n = self.map.get(key)
        if n is None:
            return None
        self._unlink(n); self._push_front(n)
        return n.val

    def put(self, key, val):
        n = self.map.get(key)
        if n is not None:
            n.val = val
            self._unlink(n); self._push_front(n)
            return
        if len(self.map) == self.cap:
            lru = self.tail.prev
            self._unlink(lru); del self.map[lru.key]
        n = Node(key, val)
        self.map[key] = n; self._push_front(n)
Pitfalls: the node must store its key, or eviction cannot delete the map entry; updating an existing key must refresh recency and must not evict; get counts as a use. In Python, collections.OrderedDict with move_to_end and popitem(last=False) is the same structure. Say so, then write the list if asked.
Staged store. The stages are easy alone; the test is whether stage 1 survives stage 3. Put liveness in one helper, so TTL changes one function and not every method.
class DB:
    """key -> field -> (value, expires_at or None)"""
    def __init__(self):
        self.data = {}

    def _live(self, key, ts):
        rec = self.data.get(key, {})
        return {f: v for f, (v, exp) in rec.items() if exp is None or ts < exp}

    def set(self, ts, key, field, value, ttl=None):
        self.data.setdefault(key, {})[field] = (value, None if ttl is None else ts + ttl)

    def get(self, ts, key, field):
        return self._live(key, ts).get(field)

    def delete(self, ts, key, field):
        if field in self._live(key, ts):
            del self.data[key][field]
            return True
        return False

    def scan(self, ts, key, prefix=""):
        return sorted((f, v) for f, v in self._live(key, ts).items() if f.startswith(prefix))

    def backup(self, ts):          # store remaining lifetime, not absolute expiry
        return {k: {f: (v, None if exp is None else exp - ts)
                    for f, (v, exp) in rec.items() if exp is None or ts < exp}
                for k, rec in self.data.items()}

    def restore(self, ts, snap):
        self.data = {k: {f: (v, None if left is None else ts + left)
                         for f, (v, left) in rec.items()}
                     for k, rec in snap.items()}
What graders check: the expiry boundary (here a field set at ts with ttl is live on [ts, ts + ttl); read the statement for which side is closed), deleting an expired field returns false, scan order is specified, and a restore recomputes expiry from the remaining lifetime. Expiry here is lazy: dead fields stay in memory until overwritten, which is fine for a timed task and worth saying aloud.
In a timed assessment, pass each stage’s tests before reading the next, and do not design for stages you have not seen beyond keeping storage access behind one or two helpers.
Follow-ups

Make the LRU cache safe for concurrent readers and writers. Where does a single lock hurt, and what do real caches do instead?
The store now holds 10 million fields and most have expired. How do you reclaim memory without a full scan on every call?
Change the eviction policy to LFU with O(1) operations. What extra structure do you need?

seniorcodingMLE REasked at OpenAI A multi-part simulation question. A grid holds susceptible, infected and wall cells, and each step every infected cell infects its four neighbours. Part 1: write one step. Part 2: how many steps until nothing changes, and how many cells are never infected? Part 3: infected cells recover after k steps and become immune. Part 4: infection succeeds with probability p per infected neighbour. Part 5: make a step fast on a large grid.

The parts reuse one state representation, so choose it for the last part and not the first: integer codes per cell, and a step that reads the old grid and writes a new one. Updating in place is the classic bug: a cell infected in this step would infect its neighbours in the same step.
from collections import deque
import numpy as np

S, I, R, W = 0, 1, 2, 3          # susceptible, infected, recovered, wall
DIRS = ((1, 0), (-1, 0), (0, 1), (0, -1))

def step(grid, age=None, recover_after=None):
    n, m = len(grid), len(grid[0])
    new = [row[:] for row in grid]
    new_age = [row[:] for row in age] if age is not None else None
    for r in range(n):
        for c in range(m):
            if grid[r][c] != I:
                continue
            for dr, dc in DIRS:
                rr, cc = r + dr, c + dc
                if 0 <= rr < n and 0 <= cc < m and grid[rr][cc] == S:
                    new[rr][cc] = I
            if recover_after is not None:          # part 3
                new_age[r][c] += 1
                if new_age[r][c] >= recover_after:
                    new[r][c] = R
    return (new, new_age) if age is not None else new
Part 2 does not need the simulation. Without recovery, a cell is infected at the step equal to its shortest-path distance from the nearest infected cell, so one multi-source BFS gives the answer in O(nm) instead of O(nm) per step:
def time_to_saturate(grid):
    n, m = len(grid), len(grid[0])
    dist = [[-1] * m for _ in range(n)]
    q = deque()
    for r in range(n):
        for c in range(m):
            if grid[r][c] == I:
                dist[r][c] = 0; q.append((r, c))
    last = 0
    while q:
        r, c = q.popleft()
        for dr, dc in DIRS:
            rr, cc = r + dr, c + dc
            if 0 <= rr < n and 0 <= cc < m and grid[rr][cc] == S and dist[rr][cc] < 0:
                dist[rr][cc] = last = dist[r][c] + 1
                q.append((rr, cc))
    unreached = sum(grid[r][c] == S and dist[r][c] < 0
                    for r in range(n) for c in range(m))
    return last, unreached
Part 3 breaks that shortcut: with recovery the front can die out before it reaches a cell, so you simulate. State the order of events inside a step (here an infected cell infects, then ages, then may recover) because the tests depend on it.
Parts 4 and 5. A susceptible cell with \(k\) infected neighbours is infected with probability \(1 - (1-p)^k\). Count neighbours with four shifted slices instead of a Python loop:
def step_np(g, p=1.0, rng=None):
    inf = (g == I)
    k = np.zeros(g.shape, dtype=int)
    k[1:, :] += inf[:-1, :]; k[:-1, :] += inf[1:, :]
    k[:, 1:] += inf[:, :-1]; k[:, :-1] += inf[:, 1:]
    hit = k > 0 if p >= 1.0 else rng.random(g.shape) < 1 - (1 - p) ** k
    out = g.copy()
    out[(g == S) & hit] = I
    return out
Slices do not wrap around, which np.roll would. Pass the random generator in, so a run is reproducible and a test can fix the seed.
Testing as you go. Check the deterministic vectorised step against the loop version on random small grids, check BFS against simulate-until-stable, and check the stochastic step by frequency: one cell between two infected cells with \(p = 0.3\) should be infected in about 51% of trials.
Follow-ups

The grid is 100,000 by 100,000 and almost empty. What representation and what update loop do you use?
With recovery and p < 1, how would you estimate the probability that the outbreak reaches a given cell, and how many runs do you need for a given error?
Your vectorised step disagrees with the loop version on one random grid in a thousand. How do you find the bug?

Rust 6% of postings

 Can state the ownership and borrowing rules and which bug classes they remove at compile time
 Can explain Send and Sync and what safe Rust still does not prevent
 Can name where Rust sits in the ML stack and how it is bound to Python (PyO3)



seniorconceptMLE AI RE What does Rust’s ownership model guarantee, what does it not guarantee, and where does Rust actually appear in ML systems?

Rules.

Every value has exactly one owner and is dropped when the owner goes out of scope (RAII, no garbage collector).
Assignment and argument passing move by default; using a moved value is a compile error.
Borrowing: at any time either any number of shared references &T or exactly one mutable reference &mut T, and no reference may outlive its referent (lifetimes).
Send and Sync mark which types may be moved to or shared between threads; shared mutable state is written as Arc<Mutex<T>>.
Errors are values: Result<T, E> with ?, and Option<T> in place of null.

Guaranteed in safe code, at compile time: no use-after-free, no double free, no iterator invalidation, no data races.
Not guaranteed: deadlocks, logic errors, leaks through Rc cycles, panics, and anything inside unsafe (which FFI to C or CUDA libraries requires).
Costs. Long compile times, a real learning curve, awkward graph-shaped data structures (use indices or arenas), and a much thinner GPU and numerical ecosystem than C++.
Where it appears. Hugging Face tokenizers and safetensors, Polars, pydantic-core, the uv and ruff tools, vector databases such as Qdrant and LanceDB, the request router of text-generation-inference, and the Candle and Burn frameworks. The usual shape is a Rust core with Python bindings through PyO3, which lets the library release the GIL and parallelise across cores.
Against C++: same performance class; Rust enforces by default what C++ leaves to discipline and sanitizers; C++ still owns GPU kernels and the existing runtimes. For an ML engineer the interview level is usually “explain ownership and read the code”, unless the role is an inference or infrastructure role that lists Rust as a requirement.
Follow-ups

Why is a data race impossible in safe Rust but a deadlock is not?
How does a Rust extension release the GIL, and why does that matter for tokenisation throughput?

title: Senior-level scope and leadership
text:
The behavioural, hiring-manager and project deep-dive rounds, which decide the level of an offer more than the coding round does. Nearly every posting asks for ownership (about 78%), cross-functional work and communication (about 60% each), and half ask for comfort with ambiguity. Interviewers look for evidence that you chose the right problem, made the decisions, measured the result and changed what other people did. title: Senior-level scope and leadership
text:
The senior bar
What separates a senior answer from a mid-level one in this area.

Leads with the decision and the measured result, then explains the alternatives that were rejected and why
Separates “I” from “we” precisely and can go three levels deep on any decision in their own project
Shows judgement about what not to do, including stopping their own work, saying no and choosing the simple solution
Frames a business request as an action, a prediction target, a label source and a metric before proposing a model
Handles disagreement on substance by naming the other side’s position fairly, finding the crux and settling it with evidence
Gives evidence of leverage beyond their own output, such as people grown, standards adopted or other teams’ decisions changed
Talks about failure and uncertainty plainly, without blame and without hedging everything

title: Senior-level scope and leadership
text:
Skills, checklists and questions
Tick an item when you can explain it without notes; ticks are saved in this browser. Open a question to see the answer.

End-to-end ownership 68% of postings

 Can present a project in the order context, decisions, alternatives, measured result, what to redo, in two minutes and in seven
 Has a decision log and a numbers sheet for two or three projects and can answer “why” three levels down
 Can tell a failure story with their own contribution to the failure and the habit that changed afterwards
 Can describe the first hour, day and week after a launch that regressed a metric
 Can explain ownership as accountability for the outcome and give an example outside their formal remit



corebehaviouralMLE AI REasked at Anthropic, OpenAI, Nvidia Walk me through the most significant project you have owned. (This is the project deep-dive; how do you structure it?)

What is tested. Whether you made the decisions, whether you understand them below the surface, and whether the result was real. It is the round that most often sets the level.
Structure.

Headline (20 s). The problem, your role, the result: one sentence each.
Context (60 to 90 s). Why it mattered and to whom, the baseline, the constraints (latency, data, team size, deadline).
Your decisions. Two or three that shaped the outcome, each as options considered, criteria, choice, evidence. Say “I” for what you decided and “we” for what the team did.
Alternatives rejected. Why, given what was known then. Include the simple baseline.
The hard part. What went wrong or surprised you, and how you found out.
Measured result. Metric, baseline, delta, how it was measured (offline set, A/B test, interval), and what did not improve.
Retrospective. What you would do differently and what it changed in your later work.

Delivery. Prepare a two-minute and a seven-minute version, and expect to be interrupted; follow the interviewer’s questions instead of finishing your script. Be ready to draw the system.
Choosing the project. Recent, you made the key calls, it has a measurable outcome, it has technical depth, and it is relevant to the role. A smaller project you drove beats a famous one you assisted.
Mistakes.

Five minutes of context before any decision.
An architecture tour with no choices in it.
No numbers. If they are confidential, give relative changes and keep the reasoning.
Unable to explain a central component that someone else built.
No failure or regret anywhere, which reads as low self-awareness.

Follow-ups

What was the simplest baseline, and how much of the gain came on top of it?
If you started again today, what would you build differently?


Reported in interviews (candidate reports on third-party sites, not verified)

OpenAI, Machine Learning Engineer, undated: The project you are most proud of (Aced (formerly Exponent))
