stafftrade-offMLE AI Design model routing for an LLM product. When does a router or a cascade save money, and when does it backfire?

Two designs.

Router: a cheap classifier (or small LLM) predicts difficulty or intent and picks a model up front. One model call per request.
Cascade: call the small model first, and escalate to the large one when a check fails (schema or business validation, a verifier, low self-consistency, a learned confidence score).

Economics. With escalation rate \(e\), expected cascade cost is \(c_s + e \cdot c_l\) against \(c_l\) for always-large. It saves money only if \(c_s + e \cdot c_l < c_l\), that is \(e < 1 - c_s / c_l\), and the escalated requests pay both latencies. A router avoids the double call but its mistakes are silent: a hard query sent to the small model simply gets a worse answer.
How to set it up. Label a traffic sample with both models’ outputs and quality grades. Sweep the threshold and plot quality against cost; choose the operating point, and check quality per slice, not only on average, because routing errors concentrate in the hard tail that matters most.
Where it backfires.

LLM self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated; prefer external checks.
Two models means two prompts, two eval suites and two cache namespaces.
A provider upgrade to either model shifts the optimal threshold.
On multi-step agent tasks, a weaker model that takes more steps can cost more per task.

Alternatives to test first. The large model at lower reasoning effort; prompt caching; a fine-tuned or distilled small model for one narrow, high-volume task with a fallback to the large model on validation failure.
Monitor the route mix, escalation rate, per-route quality and cost per completed task.
Follow-ups

How would you train the router, and what is its label?
The escalation rate doubles overnight. What happened?




seniordebuggingAI Your LLM bill tripled the week after a prompt change, with flat traffic. How do you find the cause?

Decompose spend from usage logs, before and after, per route and model:
\[
\text{cost} = \text{tasks} \times \text{calls per task} \times
(\text{uncached in} \cdot p_{in} + \text{cached in} \cdot p_{cache} + \text{out} \cdot p_{out})
\]
Then check each factor.

Cache hit rate collapsed. The most likely cause of a step change with a small edit: the change put something dynamic (date, user name, request id) near the top of the prompt, or reordered tools, so every request misses the cache. Compare cached-token fractions; diff the rendered prompt of two consecutive requests.
Input grew. New examples or documents in the prompt, multiplied by every step of every agent run.
Output grew. The new instruction elicits longer answers, more reasoning tokens, or restated context.
More calls per task. The change causes more tool calls, validation failures and retries, or loops. Compare the steps-per-task distribution and the retry rate.
Model mix changed. A routing or fallback rule now sends more traffic to the expensive model.
Not the prompt at all. A retry storm from rate limits, a batch job, or a new caller, coinciding with the change.

Fix the specific cause, then prevent recurrence: report tokens, cache hit rate, steps and cost per task in the regression suite next to quality, alert on cost per task, and set budget caps per run.
Follow-ups

How would you detect a cache-breaking change in CI?
Quality improved with the new prompt. How do you decide whether to keep it?




Forward-deployed / customer-embedded delivery 12% of postings

 Run a scoping conversation that ends in one workflow, a success metric and acceptance criteria
 List what separates a demo from production for an LLM system
 Measure delivered value against a baseline and track adoption
 Handle a customer request that is technically wrong or out of scope



seniorbehaviouralAI A customer says “we want an AI agent for our operations team”. How do you scope the engagement?

What the interviewer is testing. Whether you can turn a vague ask into a deliverable with a measurable outcome, push back constructively, and avoid building a demo nobody uses.
Structure of a strong answer.

Find the workflow, not the technology. Ask who does what today, how often, how long it takes, where errors and delays are, and what a mistake costs. Watch someone do the task if possible.
Pick one narrow, high-volume, measurable workflow where errors are detectable and recoverable. Decline the “do everything” agent for the first phase and say why.
Define success with the customer. A baseline, a target metric (handle time, error rate, throughput), and acceptance criteria on a test set they help label. Agree who signs off.
Check feasibility early. Data access, APIs and permissions, security and compliance review, the human fallback path, and who owns the system after hand-off.
Plan in thin slices. A working end-to-end version on real data in the first weeks, then widen. Write down what is out of scope.
Communicate in their terms. Risks, cost per task and expected accuracy with examples of failures, not architecture diagrams.

Mistakes that sink the answer. Starting with model or framework choices; accepting the customer’s proposed solution without understanding the problem; no baseline, so value cannot be shown; promising accuracy before seeing data; ignoring the people whose work changes; treating security review as a late step.
Follow-ups

The executive sponsor wants full autonomy on day one. What do you say?
How do you handle a request you believe will not work?




staffdesignAI Your demo impressed the customer’s executives. What stands between that demo and production, and how will you prove the system delivers value?

A demo shows that the system can work on chosen inputs. Production requires that it works on their inputs, inside their systems, with known failure behaviour.
The gaps.

Distribution. Real inputs are messier than demo inputs. Build an eval set from their data, with their experts defining what correct means, and report results by slice. This is usually the largest piece of work and the one that reveals whether the project is viable.
Integration. Their identity provider, permissions, data sources, rate limits and network constraints.
Reliability. Retries, timeouts, idempotent writes, a fallback path to a human, and defined behaviour when the model is unavailable or wrong.
Security and compliance. Data residency, retention, PII handling, vendor review, audit logs. Start this early; it sets the timeline.
Cost and latency at their volume, not at demo volume.
Operations. Monitoring, alerting, a feedback channel, a process for prompt and model updates, and a named owner after hand-off.
Adoption. Training, changes to how people work, and trust built through visible sources and easy correction.

Proving value.

Agree the primary metric and measure the baseline before launch.
Pilot with a comparison: randomised by user or team if possible; otherwise a staggered rollout, with before-and-after as the weakest option because other things change too.
Track adoption and acceptance: usage, how often outputs are accepted, edited or overridden. A tool that is not used delivers nothing.
Report cost per task next to the outcome metric, and audit a sample for errors the metric does not capture.

Risks to name. The last 20% of cases taking most of the effort, undefined success criteria, scope growth, and a pilot group that is not representative.
Follow-ups

The pilot shows no improvement in handle time but users like it. What do you conclude?
Which gap would you close first if you had two weeks?




Vector search and embedding stores 12% of postings

 Explain HNSW, IVF and product quantization and the knob each exposes for recall versus latency
 Compute the memory footprint of N vectors of dimension d with and without PQ
 Compare pre-filtering, post-filtering and filter-aware graph search under selective filters
 Say when brute force or pgvector is enough and when a dedicated vector store is needed
 Measure ANN recall against exact search and plan a re-embedding migration



coreconceptMLE AI Explain HNSW, IVF and product quantization, and the recall-latency-memory trade-off each one exposes.

Exact nearest-neighbour search is \(O(Nd)\) per query. Below roughly \(10^5\) vectors that is a few milliseconds and brute force is the right answer. Beyond that, approximate indexes trade recall for speed and memory.
HNSW (graph). A multi-layer proximity graph; search starts at the sparse top layer and greedily descends. Parameters: M (links per node, typically 16-64), efConstruction (build quality), efSearch (query-time beam: higher means better recall and slower). High recall at low latency, roughly logarithmic query scaling in practice. Costs: full vectors plus links in RAM, slow builds, deletes handled by tombstones.
IVF (partitioning). k-means splits the space into nlist cells (on the order of \(\sqrt{N}\)); a query scans the nprobe closest cells. nprobe is the recall-latency knob. Less memory overhead than a graph, needs training, and degrades when the data drifts from the trained centroids.
Product quantization (compression). Split each vector into \(m\) sub-vectors and replace each with the id of its nearest of 256 centroids: \(m\) bytes per vector. A 768-dimension float32 vector is 3,072 bytes; with \(m = 96\) it is 96 bytes, 32 times smaller. Distances come from lookup tables. It is lossy, so re-score the top candidates with full vectors.
Typical combinations. HNSW when the data fits in RAM; IVF-PQ at the billion scale; disk-based graphs (DiskANN-style) when RAM is the constraint. Scalar or binary quantization with re-scoring is a simpler alternative to PQ.
Always measure. Compute recall@k against exact search on a query sample and plot it against latency; ANN recall is a property of your data and parameters, not of the library.
Follow-ups

How much RAM do 100 million 1,024-dimension vectors need in HNSW, roughly?
What happens to an IVF index as new data arrives over months?




seniortrade-offMLE AI How does metadata filtering interact with ANN search, and when is pgvector enough versus a dedicated vector database?

Filtering. Three approaches:

Post-filter: run ANN, then drop non-matching results. With a selective filter (1% of rows match) a top-100 search returns about one usable result.
Pre-filter: select matching rows, then search exactly within them. Exact and cheap when the subset is small, linear in subset size when it is not.
Filter-aware index traversal: skip non-matching nodes during graph search. Good at moderate selectivity; at very low selectivity the graph of matching nodes is disconnected and recall collapses unless the engine falls back to brute force.

Good engines choose by estimated selectivity. If the filter is always a tenant id, use a partition or namespace per tenant instead of a filter.
pgvector is enough when the corpus is in the millions to low tens of millions of vectors, the index fits in memory, QPS is moderate, and you benefit from one system: joins with relational data, transactions, row-level security for permissions, existing backups and operations. These thresholds are rules of thumb and depend on dimension and hardware. Filtered ANN behaviour in pgvector is version-dependent, so test it with your real filters.
A dedicated store earns its place at hundreds of millions of vectors or more, with strict p99 latency at high QPS, heavy filtered or hybrid search, many tenants, or a need for built-in quantization, disk-based indexes and sharding.
Either way, plan for the operational events: a new embedding model means re-embedding everything and a dual-index migration; shorter dimensions (Matryoshka-style embeddings) and quantization cut memory at some recall cost.
Follow-ups

Your filter matches 0.1% of rows. Which strategy and why?
How would you migrate to a new embedding model with no downtime?




Structured outputs and reliability of LLM pipelines 8% of postings

 Distinguish prompt-only JSON, JSON mode and schema-constrained decoding and what each guarantees
 Design a schema that does not force the model to invent values (nullable fields, enums, reasoning before answer)
 Implement a bounded retry loop that feeds validation errors back to the model
 Explain why valid JSON can still be truncated or semantically wrong and how to catch it



coreconceptMLE AI How do you get reliable structured output from an LLM? What do JSON mode and schema-constrained decoding guarantee, and what do they not?

Three levels of guarantee:

Prompt only (“reply in JSON with these fields”). Works most of the time; failures include prose around the JSON, trailing commas, missing fields.
JSON mode. The output is syntactically valid JSON, with no guarantee about fields or types.
Schema-constrained decoding (structured outputs, strict tool calling). The schema is compiled to a grammar, and at each step tokens that would violate it are masked. Output that completes always parses and matches the schema.

What constrained decoding does not guarantee:

Completion. Hitting the output token limit leaves truncated JSON; check the finish reason.
Correct values. A date field holds a valid date, not necessarily the right one.
Full JSON Schema. Providers support a subset (limits on recursion, numeric and string constraints, optional fields); check the documentation.
No refusal. The model may still decline.

Schema design matters as much as the mechanism:

Generation is left to right, so put reasoning or evidence fields before the verdict; forcing the answer first removes the model’s chance to think.
Allow null or “unknown” so the model is not forced to invent a value.
Use enums for categories; keep nesting shallow; describe each field.
For extraction, ask for the supporting quote alongside the value so it can be verified.

Then validate anyway (types with Pydantic or JSON Schema, plus business rules such as totals that must add up), and retry with the validation error on failure.
Follow-ups

Why can constraining the output format reduce answer quality?
How would you extract fields from a scanned invoice and know which ones to trust?




seniorcodingMLE AI Write a retry-with-validation wrapper for structured output from an LLM.

from pydantic import BaseModel, ValidationError

def extract_json(text: str) -> str:
    start, end = text.find("{"), text.rfind("}")
    if start == -1 or end <= start:
        raise ValueError("no JSON object found in output")
    return text[start:end + 1]

def structured_call(llm, messages, schema: type[BaseModel], max_attempts=3, check=None):
    """llm(messages) -> str. Returns a validated `schema` instance or raises."""
    msgs, last_err = list(messages), None
    for attempt in range(1, max_attempts + 1):
        raw = llm(msgs)
        try:
            obj = schema.model_validate_json(extract_json(raw))
            if check is not None:
                check(obj)                       # business rules; raises ValueError
            return obj
        except (ValidationError, ValueError) as e:
            last_err = e
            msgs = list(messages) + [            # keep only the latest failed attempt
                {"role": "assistant", "content": raw},
                {"role": "user", "content":
                    f"That output was invalid:\n{e}\n"
                    "Return only a corrected JSON object that matches the schema."},
            ]
    raise RuntimeError(f"no valid output after {max_attempts} attempts: {last_err}")
Pitfalls an interviewer checks:

Bounded attempts. Each retry is a full paid call; two or three is the usual cap.
Feed back the specific error, not “try again”. The validator’s message tells the model which field to fix.
Do not accumulate every failed attempt in the history; it grows cost and anchors the model on its mistakes.
Separate transport errors (429, 5xx, timeouts) from validation errors; they need backoff, not a repair prompt.
Semantic checks belong in check: cross-field consistency, values present in the source text.
No side effects before validation succeeds.
Log the attempt count. A rising retry rate is an early signal of a prompt or model regression.
With schema-constrained decoding the wrapper is still needed for truncation, refusals and business rules.

Extensions: escalate to a stronger model on the last attempt; return a typed failure instead of raising so the caller can route to human review.
Follow-ups

How would you handle a response truncated by the token limit?
What would you alert on in production?




Conversational AI / voice agents 6% of postings

 Break a voice-to-voice latency budget into endpointing, ASR, LLM time to first token and TTS
 Explain turn detection and barge-in, including truncating history to what was actually spoken
 Compare a cascaded ASR-LLM-TTS pipeline with a speech-to-speech model
 Design escalation to a human with a usable handoff summary



seniordesignAI RE Design a real-time voice agent. Where does the latency go, and how do you handle turn-taking and interruptions?

Pipeline. The cascaded design is voice activity and turn detection, streaming speech recognition, the LLM, then streaming text-to-speech. The alternative is a speech-to-speech model that consumes and emits audio directly.
Latency budget. People expect a reply within a few hundred milliseconds of finishing; beyond about a second the conversation feels broken. Typical contributions (approximate, system-dependent): end-of-turn detection 200-500 ms, final transcript 100-300 ms with streaming ASR, LLM time to first token 200-500 ms, TTS time to first audio 100-300 ms, plus network. What matters is time to first audio, not total generation time.
Reducing it. Stream every stage; start TTS on the first clause rather than the full reply; use a fast model and a short, cached prompt; co-locate services; replace a fixed silence timeout with a turn-detection model that uses what was said; speak a short acknowledgement before slow tool calls.
Turn-taking and barge-in. When the user starts speaking during playback: stop audio immediately, cancel the in-flight LLM and TTS, and truncate the stored assistant turn to what was actually spoken (this needs TTS timing information), otherwise the model believes it said things the user never heard. Echo cancellation stops the agent from interrupting itself. Short back-channels (“mm-hm”) should not count as interruptions.
Cascaded versus speech-to-speech. Cascaded gives text at every stage, so guardrails, tool calling, logging and model choice are straightforward, but it loses prosody and adds latency. Speech-to-speech is faster and more natural, and harder to inspect and control.
Evaluation. p50 and p95 voice-to-voice latency, word error rate on names, numbers and domain terms, interruption handling, task completion, and escalation rate.
Follow-ups

The user gives a 16-digit number. What goes wrong and how do you make it robust?
How would you test barge-in automatically?




Agent memory and state 4% of postings

 Distinguish working context, session state and long-term memory (semantic, episodic, procedural)
 Design the write path (what, when, dedupe, conflict resolution, expiry) and the read path (always loaded versus retrieved)
 Explain memory poisoning and stale-memory failure modes and their mitigations
 Scope memory by user and tenant and support inspection and deletion



seniorconceptAI RE How would you design memory for an agent that works with the same user across many sessions?

Separate three things:

Working context: what is in the window now.
Session state: the conversation, plan, scratchpad and checkpoints for one task.
Long-term memory: what persists across sessions. Useful sub-types are semantic (facts and preferences), episodic (what happened in past sessions) and procedural (instructions and learned ways of working).

Write path. Decide who writes (the agent through an explicit tool, or a background extraction job after the session), what is written (distilled statements with a timestamp and provenance, not raw transcripts), and how conflicts resolve (a new fact supersedes or updates the old one rather than accumulating). Add expiry for things that go stale.
Read path. A small, always-loaded profile for things that matter every time; everything else retrieved on demand by search, or kept as files the agent lists and reads. Always-loaded memory costs tokens on every request and can break prompt caching if it changes often.
Failure modes.

Stale or wrong memory: an error written once is replayed forever. Keep provenance, let the agent verify against the current state, and prefer current observations over memory.
Poisoning: injected content written to memory persists across sessions and survives the end of the attack. Do not write memory from untrusted content without review.
Bloat: retrieval returns marginally relevant memories that distract.
Privacy: scope strictly by user and tenant; let users inspect and delete.

Evaluate with multi-session tasks where the answer depends on an earlier session, and measure both recall of needed memories and the rate of wrong-memory use.
Start simple: a structured profile plus notes files beats a vector store until volume demands one.
Follow-ups

The user says “I moved to Berlin” and memory says Paris. What happens on write and on read?
When is memory better implemented as fine-tuning? When is it worse?

title: Training infrastructure and data systems
text:
The senior bar
What separates a senior answer from a mid-level one in this area.

Accounts for GPU memory and step time with arithmetic (bytes per parameter, activations, bandwidth) and uses it to choose between sharding, accumulation, checkpointing and a bigger machine.
Knows what each form of parallel training splits and what it communicates, and predicts where scaling stops.
Designs data pipelines to be idempotent, replayable and correct with respect to time, so that backfills and late data do not corrupt training sets.
Chooses storage formats and layouts from the read pattern of training, and can explain why small files and random reads are the enemy.
Treats long runs as failure-prone by default, with checkpointing, preemption handling and resumable data order.
Makes experiments comparable and reproducible through tracking and lineage, and spends a tuning budget deliberately.

title: Training infrastructure and data systems
text:
Skills, checklists and questions
Tick an item when you can explain it without notes; ticks are saved in this browser. Open a question to see the answer.

Data pipelines and ETL (Spark, Beam, Airflow, Flink, Kafka) 39% of postings

 Choose between batch and streaming from a freshness requirement and say what streaming costs
 Explain a Spark job’s stages, shuffles and the effect of key skew
 Describe how a stream processor gets exactly-once results with checkpoints and idempotent or transactional sinks
 Explain event time, watermarks and late data
 Design orchestrated tasks that are idempotent and can be backfilled by partition



coretrade-offMLE AI When do you build a streaming pipeline instead of a batch one for ML features or training data? What does streaming cost?

Build streaming only when the value of freshness is demonstrated; batch is the default.
Batch. Process bounded data on a schedule (hourly, daily). Simple to reason about, easy to rerun and backfill, cheap, and complete: each run sees all the data for its window. Latency is the schedule period plus the run time.
Streaming. Process events as they arrive, with results available in seconds. Needed when a feature loses value quickly: fraud signals from the last minutes, session context for recommendations, counters that gate abuse.
What streaming costs:

Time semantics. Events arrive late and out of order, so you must define event-time windows, watermarks and what happens to late data.
State. Windowed aggregates and joins hold state that must be checkpointed, restored and bounded.
Operations. A long-running job with upgrades, rescaling and backpressure, on call around the clock.
Two code paths. Training data is usually built in batch from history, while serving features come from the stream. If the logic exists twice, the two drift apart.

How to decide:

Measure the benefit: evaluate the model with features delayed by an hour or a day. If the metric does not move, do not stream.
Consider the middle ground: micro-batches every few minutes, or computing the freshest features at request time from recent raw events.
If you stream, keep one definition of each feature that runs in both modes, or log the served feature values and train on those.

Architecturally, the “lambda” pattern runs batch and stream in parallel and merges them; the “kappa” pattern uses one streaming engine and replays the log for backfills. One code path is worth a great deal.
Follow-ups

How would you quantify what a fresher feature is worth before building anything?
What breaks when a backfill is run through a streaming job?




seniordebuggingMLE AI A Spark job that builds a training set used to take 40 minutes and now takes 6 hours. How do you find out why?

Recall how Spark executes: transformations are lazy and build a plan; an action runs it as stages separated by shuffles; each stage is a set of tasks, one per partition. Slowness is almost always in a shuffle or in a few oversized tasks.
Look at the UI before the code.

Which stage takes the time? Compare with a previous run.
In that stage, compare task durations and shuffle read sizes. A median of seconds with a maximum of hours is skew; uniformly slow tasks point to volume, resources or the plan.
Check spill to disk, garbage-collection time, failed and retried tasks.

Common causes.

Key skew. One key (a null, a bot account, a default id) holds a large share of the rows, so one task does most of a join or aggregation. Fixes: filter or handle the hot key separately, salt the key, enable adaptive skew handling.
A join that changed strategy. A table grew past the broadcast threshold, so a cheap broadcast join became a shuffle join; or a missing join condition created a partial cross product. Read the physical plan.
Input growth or layout. Many more small files, or partition pruning that stopped working because of a changed filter or a cast on the partition column, so the job scans everything.
Too few or too many partitions. Huge partitions spill and fail; tens of thousands of tiny ones drown in overhead.
Python UDFs row by row, where built-in functions or vectorised UDFs would do.
Recomputation. A DataFrame used several times without caching is recomputed from the source each time.
Cluster. Fewer executors, preempted nodes, a slow storage backend.

Then prevent it. Track input sizes and stage times per run, alert on duration, and add a data-quality check on the join keys, since skew usually signals a data problem upstream.
Follow-ups

How does salting a key fix a skewed join, and what does it cost?
What do you look for in the physical plan?




seniorconceptMLE AI How does a stream processor such as Flink reading from Kafka produce exactly-once results? Explain event time and watermarks while you are at it.

Exactly-once. Messages may be delivered more than once; what can be guaranteed is that each event affects the result exactly once. Three parts make that true.

Replayable source. Kafka keeps an ordered log per partition, and a consumer’s position is an offset. After a failure the job can re-read from a known offset.
Consistent checkpoints. The engine periodically snapshots the state of all operators together with the source offsets that state corresponds to. On failure it restores the snapshot and replays from those offsets. Internal state is then as if each event had been processed once.
Sinks that do not duplicate. Replayed events are emitted again, so the sink must be either idempotent (an upsert by key, so a repeat overwrites with the same value) or transactional (output is committed atomically with the checkpoint, a two-phase commit).

Without the third part you have exactly-once state and at-least-once output.
Event time and watermarks. Events carry the time they happened, which differs from when they are processed: mobile clients buffer, partitions lag. Windows defined on processing time give results that change on replay. Event-time windows are deterministic, but the engine must decide when a window is complete. A watermark is the engine’s assertion that no events older than time \(t\) are still expected, typically the maximum event time seen minus an allowed lateness. When the watermark passes a window’s end, the window fires.
The trade-off: a generous watermark waits longer and loses less; a tight one is fast and drops or mishandles more late events. Late events can be discarded, sent to a side output, or used to update an already-emitted result, which downstream consumers must then tolerate.
For ML, late data means features computed in the stream can differ from what a batch job would compute later over complete data. That is a source of training-serving skew unless training uses the logged served values.
Follow-ups

Why is an idempotent sink easier to operate than a transactional one?
What happens to a windowed feature when a mobile client uploads events a day late?




coreconceptMLE AI What makes a scheduled data pipeline safe to rerun and to backfill? Describe how you would structure tasks in an orchestrator such as Airflow.

The property to aim for is idempotence: running a task again for the same logical period produces the same output and no duplicates. With it, retries, reruns after a bug fix and backfills are routine; without it, each is a risk.
How to get it.

Parameterise by data interval. A task processes the interval the scheduler hands it, never “now” or “yesterday” computed from the wall clock. Then running it for a date last month does the right thing.
Write by partition, atomically. Output goes to a partition keyed by the interval and is overwritten as a whole: write to a temporary location, then swap. Never append to a shared table from a task that can be retried.
Deterministic inputs. Read input partitions for the same interval, or a pinned snapshot, not whatever the source contains at run time.
No hidden state. Everything a task needs comes from its inputs and parameters.

Structure.

A DAG of small tasks with explicit data dependencies, each with one output.
Sensors or dataset triggers that wait for upstream partitions instead of fixed sleep times.
Validation tasks between stages that fail the run on bad data, so bad partitions are not consumed.
Retries with backoff for transient failures, timeouts, and alerts with an owner.
Heavy computation in the engine (Spark, the warehouse), with the orchestrator only coordinating.

Backfills. Rerun a range of intervals after a logic change. Things to plan: the order and parallelism, downstream tasks that must rerun too, load on shared systems, and versioning of the output so that models trained on the old data can still be traced. Late-arriving data needs the same mechanism: reprocess the last few days routinely.
A useful test: can you delete any output partition and regenerate it with one command?

    F.col("updated_at").desc(), F.col("ingest_id").desc())

         .withColumn("day", F.to_date("event_ts"))
         .groupBy("day", "country")

corederivationMLE RE Estimate the GPU memory needed to train a model with one billion parameters. What are the components and which one usually dominates?

Four components.
1. Parameters. \(10^9\) parameters at 4 bytes in 32-bit floats: 4 GB.
2. Gradients. One per parameter, same size: 4 GB.
3. Optimizer state. Adam and AdamW keep two moment estimates per parameter: 8 GB. SGD with momentum keeps one: 4 GB.
So the static cost with AdamW is 16 bytes per parameter, 16 GB here, before any data has passed through the model. Mixed precision does not reduce this part: under automatic mixed precision the stored weights and the optimizer state stay in 32-bit floats.
4. Activations. Every intermediate tensor needed by the backward pass is kept until it has been used. This scales with batch size, sequence length or resolution, width and depth. For a transformer, each layer keeps several tensors of shape \([B, T, d]\) and, unless a fused attention kernel is used, attention maps of shape \([B, h, T, T]\). For large batches or long sequences this component dominates, and it is the part mixed precision halves.
Also allow for the framework’s allocator cache and fragmentation, library workspaces, and a temporary peak during the optimizer step.
Levers by component.

Activations: smaller batch with gradient accumulation; mixed precision; activation (gradient) checkpointing, which recomputes activations in the backward pass at the price of roughly one extra forward pass; shorter sequences; memory-efficient attention.
Optimizer state and gradients: sharding across GPUs (ZeRO or FSDP); an 8-bit or factored optimizer; training fewer parameters (adapters).
Parameters: sharding; lower-precision frozen weights when fine-tuning adapters.

Inference needs only the parameters and one layer’s activations at a time, which is why a model that trains on 40 GB can serve on a fraction of that.
Follow-ups

Why does automatic mixed precision not halve the parameter and optimizer memory?
Doubling the sequence length quadruples memory in one case and doubles it in another. Which is which?




seniordebuggingMLE RE A training job dies with a CUDA out-of-memory error several hours in, although the first thousands of steps ran fine. How do you debug it?

An error that appears late is rarely “the model is too big”. Something grows, or a rare input is large.
1. Read the message and the counters. It reports allocated and reserved memory. Allocated is memory held by live tensors; reserved is what the framework’s caching allocator has taken from the device. Log both, and the peak, every N steps.

Allocated memory climbing steadily means a leak of references.
Flat allocated memory with a sudden failure means a large batch.
Reserved far above allocated means fragmentation.

2. Leaks of references.

Accumulating a tensor that still carries its graph, such as total_loss += loss instead of loss.item(). The whole graph of every step stays alive.
Appending outputs or activations to a Python list for logging.
Evaluation without torch.no_grad(), so graphs are built for nothing.
A caught exception whose traceback keeps tensors alive.

3. Input-dependent peaks. With variable-length sequences or image sizes, memory is set by the largest batch, which may first appear hours in. Log the batch shape at failure. Fix with a token budget per batch instead of a fixed batch size, bucketing by length, a hard cap on length, and a test at startup that runs the worst-case batch.
4. Fragmentation. Many allocations of varying size leave free memory in pieces too small to use. Mitigate by making shapes more regular (bucketing, padding to a few sizes) and by the allocator’s configuration options; consult the current PyTorch memory-management notes for the exact settings.
5. Other processes. A second job or a zombie process on the same device, or an evaluation run that starts while training memory is still held.
6. Periodic events. Evaluation, checkpointing or logging hooks every N steps that allocate extra memory.
Calling the cache-emptying function in a loop rarely fixes anything: it returns cached blocks to the device but does not free live tensors.
Follow-ups

What is the difference between allocated and reserved memory?
How would you catch the worst-case batch before the run starts?




seniortrade-offMLE RE You have a fixed budget for training hardware. Which properties of a GPU and of the machine around it matter, and how do you choose between fewer large GPUs and more small ones?

Match the hardware to what limits the workload.
Properties of the GPU.

Memory capacity. A hard constraint: it sets the largest model, batch and sequence length without sharding or accumulation, and is the first thing to check.
Compute throughput at the precision you train in, including support for the half-precision formats you plan to use.
Memory bandwidth, which bounds many operations more than raw arithmetic does.
Links between GPUs inside a node, which determine how well multi-GPU training scales.

Properties of the machine.

CPU cores and RAM per GPU for data loading and preprocessing. Starving the GPU with too few cores is a common waste.
Local NVMe for dataset caches and checkpoints.
Network interconnect between nodes, if a job spans nodes.
Power and cooling, for on-premises hardware.

Fewer large or more small?

If one model does not fit in a small GPU’s memory, large GPUs avoid the engineering and communication cost of sharding. Memory is the deciding factor more often than speed.
If the workload is many independent jobs (hyperparameter sweeps, evaluation, small fine-tunes), more small GPUs give more parallel experiments per unit of money and less waste from one job occupying a large device.
For one large job, scaling across many GPUs is sublinear, so eight devices do not give eight times the throughput; within a single node it is usually close, across nodes it depends on the interconnect.
Availability and price per useful hour (including queue time and preemption) often matter more than list performance.

Method. Benchmark your own training step on the candidates and compute cost per unit of work, such as dollars per million training tokens or per epoch, not price per hour. Include utilisation: an expensive GPU that sits idle half the day costs twice its rate.
Follow-ups

Which workload would you put on older, cheaper GPUs?
How do you compare hardware when the available benchmarks are for a different model?

coretrade-offMLE AI RE Compare Kubernetes, Slurm and Ray for running ML training. When would you choose each?

They sit at different layers and are often combined.
Slurm. A batch scheduler from high-performance computing. You submit a job requesting nodes, GPUs and time; it queues, then runs on bare metal. Strengths: designed for multi-node tightly coupled jobs, with gang scheduling, fair-share priorities, partitions, preemption and job arrays; low overhead; researchers know it. Weaknesses: little support for long-running services, containers are an add-on, and weaker isolation and ecosystem integration.
Kubernetes. A container orchestrator built for services. Strengths: one platform for training, serving and data jobs; containers and isolation by default; autoscaling of nodes; a large ecosystem. Weaknesses: the default scheduler places pods one at a time and knows nothing of queues, quotas across teams or all-or-nothing placement for a multi-worker job, so training needs a batch scheduling layer and job operators on top (such as Kueue, Volcano, Kubeflow’s training operators). More layers to operate.
Ray. A distributed computing framework for Python, not a cluster manager. It provides tasks, actors and a shared object store, with libraries for data processing, training, tuning and serving. Strengths: one programming model from a laptop to a cluster, good for heterogeneous pipelines, hyperparameter search and RL workloads with many actors. It runs on top of Kubernetes, Slurm or virtual machines, which still do the resource allocation.
Choosing:

A research cluster with large multi-node training jobs and users who want to submit scripts: Slurm.
A company that already runs services on Kubernetes and wants one platform, elastic cloud capacity and tight integration with serving: Kubernetes plus a batch layer.
Python-centric workloads that mix data processing, training and tuning in one application: Ray on whichever of the two you have.

What matters more than the choice: queues and quotas per team, preemption with checkpointing, visibility into why a job is waiting, and accounting of GPU hours.
Follow-ups

What is gang scheduling and why does a default Kubernetes scheduler get it wrong?
How do Ray actors differ from tasks, and where would you use each?




seniorconceptMLE REasked at Anthropic On a shared GPU cluster, how do quotas, priorities and preemption work, and why can GPUs sit idle while jobs are waiting?

The policy tools.

Quota. Each team has a guaranteed share of GPUs. Guarantees prevent starvation.
Borrowing. Idle quota is lent to other teams so that capacity is not wasted. Borrowed capacity is reclaimable.
Priority. Classes such as production, interactive, standard and best-effort order the queue and decide who may preempt whom.
Preemption. When a team wants its guaranteed GPUs back, or a higher-priority job arrives, borrowed or lower-priority jobs are stopped. This is acceptable only if jobs checkpoint and resume automatically.
Fair share. Priority decays with recent usage, so a heavy user does not hold the queue indefinitely.

Why GPUs idle while jobs wait.

Fragmentation. Free GPUs are scattered: 16 free in total, but no node has 8, so an 8-GPU job cannot start. Bin-packing placement (fill nodes before opening new ones) and occasional defragmentation by migrating small jobs reduce this.
Gang scheduling. A distributed job needs all its workers at once. A scheduler that starts workers one by one lets two large jobs each hold half of what they need and deadlock. All-or-nothing admission prevents it.
Head-of-line blocking. A large job at the front waits for resources while small jobs behind it could run. Backfilling runs small jobs in the gaps if they will finish before the large job’s reservation starts, which requires time limits on jobs.
Constraints. Jobs pinned to a GPU type, zone or node pool.
Reserved but unused. Interactive sessions and notebooks holding GPUs at zero utilisation. Idle detection and time limits recover them.
Other resources. Not enough CPU or memory on the node next to the free GPU.

Measure allocation rate and utilisation separately. Allocated-but-idle GPUs are a user-behaviour problem; unallocated GPUs with a queue are a scheduler problem. Show users why their job is pending.
Follow-ups

How does backfilling work, and why does it need job time limits?
A team complains its jobs are preempted too often. What do you look at?

seniordesignMLE RE Design checkpointing and restart for long training jobs on preemptible capacity, so that a preemption costs minutes and needs no human.

What a checkpoint must contain to resume exactly.

Model parameters.
Optimizer state (moments), learning-rate scheduler state and the global step.
Gradient scaler state under mixed precision; EMA weights if used.
Random number generator states.
Data position: epoch, shard and offset, or the sampler’s state, so that the resumed run neither repeats nor skips data.
The configuration and code version, to refuse resuming with a mismatched setup.

Forgetting the optimizer or scheduler state is the classic bug: the loss jumps after resume and the learning rate restarts its warm-up.
Writing it safely.

Write to a temporary name, then rename atomically, so a preemption during a write never leaves a corrupt latest checkpoint. Keep the last few and verify on load.
Write to local disk first and upload asynchronously if the remote store is slow, so the training loop does not stall.
For sharded training, each rank writes its shard in parallel.
Choose the interval from the cost of a checkpoint and the preemption rate: frequent enough that expected lost work is small, rare enough that writing is a few percent of run time. Time-based intervals are more robust than step-based ones.

Reacting to preemption.

Handle the termination signal: the platform usually gives a notice of tens of seconds to a couple of minutes. Finish the current step, write a checkpoint, exit with a code that means “retry”.
If the notice is too short for a full checkpoint, rely on the periodic one.

Restarting without a human.

The job is submitted with a retry policy; on start it looks for the latest valid checkpoint under its run id and resumes, otherwise it starts fresh. The same code path handles first start and restart.
Metrics and logs continue under the same run id, with resumes marked.
Evaluation and export jobs watch for new checkpoints instead of living in the training process.

Test it. Kill the job at random points in CI and compare the resumed loss curve with an uninterrupted run.
Follow-ups

The loss spikes after every resume. What did the checkpoint miss?
How do you make the data order resumable with a shuffled, sharded dataset?

Method
Splits

Data parallelism (DDP)

Details worth knowing:

Data parallelism averages gradients, so the effective batch is the per-GPU batch times the number of GPUs. The learning rate and warm-up usually need retuning for the larger batch.
ZeRO comes in stages: shard the optimizer state, then also the gradients, then also the parameters. Each stage saves more memory and adds communication. FSDP corresponds to the last stage: a layer’s full parameters exist on a GPU only while that layer is computing.
Pipeline parallelism leaves stages idle at the start and end of each batch (the “bubble”); more micro-batches shrink it.
Tensor parallelism communicates inside every layer, so its cost is dominated by link speed.

Large runs combine them: tensor parallelism inside a node, pipeline across a few nodes, data parallelism across the rest.
Scaling stops when communication or the input pipeline, not computation, sets the step time, or when the larger effective batch stops improving optimisation per sample.

corecodingMLE RE Write a minimal multi-GPU training loop with PyTorch DistributedDataParallel. What changes compared with single-GPU training?

import os, torch, torch.distributed as dist
from torch.nn.parallel import DistributedDataParallel as DDP
from torch.utils.data import DataLoader, DistributedSampler

def main():
    dist.init_process_group("nccl")            # one process per GPU, via torchrun
    rank = dist.get_rank()
    local_rank = int(os.environ["LOCAL_RANK"])
    torch.cuda.set_device(local_rank)

    model = DDP(build_model().cuda(), device_ids=[local_rank])
    opt = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=lr)

    sampler = DistributedSampler(train_set, shuffle=True, drop_last=True)
    loader = DataLoader(train_set, batch_size=per_gpu_batch, sampler=sampler,
                        num_workers=8, pin_memory=True)

    for epoch in range(epochs):
        sampler.set_epoch(epoch)               # new shuffle each epoch
        for x, y in loader:
            x, y = x.cuda(non_blocking=True), y.cuda(non_blocking=True)
            loss = loss_fn(model(x), y)
            opt.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)
            loss.backward()                    # gradients are averaged across ranks
            opt.step()
        if rank == 0:
            torch.save(model.module.state_dict(), "ckpt.pt")
    dist.destroy_process_group()
What changes:

One process per GPU, each with its own data loader. The sampler gives each rank a disjoint slice; forgetting set_epoch repeats the same order every epoch.
Effective batch size is per_gpu_batch times the number of processes, so the learning rate and warm-up need adjusting.
Gradient synchronisation happens inside backward(). Every rank must execute the same parameters each step; a parameter used on only some ranks raises an error or hangs.
Side effects on rank 0 only: logging, checkpointing, evaluation reports. Save model.module, not the wrapper.
Batch normalisation statistics are per process unless converted to synchronised batch norm.
Evaluation: a distributed sampler pads the dataset so every rank gets the same count, which duplicates a few examples; gather predictions from all ranks and de-duplicate, or evaluate on one rank.
Seeds: the same seed on all ranks gives identical augmentation and dropout streams; offset by rank where independence matters, but initialise the model identically.
Failure: if one rank dies, the others hang in the next collective call unless the launcher kills the group.

Follow-ups

Validation accuracy differs slightly between a 1-GPU and an 8-GPU evaluation of the same checkpoint. Why?
How would you add gradient accumulation, and what is the effective batch then?




seniorconceptMLE RE Compare synchronous all-reduce training with asynchronous parameter-server training. Why did deep learning mostly settle on the first, and where does the second survive?

Synchronous all-reduce. Every worker computes a gradient on its share of the batch; a collective operation sums them across workers; all workers apply the identical update. Mathematically it is single-machine SGD with a larger batch, which makes it reproducible and easy to reason about. An all-reduce over a ring or tree moves about twice the gradient size per worker regardless of the number of workers, so it scales well on fast links.
Its weakness is that each step waits for the slowest worker. A straggler (a throttled node, a slow disk) slows everyone, and one failed worker stops the job. This is fine on homogeneous, reliable GPU clusters and is why it is the default there.
Asynchronous parameter server. Parameters live on server nodes. Workers pull the current parameters, compute a gradient and push it; the server applies updates as they arrive, without waiting. No worker waits for another, so stragglers and failures do not block progress, and it suits heterogeneous or preemptible workers.
Its weakness is stale gradients: a gradient was computed on parameters that have since changed. Staleness adds noise that grows with the number of workers, hurts convergence and final quality, and makes runs irreproducible. The servers also become a bandwidth bottleneck for dense models.
Why all-reduce won for dense models. GPUs made each worker fast and clusters homogeneous; networks got fast enough; and optimisation quality at large scale turned out to be sensitive to staleness.
Where parameter servers survive. Models dominated by huge sparse embedding tables, as in recommendation and advertising. Each example touches a tiny fraction of the parameters, so workers pull and push only the rows they need, the tables are too large for any one machine, and conflicts between sparse updates are rare. Hybrids keep embeddings on parameter servers and train the dense layers synchronously.
Middle grounds exist: synchronous training with backup workers that drops the slowest few gradients each step, and local SGD, where workers take several local steps between averaging to cut communication.
Follow-ups

Why does gradient staleness hurt more as you add workers?
Your recommendation model has a 500 GB embedding table. How does training communicate it?




seniortrade-offMLE RE A model you need to train or fine-tune does not fit in the memory of the GPUs you have. What are your options, cheapest first?

First find out which component overflows: activations (scales with batch and sequence) or parameters plus optimizer state (fixed). The remedies differ.
If activations overflow.

Smaller batch with gradient accumulation. Run \(k\) small batches, accumulate gradients, step once. Same effective batch, \(k\) times less activation memory, no quality cost except with batch-statistics layers. Free.
Mixed precision. Halves activation memory and speeds up the step.
Activation checkpointing. Store only some activations and recompute the rest during the backward pass. Large memory saving for roughly one extra forward pass of compute.
Shorter sequences or lower resolution, or a memory-efficient attention implementation.

If parameters and optimizer state overflow.

Train fewer parameters. For fine-tuning, adapters such as LoRA leave the base model frozen, so there are no gradients or optimizer state for it, and the frozen weights can be loaded in lower precision.
A lighter optimizer. SGD or a memory-reduced Adam variant in place of full two-moment state.
Shard across GPUs with FSDP or ZeRO, so each device holds a fraction of parameters, gradients and optimizer state. Costs communication and needs several GPUs.
Offload to CPU memory or disk. Works, and is slow; a last resort for training, acceptable for occasional inference.

If a single layer’s computation overflows even alone, you need tensor parallelism or a different architecture.
Or change the hardware. Renting a larger-memory GPU for the duration of the job is often cheaper than the engineering time for options 7 and beyond.
State the trade for each: accumulation costs nothing but wall-clock per update; checkpointing costs compute; adapters change what is learned; sharding costs communication and complexity. Combine the free ones first, measure peak memory after each step, and keep a worst-case batch test in the pipeline.
Follow-ups

Does gradient accumulation give exactly the same result as the large batch?
When is LoRA not an acceptable substitute for full fine-tuning?




staffderivationMLE RE A job runs on 500 nodes. How often should it checkpoint? Derive the interval from the failure rate and the cost of a checkpoint.

Failure rate of the job. If each node fails independently with mean time between failures \(m\), a job on \(N\) nodes that needs all of them fails with rate \(N / m\), so its mean time between failures is
\[M = m / N.\]
With \(m\) = 5 years per node and \(N = 500\): \(M \approx 3.65\) days \(\approx 88\) hours. Large jobs fail routinely even on reliable hardware, and preemptions add to the rate.
The trade-off. Let \(\delta\) be the time to write a checkpoint and \(\tau\) the interval between checkpoints.

Overhead from writing: a fraction \(\delta / \tau\) of the run.
Expected rework after a failure: on average half an interval, \(\tau / 2\), lost once every \(M\), a fraction \(\tau / (2M)\).

Total waste as a fraction of run time:
\[w(\tau) \approx \frac{\delta}{\tau} + \frac{\tau}{2M}.\]
Setting the derivative to zero gives Young’s approximation:
\[\tau^* = \sqrt{2\, \delta\, M}, \qquad w(\tau^*) = \sqrt{2\delta / M}.\]
Numbers. With \(\delta = 2\) minutes and \(M = 88\) hours \(= 5280\) minutes: \(\tau^* = \sqrt{2 \cdot 2 \cdot 5280} \approx 145\) minutes, and the waste is about \(\sqrt{4 / 5280} \approx 2.8\%\). On preemptible capacity with \(M = 2\) hours: \(\tau^* \approx 22\) minutes and waste about 18%, before restart time.
What the formula teaches.

The interval grows with the square root of the checkpoint cost, so making checkpoints cheaper (asynchronous upload, parallel per-rank writes, incremental state) pays twice: lower overhead and shorter intervals.
Add the restart time (rescheduling, loading, warm-up) to the cost of each failure; when it is large, reducing it matters more than tuning \(\tau\).
The approximation assumes \(\delta \ll \tau \ll M\). When failures are very frequent, the job spends most of its time recovering, and the remedy is fewer nodes per job, redundancy or more reliable capacity.
If the platform gives notice before preemption, a checkpoint on notice removes most rework and the periodic interval can be long.

Follow-ups

How does the answer change if a failed node can be replaced without restarting the whole job?
What would you measure in production to set these parameters?




seniorderivationRE MLEasked at OpenAI, Anthropic, Google A matrix multiply Y = XW, with X of shape (B, d_in) and W of shape (d_in, d_out), is split across P devices. Give the ways to shard it, the communication each needs in the forward and backward pass, and a performance model: FLOPs, memory, network. Then apply it to a feed-forward block.

Single device. \(2\,B\,d_\text{in}\,d_\text{out}\) FLOPs (a multiply and an add per term), \(d_\text{in} d_\text{out}\) weights, and with upstream gradient \(G = \partial L/\partial Y\): \(\partial L/\partial W = X^\top G\) and \(\partial L/\partial X = G W^\top\).
Three ways to shard.









Shard
Each device holds
Forward communication
Backward communication




Batch rows
all of \(W\), \(B/P\) rows of \(X\)
none
sum \(X^\top G\) across devices: all-reduce of \(d_\text{in} d_\text{out}\) values


Columns of \(W\) (output dim)
\(W[:, c_p]\), all of \(X\)
none to compute; \(Y\) is the concatenation of the parts
\(\partial L/\partial W\) is local; \(\partial L/\partial X = \sum_p G[:, c_p]\, W[:, c_p]^\top\): all-reduce of \(B d_\text{in}\) values


Rows of \(W\) (input dim)
\(W[r_p, :]\), \(X[:, r_p]\)
\(Y = \sum_p X[:, r_p]\, W[r_p, :]\): all-reduce of \(B d_\text{out}\) values
every device needs \(G\); both gradients are then local



Batch sharding replicates the weights, so it scales throughput and not model size. The other two split the weights, which is what you need when \(W\) does not fit on one device. The pattern to remember: wherever the forward pass concatenates, the backward pass sums, and the reverse.
Feed-forward block (\(d \to 4d \to d\)). Shard the first matrix by columns and the second by rows, on the same partition of the hidden units. Each device computes its own slice of the hidden layer, applies the nonlinearity (elementwise, so local), and multiplies by its rows of the second matrix. The hidden activations never leave the device. The cost is one all-reduce of \(B d\) values at the output, and one in the backward pass for the gradient with respect to the input.
Performance model.

Compute time is FLOPs divided by the FLOP rate the device actually achieves.
Communication time is bytes divided by link bandwidth, plus latency per message. A ring all-reduce moves about \(2(P-1)/P\) times the tensor size per device.
Memory per device is the weight shard, the activations kept for the backward pass, and communication buffers.

Worked example, with \(d = 8192\), \(B = 4096\) token positions, 16-bit floats, \(P = 8\): each matrix has 268M weights, 537 MB. The block costs \(4.4 \times 10^{12}\) FLOPs. At an assumed \(10^{14}\) FLOP/s per device that is 44 ms on one device and 5.5 ms on eight. The all-reduce tensor is 67 MB; at an assumed 50 GB/s it takes about 2.3 ms. So communication is already 30% of the step, and it does not shrink as devices are added, while compute per device does. That ratio, not the FLOP count, sets the scaling limit.
Roofline check. Arithmetic intensity is FLOPs per byte moved through memory. For a large batch the weights are reused across rows, intensity is high and the multiply is compute-bound. For \(B = 1\), each 2-byte weight is read once for 2 FLOPs: 1 FLOP per byte, which is bound by memory bandwidth, and more compute does not help. The attainable rate is \(\min(\text{peak FLOP/s},\ \text{intensity} \times \text{memory bandwidth})\).
What to verify. The assumed rates: measure them. And the identities: split a small random example in NumPy and compare with the unsharded result.
Follow-ups

Communication is 30% of the step at eight devices. What are your options to reduce it?
Which sharding would you choose when the batch is one long sequence, and why?

Simulation, sandboxes and RL environments 16% of postings

 Design an isolated, resettable sandbox for agents that execute code
 Trade simulator fidelity against speed and explain domain randomisation



coreconceptMLE RE Describe the standard interface of an RL environment. Which details of it cause bugs in training code?

The de facto interface (Gymnasium, formerly OpenAI Gym):
obs, info = env.reset(seed=seed)
while True:
    action = policy(obs)
    obs, reward, terminated, truncated, info = env.step(action)
    if terminated or truncated:
        obs, info = env.reset()
plus declared observation and action spaces (shape, type, bounds; discrete or continuous) that the agent’s networks are built from.
Details that cause bugs:

Termination versus truncation. terminated means the episode ended inside the task (goal reached, failure). truncated means it was cut off from outside, usually by a time limit. On termination the value of the next state is zero; on truncation it is not, and the learner should bootstrap from the final observation. Treating a time limit as termination teaches the agent that the world ends at step \(T\).
Auto-reset in vectorised environments. When one of \(N\) parallel environments finishes, the vector wrapper resets it immediately and returns the first observation of the new episode; the final observation of the old one is delivered separately in info. Bootstrapping from the wrong one is a silent error. The exact convention has changed between library versions, so check the one in use.
Seeding and determinism. The environment, the action-space sampler and the policy each have their own random generator. Reproducible runs need all of them seeded, and parallel environments need distinct seeds.
Spaces. Actions outside the declared bounds are clipped or rejected depending on the environment; observation scaling and types (bytes versus floats) are a frequent source of a policy that cannot learn.
Wrappers. Frame stacking, action repeat, reward clipping and normalisation change the problem. Normalisation statistics are part of the policy and must be saved with it and frozen for evaluation.
Reward and info. Evaluation should report the unmodified task reward, not the clipped or shaped one used for training.

Vectorisation. Running many environments in parallel, in processes or batched on a GPU, is the main throughput lever; the policy then acts on a batch of observations in one forward pass.
A unit test worth having: a random policy and a scripted policy run through the full wrapper stack, with checks on shapes, ranges and episode boundaries.
Follow-ups

What is the effect on the learned value function of treating time limits as termination?
How do you evaluate a policy that was trained with normalised observations?




seniordesignMLE AI RE Design the sandbox infrastructure for running agents that execute code, either to evaluate them on tasks or to collect training episodes. What do isolation, reset and scale require?

Treat everything the agent runs as untrusted: it may be wrong, destructive or adversarial, and it runs thousands of times in parallel.
Isolation.

Compute boundary. Ordinary containers share the host kernel, which is a thin wall for untrusted code. Use a stronger boundary for anything exposed to arbitrary commands: a user-space kernel sandbox, a microVM, or a full virtual machine. Choose by threat model and by start-up time.
Resources. Limits on CPU, memory, disk, process count and wall-clock time per command and per episode, so a runaway loop cannot starve neighbours.
Network. Denied by default. Where a task needs packages or an API, allow specific hosts through a proxy, or better, mirror them inside. Open egress enables data exfiltration and makes results depend on the outside world.
Credentials. None inside the sandbox. If a tool needs one, a broker outside performs the call.

Reproducibility and reset.

Each task is an immutable image or snapshot with dependencies pinned. Every episode starts from the same state; nothing persists between episodes.
Sources of nondeterminism (time, random seeds, network) are fixed or recorded.
Snapshot and restore let search-style methods branch from an intermediate state.

Scoring.

The check runs outside the agent’s reach: tests and expected outputs are not present in the sandbox during the episode, or are restored from a trusted copy before scoring, so that the agent cannot pass by editing the tests.
Validate each task: the reference solution passes, an empty solution fails, and the outcome is stable across repeated runs.

Scale and throughput.

A pool of pre-warmed sandboxes, since start-up time otherwise dominates short episodes.
A scheduler that packs sandboxes onto nodes separately from the GPU fleet running the model; the two scale independently.
Asynchronous episodes with timeouts and retries for infrastructure failures, which must be distinguished from agent failures in the results.

Observability. Full trajectories: commands, outputs, file diffs, timings and resource use. These are both the debugging record and the training data.
Risks to state: flaky tasks that add noise to every comparison, environment exploits that inflate scores, and leakage of task solutions into training data.
Follow-ups

How do you tell an infrastructure failure from an agent failure in aggregate results?
What stops an agent from passing a task by modifying the tests?




seniortrade-offMLE RE How do you trade simulator fidelity against speed for training a policy, and how do you get a policy trained in simulation to work in the real system?

The trade. RL needs very many samples, so simulator throughput bounds how much the policy can learn; but whatever the simulator gets wrong, the policy will exploit or be surprised by. Higher fidelity (finer physics steps, realistic rendering, accurate contact and sensor models) costs speed.
Rules for spending fidelity:

Put it where the policy’s decisions are sensitive: contact and friction for manipulation, actuator delay and dynamics for locomotion, sensor noise for perception. Elsewhere, cheap approximations are fine.
Prefer many fast, slightly wrong environments with variation over a few accurate ones. Simulators that run thousands of environments in parallel on a GPU changed what is practical.
Test the choice empirically: does performance in the high-fidelity or real system track performance in the fast simulator across checkpoints?

Closing the gap between simulation and reality.

Domain randomisation. Randomise the parameters you are unsure of (masses, friction, delays, lighting, textures, noise) during training, so that reality looks like one more sample from the training distribution. Too little fails to cover reality; too much makes the task needlessly hard and the policy overly conservative.
System identification. Measure the real system and fit the simulator’s parameters to it, then randomise around those values.
Model what bites. Latency, actuator limits and sensor noise matter more than visual polish.
Adaptation. Give the policy a history of observations so that it can infer the dynamics it is in, or fine-tune on a small amount of real data.
Residual or hybrid control. Learn a correction on top of a classical controller that already works.

Evaluation. Real-world success on a fixed protocol is the metric; simulation metrics are proxies. Evaluate across randomisation ranges to find where the policy breaks, and keep a set of real failure cases that are reproduced in simulation and added to training.
The same reasoning applies outside robotics: a simulated user or market is a model with a fidelity gap, and a policy optimised against it must be validated online.
Follow-ups

How do you choose the ranges for domain randomisation?
Your policy succeeds in simulation and fails on hardware. What is your first measurement?

 Choose a hyperparameter search method for a given budget and explain early stopping of trials
