coreconceptMLE RE What should be recorded for every training run, and what do tools such as MLflow or Weights and Biases give you beyond a spreadsheet?

What to record, automatically and at the start of the run where possible:

Code: commit hash, whether the working tree was dirty, and the diff if it was.
Configuration: the fully resolved hyperparameters after defaults and overrides, not only what was passed on the command line.
Data: dataset name and version or snapshot id, the split definition, preprocessing version.
Environment: container image, key library versions, hardware, number of devices.
Randomness: seeds.
Metrics over time: training and validation loss, learning rate, gradient norm, throughput, memory. Curves, not only final values.
Evaluation: metrics on named, versioned evaluation sets and slices.
Artefacts: checkpoints, the final model, sample predictions, plots.
Lineage and notes: parent run for fine-tunes or resumes, the hypothesis the run was testing, and the conclusion.

What a tracking tool adds.

Capture with a few lines of code, so that recording does not depend on discipline.
A queryable store: filter and sort hundreds of runs, group by a hyperparameter, plot curves on top of each other.
Artefact storage linked to runs, and a path from a run to a registered model.
Live monitoring of running jobs, with alerts on divergence.
Sharing: a link to a comparison instead of a screenshot, and reports that record why a decision was taken.

What tools do not give you.

Comparability. Two runs are comparable only if they used the same evaluation set and code. Enforce versioned evaluation, and compare against the baseline rerun under the same conditions.
Significance. One run per configuration says little; record seed variance and report differences against it.
Hygiene. Naming, tagging, deleting failed runs and writing the conclusion remain human work.

Choosing between tools is secondary (hosted or self-hosted, cost, integration with the scheduler and registry). The practice that matters is that no result enters a decision or a paper unless its run record can be opened.
Follow-ups

A colleague reports a 0.5 point gain from a single run. What do you ask for?
How do you track experiments on prompts and LLM pipelines where there is no training run?




seniortrade-offMLE RE You have a budget of 200 GPU-days to tune a model’s hyperparameters. How do you spend it? Compare grid search, random search, Bayesian optimisation and early-stopping methods.

Methods.

Grid search. Exhaustive over a lattice. Wastes trials: if only two of six hyperparameters matter, most grid points repeat the same values of the ones that do. Acceptable for one or two dimensions.
Random search. Sample each hyperparameter independently. Every trial tests a new value of every dimension, so it covers the important ones far better for the same budget. Trivially parallel. The baseline to beat.
Bayesian optimisation. Fit a model of the objective from past trials and choose the next trial to balance exploring and exploiting. More sample-efficient when each trial is expensive and the dimension is modest; inherently sequential, though batched variants exist; less advantage when the objective is noisy.
Early stopping of trials (successive halving, Hyperband, ASHA). Start many configurations with a small budget, keep the best fraction, give them more, repeat. Most compute goes to promising configurations. Usually the largest gain, and it combines with random or Bayesian sampling.
Population-based training. Mutate hyperparameters during training, which yields schedules rather than fixed values.

Spending the budget.

Reduce the space first. Fix what is known from prior work; search the few that matter most (learning rate, weight decay, warm-up, batch size, a regularisation strength), on log scales where appropriate.
Use a cheap proxy where it predicts the full result: a smaller model, a data subset or shorter training. Check the rank correlation on a few configurations first.
Run random sampling with early stopping across the bulk of the budget.
Reserve a share (perhaps a quarter) to rerun the top few configurations with several seeds to full length. Search winners are selected partly by luck.
Report the final result on a test set not used for selection.

Pitfalls. Early stopping favours configurations that start fast, such as high learning rates, over those that finish best. Noise between seeds can exceed the differences being optimised. The best configuration at small scale may not transfer to large scale, particularly the learning rate. And a tuned method compared with an untuned baseline is not a fair comparison.
Follow-ups

Why does random search beat grid search when only some hyperparameters matter?
How do you check that a short-training proxy ranks configurations the same way as full training?




seniordesignMLE RE Design experiment tracking and lineage for an organisation of fifty people training models, so that any deployed model can be traced back to its data and code.

Goal. From any model in production, answer in minutes: which run produced it, with what code, configuration and data, evaluated on what, approved by whom. And the reverse: which models used this dataset.
Entities and links.

Dataset version: immutable snapshot id, the query or pipeline run that built it, its validation report.
Run: code commit, resolved configuration, image digest, input dataset versions, parent run if resumed or fine-tuned, metrics, artefacts.
Evaluation result: model artefact, evaluation set version, evaluation code version, metrics by slice.
Registered model version: the artefact, its run, its evaluation results, its stage and approval record.
Deployment: registered version, serving configuration, time and environment.

Every link is written by tooling, not by people.
How it is captured.

The job launcher injects the run id, commit and image; the training library logs configuration and metrics; the data client records which dataset versions were read. A run started from uncommitted code is flagged and cannot be promoted.
Evaluation is a separate, versioned job that writes results against the artefact, so that all candidates are measured the same way.
Promotion to the registry requires the links to exist.

Organisation.

Projects and tags by team and model family; a naming convention; retention rules that keep registered models and their lineage indefinitely and expire the artefacts of abandoned runs.
Shared dashboards comparing candidates with the current production model.
Access control for sensitive datasets carried through to their derived artefacts.
Cost per run from the scheduler, attached to the run.

Build or buy. A hosted tracker or an open-source one covers runs and artefacts; the lineage to datasets and deployments usually needs integration work with your own data platform and deployment system. Start with enforced capture at launch, since retrofits fail on the runs that matter most.
Check. Pick a random production model each quarter and reproduce it from its record.
Follow-ups

How do you handle exploratory work in notebooks without losing lineage?
A dataset must be deleted for legal reasons. What does your system tell you?




Dataset engineering at scale (loaders, sharding, petabyte data) 12% of postings

 Explain why training data is packed into shards and how shuffling works on sequential data
 Split shards across distributed ranks and loader workers without duplication
 Design a preprocessing pipeline for a very large dataset, including what is done offline



coreconceptMLE RE Why do large training datasets get packed into shards, and how do you shuffle data that can only be read sequentially?

Why shards. Storing each example as its own file fails at scale: millions of small files overload file-system metadata and object-store request limits, and random access to remote storage is slow. Packing examples into shards, large files of perhaps a few hundred megabytes to a few gigabytes that are read front to back, replaces millions of random reads with a few thousand sequential ones. Sequential reads are what disks, networks and object stores do best, and whole shards can be cached, prefetched and assigned to workers. Common containers are tar-based shards, record files and columnar files.
Shuffling sequential data. You cannot draw a uniformly random example from the whole dataset without random access. The standard approximation has two levels:

Shuffle the order of shards each epoch.
Shuffle within a buffer: keep a buffer of \(k\) examples; emit a random one and replace it with the next example read.

Reading several shards in parallel and interleaving them mixes further.
How good is it? It depends on how the shards were written. If shards were filled from already-shuffled data, each is a random sample and shard-level shuffling is nearly as good as a global shuffle. If shards were written in source order (by date, by class, by crawl domain), consecutive examples are correlated, and a buffer smaller than a shard cannot fix it. The cure is a one-time global shuffle when the shards are created.
Poor shuffling shows up as a loss curve with periodic structure, or as degraded results with batch-statistics layers.
Related design points.

Shard count well above the number of workers times ranks, so the work divides evenly.
Assign whole shards to distributed ranks and loader workers so no example is read twice.
“Epoch” becomes approximate; many pipelines define it as a number of steps over an infinite, reshuffled stream.
Record the shard and offset in checkpoints to resume without repeating data.
Keep an index (example id to shard and offset) for debugging and for removing examples.

Follow-ups

Your shards were written in chronological order. What goes wrong and how do you fix it without rewriting everything?
How large should the shuffle buffer be?




seniorcodingMLE RE Write a PyTorch IterableDataset over a list of shards that works with several data-loader workers and several DDP processes without duplicating examples, and shuffles with a buffer.

import random
from torch.utils.data import IterableDataset, get_worker_info

class ShardedDataset(IterableDataset):
    def __init__(self, shards, read_shard, rank=0, world_size=1,
                 buffer_size=10_000, seed=0):
        self.shards, self.read_shard = list(shards), read_shard
        self.rank, self.world_size = rank, world_size
        self.buffer_size, self.seed, self.epoch = buffer_size, seed, 0

    def set_epoch(self, epoch):
        self.epoch = epoch

    def __iter__(self):
        # Same permutation on every rank and worker, new each epoch.
        shards = self.shards[:]
        random.Random(self.seed + self.epoch).shuffle(shards)
        shards = shards[self.rank::self.world_size]        # split across processes
        info = get_worker_info()
        wid = 0
        if info is not None:
            wid = info.id
            shards = shards[wid::info.num_workers]         # split across workers
        rng = random.Random(hash((self.seed, self.epoch, self.rank, wid)))
        buf = []
        for shard in shards:
            for sample in self.read_shard(shard):
                if len(buf) < self.buffer_size:
                    buf.append(sample)
                    continue
                i = rng.randrange(self.buffer_size)
                yield buf[i]
                buf[i] = sample
        rng.shuffle(buf)
        yield from buf
What an interviewer checks:

No duplication. With an iterable dataset every worker gets a copy of the dataset object; without the split by worker id, each worker yields everything and the model sees each example num_workers times. The same applies across DDP ranks.
Consistent global order. All ranks and workers must shuffle the shard list with the same seed before slicing, or the slices overlap.
Different randomness per worker for the buffer, or all workers emit in the same pattern.
Uneven lengths. Ranks receive different numbers of examples when shards differ in size. DDP needs the same number of steps on every rank, so define an epoch as a fixed number of steps and loop the stream, or drop the excess.
Epoch propagation. With persistent workers, calling set_epoch in the main process does not reach the worker copies; derive the epoch inside the worker or recreate the loader.
Shard count should be much larger than ranks times workers.

For resumability, also expose the current shard and offset so a checkpoint can record them.
Follow-ups

What happens with 4 shards, 2 ranks and 8 workers per rank?
How would you make every rank produce exactly the same number of batches?




staffdesignMLE RE Design the data preparation and loading system for training on a multimodal dataset of billions of examples. What is computed offline, what online, and how is the dataset versioned?

Principles. Do expensive, deterministic work once, offline. Keep the per-step path to sequential reads plus cheap, random transformations. Make every stage rerunnable and every dataset version addressable.
Offline pipeline, a distributed batch job per stage with outputs in object storage:

Ingest and normalise. Fetch raw items, validate, convert to a few canonical encodings and sizes. Record source, licence and timestamps as metadata.
Filter. Corrupt files, too small or too long items, unsafe or disallowed content, low-quality pairs by model-based scores. Keep the scores as columns so thresholds can change without recomputation.
Deduplicate. Exact duplicates by content hash; near-duplicates by perceptual hash or embedding similarity. Also remove overlap with evaluation sets.
Precompute what is deterministic and expensive. Tokenisation of text, resizing to a bounded resolution, optional embeddings or latents from a frozen encoder.
Global shuffle and shard. Write shards of roughly equal size with examples in random order, plus a metadata table with one row per example (id, shard, offset, lengths, scores, source).

Online, in the loader.

Sequential shard reads with parallel workers, prefetching and a local NVMe cache.
Decoding and random augmentation, on CPU workers or on the GPU.
Sampling policy: mixing sources at chosen ratios, and bucketing by length or aspect ratio so batches pad little.
Batching by a token or pixel budget instead of a fixed count.

Versioning. A dataset version is a manifest: the list of shards with checksums, the filter thresholds and the code version of each stage. New versions are new manifests that reuse unchanged shards. Removing examples (a takedown or a discovered bug) is done with a deny-list applied at load time immediately, and by rewriting the affected shards in the next version.
Operations.

Throughput target derived from the training step: examples per second per GPU times GPUs, with headroom, tested before the run.
Per-stage statistics and samples for inspection; data bugs are found by looking.
Resumable loading: checkpoints record position in the manifest.
Cost: the offline stages are embarrassingly parallel and suit preemptible capacity.

The main risks are silent quality problems in filtering, duplicates leaking into evaluation, and a loader that cannot keep the GPUs fed.
Follow-ups

Which precomputations would you avoid because they freeze a decision you may want to change?
How do you remove one million examples from a dataset that a run is currently training on?




Data lakes, warehouses and storage formats 11% of postings

 Explain how a columnar format enables column pruning and predicate pushdown
 Say what a table format adds on top of files in object storage
 Choose a partitioning scheme and avoid the small-files problem



coreconceptMLE AI Why are analytical and training tables stored in a columnar format such as Parquet? What does the file layout buy you, and when is it the wrong format?

Layout. A Parquet file stores data column by column inside row groups (chunks of rows, typically tens to hundreds of megabytes). Each column chunk is divided into pages, encoded and compressed separately, and the file footer records the schema and statistics such as minimum, maximum and null count per column chunk.
What that buys.

Column pruning. A query that needs 5 of 300 columns reads only those 5. Analytical and feature queries usually touch few columns of wide tables.
Predicate pushdown. A reader skips a row group when the statistics show that no row can match the filter, without decompressing it. It works well when the data is sorted or clustered on the filter column.
Compression. Values in one column are similar, so dictionary and run-length encoding plus a general compressor shrink the data several times more than a row format would.
Vectorised reads. Engines process a column as an array, which is CPU-efficient.
A self-describing, typed schema, readable by every engine.

When it is the wrong format.

Point lookups and updates of single rows. Files are immutable, and reading one row means decoding a page of each needed column. Use a key-value or relational store.
Row-at-a-time streaming writes. A row-oriented format such as Avro suits logs and message payloads; convert to Parquet in batches.
Large binary objects per row, such as images, audio or long token arrays for training with random access. Sharded archives or formats designed for it serve better; keep metadata in Parquet and the payload elsewhere.
Many tiny files. The per-file overhead of footers and listing destroys the benefit.

Practical knobs. Row group size (larger compresses and scans better; smaller skips better), sort order within files, compression codec (fast versus dense), and target file size of a few hundred megabytes to a gigabyte.
Follow-ups

A filter on an unsorted high-cardinality column gets no benefit from pushdown. Why?
How would you store a dataset of images with labels and metadata?




seniorconceptMLE AI What do table formats such as Iceberg, Delta Lake or Hudi add on top of Parquet files in object storage? Why does that matter for ML?

A directory of Parquet files is not a table. Readers find files by listing, which is slow and can observe a half-finished write; there are no transactions, no safe concurrent writers and no way to change the schema or delete rows cleanly.
A table format adds a metadata layer that states exactly which data files make up the table at each version.

Atomic commits. A write produces new data files and then publishes a new metadata version in one atomic step. Readers see the old snapshot or the new one, never a mix. Concurrent writers are handled by optimistic concurrency: a writer commits only if the table has not changed in a conflicting way, otherwise it retries.
Snapshots and time travel. Every commit is a snapshot that can be queried by id or timestamp until it is expired.
Schema evolution. Add, rename or drop columns without rewriting data, because columns are tracked by id.
Row-level changes. Updates, deletes and merges, implemented by rewriting the affected files (copy-on-write) or by writing delete and delta files merged at read time (merge-on-read). This is what makes deletion requests and late corrections feasible on a lake.
Planning without listing. File lists and per-file column statistics live in metadata, so the engine prunes files before touching storage. Partitioning can be derived from columns and changed over time.
Maintenance. Compaction of small files, expiry of old snapshots, removal of orphan files. These jobs must actually be run.

Why it matters for ML.

Reproducibility: a training set is a query against a snapshot id, which pins the exact data.
Consistency: a training job never reads a partially written partition.
Backfills and corrections are atomic replacements of partitions.
Incremental processing: read only what changed between two snapshots to update features.
Lineage and audit: who changed what, when.

The combination of open table formats on object storage with warehouse-style engines is what people mean by a lakehouse.
Follow-ups

Copy-on-write or merge-on-read for a table with frequent small updates and heavy scans?
How long should snapshots be retained if models must be reproducible for a year?




coretrade-offMLE AI How do you choose a partitioning scheme for a large table, and what is the small-files problem?

Purpose. Partitioning splits a table into directories or file groups by the value of one or more columns, so that a query filtering on those columns reads only the matching parts. It also defines the unit of an idempotent write: overwrite one partition.
Choosing the key.

Partition on the columns that almost every query filters on. For event data that is the event date, sometimes with one more low-cardinality column such as region.
Keep cardinality low enough that each partition holds at least hundreds of megabytes. Partitioning by user id or by hour and country and device creates millions of tiny partitions.
Match the write pattern: daily jobs write daily partitions.
For high-cardinality columns that queries filter on, do not partition. Sort or cluster the data on that column within files, or bucket by its hash, so that file statistics prune the read.

The small-files problem. Thousands or millions of files of a few kilobytes or megabytes each. Causes: over-partitioning, streaming or micro-batch writers committing often, and jobs with many output tasks each writing a file per partition.
Why it hurts:

Listing and opening files dominates query time; object stores charge and throttle per request.
Each file carries its own footer and metadata, and compression works poorly on small chunks.
Query planning slows as metadata grows.
For training, loaders spend their time opening files instead of reading data.

Fixes: compact small files into target-sized ones (a few hundred megabytes to a gigabyte) with a scheduled job; repartition by the partition key before writing so each partition is written by one task; coarsen the partitioning; batch streaming commits.
Related choice. A warehouse manages storage and layout for you and suits business analytics; a lake of open files is cheaper and open to any engine and to training jobs; a lakehouse puts table semantics on the lake to get both.
Follow-ups

A table partitioned by date is always queried by user id. What do you change?
How do you compact files while other jobs are reading and writing the table?




HPC, networking and storage for ML 9% of postings

 Explain why multi-node training needs a low-latency, high-bandwidth interconnect
 Compare object storage, a parallel file system and local NVMe for training data and checkpoints



seniorconceptMLE RE Why does multi-node training need a special network? What do InfiniBand and RDMA give you that ordinary Ethernet with TCP does not?

The requirement. Synchronous distributed training exchanges data every step: gradients in data parallelism, parameters in sharded training, activations in tensor parallelism. A model with \(10^9\) parameters has 4 GB of 32-bit gradients, and an all-reduce moves about twice that per worker per step. On a 10 Gb/s link (about 1.2 GB per second) that alone takes several seconds, longer than the computation. The step time is then set by the network, and adding nodes adds nothing.
What a high-performance interconnect provides.

Bandwidth: 100 to 400 Gb/s per link and more, with several links per node.
Low, predictable latency: microseconds, which matters because collective operations consist of many small synchronised exchanges.
RDMA (remote direct memory access): the network card reads and writes application memory directly, bypassing the kernel’s network stack and avoiding copies and context switches. With GPU-aware variants, data moves between GPU memories on different nodes without passing through host memory.
Lossless transport and a suitable topology, such as a fat tree with full bisection bandwidth, so that many simultaneous node pairs do not contend.

InfiniBand is a network technology designed around these properties. RoCE provides RDMA over Ethernet hardware and needs careful configuration to be lossless.
Inside a node there is a similar hierarchy: direct GPU-to-GPU links are faster than going through the PCIe bus, and which GPUs share a switch or a CPU socket affects communication cost. Process placement should respect that topology, including NUMA locality for host memory.
When it matters less. Small models, infrequent synchronisation, embarrassingly parallel work such as sweeps and batch inference, and single-node jobs.
Diagnosing a network-bound job. Throughput per GPU drops as nodes are added while GPU utilisation falls; a profiler shows time in collective communication; and the same job scales well inside one node.
Follow-ups

Estimate the communication time per step for a model you have trained.
Why can a job scale well to 8 GPUs in one node and badly to 16 across two?




seniortrade-offMLE RE Where should training data and checkpoints live: object storage, a parallel file system or local NVMe? What are the failure modes of each?









Storage
Strengths
Weaknesses




Object storage (S3, GCS)
Cheap, durable, effectively unlimited, accessible from anywhere, high aggregate throughput with many parallel readers
High latency per request (tens of milliseconds), no POSIX semantics, request costs and rate limits; terrible for many small random reads


Parallel or distributed file system (Lustre, GPFS and similar)
POSIX interface, high throughput shared by all nodes, good for large files
Metadata servers choke on millions of small files; shared by all jobs, so one job’s bad pattern hurts everyone; costly to run


Local NVMe on the node
Fastest, lowest latency, no network
Ephemeral and limited in size; gone when the node is reclaimed; must be filled first



The pattern that works.

Source of truth in object storage, as large shards (hundreds of megabytes to a few gigabytes each) read sequentially. Sequential reads of large objects turn the store’s weakness into a non-issue, and many shards read in parallel give high throughput.
A cache on local NVMe for datasets that fit, filled at job start or lazily on first read. For multi-epoch training the second epoch is then local.
A parallel file system where a POSIX interface is required or where the organisation already runs one, with data still packed into large files.

Failure modes to recognise.

Millions of small files (one image or one JSON per example): metadata operations dominate and listing a directory takes minutes.
Random access into remote storage from a shuffling loader.
Throttling by the object store under a burst of requests from hundreds of workers.
Cross-region reads: slow and billed.
Every job copying the same dataset to local disk separately, with no shared cache.

Checkpoints. Large sequential writes. Write to local disk and upload asynchronously, or write in parallel per rank, so that the training loop does not stall on a slow remote write. Keep retention rules, since checkpoints of large models fill storage quickly. Measure the time to write and to restore, because both enter the fault tolerance calculation.
Diagnosis. High I/O wait and idle GPUs point to storage; compare throughput with the dataset on local disk to confirm.
Follow-ups

Why are large sequential shards so much better than individual files on every one of these systems?
How would you share one dataset cache among many jobs on the same nodes?




ML framework internals and compilers 8% of postings

 Explain reverse-mode automatic differentiation and what the framework stores for the backward pass
 Implement a minimal scalar autograd engine
 Explain what a graph compiler such as torch.compile or XLA does and what causes recompilation



coreconceptMLE RE How does reverse-mode automatic differentiation work in a framework like PyTorch? What is stored during the forward pass, and why is reverse mode the right choice for training?

The idea. A program computing a loss is a composition of elementary operations whose derivatives are known. Automatic differentiation applies the chain rule to that composition exactly, neither symbolically nor by finite differences.
Forward pass, recording. As each operation runs, the framework creates a node that remembers its inputs and whatever is needed to compute its local derivative (often the input or output values). The result is a directed acyclic graph from parameters to the loss. In PyTorch this graph is built dynamically, fresh on every forward pass, which is why ordinary Python control flow works.
Backward pass. Starting from \(\partial L / \partial L = 1\), walk the graph in reverse topological order. Each node receives the gradient of the loss with respect to its output and multiplies it by its local Jacobian to produce gradients for its inputs: a vector-Jacobian product. The full Jacobian is never formed. Gradients arriving at a tensor along several paths are summed.
Why reverse mode. For a function from \(n\) inputs to \(m\) outputs, forward mode costs one pass per input and reverse mode one pass per output. Training has millions of parameters and one scalar loss, so reverse mode yields all gradients for a small constant multiple of the cost of the forward pass.
The price is memory. Every intermediate value needed by a backward function is kept alive until the backward pass uses it. This is the activation memory of training, and it is why inference under a no-gradient context needs so much less.
Practical consequences.

The graph is freed after backward() by default; a second backward through it needs it to be retained.
In-place modification of a tensor that a backward function saved invalidates the gradient; the framework detects it through version counters and raises an error.
Detaching a tensor cuts the graph: no gradient flows past it.
Gradients accumulate into .grad across calls, so they are zeroed each step.
Non-differentiable points get a conventional subgradient; integer and indexing operations pass no gradient to the indices.
Higher-order derivatives come from differentiating the backward computation itself.

Follow-ups

When would forward-mode differentiation be the better choice?
Why does an in-place operation sometimes break the backward pass and sometimes not?




seniorcodingMLE REasked at OpenAI Implement a minimal scalar reverse-mode autodiff engine in Python that supports addition, multiplication and tanh, with a backward method.

import math

class Value:
    def __init__(self, data, parents=()):
        self.data, self.grad = float(data), 0.0
        self._parents = parents
        self._backward = lambda: None

    def __add__(self, other):
        other = other if isinstance(other, Value) else Value(other)
        out = Value(self.data + other.data, (self, other))
        def backward():
            self.grad += out.grad
            other.grad += out.grad
        out._backward = backward
        return out

    def __mul__(self, other):
        other = other if isinstance(other, Value) else Value(other)
        out = Value(self.data * other.data, (self, other))
        def backward():
            self.grad += other.data * out.grad
            other.grad += self.data * out.grad
        out._backward = backward
        return out

    __radd__, __rmul__ = __add__, __mul__

    def tanh(self):
        t = math.tanh(self.data)
        out = Value(t, (self,))
        def backward():
            self.grad += (1.0 - t * t) * out.grad
        out._backward = backward
        return out

    def backward(self):
        order, seen = [], set()
        def visit(v):
            if v not in seen:
                seen.add(v)
                for p in v._parents:
                    visit(p)
                order.append(v)
        visit(self)
        self.grad = 1.0
        for v in reversed(order):
            v._backward()
What the interviewer looks for:

Accumulate with +=. A value used twice, as in y = x * x, receives gradient from both uses; assignment would keep only one.
Topological order. A node’s gradient must be complete before it is propagated to its parents, so process nodes in reverse topological order, not in a naive recursive walk that could visit a shared node early.
Closures capture what the local derivative needs: the other operand for multiplication, the output for tanh. This is the stored state that costs memory in a real framework.
Seeding the output’s gradient with 1.
A check: compare with a finite difference, \((f(x + \epsilon) - f(x - \epsilon)) / 2\epsilon\), on a small expression.

Limits to mention: gradients must be zeroed before a second backward call; the recursive sort overflows the stack on very deep graphs, so use an iterative one; and a real engine works on tensors, where each local derivative becomes a vector-Jacobian product with broadcasting to undo.
Follow-ups

Add subtraction, division and a power operation using what is already there.
What changes when values are tensors and addition broadcasts?


Reported in interviews (candidate reports on third-party sites, not verified)

seniorconceptMLE RE What does a graph compiler such as torch.compile or JAX’s jit do for a model, and what commonly goes wrong when you turn it on?

Why compile. Eager execution runs one operation at a time from Python: every operation pays interpreter and dispatch overhead and writes its own intermediate tensor, and the framework never sees more than one operation ahead. A compiler captures a region of the program as a graph and optimises it as a whole.
What it does.

Capture. torch.compile intercepts Python execution, records tensor operations into a graph and inserts guards: conditions on input types, shapes and relevant Python values under which the captured graph is valid. JAX’s jit instead traces the function once with abstract values standing for arrays of a given shape and type.
Optimise. Remove dead code, fold constants, fuse chains of elementwise operations into single kernels, eliminate intermediate tensors, plan memory. With training, the backward computation is captured and optimised too.
Generate code for the target device and cache it. Later calls that satisfy the guards skip Python for that region.

Gains are largest for models with many small operations and Python overhead, and small for models already dominated by a few large library kernels.
What goes wrong.

Recompilation. A new input shape, type or guarded Python value fails the guards and triggers a compile. Variable sequence lengths can cause a compile on many steps. Remedies: pad or bucket to a few shapes, or mark dimensions as dynamic.
Compile time. The first call takes seconds to minutes, which hurts short jobs, tests and serving cold starts.
Graph breaks (PyTorch). Unsupported Python constructs, data-dependent control flow, calls into other libraries or printing a tensor split the region; each piece is compiled separately and the benefit shrinks.
Tracing semantics (JAX). Python control flow on array values cannot be traced; it must be expressed with the library’s structured control-flow functions. Side effects run only at trace time. Functions must be pure, with randomness passed explicitly.
Numerical differences. Fusion and reordering change floating-point results slightly.
Debugging. Errors refer to generated code; start by disabling compilation to localise the problem.

Adopting it. Measure steady-state step time and compile time separately, log recompilation counts, and keep an eager mode switch. Check the current documentation; this area changes quickly between releases.
Follow-ups

Your training loop recompiles every few steps. How do you find the cause?
Why must a function be pure for JAX to compile it correctly?




Feature stores and online/offline consistency 3% of postings

 Describe the offline and online stores and how one definition feeds both
 Explain point-in-time correctness and write a point-in-time join



coreconceptMLE What problem does a feature store solve? Describe its parts and what point-in-time correctness means.

A feature store exists to make the features a model sees in training identical to those it sees in serving, and to let teams reuse features instead of rebuilding them.
Parts.

Feature definitions. One declared transformation per feature, with an entity key (user, item), a timestamp, an owner and a version. The same definition feeds both stores.
Offline store. The full history of feature values with timestamps, in a warehouse or lake. Used to build training sets.
Online store. The latest value per entity in a low-latency key-value store. Used at inference with a budget of a few milliseconds.
Materialisation. Batch and streaming jobs that compute features and write them to both stores.
Serving API and registry. Fetch a feature vector by entity keys; discover features, lineage and consumers.
Monitoring. Freshness, null rates and the distribution of online against offline values.

Point-in-time correctness. A training example is an event at time \(t\) with a label. Its features must be the values that were available just before \(t\), as serving would have seen them. Joining the latest value of each feature instead leaks the future: a “purchases in the last 30 days” feature computed today includes the very purchase you are predicting. The offline join is therefore an as-of join: for each example, the most recent feature row with a timestamp earlier than the event’s.
The timestamp that matters is when the value became available to serving, not the event time of the underlying data. A daily batch feature for day \(d\) that lands at 6 am on day \(d + 1\) must not be used for events before that.
When you do not need one. A single team with a few batch features can keep one shared transformation library and log served features for training. Logging the feature vector at prediction time and training on those logs gives consistency by construction; its cost is that a new feature has no history until it has been logged for a while.
Follow-ups

Why is the availability time, not the event time, the right timestamp for the join?
What are the trade-offs of training only on features logged at serving time?




seniorcodingMLE Write a point-in-time join: for each labelled event, attach the most recent feature value known strictly before the event. Show it in pandas and in SQL.

import pandas as pd

def point_in_time_join(labels, features, key="user_id", ts="ts", max_age=None):
    """labels:   [key, ts, label]
    features: [key, ts, f1, ...], ts = time the value became available.
    max_age:  optional pd.Timedelta; older feature values are treated as missing."""
    labels = labels.sort_values(ts)
    features = features.sort_values(ts)
    return pd.merge_asof(
        labels, features, on=ts, by=key,
        direction="backward",          # latest feature row at or before the event
        allow_exact_matches=False,     # strictly before: no same-instant leakage
        tolerance=max_age)
The same in SQL, portable across warehouses:
SELECT *
FROM (
  SELECT l.*, f.f1,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY l.label_id ORDER BY f.ts DESC) AS rn
  FROM labels l
  LEFT JOIN features f
    ON f.user_id = l.user_id AND f.ts < l.ts
) t
WHERE rn = 1;
What to say:

merge_asof requires both frames sorted by the time column; by restricts matches to the same entity.
Strict inequality. A feature row with the same timestamp as the event may already contain the event’s outcome.
Left join. Events with no earlier feature row keep a null, which is what serving would have seen for a new user. Dropping them biases the training set.
Staleness bound. Serving may expire old values (a TTL in the online store). Apply the same bound offline with tolerance, or training sees values serving would not have.
Availability time. If ts is the event time of the source data rather than when the feature landed, add the pipeline delay before joining.
Cost. The SQL form joins every label to all earlier feature rows for the entity before filtering, which explodes for long histories. Engines with an as-of join, or a range-bounded join on a window of days, avoid that.
Test. Build a tiny fixture where the naive latest-value join gives a different answer, and assert the difference.

Follow-ups

How would you verify on real data that a training set has no future leakage?
How does the join change when features are updated by a stream rather than a daily batch?

title: Evaluation and experimentation
text:
The senior bar
What separates a senior answer from a mid-level one in this area.

Starts from the decision the evaluation must support and from failure modes seen in real outputs, not from a generic metric or an off-the-shelf benchmark.
Reports uncertainty with every number (examples, trials, confidence interval, paired comparison) and knows the noise floor before claiming a gain.
Validates graders, whether LLM judges or human raters, against a trusted reference and treats the grader version as part of the metric definition.
Separates north-star, proxy and guardrail metrics, and can give concrete mechanisms by which an offline win turns into an online loss.
Designs experiments with a decision rule written in advance, the correct randomisation unit and adequate power, and handles peeking, multiple comparisons, novelty and interference.
Runs error analysis as a loop from raw traces to a failure taxonomy to new test cases and targeted fixes, and checks slices rather than averages.
Monitors production quality without labels through traces, proxy signals and sampled grading, and can tell a data bug from drift.

title: Evaluation and experimentation
text:
Skills, checklists and questions
Tick an item when you can explain it without notes; ticks are saved in this browser. Open a question to see the answer.

Model evaluation and benchmarks 58% of postings

 Build an eval from nothing, from task definition and success criteria to a versioned set wired into CI
 Compute the standard error of an accuracy and say how many examples a given difference needs
 Compare two systems with a paired test and explain why pairing shrinks the interval
 Implement a paired bootstrap confidence interval and choose the right resampling unit
 Explain contamination, adaptive overfitting and saturation, and how to detect each
 Design the full eval system for a product, including datasets, graders, runner, gates and online checks



coreconceptMLE AI RE You have just joined a team shipping an LLM feature with no evaluation at all. How do you build one from zero?


Define the task and what good means. Write success criteria with the people who own the product: what a correct output is, what is unacceptable, and what decision the eval must support (ship this prompt, pick this model).
Collect 50-200 real inputs. From logs, support tickets or subject experts. Stratify by intent or slice, and include known failures, edge cases and inputs where the right behaviour is to refuse or ask.
Read outputs before writing graders. Run the current system, read 50-100 outputs, and note what goes wrong. The failure modes you find determine what to grade.
Choose graders per criterion. Code checks where the criterion is objective (schema, exact answer, tests pass); an LLM judge with a narrow rubric where it is not; human labels to calibrate the judge. Each example carries a reference answer or the rubric.
Baseline and uncertainty. Record the score with a confidence interval. At 80% accuracy, 100 examples give about ±8 points at 95% confidence and 1,000 give about ±2.5, so a small set only detects large differences.
Version and split. Version the dataset, graders and prompts together. Keep a held-out portion that is not used while iterating on the prompt.
Wire it in. Run on every change; show per-slice scores and the examples that flipped.
Grow it. Each production failure becomes a test case; refresh from current traffic.

Common mistakes: starting with generic metrics (“helpfulness 1-5”) before looking at data, an unvalidated judge, and a set made only of easy synthetic cases.
Follow-ups

How do you get reference answers when experts disagree?
What tells you the eval set has become too easy?




seniorconceptMLE AI RE What makes a benchmark result untrustworthy? Cover contamination, overfitting and saturation, and say how you would report results properly.

Contamination. Test items, or close paraphrases, were in the training data, so the score measures recall. Public benchmarks are scraped into pretraining corpora. Signs: a large drop on freshly written or post-cutoff items, on rephrased questions, or when answer options are reordered; the model completing a test item verbatim. Mitigations: private held-out sets, periodically refreshed items, and canary strings in published data.
Overfitting to the benchmark. Repeatedly choosing models, prompts and hyperparameters on the same test set selects for noise in that set, even with no leakage. Keep a development split for iteration and look at the test split rarely. Community-wide reuse has the same effect over years.
Saturation. When scores approach the ceiling, remaining differences are within noise and within the label error rate. A benchmark with 3% wrong labels cannot distinguish 96% from 97%.
Construct validity. A benchmark is a sample of some skill. Check that it resembles your task; a leaderboard gain may not transfer.
Reporting.

Number of items and a confidence interval for every score.
Paired comparison between systems on the same items.
Variance across seeds or repeated runs for sampled outputs.
The full setup: prompt, few-shot examples, decoding settings, tools, scaffold and budgets. Agent benchmark scores depend heavily on the harness.
Cost and latency next to accuracy.
Which results were selected after looking at the test set.

Follow-ups

How would you test a model for contamination on a benchmark you did not create?
Your team has tuned on the same test set for a year. What now?




seniorderivationMLE AI RE Model B scores 83% and model A 80% on your 500-example eval. Is B better? Show the calculation.

It depends on whether the comparison is paired, and it should be, since both models ran on the same examples.
Unpaired view. The standard error of an accuracy is \(\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}\). The difference has
\[
\mathrm{SE} = \sqrt{\tfrac{0.80 \cdot 0.20}{500} + \tfrac{0.83 \cdot 0.17}{500}} \approx 0.0245,
\]
so the 95% interval is \(3 \pm 4.8\) points: not significant.
Paired view. With per-example scores \(a_i, b_i\) and \(d_i = b_i - a_i\),
\[
\mathrm{Var}(\bar d) = \frac{\sigma_A^2 + \sigma_B^2 - 2\,\mathrm{Cov}(a, b)}{n}.
\]
Two models tend to get the same examples right, so the covariance is positive and the variance shrinks. For binary scores only discordant examples matter. Suppose A alone is right on \(n_{10} = 10\) and B alone on \(n_{01} = 25\) (difference \(15/500 = 3\) points):

McNemar: \(\chi^2 = (n_{01} - n_{10})^2 / (n_{01} + n_{10}) = 225/35 \approx 6.4\), \(p \approx 0.011\).
\(\mathrm{SE}(\bar d) = \sqrt{n_{01} + n_{10} - (n_{01} - n_{10})^2/n}\,/\,n \approx 0.0118\), so the interval is \(3 \pm 2.3\) points.

Same data, significant once paired. With 60 and 75 discordant examples instead, the same 3 points would not be.
Caveats.

This covers sampling of examples only. If outputs are sampled, add run-to-run variance by repeating runs.
Examples that share a source document or user are not independent; use clustered standard errors or a cluster bootstrap.
If B is the best of many variants tried on this set, the p-value is optimistic.

Sizing. To detect a difference \(\delta\), the interval half-width must be below \(\delta\); halving the detectable difference needs four times the examples.
Follow-ups

Why does a paired test need fewer examples?
What changes if each example is graded on a 1-5 scale instead of pass/fail?




seniorcodingMLE AI RE Implement a bootstrap confidence interval for the difference in a metric between two systems evaluated on the same examples.

import numpy as np

def paired_bootstrap_diff(a, b, n_boot=10_000, alpha=0.05, seed=0, groups=None):
    """a, b: per-example scores of systems A and B on the SAME examples, shape (n,).
    groups: optional cluster id per example (user, document); resample clusters if given."""
    a, b = np.asarray(a, float), np.asarray(b, float)
    assert a.shape == b.shape and a.ndim == 1
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    if groups is None:
        units = [np.array([i]) for i in range(len(a))]
    else:
        groups = np.asarray(groups)
        units = [np.flatnonzero(groups == g) for g in np.unique(groups)]
    diffs = np.empty(n_boot)
    for t in range(n_boot):
        pick = rng.integers(0, len(units), size=len(units))     # resample units with replacement
        idx = np.concatenate([units[j] for j in pick])
        diffs[t] = b[idx].mean() - a[idx].mean()                # same idx for both: paired
    lo, hi = np.quantile(diffs, [alpha / 2, 1 - alpha / 2])
    return {"diff": b.mean() - a.mean(), "ci": (lo, hi), "significant": not (lo <= 0 <= hi)}
Pitfalls an interviewer checks:

Pairing. Use the same resampled indices for both systems. Resampling them independently throws away the correlation and widens the interval.
Unit of resampling. Resample the independent unit: the conversation, user or source document, not the turn or chunk. Otherwise the interval is too narrow.
Metrics that are not means. For corpus-level F1, BLEU or AUC, recompute the metric on each resample; do not average per-example values.
Replicates. At least 1,000; 10,000 for stable tails.
Small or skewed samples. The percentile interval has poor coverage; use BCa or a permutation test for the p-value.
What it does not cover. Only example sampling. For stochastic systems, also resample over repeated runs.
Speed. For the simple mean, draw an index matrix of shape (n_boot, n) and vectorise.

Follow-ups

How would you turn this into a p-value?
When does the bootstrap fail outright?




staffdesignMLE AI RE Design the evaluation system for an AI assistant product used by several teams, covering offline evaluation, release gating and production.

Goals. Any change to prompt, model, tools or retrieval gets a trustworthy quality, cost and latency read within minutes to hours; regressions are caught before release; production quality is visible continuously.
Datasets. Versioned and owned.

Golden sets per capability and slice, with references or rubrics.
A regression set built from past incidents.
Safety and adversarial sets.
A rolling sample of recent production traffic, privacy-filtered.
A held-out set that prompt authors do not see.

Graders. A library of code checks and LLM judges, each with a measured error rate against a human-labelled calibration set, a pinned judge version, and tests. A human review queue for calibration and ambiguous cases.
Runner. Executes a system configuration against a dataset in parallel, with sandboxed tools for agent tasks, multiple trials per case, cached model outputs keyed by configuration, and per-run cost accounting. Every run records the dataset version, grader versions, code commit, model snapshot and prompt version.
Results. A store and UI with per-slice scores and confidence intervals, paired comparison against a baseline, the list of flipped examples, and a link from every score to the trace.
Gates. A smoke suite on every change; the full suite nightly and before release; explicit thresholds for guardrail criteria (safety, format validity, groundedness) and a non-inferiority margin for the primary metric.
Online. The same graders score a sample of production traces; implicit signals (regenerate, edit, abandon, escalate) and A/B tests measure user impact; canary prompts detect upstream model changes.
The loop. Production failures and review-queue findings flow back into datasets; judges are re-calibrated on a schedule.
Trade-offs to state. Suite cost and runtime against coverage, handled by tiering; flaky cases quarantined and fixed, not ignored; one shared platform against team-specific rubrics; and the risk of the suite becoming the target, countered by refreshing it from live traffic.
Follow-ups

How do you stop teams from tuning to the shared golden set?
What is the first thing you would build with two engineers and one month?
How do you decide the release threshold for the primary metric?




Monitoring, drift and observability 45% of postings

 Distinguish covariate shift, prior shift and concept drift and what each needs to detect
 Compute PSI and explain why statistical tests over-alert at scale
 Specify what an LLM trace must contain
 Monitor quality without labels using sampled grading, implicit user signals and operational proxies
 Investigate a quality drop with no deploy, including upstream model and data dependencies



coreconceptMLE AIasked at Nvidia What is the difference between data drift and concept drift, how do you detect each, and what do you do about it?


Covariate (data) drift: the input distribution \(P(X)\) changes; the relation \(P(Y \mid X)\) may be intact.
Prior (label) shift: the class balance \(P(Y)\) changes.
Concept drift: \(P(Y \mid X)\) changes. The same input now has a different right answer (new fraud pattern, changed user intent, a policy change).

Detection.

Inputs. Compare a recent window with a reference per feature: population stability index, \(\mathrm{PSI} = \sum_i (a_i - e_i)\ln(a_i/e_i)\) over bins with reference share \(e_i\) and current share \(a_i\); Kolmogorov-Smirnov or chi-square tests; for text and images, distances between embedding distributions or a classifier trained to tell the windows apart.
Outputs. Shifts in the score distribution and predicted class mix.
Performance. The only direct evidence of concept drift is labelled outcomes. When labels are delayed, use early proxies, a small fast-labelled sample, or delayed evaluation by cohort.

Caveats.

At large volume every statistical test is significant. Alert on effect sizes with thresholds learned from normal week-to-week variation. Common PSI cut-offs (0.1, 0.25) are conventions.
Drift is not degradation. Many input shifts do not hurt; concept drift can hurt with no visible input shift.
Most drift alerts are pipeline faults: a schema change, a unit change, a spike in nulls, a broken upstream job. Check data quality first.

Response. Fix the pipeline if it is a bug. Otherwise retrain or fine-tune on recent data, recalibrate if only the base rate moved, add features for the new pattern, or fall back to a safer policy. Scheduled retraining with monitored evaluation handles gradual drift; alerts handle abrupt changes.
Follow-ups

Labels arrive 30 days late. How do you know today that the model is failing?
Which drift alerts would you page on, and which only log?


Reported in interviews (candidate reports on third-party sites, not verified)

Nvidia, Machine Learning Engineer, Feb 2026: Bias-variance trade-off, calibration and model drift (PracHub)





seniorconceptAI MLE How do you monitor the quality of an LLM product in production when you have no labels?

Start with traces. One trace per user request, with a span for each model call, retrieval and tool call, recording: inputs and outputs (under a PII policy), prompt and model versions, tokens in and out including cached, latency including time to first token, cost, finish reason, retries and errors, and identifiers that join it to the user session and to downstream outcomes. OpenTelemetry is the common transport; its conventions for generative AI are still evolving.
Quality signals without labels.

Sampled automated grading. Run the offline graders (validated judges and code checks for groundedness, format validity, policy adherence) on a sample of live traces. This is the closest thing to a continuous quality number.
Implicit user signals. Regenerate and rephrase rates, edits to the output before use, acceptance of suggestions, abandonment, escalation to a human, explicit thumbs. Each is biased; the trend is informative.
Operational proxies. Tool error rate, validation-retry rate, refusal rate, steps per task, runs ended by a budget, empty retrievals.
Input drift. Clusters of intents over time; a new cluster is a use case the eval set does not cover.
Canaries. A fixed set of prompts replayed on a schedule detects changes in the upstream model or in dependencies independent of traffic mix.

Alerting. Rates with baselines from normal variation, segmented by route, tenant, model version and prompt version; comparison before and after every deploy; alerts on cost per task and latency percentiles alongside quality.
Close the loop. Route low-scoring and user-flagged traces to a review queue, label them, add them to the eval set, and periodically re-validate the online judges against those labels.
Follow-ups

Thumbs-down rate is 0.5% of sessions. How much can you learn from it?
What would you sample more heavily than uniform, and how do you keep the estimate unbiased?




seniordebuggingMLE AI A production quality metric dropped on Tuesday and your team deployed nothing. How do you investigate?

Is the drop real? Check the measurement before the system: a logging or pipeline change, a grader or judge update, a change in sampling, missing data for part of the day.
Characterise it. A step or a ramp? All traffic or one slice (tenant, locale, platform, route, model version)? The shape and scope narrow the cause more than anything else.
Things that change without your deploy.

Upstream model. A provider updated the model behind an alias, changed a default, or your traffic is on a fallback model because of rate limits or an outage. Canary prompts and the logged model id show this.
Dependencies. The retrieval index failed to refresh or was rebuilt, an embedding or feature service changed, a tool’s API changed its response format, timeouts are truncating context.
Data. An upstream schema or unit change, a spike in nulls, a late batch job.
Traffic mix. A new customer, a campaign, bot traffic, a seasonal shift in intents. Compare quality at fixed mix.
Other teams’ changes. Feature flags, experiments, configuration, shared prompts or libraries.
Infrastructure. Region failover, capacity limits, cache expiry.

Method. Line up the drop time against change logs of every dependency. Diff traces for similar inputs before and after: retrieved context, tool results, model id, token counts, finish reasons. Replay a fixed set of requests against the current system to see whether the change reproduces independent of traffic.
Mitigate and learn. Pin or roll back the dependency, or switch route, before the root cause is fully understood if users are affected. Then add the monitor that would have caught it at the source: a canary, a dependency version in every trace, an index freshness check, or a data-quality gate.
Follow-ups

The drop affects only one tenant. What are the first three things you check?
How do you tell a traffic mix change from a real degradation?




seniordesignMLE REasked at OpenAI Design out-of-distribution detection for a deployed classifier: how do you score a single input, how do you evaluate the detector, and how do you monitor it in production?

Say which shift you mean. Covariate shift (familiar classes, new input style: a new camera, a new language), semantic shift (a class the model never saw), and label shift (class frequencies move). A per-input detector targets the first two; label shift is a population-level question.
Per-input scores, cheapest first:

Maximum softmax probability. The baseline; weak because networks are confidently wrong far from the training data.
Energy, \(T \log \sum_c e^{z_c/T}\) on the logits: free, and usually better than the softmax maximum.
Feature distance: Mahalanobis distance to the nearest class mean in the penultimate layer, or distance to the k-th nearest training embedding. Strong on semantic shift, needs no retraining.
Disagreement across an ensemble: best quality, several times the cost.
Likelihood from a generative model is unreliable alone: such models can assign higher likelihood to out-of-distribution images than to their training data.

import numpy as np

def fit_mahalanobis(feats, labels):
    classes = np.unique(labels)
    mu = np.stack([feats[labels == c].mean(0) for c in classes])
    centred = feats - mu[np.searchsorted(classes, labels)]
    prec = np.linalg.pinv(centred.T @ centred / len(feats))   # shared covariance
    return mu, prec

def mahalanobis_score(x, mu, prec):                           # higher = more in-distribution
    d = x[:, None, :] - mu[None]
    return -np.einsum("ncd,de,nce->nc", d, prec, d).min(1)

def fpr_at_tpr(id_scores, ood_scores, tpr=0.95):
    thr = np.quantile(id_scores, 1 - tpr)
    return float((ood_scores >= thr).mean())
Evaluation. AUROC and the false-positive rate at 95% true-positive rate, reported separately for near shifts (similar classes, a new time period, a new region or device) and far ones (unrelated data). Far shifts flatter every method. Build the test sets from real held-out shifts in your own data; set the threshold on in-distribution validation data only, since real shifts are not known in advance.
Production design.

Per request: compute the score from activations the model already produces; above threshold, abstain, route to a fallback or a human, and log the input.
Population level: compare windows of scores, embeddings and predicted-class frequencies with a reference window, using a two-sample test or a classifier trained to tell the windows apart. Many small shifts never trip the per-input threshold and still move accuracy.
Close the loop: sample flagged inputs for labelling, measure accuracy on them, and add them to training or to the evaluation set.
Monitor the detector: flag rate over time, precision of flags from the labelled sample, and accuracy on unflagged traffic.

Failure modes. A flag rate that follows a benign traffic mix change and pages people for nothing; thresholds that go stale after each retrain because the feature space moved; the detector passing inputs that are in-distribution for the features and still adversarial; and treating “not flagged” as “correct”, which it is not.
Follow-ups

The flag rate doubled overnight and accuracy on a labelled sample did not move. What happened and what do you change?
Why can a generative model give higher likelihood to data it was never trained on?
How would you adapt this to a generative language model, where there are no class logits?

coreconceptMLE AI RE How do you design an ablation study so that its conclusions can be trusted?

An ablation attributes a result to a cause. It is trustworthy when the only difference between two runs is the thing being claimed.

A strong, equally tuned baseline. Most false gains come from a tuned new method against an untuned baseline. Give both the same tuning budget.
One change at a time. If the new run changes the architecture, the learning rate and the data, the gain cannot be assigned. Either add components one by one to the baseline or remove them one by one from the full system; do both when interactions are likely.
Hold everything else fixed. Data and splits, preprocessing, compute or step budget, evaluation code, decoding settings. Compare at equal parameters or equal compute, and say which.
Know the noise floor. Run the baseline with several seeds (three to five at least) and measure the standard deviation of the metric. A difference smaller than about two standard errors is not evidence. For LLM applications the analogues are sampling variance and eval-set size.
Report all runs. Mean and spread across seeds, not the best seed; include the variants that did not help.
Check the mechanism. If the claim is “the gain comes from X”, a control that removes X’s supposed mechanism while keeping its parameter count or compute should lose the gain.
Record enough to reproduce. Code commit, config, seeds, data version, environment.

Typical traps: test-set selection of checkpoints or hyperparameters, different amounts of training between arms, an evaluation bug that favours one output format, and concluding from a single seed.
Follow-ups

Compute allows three seeds for one configuration or one seed for three. Which do you choose?
Two components each give nothing alone and a gain together. How do you present that?




seniortrade-offMLE AI RE You tried 30 variants and one beats the baseline by 0.4 points with p = 0.03. Do you believe it?

Not yet. With 30 comparisons at \(\alpha = 0.05\) and no real effects, the chance that at least one looks significant is \(1 - 0.95^{30} \approx 79\%\). A p-value of 0.03 for the best of 30 is what noise produces.
Corrections.

Bonferroni: require \(p < \alpha/m = 0.0017\). Simple and conservative.
Holm: step-down version, uniformly more powerful than Bonferroni.
Benjamini-Hochberg: controls the false discovery rate, appropriate when screening many candidates and some false leads are acceptable.

The better remedy is replication. Select on one set of data and confirm on another: rerun the winning variant and the baseline with new seeds, or evaluate on a held-out set that played no part in choosing it. Expect the confirmed gain to be smaller than 0.4 because the best of many is biased upward.
Also ask.

Is 0.4 above the noise floor from seed-to-seed variation of the baseline?
Was the baseline tuned as much as the variants?
Were the 30 variants chosen in advance, or did choices adapt to earlier results (stopping rules, metric choice, subsets)? Undisclosed flexibility inflates false positives beyond the simple count.
Is there a reason to expect this variant to work? A mechanism raises the prior; an arbitrary winner lowers it.

Pre-registration in an engineering setting. Before the runs, write down the primary metric, the eval set, the comparison, the decision threshold and the stopping rule. Exploratory findings are fine, labelled as such and confirmed before anyone depends on them.
Follow-ups

When is false discovery rate control the right choice over family-wise error control?
How many seeds would you run to confirm a 0.4-point gain?




seniorconceptMLE RE A result from six months ago cannot be reproduced. What should have been recorded, and how do you make experiments reproducible by default?

What determines a result. Code, configuration, data, randomness, environment and the evaluation procedure. Each needs an identifier stored with the result.

Code: the commit hash, plus a diff if the tree was dirty.
Configuration: the fully resolved config after defaults and overrides, not only the command line.
Data: dataset version or content hash, split definition, preprocessing and tokenizer versions, and any filtering.
Randomness: seeds for initialisation, data order, augmentation and sampling.
Environment: container image or lockfile, library versions, hardware type, precision settings.
Evaluation: eval set version, metric code version, decoding settings, grader or judge version, checkpoint-selection rule.
For LLM applications: model snapshot id, prompt and tool-definition versions, sampling settings, and stored raw outputs.

Make it the default. The launcher records all of this automatically to the experiment tracker; runs from uncommitted code are refused or flagged; results tables are generated from tracked runs and never typed by hand; each headline number links to its run.
What reproducibility means. Bit-exact reruns are often unattainable on GPUs (non-deterministic kernels, different hardware, parallel data loading). The practical target is statistical: a rerun lands within the seed-to-seed spread. That spread must be known, which is another reason to run several seeds.
When a result does not reproduce. Diff the recorded items first; common culprits are a changed dataset behind an unchanged name, a library upgrade, a default that changed, a single lucky seed, and evaluation on a different checkpoint.
Follow-ups

Which sources of non-determinism remain after fixing all seeds?
How do you handle a dataset that is updated in place?

seniorconceptMLE AI REasked at Apple When is an LLM judge trustworthy? How do you validate one and what biases do you look for?

A judge is a classifier and is trusted only as far as it has been measured.
Validation.

Label 100-300 outputs by humans, ideally two per item, on the same rubric.
Report judge-human agreement (Cohen’s \(\kappa\) for categories, rank correlation for scores) next to human-human agreement, which is the ceiling.
Look at the confusion matrix: a judge that passes everything has high agreement when most outputs are good, and no power to detect regressions.
Hold out part of the labelled set from rubric tuning.

Known biases.

Position: in pairwise comparison, a preference for the first or second answer. Run both orders and count only consistent verdicts.
Verbosity: longer answers score higher.
Self-preference: judges tend to favour outputs from their own model family.
Leniency and compression: scores bunch at the top of a 1-5 scale.
Rubric sensitivity: small wording changes move scores.

Mitigations. Binary or three-level criteria with explicit definitions and examples; one criterion per call; reasoning before the verdict; a judge at least as capable as the system under test and preferably from a different family; pinned judge version.
Correcting for judge error. If the judge has true positive rate TPR and false positive rate FPR on the labelled set, an observed pass rate \(p_{obs}\) implies a true rate \(\hat p = (p_{obs} - \mathrm{FPR}) / (\mathrm{TPR} - \mathrm{FPR})\). With TPR 0.9 and FPR 0.2, an observed 76% corresponds to 80%.
Re-validate whenever the judge model, the rubric or the product’s output distribution changes.
Follow-ups

Judge-human agreement is 85% and human-human is 80%. What does that mean?
How does the correction formula behave when TPR is close to FPR?

seniortrade-offAI RE Pairwise or pointwise judging? And what makes a rubric good?

Pointwise assigns each output an absolute verdict or score. It scales linearly in outputs, gives a level you can threshold and track over time, and suits regression gates and production monitoring. Its weakness is calibration: absolute scores drift between raters and judge versions, and bunch at the top of the scale.
Pairwise asks which of two outputs is better. People and models are more consistent at comparing than at absolute scoring, so it detects smaller differences with fewer examples. Its weaknesses: no absolute level (both can be bad), position bias, intransitive preferences, and quadratic growth in comparisons with many systems, handled by sampling pairs and fitting Elo or Bradley-Terry ratings. Allow ties.
Use pairwise for selecting between two prompts or models; use pointwise pass/fail for gates, monitoring and anything that needs a stable number.
Rubric design.

Decompose quality into independent criteria (correct, grounded, complete, follows format) and grade each separately.
Prefer binary or three levels with observable definitions. A 1-10 scale has levels nobody can distinguish.
Give anchor examples for each level, including borderline cases with the reasoning.
Say what to ignore (length, style) if it should not count.
Treat critical failures (unsafe, fabricated fact) as separate gates; averaging hides them.
Pilot the rubric on 30-50 items with two raters, find where they disagree, and revise the wording until agreement is acceptable.

A rubric that humans cannot apply consistently will not be applied consistently by a model.
Follow-ups

How many pairwise comparisons would you need to rank five systems?

seniorconceptAI REasked at OpenAI How is evaluating an agent different from evaluating a single model response?

An agent produces a trajectory with side effects, is more variable, and costs far more per example.
Outcome versus trajectory grading.

Outcome: check the final environment state (tests pass, the record has the right values, the file exists). It accepts any valid path, so prefer it for task success.
Trajectory: check the steps (tools used, unnecessary calls, policy violations such as acting without confirmation, efficiency). Use it for diagnosis and for constraints that must hold along the way. Requiring one exact path penalises valid alternatives.

Environments. Sandboxed and resettable with a deterministic start state: containers, seeded databases, mocked or recorded external services. No state may leak between runs. Live dependencies (the web, third-party APIs) make results non-stationary.
Variance. Run each task \(k\) times. Report mean success with a confidence interval, and if reliability matters, the fraction of tasks solved in all \(k\) trials, which is much lower than the mean for unreliable agents. Separate infrastructure failures (timeouts, sandbox errors) from agent failures.
Cost. Record tokens, steps, wall-clock time and money per task; a method that gains two points at three times the cost is a different trade. Tier the suites: a small smoke set per change, the full set nightly.
Grader validity. Confirm that a reference solution passes and a do-nothing agent fails. Read transcripts: agents find shortcuts such as editing the tests, hard-coding expected output or exploiting a lenient check.
Reporting. State the harness, tools, step and token budgets with the score, since the same model scores differently under different scaffolds.

seniordebuggingAI RE You upgraded the judge model and quality scores moved by several points overnight with no product change. What do you do?

Confirm the cause. Take a frozen set of stored product outputs and score them with the old and the new judge. Identical outputs with different scores isolate the judge effect from any product change.
Decide which judge is right. Score the human-labelled calibration set with both. Compare agreement with humans, true and false positive rates, and the score distribution. Read the items where the judges disagree, grouped by criterion and slice: the new judge may be stricter on one criterion, more lenient on long answers, or reading the rubric differently.
Repair the time series.

The judge version is part of the metric definition. Scores from different judge versions are not comparable and should never share a trend line without a marked break.
If the new judge agrees with humans at least as well, adopt it and re-baseline: re-score stored historical outputs with it, or run both judges in parallel for an overlap period and publish the offset.
If it agrees worse, stay on the pinned old version and adjust the rubric for the new one before switching.

Prevent recurrence.

Pin a dated judge snapshot; never a moving alias.
Store raw outputs so they can be re-scored.
Run the calibration set through the judge in CI and alert when judge-human agreement or the judge’s pass rate on a fixed reference set moves.
Version rubric, judge model and judge prompt together and log them with every score.

The same procedure applies when the rubric is edited, which is a more frequent cause than model upgrades.

coreconceptMLE AI REasked at Meta, TikTok Which classification metric do you use when positives are rare, and why is accuracy or ROC-AUC not enough?

Definitions: precision \(= TP/(TP+FP)\), recall \(= TP/(TP+FN)\), false positive rate \(= FP/(FP+TN)\). ROC-AUC is the probability that a random positive is scored above a random negative. PR-AUC summarises precision over recall.
Accuracy is uninformative under imbalance: at 1% prevalence, predicting all negative scores 99%.
ROC-AUC does not depend on prevalence, which is its use and its trap. A false positive rate of 1% sounds excellent, but at 1% prevalence with 90% recall,
\[
\text{precision} = \frac{0.01 \cdot 0.90}{0.01 \cdot 0.90 + 0.99 \cdot 0.01} \approx 0.48,
\]
so half the alerts are wrong. Precision is what the reviewer or user experiences.
Use PR-AUC to compare models on rare positives (its baseline is the prevalence, not 0.5), and report the operating point the product uses: recall at a fixed precision, or precision at the top \(k\) if review capacity is fixed.
Threshold comes from costs: flag when \(p > c_{FP} / (c_{FP} + c_{FN})\), which requires calibrated probabilities.
Calibration is separate from ranking. AUC is unchanged by any monotonic transform of the scores. If scores are used as probabilities (expected value, thresholds from costs, bids), also measure log loss, Brier score or a reliability plot.
Caveats. Precision and PR-AUC change when prevalence changes, so they are not comparable across datasets with different base rates. If negatives were downsampled for training or evaluation, correct for it before reporting precision.
Follow-ups

Two models have the same ROC-AUC. How can one be much better in production?
