How often should a production model be retrained? Compare scheduled, triggered and continuous training.


Retrain as often as the world changes relative to what the model learned, and no more, because each retrain is a release with risk and cost.

Scheduled (daily, weekly, monthly). Simple and predictable. Choose the period from a backtest: train on data up to time \(t\), evaluate on windows further and further ahead, and read how fast the metric decays. If a month-old model loses nothing, weekly retraining buys nothing.
Triggered. Retrain when a monitor fires: input drift past a threshold, the outcome metric dropping, or enough new labelled data. Efficient, but depends on monitors that are neither noisy nor blind, and labels may arrive too late to trigger in time.
Continuous or online. Incremental updates from a stream, used where freshness is the product (ads, feeds, fraud). Highest operational burden: any bad data flows into the model within minutes, so it needs strict input validation, automatic rollback and periodic full retrains to reset accumulated error.

Things that complicate the choice:

Label delay. If outcomes arrive after 30 days, the newest month has incomplete labels. Train on matured data or model the delay explicitly.
Feedback loops. The model’s decisions shape its next training set; keep some exploration or holdout traffic.
Stability. Frequent retrains can churn predictions for the same input. Measure prediction churn between versions and warm-start if it matters.
Gates. Every automatic retrain needs the same evaluation gates as a manual release, compared against the current production model on the same fresh data.

For LLM-based systems the equivalent questions are when to refresh the retrieval index, the prompts and the evaluation set, and when to re-qualify on a new model version.

What is hidden technical debt in ML systems? Give the forms you have seen and how you contain them.


ML systems accumulate debt in places that ordinary code review does not see, because behaviour depends on data and on other models. The main forms, following the well-known Google paper on the topic:

Entanglement. Changing anything changes everything: adding a feature or altering one input distribution shifts the weights of all others. No change is isolated, so every change needs a full evaluation.
Hidden feedback loops. The model influences the data it is later trained on, or two systems influence each other through the world.
Undeclared consumers. Other teams read your model’s scores or logs without telling you; a recalibration then breaks their thresholds.
Unstable data dependencies. Input signals owned by other teams change meaning over time; unused or weakly useful features stay in the model and remain a liability.
Pipeline jungles and glue code. Data preparation grows by accretion into scrapes, joins and intermediate files that nobody can test end to end.
Configuration debt. Thresholds, feature lists and learning settings spread across files with no validation or history.
Dead experimental paths. Flags for abandoned experiments left in the serving code.

Containment: version and validate input data with contracts; register consumers and expose a calibrated, versioned output; delete features that do not pay for themselves; keep preprocessing in one library shared by training and serving; treat configuration as code with review; and schedule the removal of experiment branches at launch time. The useful interview move is to name one of these that caused a real incident and what the fix was.

What does a model registry do, and what exactly do you version so that a model can be reproduced and rolled back?


A registry is the source of truth for which model artefacts exist, where each came from and which one is serving. For every version it stores the artefact and its metadata, and it controls promotion between stages (for example candidate, staging, production, archived) with a record of who or what approved each move.
To reproduce a model you need all of:

Code: the commit of the training code and of the shared preprocessing library.
Data: an immutable snapshot or a query pinned to a table version, including the label definition and the split.
Configuration: hyperparameters, feature list, random seeds.
Environment: container image digest, library versions, hardware type where it affects numerics.
Outputs: metrics on the fixed evaluation sets, the evaluation set versions and the training logs.

Lineage links these: from a serving model you can reach the run, the data and the code, and from a dataset you can list every model trained on it, which is what you need for an incident or a deletion request.
What is deployed is more than weights: the preprocessing and postprocessing, the input and output schema, thresholds and calibration, and for LLM systems the prompt, the tool definitions and the pinned model identifier. Version them as one unit, because rolling back the weights without the matching feature transformation is a common way to turn a rollback into a second incident.



Two runs from the same commit and data give different metrics. What are the causes?

You are asked to reproduce a model trained six months ago, and the retrained model scores noticeably worse. Where do you look?


Assume nothing was pinned until shown otherwise, and compare the two runs layer by layer.

Data. Most often the cause. Was the training set a snapshot or a query against a live table? Rows get backfilled, corrected, deleted for privacy or deduplicated differently. Compare row counts, label rates and feature distributions with whatever statistics the old run logged. Check that the split is the same: a random split with an unpinned seed or a changed user-to-split hash changes the test set itself.
Labels and features. Did a label definition or a feature’s computation change upstream, so the same column name now means something else?
Evaluation. Is the metric computed by the same code on the same evaluation set? A changed tokenizer, threshold or metric library version moves numbers without any model change.
Environment. Library versions change defaults (initialisation, optimiser epsilon, data-loader ordering, mixed-precision behaviour). Use the old container image if it exists.
Configuration. Hyperparameters that lived in a notebook or an environment variable and never reached the tracked config; the number of training steps; early stopping on a different validation set.
Nondeterminism. Seeds, data order with multiple workers, nondeterministic GPU operations and distributed reduction order give run-to-run variance. Measure it with a few seeds: a gap inside that variance is not a reproduction failure.

Then fix the process: immutable dataset versions, image digests in the run record, and a periodic “retrain from the registry record” job that proves reproduction still works.

Design the monitoring for a model whose labels arrive weeks after the prediction. What do you alert on?


Monitor four layers, from the fastest and least specific signal to the slowest and most meaningful.

Service. Latency percentiles, error and timeout rates, saturation, and the share of requests answered by a fallback or default. Alert as for any service.
Inputs. Per-feature null rate, range, cardinality and distribution against a training reference; freshness of every upstream table and feature; schema. These catch most real incidents (a broken pipeline) within minutes.
Predictions. Score distribution, the rate of each predicted class, the share above the decision threshold, and agreement with the previous model version on shadow traffic. A shift here with stable inputs suggests a serving or version problem.
Outcomes. Once labels mature: the metric itself, calibration and performance by slice. Until then use proxies that arrive sooner, such as user corrections, early partial labels, or a small human-labelled sample each day.

Alert design:

Page only on signals that are actionable and specific: staleness, null-rate jumps, fallback rate, prediction-rate change beyond a band learned from history. Send drift statistics on individual features to a dashboard, since with hundreds of features some always look significant.
Compare with the same hour last week to absorb seasonality.
Monitor by slice; aggregate metrics hide a broken segment.
Log inputs, model version and prediction for every request with a join key, so that outcomes can be attached later and any incident can be replayed.

The delayed labels also mean the newest training data is incomplete, which the retraining pipeline must handle.

Implement the population stability index for one numeric feature in NumPy. How do you read it, and what are its limits?


PSI compares the binned distribution of a feature in production (actual, \(a_i\)) with a reference such as the training set (expected, \(e_i\)):
\[\mathrm{PSI} = \sum_i (a_i - e_i) \ln \frac{a_i}{e_i}.\]
It is a symmetrised KL divergence over bins, so it is non-negative and zero only when the binned distributions match.
import numpy as np

def psi(expected, actual, bins=10, eps=1e-6):
    """PSI of `actual` against the reference sample `expected`."""
    edges = np.quantile(expected, np.linspace(0, 1, bins + 1))
    edges[0], edges[-1] = -np.inf, np.inf      # catch out-of-range values
    edges = np.unique(edges)                   # ties collapse bins
    e = np.histogram(expected, edges)[0] / len(expected)
    a = np.histogram(actual, edges)[0] / len(actual)
    e, a = np.clip(e, eps, None), np.clip(a, eps, None)
    return float(np.sum((a - e) * np.log(a / e)))
Reading it: the usual rule of thumb is below 0.1 stable, 0.1 to 0.25 worth a look, above 0.25 a significant shift. These thresholds are convention, not theory.
Limits to state:

Bins come from the reference only; quantile bins give equal expected mass, which keeps the estimate stable.
It depends on the number of bins and on sample size. Small samples inflate it, so compare windows of similar size or calibrate the threshold by bootstrapping the reference against itself.
Nulls need their own bin; dropping them hides the most common failure.
It is univariate. It misses changes in the relationship between features and says nothing about whether the shift hurts the model. Weight alerts by feature importance and confirm with prediction and outcome metrics.

Design an automated retraining pipeline that promotes models to production without a human in the loop. What makes that safe?


Automation is safe only if every judgement a careful engineer would make at release time is encoded as a gate, and a failure of any gate leaves the current model serving.
Pipeline.

Data build: materialise an immutable training snapshot. Gate on data validation: schema, volume against expectation, null rates, label rate, freshness.
Train: pinned code, configuration and image. Gate on training health: loss within a band of previous runs, no NaN, expected duration.
Evaluate: the candidate and the current production model on the same fresh held-out window and on fixed regression sets and slices. Gate on no regression beyond noise overall and on protected slices, calibration within tolerance, and bounded prediction churn against production.
Package and verify: load the artefact in the serving image, replay recorded requests, compare outputs with the training-side predictions (skew test), check latency and memory.
Release: canary with automatic rollback on service and prediction guardrails, then full rollout. Register lineage and the gate results.

What makes it safe.

The gates compare with the live model, not with fixed thresholds that go stale.
A bounded rate of change: at most one promotion per period and a freeze switch.
Rollback is one action and restores model and preprocessing together.
The pipeline alerts when it has not produced a model for longer than expected, since silent failure means an ageing model.
Periodic human review of gate statistics, and a holdout of traffic on an older model to detect slow degradation that step-to-step comparisons cannot see.

State where you would keep a human: changes to features, labels, architecture or the gates themselves.

Map a typical ML system, training plus online inference, onto cloud building blocks. What do you need from each?


Five groups of services, the same on AWS, GCP and Azure under different names.

Compute. Virtual machines and GPU instances for training; an orchestrator for containers (managed Kubernetes, or a managed training and endpoint service) for jobs and serving; serverless functions for glue. Decide per workload between on-demand, reserved or committed capacity, and spot or preemptible capacity.
Storage. Object storage (S3, GCS, Blob) for datasets, checkpoints and model artefacts: cheap, durable, high throughput, no in-place edits. Block storage and local NVMe for scratch and data caches. A warehouse or lakehouse for analytical tables. A low-latency key-value store for online features.
Network. A virtual private network with private subnets, load balancers in front of serving, private endpoints to storage and managed services, and a gateway or CDN at the edge. Data location matters because cross-zone and cross-region transfer and egress are billed and slow.
Identity and secrets. Roles for people and service accounts for workloads, scoped to the buckets and services each needs; a secrets manager and a key-management service; audit logs.
Managed ML and data services. Training and endpoint platforms, model APIs, managed streaming, workflow orchestration, monitoring.

A training job then reads as: an orchestrated container on GPU nodes, with a service account allowed to read one dataset prefix and write one checkpoint prefix, in the same region as the data. Online inference: an autoscaled deployment behind a load balancer, reading features from the online store, pulling the artefact from the registry bucket at start, exporting metrics and logs.

What changes if the data may not leave one country?





How do you set up identity, permissions and networking for ML workloads in the cloud so that a compromised notebook or job does limited damage?


Start from least privilege and from the assumption that any single workload can be compromised, for instance through a malicious package or a poisoned model file.
Identity.

Every workload runs as its own service account or role with a narrow policy: this training job may read this dataset prefix and write that checkpoint prefix. No shared “ML team” role with access to everything.
Short-lived credentials issued by the platform (workload identity, instance roles), never long-lived keys in code, images or notebooks.
People get access through groups, with elevated access granted temporarily and logged.
Separate accounts or projects for development, staging and production, so that an experiment cannot touch production data or endpoints.

Network.

Workloads in private subnets without public addresses; inbound traffic only through a load balancer or gateway.
Private endpoints to object storage and managed services, so data does not cross the public internet.
Egress control: training jobs and notebooks reach only an internal package mirror and approved hosts. Open egress is how data is exfiltrated.

Data.

Encryption at rest with managed keys and in transit with TLS.
Sensitive datasets in separate buckets with their own policies and access logs.

Detection. Audit logs on data access and permission changes, with alerts on unusual volume or new principals.
The trade-off is friction: researchers want broad access and open internet. The answer is a paved path, such as a sandbox project with de-identified data and a package mirror, rather than exceptions.

Your team’s cloud bill for ML has doubled. Where do you look, and which levers do you pull first?


First attribute the bill: by service, by team or project tag, and by workload type (training, inference, storage, data transfer). Untagged spend is usually the first finding.
Compute, usually the largest part.

Idle and oversized resources: notebooks and development GPUs left running, endpoints with a minimum replica count sized for peak, GPU instances at 20% utilisation. Measure utilisation per instance; shut down on idle; right-size.
Pricing model: steady baseline load on committed or reserved capacity; fault-tolerant training and batch inference on spot or preemptible instances, which are much cheaper but can be reclaimed, so they need checkpointing and retries; on-demand only for the remainder.
Efficiency: batching, a smaller or quantised model, mixed precision, caching of repeated requests, moving offline work from online endpoints to batch jobs.

Storage. Checkpoints and intermediate datasets kept forever, many copies of the same dataset, everything in the hot tier. Add lifecycle rules, retention for checkpoints (keep the best and the last few) and colder tiers for archives.
Network. Egress and cross-region or cross-zone transfer: training in one region on data in another, or chatty services across zones. Co-locate compute and data.
Managed-service premiums. Convenience pricing on managed endpoints, logging and monitoring ingestion, and per-token model APIs. Check log volume and sampling.
Then make it stay fixed: budgets and alerts per team, cost per unit of work on a dashboard (per training run, per thousand predictions), and quotas. Report the result as unit cost, since total spend should grow with usage.

Managed ML platform (SageMaker, Vertex AI, Azure ML) or your own stack on Kubernetes? How do you decide?


Decide by team size, workload shape and how far your needs are from the platform’s defaults.
Managed platform. Training jobs, endpoints, pipelines, a registry and monitoring without running the control plane. Strengths: fast start, security and compliance features built in, autoscaling endpoints, little operations staff needed. Costs: a price premium on compute, quotas and limited instance choice, opinions that are hard to bend (custom schedulers, unusual serving patterns, multi-node training topologies), and coupling of code to one provider’s SDK.
Own stack on Kubernetes with open components for scheduling, serving, workflows and tracking. Strengths: full control over scheduling and bin-packing of GPUs, any serving runtime, portability across clouds and on-premises, lower unit cost at scale. Costs: a platform team to build, upgrade and be on call for it; you own security patches, GPU drivers and cluster upgrades.
Rules of thumb:

A few engineers and standard workloads: managed, and spend the time on the product.
Large or unusual GPU workloads, strict cost targets, multi-cloud or on-premises requirements, or dozens of teams needing shared quota and fair scheduling: own platform, when there are people to run it.
Hybrids are common: managed Kubernetes and managed data services underneath, with your own job and serving layer on top; or model APIs for inference and your own stack for evaluation and data.

Keep the exit cheap either way: containers as the unit of work, artefacts in open formats in your own bucket, and a thin internal interface in front of provider SDKs.

RUN python3 -m venv /opt/venv

    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/* && useradd --create-home app
COPY --from=build /opt/venv /opt/venv

What to explain:

Layer order. Dependencies before source code, so a code change rebuilds only the last layer.
Size. A runtime base, not devel; no build tools or pip cache in the final stage. Framework wheels with bundled CUDA libraries are several gigabytes, and image size is pull time, which is cold-start time.
Reproducibility. A lock file with hashes, a pinned base digest, no latest.
Safety. Non-root user, no secrets in layers or build arguments, a .dockerignore.
Weights. Usually not baked in: pull them at start from the registry, or mount a volume, so that image and model version independently. Bake them in only when cold-start time dominates.
CUDA. The kernel driver lives on the host and is exposed by the NVIDIA container runtime; the image carries the user-space CUDA libraries. The host driver must be at least as new as the image’s CUDA version requires. PyTorch wheels ship their own CUDA libraries, so the image’s system CUDA matters mainly for other runtimes.

Which Kubernetes objects does an ML inference service use, and what do resource requests, limits and probes do for a GPU workload?


The objects:

Pod: one or more containers scheduled together on a node; the unit that gets a GPU.
Deployment: keeps N replicas of a pod template running and performs rolling updates. A Job runs a pod to completion (training, batch inference); a StatefulSet gives stable identities and volumes.
Service: a stable virtual address that load-balances across ready pods. Ingress or a gateway exposes it outside the cluster.
ConfigMap and Secret: configuration and credentials injected at run time.
HorizontalPodAutoscaler: changes the replica count from a metric.
Node pools with labels and taints: GPU nodes are tainted so that only pods that tolerate the taint and request a GPU land on them.

Requests and limits. The scheduler places a pod by its requests. CPU above the limit is throttled; memory above the limit gets the container killed (OOMKilled). GPUs are an extended resource such as nvidia.com/gpu: 1, exposed by a device plugin. They are integers and by default not shared: one pod gets the whole device unless time-slicing or partitioning is configured. Set CPU and memory for the data-loading and tokenisation work too, since a throttled CPU starves the GPU.
Probes.

Startup: gives slow model loading time before other probes begin.
Readiness: the pod receives traffic only when the model is loaded and warmed up. Without it, a rolling update sends requests to pods that are still loading weights.
Liveness: restarts a hung process. Keep it cheap and separate from readiness, or a busy GPU causes restarts under load.

Also set a termination grace period and drain in-flight requests on SIGTERM.



What happens during a rolling update if readiness is missing and the model takes 90 seconds to load?
How would you let two small models share one GPU?





What does infrastructure as code give an ML team, and what are the failure modes of a tool like Terraform?


Infrastructure as code declares the desired resources (networks, clusters, node pools, buckets, roles, endpoints) in version-controlled files, and a tool makes reality match.
What it gives:

Reproducibility. A new environment or region is a parameter change, and staging can really mirror production.
Review and history. Changes to permissions or cluster shape go through pull requests; you can see who changed what and revert it.
Disaster recovery and audit. The definition of the infrastructure exists outside the cloud console.

How Terraform works, in one breath: providers map resource types to cloud APIs; a state file records what the tool believes exists; plan diffs configuration against state and reality; apply executes the diff; modules package reusable pieces.
Failure modes to know:

State. It must live in a shared, locked, encrypted backend. Two concurrent applies or a lost state file are serious. State can contain secrets.
Drift. Manual console changes diverge from the code; the next apply reverts them or fails. Detect drift with scheduled plans and remove console write access.
Destructive plans. Renaming a resource or changing an immutable field becomes destroy-and-recreate, which for a database or bucket is data loss. Read the plan; protect stateful resources against deletion.
Blast radius. One giant configuration means every change risks everything. Split by environment and by layer (network, cluster, applications).
Boundary with the cluster. Terraform suits long-lived infrastructure; workloads inside Kubernetes are better managed by manifests or a GitOps controller.

For ML specifically: put GPU node pools, quotas and service accounts in code, since these are what an incident or a new region needs first.



Someone resized a node pool in the console during an incident. What happens next?
How do you keep secrets out of state and out of the repository?





A training container runs fine on your workstation but in the cluster it is killed, hangs or runs several times slower. What are the usual causes?


Work through what differs between the two environments: resources, devices, storage and network.
Killed.

OOMKilled: the memory limit is lower than the workstation’s RAM. Data-loader workers multiply memory, and page cache for memory-mapped data counts toward the limit on some configurations. Check the pod’s last state and raise the limit or reduce workers.
Shared memory: PyTorch workers pass tensors through /dev/shm, which defaults to 64 MB in containers. The symptom is a bus error or a hang. Mount a memory-backed volume at /dev/shm.
Preemption or eviction: spot nodes reclaimed, or ephemeral storage exhausted by checkpoints written to the container filesystem.

Fails at start.

CUDA mismatch: host driver older than the image’s CUDA libraries need, or no GPU requested so none is visible.
Permissions: running as non-root with a read-only filesystem, or a service account without access to the bucket.

Slow.

CPU throttling: a CPU limit of 2 with 16 data-loader workers. Libraries read the node’s core count, not the container’s limit, and oversubscribe threads. Set the worker and thread counts from the limit.
Storage: reading many small files from network or object storage instead of local NVMe. Look at I/O wait; use sharded archives and a local cache.
Different hardware: another GPU model, or a neighbour sharing the device or the node’s memory bandwidth.
Network: downloading the dataset or the model at every start.

Method: compare GPU utilisation, CPU throttling counters, I/O wait and memory between the environments before changing the code.

Why does the process see 96 cores when its limit is 4, and what breaks because of it?

Design a cache for model predictions or LLM responses. What goes in the key, how do you invalidate, and when is caching the wrong answer?


Key. Everything the output depends on, and nothing else: a hash of the normalised input, the model and preprocessing version, the prompt or feature-set version, decoding parameters, and any per-user or per-tenant context that changes the answer. Omitting the version serves old outputs after a deploy; omitting the tenant leaks one customer’s answer to another.
Value and policy. Store the output with its creation time and version. Set a TTL from how fast the underlying facts change. Bound the size with LRU or LFU eviction.
Invalidation.

Version in the key makes a model or prompt change an automatic miss, with no purge.
Event-driven deletes when a source document or feature changes.
TTL as the backstop.

Operational hazards.

Stampede: a popular key expires and many requests recompute it at once. Use single-flight (one computation per key, others wait), stale-while-revalidate, and jittered TTLs.
Cold start after deploy: a version bump empties the cache exactly when the new version is under most scrutiny. Pre-warm the top keys.
Negative caching: cache failures briefly, or an outage is amplified by retries.

Variants. Exact-match caching works when inputs repeat (popular queries, item embeddings, classification of repeated content). Semantic caching returns a stored answer for a similar query by embedding distance; it raises the hit rate and can return a wrong answer for a query that differs in one important word, so it needs a strict threshold and an evaluation. Precomputation is a cache filled ahead of time by a batch job.
When not to cache. Personalised or fast-changing outputs, sampled generations where variety is intended, low repetition (measure the hit rate first), and sensitive outputs that should not be stored.



How would you estimate the hit rate before building it?

You run long inference jobs through a queue. Explain at-most-once, at-least-once and exactly-once delivery, and what your workers must do as a result.


A queue decouples producers from workers and absorbs bursts. Its delivery guarantee decides what the worker code must tolerate.

At-most-once. The message is acknowledged before processing. A crash loses the job. Acceptable only for work that can be dropped.
At-least-once. The message is acknowledged after processing; if the worker dies or the visibility timeout expires first, it is redelivered. Nothing is lost, but a job can run twice, including when the first run actually finished and only the acknowledgement was lost. This is what almost every system provides.
Exactly-once. Not achievable as pure delivery over an unreliable network. What systems offer is exactly-once effect: at-least-once delivery plus idempotent or transactional processing.

So workers must be idempotent:

Give every job an idempotency key. Before doing work, or atomically with writing the result, check whether that key is already complete.
Write results with an upsert keyed by the job id, never an append.
For side effects outside your store (sending a message, charging a customer), pass the idempotency key downstream or record intent and completion transactionally.

Other things to design:

Visibility timeout longer than the worst-case processing time, or a heartbeat that extends it. A GPU job that outlives its timeout is run twice concurrently.
Retries with backoff and a dead-letter queue after N attempts, so that a poison message does not block the queue forever.
Ordering only where needed, per key, since global ordering costs throughput.
Backlog age as the main metric for autoscaling and alerting.

A log such as Kafka differs from a task queue: consumers track an offset in an ordered, replayable partition, which suits event pipelines; per-message acknowledgement and retries suit job processing.



Where exactly does the duplicate come from when a worker finishes just as its timeout expires?
How do you make “send the user an email with the result” idempotent?





Give me a threat model for an ML system. What can an attacker do that they could not do to an ordinary web service?


Everything that applies to a web service applies here (authentication, injection, secrets, dependencies). The ML-specific surface is the data, the model artefact and the model’s behaviour.
Training time.

Data poisoning: an attacker who can influence training data, such as user-submitted content, scraped pages or a feedback signal, inserts examples that degrade the model or plant a backdoor triggered by a specific pattern.
Supply chain: pretrained weights, datasets and packages from public hubs. Pickle-based model files execute arbitrary code when loaded. Prefer weight-only formats such as safetensors, verify hashes, scan and pin dependencies, and load untrusted artefacts in a sandbox.

Inference time.

Evasion: inputs crafted to be misclassified, which matters most for fraud, abuse and malware detection where the adversary adapts.
Extraction: repeated queries to copy the model’s behaviour or recover its decision boundary. Rate limits and monitoring raise the cost.
Privacy attacks: membership inference (was this record in the training set?) and training-data extraction, to which models that memorise are vulnerable.
Prompt injection and unsafe tool use for LLM systems.
Resource abuse: expensive inputs as denial of service, or stolen API keys used for free inference.

Infrastructure. Over-broad access to training data, credentials in notebooks, unauthenticated internal endpoints, and prompt or request logs that contain sensitive data.
Mitigation follows from asking, for each asset (data, weights, predictions), who can read or influence it and what the worst outcome is. Then apply least privilege, provenance and validation for data and artefacts, rate limiting and abuse monitoring at the endpoint, and a response plan that includes retraining from clean data.



How would you detect that a feedback signal is being manipulated?
Why is loading a pickle file from a model hub dangerous, concretely?





Your training data and request logs contain personal data. How do you handle it, and what happens when a user asks for their data to be deleted?


Minimise first. Collect and keep only the fields the model needs. Drop or coarsen the rest at ingestion (precise location to region, birth date to age band). Data that was never stored needs no protection.
Separate identity from content. Replace direct identifiers with pseudonymous keys and keep the mapping in a separate, tightly controlled store. Pseudonymised data is still personal data, since it can often be re-identified by joining, but the separation limits who can do so.
Scrub free text. Logs, prompts and transcripts contain names, emails and account numbers. Run detection and redaction before the text reaches analytics or training stores, and measure the detector’s recall on a labelled sample, because it is not perfect.
Control and record access. Role-based access to raw data, de-identified views for most work, access logs, and encryption. Set retention periods per dataset and enforce them with lifecycle rules, not by convention.
Deletion requests. Deleting the source row is the easy part. You need lineage to find the derived copies: feature tables, training snapshots, caches, embeddings in a vector index, evaluation sets, backups. Practical design: key everything by the pseudonymous id, run a periodic deletion job across all registered stores, and rebuild derived datasets from sources on a schedule so that deletions propagate.
Models. A trained model may have memorised the record. The dependable remedy is retraining without it at the next scheduled cycle; machine unlearning methods exist but are not yet something to rely on for guarantees. How regulators treat already-trained models is not settled everywhere, so this is a decision to take with legal counsel, and the engineering job is to make retraining and lineage cheap.
Purpose limitation also applies: data collected to provide a service is not automatically usable for training. Record the permitted purposes with the dataset.



How do you find every place a user’s data has been copied to?
What would you log from an LLM product’s requests, and for how long?

Explain differential privacy and federated learning. What does each guarantee, and what does it cost?


Differential privacy is a property of an algorithm. A randomised mechanism \(M\) is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-differentially private if for any two datasets \(D, D'\) differing in one record and any set of outputs \(S\):
\[\Pr[M(D) \in S] \le e^{\varepsilon} \Pr[M(D') \in S] + \delta.\]
The output barely depends on any one individual, whatever the attacker already knows. Smaller \(\varepsilon\) is stronger. Guarantees compose: every release from the same data spends budget.
For model training the standard method is DP-SGD: compute per-example gradients, clip each to norm \(C\), sum, add Gaussian noise with standard deviation \(\sigma C\), and step. A privacy accountant converts the noise level, sampling rate and number of steps into \((\varepsilon, \delta)\). Costs: lower accuracy, most painful for small datasets and rare subgroups; per-example gradients are slower and use more memory; large batches are needed; and the reported \(\varepsilon\) is only meaningful if the unit of privacy (record or user) is chosen correctly.
Federated learning is a system architecture. Data stays on devices or in silos; each client computes an update on local data, and a server aggregates the updates (FedAvg averages client weights after several local steps). It reduces central collection of raw data. It is not a privacy guarantee by itself: updates can leak training examples. It is combined with secure aggregation, so the server sees only the sum, and with differential privacy on the aggregate.
Costs of federation: clients have different data distributions, which slows or biases convergence; devices are unreliable and heterogeneous; debugging without seeing the data is hard; and communication is the bottleneck.
One sentence to remember: differential privacy limits what the output reveals; federated learning limits where the input travels.



Why is clipping per example, and not per batch, necessary for the guarantee?
What does an epsilon of 8 mean in practice, and how would you explain it to a product manager?





You sell an LLM-based product to enterprises. Design tenant isolation and the controls a security review will ask for.


A security questionnaire asks, in effect: can another customer see our data, can your staff, where does it go, and can you prove it.
Tenant isolation.

Every request carries a tenant identity established at authentication, and every data access is filtered by it in the data layer, not in the prompt. Row-level security or separate schemas, indexes or databases per tenant, chosen by the isolation a customer tier requires.
Retrieval indexes are per tenant, or filtered by tenant and document permissions at query time, before the model sees anything.
Caches, conversation memory and logs are keyed by tenant. A shared response cache without the tenant in the key is a classic leak.
No training or fine-tuning of shared models on a tenant’s data unless the contract allows it; per-tenant adapters stay per tenant.

Data flow. Document which sub-processors receive data (model providers, vector stores, monitoring), with data-processing agreements and retention settings. Offer regional processing when data residency is required.
Access by your own staff. Production data is inaccessible by default; break-glass access is time-limited, approved and logged. Debugging uses redacted traces.
Standard controls. Single sign-on and role-based access for customer users, encryption at rest and in transit, customer-visible audit logs of who asked what and which documents were retrieved, configurable retention and deletion, secrets management, dependency and vulnerability scanning, and an incident response process. Certifications such as SOC 2 or ISO 27001 are evidence that these operate.
Model-specific. Treat retrieved documents and tool outputs as untrusted input, limit what tools can do on a user’s behalf to that user’s own permissions, and test for cross-tenant leakage as part of the evaluation suite.



How would you test that tenant A can never retrieve tenant B’s documents?
A customer asks that their prompts never be stored. What breaks, and what do you offer?





What is a data contract, and where do you put data validation in an ML pipeline?


A data contract is an explicit agreement between the producer of a dataset and its consumers: the schema (names, types, nullability), the semantics and units of each field, allowed values and ranges, freshness and completeness expectations, the owner, and how changes are announced and versioned. Its purpose is to turn a silent upstream change into a failed check on the producer’s side.
Validation belongs at three points, each catching a different failure:

At ingestion, on each batch or stream window. Schema and types, primary-key uniqueness, null rates, value ranges and categories, row counts against expectation, and freshness. Bad data is quarantined before it spreads to derived tables.
Before training, on the assembled training set. Label rate and label distribution, feature distributions against the previous snapshot, duplicates, and leakage between splits. Fail the pipeline; do not train.
At serving, on each request. Type and range checks, missing features, and unknown categories, with a defined fallback and a counter. Then compare serving distributions with training.

Kinds of check, from cheap to subtle: schema; volume and freshness; per-column statistics (nulls, min, max, distinct count, quantiles); cross-column rules (end after start); referential integrity; distribution comparison with a reference.
Practical points: thresholds learned from history with tolerance bands work better than hand-set constants; classify checks into blocking and warning, or people learn to ignore them; every check needs an owner who is paged; and the expectations should be stored with the dataset version so that training and serving validate against the same definition.



Which checks block the pipeline and which only warn, and how do you decide?
How do you validate a free-text or image column?





Write a small validation function for a pandas DataFrame that a training pipeline can run as a gate. What would you add for production?


import pandas as pd

def validate(df: pd.DataFrame, spec: dict, min_rows: int = 1) -> list[str]:
    """spec: {col: {"dtype": str, "max_null": float, "min": x, "max": x,
    "values": set, "unique": bool}}. Returns a list of problems; empty means pass."""
    errs = []
    if len(df) < min_rows:
        errs.append(f"only {len(df)} rows, expected at least {min_rows}")
    for col, rule in spec.items():
        if col not in df.columns:
            errs.append(f"{col}: missing column")
            continue
        s = df[col]
        if "dtype" in rule and str(s.dtype) != rule["dtype"]:
            errs.append(f"{col}: dtype {s.dtype}, expected {rule['dtype']}")
        null_rate = s.isna().mean()
        if null_rate > rule.get("max_null", 0.0):
            errs.append(f"{col}: null rate {null_rate:.3f}")
        v = s.dropna()
        if "min" in rule and (v < rule["min"]).any():
            errs.append(f"{col}: values below {rule['min']}")
        if "max" in rule and (v > rule["max"]).any():
            errs.append(f"{col}: values above {rule['max']}")
        if "values" in rule:
            extra = set(v.unique()) - rule["values"]
            if extra:
                errs.append(f"{col}: unexpected values {sorted(extra)[:5]}")
        if rule.get("unique") and v.duplicated().any():
            errs.append(f"{col}: duplicate values")
    return errs
The pipeline calls it and fails when the list is non-empty, logging every problem, not only the first.
What production adds:

Distribution checks against the previous snapshot (quantiles, category shares, label rate), with tolerance bands learned from history.
Freshness and volume relative to the same weekday, not a constant.
Cross-column and cross-table rules: timestamps in order, foreign keys present, no overlap between train and test keys.
Severity levels and quarantine of bad partitions instead of all-or-nothing.
Scale: the same rules compiled to SQL or Spark for data that does not fit in memory. Libraries such as Great Expectations, pandera or TFDV provide this; the logic is what an interviewer wants to see.
The spec versioned next to the dataset, and reused for serving-time checks.




How would you check that no user appears in both the training and the test split?
Where do the thresholds come from, and who updates them?





A model has been slowly getting worse for two weeks. You find that an upstream team changed how a field is populated, so one feature is now null for a third of rows. What do you do now and what do you change afterwards?


Contain. Decide quickly between rolling the upstream change back, patching the feature computation to read the new source, or serving without the feature. If the model degrades gracefully with the feature missing, a temporary imputation matching what training saw may be enough; if the null is being mapped to a default such as zero that means something else to the model, fix that first, since a wrong value is worse than a missing one.
Assess the damage. Three places are affected:

Serving for two weeks: quantify the metric loss and who was affected.
Logged features: any training data built from this period contains the broken feature. Mark the range.
Models retrained during the period: they learned from corrupted data and may now depend on the null pattern. Check whether an automatic retrain was promoted.

Repair the data. Backfill the feature for the affected dates from the corrected source if it can be recomputed as of each event’s time; otherwise exclude the range or keep it with an explicit missing indicator. Rebuild downstream tables and retrain from clean data. Backfills must be idempotent and must not overwrite point-in-time correctness.
Prevent.

A null-rate and distribution check on this feature at ingestion and at serving, with an alert that pages its owner. Two weeks of unnoticed decay means input monitoring was missing or ignored.
A data contract with the upstream team, with schema and semantics tests in their deployment pipeline and a registered list of consumers.
A data-validation gate before every retrain.
A feature-importance-weighted view of input health, so that the features that matter get the strict thresholds.

In the retrospective, the question is not who changed the field but why the system allowed a silent change to reach a model.



How would you have detected this on day one?
The backfilled values differ slightly from what was served. Which do you train on?





Design the golden path of an internal ML platform, from a new idea to a model in production. What do you standardise and what do you leave open?


A golden path is the supported, pre-wired way to do the common thing. The aim is that the easiest route is also the correct one, while unusual work remains possible.
The path.

Start: a project template creates a repository with the training entry point, configuration, tests, a container build, CI and a pipeline definition. First run in under an hour.
Develop: the same container locally and remotely; one command submits a job to the shared cluster; data access through a client that records which dataset version was read.
Track: runs are logged automatically with code version, data version, configuration and metrics. No extra code.
Evaluate: a standard report against the current production model and required slices.
Register and deploy: one command or a merge promotes a registered model to a serving template with autoscaling, logging, monitoring and a canary already wired.
Operate: dashboards and alerts exist by default; ownership and on-call are assigned at registration.

Standardise the interfaces and the things that are expensive to get wrong: artefact and metadata formats, lineage, the deployment and rollback mechanism, security defaults, monitoring, cost attribution.
Leave open the modelling: frameworks, architectures, training loops. Provide escape hatches at each layer (bring your own container, your own serving code behind the standard contract), so that the 10% of unusual projects do not have to leave the platform entirely.
Product discipline. Treat teams as customers: interview them, build for the most common painful workflow first, write documentation as part of the feature, keep backwards compatibility, and publish what is and is not supported. A platform that is mandated but worse than the home-grown scripts will be routed around.



Which part would you build first and why?
A research team says the platform slows them down. How do you respond?





How do you measure whether internal ML tooling or a platform is working?


Measure outcomes for the teams that use it, not the platform’s own output.
Flow metrics, adapted from the DORA set to ML:

Lead time: from a merged change, or a new training run, to a model serving production traffic. Also time from project start to first deployed model.
Deployment frequency: model and pipeline releases per team per month.
Change failure rate: share of model releases that are rolled back or cause an incident.
Time to restore: how long a bad model or broken pipeline takes to detect and roll back.

Adoption. Share of production models on the platform; active users; and voluntary adoption, which is the honest signal. Track the escape rate: projects that started on the golden path and left it, with the reason.
Friction. Time to first successful run for a new engineer; queue wait time for compute; CI and build duration; number of manual steps and handoffs in a release; support tickets per user and their categories.
Efficiency. Cluster utilisation, cost per training run or per thousand predictions, and idle resources.
Qualitative. A short regular survey and interviews. Ask what people did the last time they shipped a model and where they waited.
Cautions: counts such as the number of pipelines or experiments are activity, not value, and are easily inflated. Speed metrics must be read together with failure metrics, or teams ship faster by skipping gates. And attribute carefully: compare the same team before and after, or teams on and off the platform, while acknowledging that early adopters differ.
The summary for leadership is one sentence per quarter: how long it takes a team to go from idea to a monitored production model, and how that changed.



Which single metric would you report if you could pick only one?
How would the metrics differ for a platform serving LLM application teams?





Tell me about a time you had to get other teams to adopt a tool, platform or standard you built. What did you do when they resisted?


What the interviewer is testing. Whether you can create leverage beyond your own code: understanding other teams’ incentives, earning adoption instead of demanding it, and staying with the work through migration, which is the unglamorous part.
Structure of a strong answer.

The problem in their terms: what the teams were losing without the standard (incidents, weeks per launch, duplicated work), with a number.
Discovery: whom you talked to and what you learned about why the existing way persisted. Resistance usually has a real reason: migration cost, a missing feature, a deadline, or loss of control.
Design for adoption: a first version aimed at one team’s concrete pain, a migration path that is incremental, compatibility with what they already run, documentation and a working example.
The first adopters: how you picked a team that would benefit and be vocal, did part of the migration work for them and published their result.
Handling resistance: what you changed in response to valid objections, what you declined, and when you escalated or accepted that a team would not migrate.
Outcome: adoption, the metric that moved, and what you would do differently.

Mistakes that sink the answer.

Presenting a mandate from leadership as the adoption strategy.
Describing the teams as wrong or slow, with no account of their reasons.
No measured outcome, or an outcome measured in features shipped.
Stopping the story at launch, with the old system still running in parallel.

Use a real example and be specific about one objection you had not anticipated.



What did you do for the team that had a legitimate reason not to migrate?

Define a Markov decision process and the value functions, and write the Bellman equations. What does the Markov assumption buy you, and what do you do when it does not hold?


An MDP is \((\mathcal S, \mathcal A, P, r, \gamma)\): states, actions, transition kernel \(P(s' \mid s, a)\), reward \(r(s, a)\) and discount \(\gamma \in [0, 1)\). A policy \(\pi(a \mid s)\) induces
\[V^\pi(s) = \mathbb E_\pi\Big[\sum_{t \ge 0} \gamma^t r_t \,\Big|\, s_0 = s\Big], \qquad
Q^\pi(s, a) = r(s, a) + \gamma\, \mathbb E_{s' \sim P}\big[V^\pi(s')\big].\]
Bellman expectation equation: \(V^\pi(s) = \sum_a \pi(a \mid s)\, Q^\pi(s, a)\). Bellman optimality equation:
\[Q^*(s, a) = r(s, a) + \gamma\, \mathbb E_{s'}\big[\max_{a'} Q^*(s', a')\big],\]
and the greedy policy with respect to \(Q^*\) is optimal. The advantage \(A^\pi = Q^\pi - V^\pi\) says how much better an action is than the policy’s average.
The Markov property (the next state and reward depend only on the current state and action) is what makes these recursions valid: the value of a state does not depend on how you got there, so one function of the state is enough and dynamic programming applies.
When the agent sees only an observation, the problem is a POMDP. Practical fixes are to build a state that is closer to Markov: stack recent frames, feed the history to a recurrent or transformer policy, or maintain a belief state. Symptoms of a non-Markov state are a value function that cannot fit and behaviour that oscillates in states that look identical to the agent.



Why must \(\gamma\) be below 1 in a continuing task, and what replaces it in the average-reward setting?
Is a chat conversation with a language model an MDP? What is the state?





Implement value iteration for a tabular MDP in NumPy and return the greedy policy. Why does it converge, and how many iterations do you need?


import numpy as np

def value_iteration(P, R, gamma=0.99, tol=1e-8, max_iter=10_000):
    """P: [S, A, S] transition probabilities, R: [S, A] expected rewards."""
    V = np.zeros(P.shape[0])
    for _ in range(max_iter):
        Q = R + gamma * (P @ V)        # [S, A]
        V_new = Q.max(axis=1)
        done = np.max(np.abs(V_new - V)) < tol
        V = V_new
        if done:
            break
    Q = R + gamma * (P @ V)
    return V, Q.argmax(axis=1)
Convergence: the Bellman optimality operator \(T\) is a \(\gamma\)-contraction in the max norm, \(\lVert TV - TU \rVert_\infty \le \gamma \lVert V - U \rVert_\infty\), so it has a unique fixed point \(V^*\) and \(\lVert V_k - V^* \rVert_\infty \le \gamma^k \lVert V_0 - V^* \rVert_\infty\). Reaching error \(\epsilon\) takes about \(\log(1/\epsilon) / (1 - \gamma)\) sweeps, each costing \(O(S^2 A)\). If successive iterates differ by less than \(\delta\), the result is within \(\gamma \delta / (1 - \gamma)\) of \(V^*\).
What an interviewer checks: the max is over actions and the expectation over next states (not the reverse); terminal states have zero outgoing value; the greedy policy is extracted from \(Q\), not from \(V\) alone. Policy iteration is the alternative: exact evaluation by solving a linear system (\(O(S^3)\)) and then greedy improvement, with far fewer but more expensive iterations.

What is the difference between on-policy and off-policy learning? Use SARSA and Q-learning as the example, and explain the deadly triad.


Both learn \(Q\) by temporal-difference updates; they differ in the target.

SARSA (on-policy): \(Q(s,a) \leftarrow Q(s,a) + \alpha\,[r + \gamma Q(s', a') - Q(s,a)]\) with \(a'\) the action the behaviour policy actually takes next. It learns the value of the policy it is following, exploration included.
Q-learning (off-policy): the target is \(r + \gamma \max_{a'} Q(s', a')\). It learns the value of the greedy policy whatever policy generated the data.

Consequences. Off-policy methods can learn from a replay buffer, from old policies or from another agent’s data, which is why they are sample efficient. On-policy methods need fresh data after every update but optimise the thing they measure. The classic illustration is cliff walking: SARSA with \(\epsilon\)-greedy learns the safer path because it accounts for its own random steps, while Q-learning learns the edge path that is optimal only without exploration.
The deadly triad: function approximation, bootstrapping (targets built from the current estimate) and off-policy data together can make value estimates diverge. Any two are safe in theory. Practical methods keep all three and add stabilisers: target networks, double estimators, replay with limited staleness, and clipped or conservative targets.



Is PPO on-policy? It reuses each batch for several epochs.

Why did deep Q-learning need a replay buffer and a target network, and what does Double DQN fix?


Naive Q-learning with a network regresses \(Q_\theta(s,a)\) onto \(r + \gamma \max_{a'} Q_\theta(s', a')\). Two things break supervised-learning assumptions.

Correlated, non-stationary data. Consecutive transitions are highly correlated and their distribution shifts as the policy changes. A replay buffer samples past transitions uniformly, which decorrelates minibatches and reuses each transition many times.
Moving targets. The target depends on the parameters being updated, so each step chases itself. A target network \(Q_{\bar\theta}\), copied every few thousand steps or updated by Polyak averaging, holds the target fixed for a while.

Overestimation. The max over noisy estimates is biased upward: \(\mathbb E[\max_a \hat Q(s,a)] \ge \max_a \mathbb E[\hat Q(s,a)]\), and bootstrapping propagates the bias. Double DQN decouples selection from evaluation:
\[y = r + \gamma\, Q_{\bar\theta}\big(s', \arg\max_{a'} Q_\theta(s', a')\big).\]
Continuous-control methods use the same idea as clipped double Q (the minimum of two critics).
Details that matter in an implementation: bootstrap with zero only on true termination and not on a time-limit truncation; use a Huber loss or clip gradients because TD errors are heavy-tailed; start learning only after the buffer has some data. Later additions (prioritised replay, dueling heads, n-step targets, distributional values) are incremental on top of these.

Derive the policy gradient. Why can you subtract a baseline, and why does only the reward-to-go multiply each log-probability?


Objective: \(J(\theta) = \mathbb E_{\tau \sim p_\theta}[R(\tau)]\) with \(p_\theta(\tau) = \rho(s_0) \prod_t \pi_\theta(a_t \mid s_t)\, P(s_{t+1} \mid s_t, a_t)\).
Log-derivative trick. \(\nabla_\theta p_\theta = p_\theta \nabla_\theta \log p_\theta\), so
\[\nabla_\theta J = \mathbb E_\tau\big[R(\tau)\, \nabla_\theta \log p_\theta(\tau)\big]
= \mathbb E_\tau\Big[R(\tau) \sum_t \nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(a_t \mid s_t)\Big],\]
because the initial-state and dynamics terms do not depend on \(\theta\). No model of the environment is needed and the reward need not be differentiable.
Causality. An action at time \(t\) cannot affect rewards before \(t\); those terms have zero expectation, so \(R(\tau)\) can be replaced by the reward-to-go \(G_t = \sum_{t' \ge t} \gamma^{t'-t} r_{t'}\).
Baseline. For any \(b(s)\) that does not depend on the action,
\[\mathbb E_{a \sim \pi_\theta}\big[\nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(a \mid s)\, b(s)\big]
= b(s)\, \nabla_\theta \sum_a \pi_\theta(a \mid s) = b(s)\, \nabla_\theta 1 = 0,\]
so subtracting it leaves the gradient unbiased and, with \(b = V^\pi\), cuts variance sharply. The result is
\[\nabla_\theta J = \mathbb E\Big[\sum_t \nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(a_t \mid s_t)\, A^\pi(s_t, a_t)\Big].\]
The estimator is unbiased only for data sampled from the current \(\pi_\theta\), which is why vanilla policy gradient is on-policy and uses each batch once.



What changes in the derivation for a deterministic policy?
Where does the variance come from, and which terms of the estimator reduce it?





What is generalized advantage estimation? Write it down and explain what lambda trades off.


The policy gradient needs an estimate of \(A^\pi(s_t, a_t)\). Two extremes:

Monte Carlo: \(G_t - V(s_t)\). Unbiased, high variance because it sums many random rewards.
One-step TD: \(\delta_t = r_t + \gamma V(s_{t+1}) - V(s_t)\). Low variance, biased whenever \(V\) is wrong.

The \(n\)-step estimator \(\hat A_t^{(n)} = \sum_{l=0}^{n-1} \gamma^l r_{t+l} + \gamma^n V(s_{t+n}) - V(s_t)\) interpolates, and it telescopes into a sum of TD errors, \(\hat A_t^{(n)} = \sum_{l=0}^{n-1} \gamma^l \delta_{t+l}\). GAE is the exponentially weighted average of all of them with weights \((1 - \lambda)\lambda^{n-1}\):
\[\hat A_t^{\mathrm{GAE}(\gamma, \lambda)} = \sum_{l \ge 0} (\gamma \lambda)^l\, \delta_{t+l},
\qquad \hat A_t = \delta_t + \gamma \lambda\, \hat A_{t+1}.\]
\(\lambda = 0\) gives one-step TD and \(\lambda = 1\) gives Monte Carlo with a baseline. Lower \(\lambda\) trusts the critic more: less variance, more bias. Values of 0.9 to 0.97 with \(\gamma\) near 0.99 are the usual starting point. The value target is \(\hat A_t + V(s_t)\).
\(\gamma\) plays a similar role: even in an undiscounted task, using \(\gamma < 1\) in the estimator reduces variance by ignoring far-future rewards at the price of bias.

Implement GAE for a batch of parallel environments in PyTorch, handling episode boundaries. What are the usual bugs?


import torch

@torch.no_grad()
def gae(rewards, values, dones, last_value, gamma=0.99, lam=0.95):
    """rewards, values, dones: [T, N]; last_value: [N] is V(s_T).
    dones[t] = 1 if the episode terminated at step t."""
    T = rewards.shape[0]
    adv = torch.zeros_like(rewards)
    next_adv = torch.zeros_like(last_value)
    next_value = last_value
    for t in reversed(range(T)):
        nonterminal = 1.0 - dones[t]
        delta = rewards[t] + gamma * next_value * nonterminal - values[t]
        next_adv = delta + gamma * lam * nonterminal * next_adv
        adv[t] = next_adv
        next_value = values[t]
    returns = adv + values
    return adv, returns
Pitfalls an interviewer looks for:

Boundary mask. Both the bootstrap value and the running advantage must be zeroed across a termination, otherwise credit leaks between episodes.
Truncation is not termination. If the episode ended on a time limit, the state still has value: bootstrap from \(V\) of the final observation instead of zero. Treating truncation as termination biases values down and matters a lot in long-horizon tasks.
Off-by-one. dones[t] must refer to the transition out of step t; many environment wrappers report it one step later.
Gradients. Advantages and returns are targets, so compute them without gradient.
Normalisation. Advantages are usually standardised per minibatch for the policy loss; returns are not.

Explain the PPO clipped objective and write the loss in PyTorch. Which implementation details decide whether it works?


PPO wants several gradient epochs from each on-policy batch without moving the policy so far that the batch stops being representative. With the ratio \(r_t(\theta) = \pi_\theta(a_t \mid s_t) / \pi_{\text{old}}(a_t \mid s_t)\):
\[L^{\text{CLIP}} = \mathbb E_t\Big[\min\big(r_t \hat A_t,\ \operatorname{clip}(r_t, 1 - \epsilon, 1 + \epsilon)\, \hat A_t\big)\Big].\]
The min makes it a pessimistic bound: the objective gains nothing from pushing the ratio beyond the interval in the direction that helps, but still penalises moves that hurt. It is a first-order stand-in for TRPO’s KL trust region.
def ppo_loss(logp_new, logp_old, adv, values, returns, entropy,
             clip=0.2, vf_coef=0.5, ent_coef=0.01):
    adv = (adv - adv.mean()) / (adv.std() + 1e-8)
    ratio = (logp_new - logp_old).exp()
    surr = torch.min(ratio * adv, ratio.clamp(1 - clip, 1 + clip) * adv)
    policy_loss = -surr.mean()
    value_loss = 0.5 * (values - returns).pow(2).mean()
    loss = policy_loss + vf_coef * value_loss - ent_coef * entropy.mean()
    approx_kl = (logp_old - logp_new).mean()
    return loss, approx_kl
Details that matter as much as the objective: GAE with advantage normalisation; logp_old, advantages and returns fixed during the epochs; stopping the epochs early when the approximate KL exceeds a threshold (around 0.01 to 0.03); learning-rate annealing; gradient clipping; observation and reward normalisation; correct truncation handling. Clipping alone does not bound the KL, so monitor it and the fraction of clipped samples.



The approximate KL spikes after the second epoch. What do you change?

PPO or an off-policy actor-critic such as SAC? How do you choose?


Choose by what is scarce: environment samples or engineering and wall-clock time.
PPO (on-policy). Uses each batch for a few epochs and then discards it. Sample hungry, but simple, robust to hyperparameters, works for discrete and continuous actions, and scales almost linearly with parallel environments. It is the default when a fast simulator exists (thousands of environments on a GPU) and for fine-tuning large policies where stability matters more than sample count.
SAC, TD3, DQN family (off-policy). Reuse every transition many times through a replay buffer, so they need often an order of magnitude fewer environment steps. SAC maximises reward plus entropy, \(J = \mathbb E[\sum_t r_t + \alpha\, \mathcal H(\pi(\cdot \mid s_t))]\), with twin critics and a tuned temperature. The price is the deadly triad: more moving parts, sensitivity to the update-to-data ratio, and value overestimation. They are the default when samples are expensive, as with real robots or slow simulators.
Other deciding factors:

Existing logged or demonstration data can seed an off-policy buffer but not PPO.
Very large or structured action spaces (token sequences) favour policy-gradient methods.
A learned critic for long token sequences is hard, which is one reason language-model RL often uses policy-gradient methods with simple baselines.

How do RL agents explore, and what do you do when the reward is so sparse that random exploration never finds it?


Exploration methods, roughly in order of sophistication:

Undirected noise. \(\epsilon\)-greedy, Boltzmann sampling, Gaussian action noise, or an entropy bonus that keeps a stochastic policy from collapsing. Cheap, and enough when reward is dense.
Optimism. Optimistic initial values, upper confidence bounds, count-based bonuses \(\propto 1/\sqrt{N(s)}\), with pseudo-counts or hashing for large state spaces.
Posterior sampling. Act greedily under a sampled value function (bootstrapped ensembles approximate this); gives temporally consistent exploration.
Intrinsic motivation. Reward prediction error or novelty, for example random network distillation. Prediction-error curiosity is attracted to irreducible noise (the “noisy TV” problem), which is why novelty measured on a fixed random target works better than forward-model error.

When the reward is too sparse for any of these, change the problem rather than the noise:

Demonstrations, to seed the policy or the replay buffer.
A curriculum from easy start states or short horizons, or resets to states near the goal.
Potential-based shaping from a distance or progress measure.
Hindsight relabelling for goal-conditioned tasks.
Hierarchy or skills learned beforehand.

In products the constraint is usually safety and cost, not novelty: exploration is bounded to a small traffic share, to reversible actions, and logged with propensities so that it can be reused offline.

What is offline RL, why does a standard off-policy algorithm fail on a fixed dataset, and what are the main fixes?


Offline RL learns a policy from a fixed log of transitions with no further interaction. It matters wherever exploration is costly or unsafe: recommendation logs, medical or industrial records, robot datasets.
Why naive off-policy learning fails. The Bellman target takes \(\max_{a'} Q(s', a')\) over all actions, including ones the dataset never contains. The network’s values there are arbitrary extrapolations, the max picks the largest errors, and bootstrapping spreads them. Online, the agent would try those actions and be corrected; offline, nothing corrects them. The learned policy then leaves the data distribution.
Families of fixes.

Policy constraint: keep the policy close to the behaviour policy (BCQ, TD3+BC, a KL or behaviour-cloning term).
Value pessimism: push down Q-values for actions outside the data (CQL) or subtract an uncertainty penalty from an ensemble.
In-sample learning: never query unseen actions; IQL fits an expectile of the value from dataset actions only, then extracts a policy by advantage-weighted regression.
Sequence modelling: condition a behaviour-cloning model on the return to go.

What a senior answer adds: how much the result depends on the data. With narrow expert data, behaviour cloning is a strong baseline and often wins; offline RL helps when the data is broad and suboptimal, so that good trajectories can be stitched from parts. Evaluation is the hard part, since off-policy evaluation is itself unreliable; plan a guarded online test.

Your RL agent’s return is flat after many hours of training. How do you debug it?


RL fails silently, so work from the cheapest certainty outwards.

Environment and reward. Step it by hand or with a scripted policy. Can a known good policy get reward? Are observations in a sane range, is the reward scale reasonable (returns of order 1 to 100), are terminations and time limits reported correctly?
A problem the code must solve. Run the same code on a small known task (a classic control problem or a shortened version of your task). If that fails, the bug is in the algorithm code, not in the difficulty of the task.
Diagnostics instead of the return curve.

Policy entropy: collapsed to zero early means premature convergence; never decreasing means the policy is not learning.
Approximate KL and clip fraction per update: zero means the step is too small or advantages are zero; large means the step is too big.
Value explained variance: near zero or negative means the critic is useless, so advantages are noise.
Gradient norms and the advantage distribution.

Usual culprits. Advantages not normalised, observations not normalised, truncation treated as termination, done flags off by one, old log-probabilities recomputed after the update, wrong action scaling or clipping, reward that is too sparse for the exploration used, a learning rate tuned on another task.
Variance. Run at least three to five seeds before concluding anything; one flat seed is common.

Finally, watch episodes. Many “not learning” cases are an agent that learned an unintended behaviour the reward allows.

A team wants to “use RL” for a product decision problem. How do you decide whether RL is the right tool?


Ask what structure the problem really has, and take the simplest formulation that fits.

Supervised learning if the right action is known for past cases, or if the outcome of each action can be predicted and then optimised directly (predict, then choose).
Contextual bandit if you choose an action, see a reward for that action only, and the action does not change what you see next. Most ranking, pricing and notification decisions are treated this way.
Full RL only if actions have delayed consequences through the state: today’s action changes tomorrow’s options. Examples are control, games, multi-step agents, inventory and long-term user value.
A solver if the objective and constraints are known and the uncertainty is small.

What full RL costs: far more data than supervised learning; a simulator or a safe way to explore; a reward that will be exploited wherever it differs from intent; evaluation that requires either online runs or unreliable off-policy estimates; and unstable training with seed variance.
So the bar is: sequential structure that a myopic policy demonstrably loses on, a measurable long-horizon objective, and either a faithful simulator or logged data with enough coverage plus a guarded online test. A strong answer proposes a baseline (a heuristic, a myopic model or a bandit) and states the gap RL would have to close to pay for itself.

Why does behaviour cloning degrade over long horizons, and how does DAgger fix it?


Behaviour cloning is supervised learning of \(\pi(a \mid s)\) on expert state-action pairs. Training states come from the expert’s distribution, but at test time the states come from the learner’s own actions. A small mistake moves the agent to a state the expert rarely visited, where the policy is worse, which causes a larger mistake. This is covariate shift created by the policy itself.
The standard result (Ross and Bagnell): if the policy errs with probability \(\epsilon\) per step on the expert’s distribution, the expected cost over horizon \(T\) can grow as \(O(\epsilon T^2)\), not \(O(\epsilon T)\), because after the first error the agent may be off-distribution for the rest of the episode.
DAgger closes the loop: run the current policy, ask the expert for the correct action in the states the policy visited, aggregate those labels into the dataset and retrain. The training distribution converges to the learner’s own state distribution, and the bound becomes \(O(\epsilon T)\).
Its cost is an expert who can be queried on arbitrary states, which is easy for a scripted or planning expert and awkward for humans. Alternatives that need no queries: inject noise during demonstration collection so the data contains recoveries, augment with synthetic perturbations and corrective labels, predict chunks of actions to shorten the effective horizon, or fine-tune with RL after cloning.

You have a large log of human operators doing a multi-step task and a simulator of medium fidelity. Design the pipeline that turns this into a deployable policy.


1. Data. Segment the log into episodes with outcomes, filter out failed or idle segments, and check coverage: which states and recoveries are present. Split by operator and by time so the evaluation does not leak.
2. Clone first. Train a behaviour-cloning policy. Human data is multimodal (two valid ways to do the same step), and a regression head averages the modes into an invalid action, so use a categorical head over discretised actions, a mixture, or a generative action head. Give the policy enough history to be Markov, but watch for causal confusion: with history the model can learn to copy the previous action instead of reading the observation.
3. Evaluate in closed loop. Held-out action error does not predict task success. Use the simulator for success rate, time to complete and safety violations, with scenario sets for rare cases.
4. Improve past the demonstrations. Fine-tune with RL in the simulator, starting from the cloned policy and keeping a cloning or KL term so the policy stays near human-like behaviour where the simulator is wrong. Randomise simulator parameters to cover the fidelity gap. Use a sparse task reward plus constraints rather than an elaborate shaped reward.
5. Deploy with guards. Shadow mode against operators, then assisted mode with human takeover. Log interventions; they are DAgger labels for the next round.

What is potential-based reward shaping, and why does it leave the optimal policy unchanged?


Shaping adds a term \(F\) to the reward to give the agent denser feedback. Arbitrary shaping changes what is optimal: reward “progress” and the agent may learn to oscillate to collect it repeatedly. Potential-based shaping (Ng, Harada and Russell, 1999) restricts \(F\) to the difference of a potential \(\Phi\) over states:
\[F(s, a, s') = \gamma\, \Phi(s') - \Phi(s).\]
Why it is safe. Along any trajectory the shaping terms telescope:
\[\sum_{t \ge 0} \gamma^t \big(\gamma \Phi(s_{t+1}) - \Phi(s_t)\big) = -\Phi(s_0),\]
assuming the discounted potential vanishes at the end (bounded \(\Phi\) with \(\gamma < 1\), or \(\Phi = 0\) at terminal states). So every policy’s return from \(s_0\) shifts by the same constant. Equivalently \(Q'^*(s, a) = Q^*(s, a) - \Phi(s)\): the shift does not depend on the action, so the \(\arg\max\) is unchanged. The result is also necessary in the sense that, without knowledge of the dynamics, only potential-based shaping guarantees invariance.
What makes a good potential. The ideal is \(\Phi = V^*\), which makes the one-step greedy action optimal; in practice use a rough estimate of progress, such as negative distance to the goal. Any cycle in state space collects zero net shaping, which is exactly what prevents the oscillation exploit.
Caveats: the terminal potential must be zero in episodic tasks, and shaping changes learning speed and exploration, so a bad potential can still slow learning even though the optimum is preserved.

Agents exploit their reward. How do you design a reward, and what process catches specification gaming before it ships?


Treat the reward as a specification that an optimiser will satisfy literally. Wherever it differs from what you want, a strong enough learner finds the difference: collecting a progress bonus in a loop, exploiting a simulator bug, satisfying a test by special-casing it, or maximising a learned judge’s score with text the judge likes rather than a correct answer.
Design principles.

Reward the outcome, not the proxy for it. Prefer a sparse, verifiable task result and add density through potential-based shaping, not through extra terms.
Make constraints explicit as penalties or hard terminations (safety, cost, time), and check that no behaviour earns more by violating them.
Keep the reward bounded and on a known scale; unbounded terms dominate.
If the reward is a learned model, assume it is exploitable: use ensembles, cap its contribution, refresh it on policy outputs and hold out a separate judge for evaluation only.

Process.

Before training, ask what the laziest policy that scores well would do, and red-team the reward on paper.
During training, watch episodes at every checkpoint and track metrics that are not in the reward (task success by an independent check, constraint violations, diversity). Divergence between reward and those metrics is the signal.
Evaluate on held-out tasks and with a grader the policy was never trained against.
Keep the reward function versioned with the run, so a change in behaviour can be traced.
