Design an evaluation platform for LLM products used by many teams.


Clarify. Teams ship prompts, retrieval pipelines, agents and model upgrades. They need to know, before and after release, whether a change is better. Assume 30 teams, suites of about 2,000 cases, and hundreds of evaluation runs per day.
Metrics. For the platform: time from change to trusted result, share of releases gated by an evaluation, agreement between automated graders and humans, agreement between offline results and online outcomes, cost per run.
Data and labels. Versioned datasets with provenance: curated cases, sampled production traces (with privacy filtering), adversarial cases, and regression cases added from incidents. Human labels with a rubric and measured inter-rater agreement. A held-out split per suite that developers do not iterate on.
Architecture.

Evaluation as code: a suite declares dataset version, system under test, graders and aggregation.
Runner: parallel, rate-limited, resumable, with response caching keyed by model, prompt and parameters.
Graders: exact and programmatic checks first; LLM judges with a rubric for open-ended output, each validated against human labels before use and re-validated when the judge model changes; human review queues for samples and disagreements.
Agent evaluation: scoring of final state in a sandboxed environment, plus trajectory checks.
Results store and reports: scores with confidence intervals, per-slice tables, diffs of individual cases between two runs.
Gates: CI blocks a release on a significant regression in a required suite.
Online: sample production traces, run the same graders, alert on drift.

Serving. Statistics determine the size. With \(n=2{,}000\) and a pass rate of 0.8 the standard error is \(\sqrt{0.8\cdot0.2/2000}\approx0.9\) points, so two independent runs must differ by about 2.5 points to be distinguishable; paired comparison on the same cases (a paired bootstrap or McNemar’s test) resolves much smaller differences. Cost: 2,000 cases x 3 samples x 20 configurations is 120k generations per day per team before judging, so caching and a small smoke subset matter.
Evaluation and launch. Evaluate the evaluators: judge-human agreement per suite, and whether offline wins predict online wins on past launches. Start with two or three teams and their real release decisions.
Failure modes and iteration. Judges that prefer longer or same-family outputs, suites overfitted by repeated iteration, contamination of public benchmarks, stale datasets after the product changes, nondeterminism read as regression, gates so noisy that teams bypass them.
What a senior answer adds. Graders treated as models with their own validation, every number reported with uncertainty, an explicit link from offline suites to online metrics, and dataset maintenance treated as ongoing work with an owner.



How do you validate an LLM judge, and what agreement level is enough?
A team’s change shows +1.2 points. Is it real?
How do you stop a suite from being overfitted over six months of use?





Design a multi-tenant LLM inference platform serving several models to internal and external customers.


Clarify. Assume 2,000 requests per second at peak, 1,500 prompt tokens and 300 output tokens on average, a handful of base models plus tenant fine-tunes, interactive and batch traffic. Targets: time to first token under 500 ms at p95, steady streaming speed, 99.9% availability.
Metrics. Time to first token, tokens per second per stream, error and rejection rates per tenant, GPU utilisation, cost per million tokens, fairness between tenants under overload.
Data and labels. Traces of request sizes and arrival patterns per tenant drive capacity planning and load tests. Quality evaluations gate every engine, quantisation or model change.
Architecture.

Gateway: authentication, quotas and rate limits in tokens per minute, request validation, usage metering.
Router: sends requests to a replica that already holds the prompt prefix in cache (session or prefix affinity); spills over when queues grow.
Scheduler in each replica: continuous batching, priority classes (interactive above batch), per-tenant fair queueing, admission control on queued tokens.
Engine: paged KV cache, prefix caching, quantised weights where evaluations allow, LoRA adapters loaded on a shared base model for tenant fine-tunes.
Control plane: model registry, placement, autoscaling on queue time and tokens in flight (GPU utilisation is a poor signal), warm pools because loading 100+ GB of weights takes minutes.

Serving. Demand is 2,000 x 300 = 600k output tokens per second. At an assumed 2,000 output tokens per second per 4-GPU replica of a 70B-class model within the latency target, that is 300 replicas, 1,200 GPUs, about 1,600 with 30% headroom; the per-replica figure must come from load tests. Memory bounds concurrency: with 80 layers and 8 KV heads of dimension 128 in fp16, the cache is \(2\cdot80\cdot8\cdot128\cdot2\) bytes, about 0.33 MB per token, or 2.6 GB for an 8k context. Weights take 140 GB of a 320 GB replica, leaving room for roughly 55 full 8k contexts.
Evaluation and launch. Load tests replaying real traces; canary each engine or model version with automatic rollback on latency or quality regressions; shadow traffic for new quantisation.
Failure modes and iteration. One tenant’s long prompts starving others, retry storms after a brownout (return 429 with retry-after, shed batch load first), cache-affinity hot spots, slow cold starts during a spike, GPU failures, regional outage. Offer a cheaper batch tier to fill off-peak capacity.
What a senior answer adds. Capacity planning in tokens and KV memory rather than requests; isolation and fairness as first-class requirements; cost attribution per tenant; a degradation ladder (shed batch, shorten maximum output, route to a smaller model); and multi-region failover with headroom planned for it.



Why is autoscaling on GPU utilisation misleading for LLM serving?
How do you serve 500 tenant fine-tunes without 500 deployments?
A tenant sends 100k-token prompts. What breaks, and how do you contain it?





Design a fine-tuning and post-training pipeline for a domain model, supervised fine-tuning followed by RL or preference tuning, with evaluation gates.


Clarify. A base model must reach a quality bar on a domain task (assume structured generation with a checkable outcome), at a fixed serving budget, with releases every few weeks. The pipeline must be repeatable by someone who did not build it.
Metrics. A primary task metric from held-out data, an independent quality measure that is not the training reward (human or a separate judge), general-capability and safety regression suites, and behaviour drift from the previous release. Launch criteria are written before training.
Data and labels. Supervised set from curated demonstrations and filtered teacher outputs: deduplicated, split by source and time to prevent leakage, with a manifest of versions and filters. For RL: a prompt set covering the deployment distribution, and a reward. Reward preference order: verifiable outcomes (tests pass, exact match, measured downstream effect), then a learned reward model, then an LLM judge. Preference pairs for DPO come from human or outcome comparisons.
Architecture.

Supervised fine-tuning (full or LoRA), with checkpoint selection on validation.
Gate 1: task metric at or above the incumbent; no regression on general and safety suites; output format valid.
Policy-gradient RL (PPO or GRPO style) or DPO from the gate-1 checkpoint, with a KL or reference-policy constraint, low learning rate, and frequent checkpoints.
Gate 2: reward improves on held-out prompts and the independent measure improves too; drift is bounded; a reward-hacking audit of high-reward samples by reading them.
Registry entry with lineage (data, config, code, parent checkpoint), then shadow and A/B.

Serving. Supervised stage: 200k examples x 1k tokens x 3 epochs is 600M tokens; at an assumed 4k tokens per second per GPU that is about 42 GPU-hours. RL is dominated by rollouts and reward: 2,000 steps x 256 prompts x 8 samples is 4.1M rollouts and 1.2B generated tokens; if a reward call takes 2 seconds, that is about 2,300 hours of reward compute, so it needs around 100-way parallelism to finish in a day. Reward throughput and reliability are designed first.
Evaluation and launch. Compare candidates on the same frozen benchmark, with intervals. Online A/B decides. Keep the incumbent deployable for rollback.
Failure modes and iteration. Reward hacking (length, format tricks, exploiting judge preferences), collapse of output diversity, forgetting of general ability, gains that come from changing how often the model acts and not how well, a reward service outage that corrupts a run, overfitting the benchmark across many checkpoints.
What a senior answer adds. Independence between the training reward and the release metric; gates defined before training; a decomposition of gains into behaviour-rate and per-decision quality; and provenance complete enough to rebuild any released checkpoint.



Reward goes up for 1,000 steps while the independent metric falls. What do you do?
When would you choose DPO over policy-gradient RL here?
How do you choose which RL checkpoint to ship?




Meta, Machine Learning Engineer, Sep 2025: Asynchronous RLHF-style post-training system for a production chat model (PracHub)





Design embedding retrieval over a billion items for semantic search.


Clarify. 1B items, 768-dimensional embeddings, 5k QPS at peak, top 100 results in 50 ms at p99, 10M inserts or updates per day, metadata filters on some queries.
Metrics. ANN recall@100 against exact search on a sample, end-to-end recall against labelled relevance, p50 and p99 latency, cost per query, index freshness (time from write to searchable).
Data and labels. Query-item relevance from clicks and judgments to train and evaluate the encoder; a fixed sample of queries with exact nearest neighbours to measure index recall separately from model quality.
Architecture. Memory decides the index type.

Raw vectors: 1B x 768 x 4 bytes is 3.07 TB. An in-memory HNSW graph adds links (with degree 32, about 256 bytes per vector at the base layer, another 256 GB), so more than 3.3 TB of RAM across the fleet per replica.
IVF with product quantisation: 64-byte codes take 64 GB plus ids. With about 1M inverted lists and 64 probes, a query scans about 64k codes. Recall is lower, so re-score the top 1,000 with full-precision vectors read from SSD.
Graph index on SSD with compressed vectors in memory is the third option, with similar re-scoring.

I would choose compressed vectors in memory with full-precision re-scoring, sharded into 20 shards of 50M, each replicated three times, queried by scatter-gather with a merge of the top results.

Filters: push selective filters into the index (per-partition indexes or filtered search), and fall back to exact search over the subset when the filter matches few items.
Freshness: a small in-memory index for recent writes, merged periodically; deletions by tombstone.

Serving. p99 of a fan-out is governed by the slowest shard, so use hedged requests and per-shard timeouts with partial results. Re-embedding after an encoder upgrade: at an assumed 2,000 items per second per GPU, 1B items take about 140 GPU-hours; build the new index beside the old one and switch atomically, because query and item vectors from different encoder versions are not comparable.
Evaluation and launch. Plot recall against latency for index parameters (probes, re-score depth) and pick the knee. Shadow queries against exact search weekly. A/B the end-to-end effect.
Failure modes and iteration. Recall falling as the data distribution moves away from the trained quantiser, filtered queries with poor recall, shard imbalance, a mixed-version index during migration, tail latency from SSD reads.
What a senior answer adds. Index recall and model recall measured separately; memory and cost arithmetic driving the index choice; a migration plan for encoder upgrades; and hybrid retrieval with lexical search where exact terms matter.



Recall@100 dropped from 0.95 to 0.88 over three months with no code change. Why?
How would shorter or binary embeddings change the design?
A filter matches 0.1% of items. What happens to ANN recall and what do you do?





Design real-time fraud detection for card payments.


Clarify. Assume 100M transactions per day: 1,200 per second on average and 5,000 at peak. A decision is needed inside the authorisation flow; the model has 30 ms of a 100 ms budget. Fraud is about 0.1% of transactions. Actions: approve, step-up authentication, decline, or queue for review.
Metrics. Fraud loss prevented in currency (value-weighted recall), false-decline rate and the revenue it costs, step-up rate, review-queue volume. Offline: precision-recall AUC and recall at fixed false-positive rates, on a later time slice.
Data and labels. Chargebacks arrive weeks to months later, so recent data is partly unlabelled: train with a maturity cut-off and add faster signals (customer reports, analyst decisions). Declined transactions have no outcome, which biases training toward the current policy; approve a small random sample of low-value flagged transactions to learn from. Labels are noisy (“friendly fraud”).
Architecture.

Features: velocity counts and sums over windows (1 minute to 30 days) per card, device, IP address and merchant; deviation from the cardholder’s history; device and network signals; graph features such as cards sharing a device. Streaming aggregates are written to an online store; all features are computed point-in-time for training.
Model: gradient-boosted trees as the main scorer, with sequence or graph embeddings as inputs when they earn their latency.
Rules engine in parallel: hard policy, and fast response to a new attack before the model is retrained.
Decision: thresholds from expected cost, \(p\cdot L_{\text{fraud}}\) against \((1-p)\cdot L_{\text{decline}}\), with a middle band sent to step-up authentication.

Serving. 100k fraudulent transactions per day. If 200 analysts review 150 cases each, capacity is 30k per day, 0.03% of volume, so nearly every decision is automatic. Flagging 0.5% of transactions (500k per day) at 60% recall catches 60k frauds at 12% precision: 440k legitimate customers affected, which is why the middle band gets a step-up and not a decline. Feature reads under 5 ms, model under 10 ms; on a feature-store timeout, fall back to rules and a model without streaming features.
Evaluation and launch. Backtest on time-ordered data, shadow-score live traffic, then ramp with a control group. Monitor score distributions, feature freshness and approval rates per segment.
Failure modes and iteration. Adversaries adapt within days, so retrain frequently and watch for new clusters among false negatives. Feedback loops from blocked transactions, merchant outages that look like attacks, regional and segment disparities in false declines, feature pipeline lag.
What a senior answer adds. Decisions framed as costs with three actions; label delay and selection bias handled explicitly; review capacity as a design constraint; and a fallback that keeps payments flowing when a component fails.



How do you evaluate a new model when the old model’s declines hide the outcomes?
A new attack pattern appears at 2 a.m. What in your design responds, and how fast?
How do you set thresholds differently for a 5-unit and a 5,000-unit transaction?




Google, Machine Learning Engineer, Jan 2026: Fraud detection system (PracHub)
TikTok, Data Scientist, Jul 2025: Real-time card fraud detection (PracHub)





Design a content moderation system for a platform with text, image and video uploads.


Clarify. Assume 500M items per day, about 5,800 per second, of which 100M are videos. Policies cover many categories with different severity; the most severe must be blocked before publication, others can be actioned after. Policies change and differ by region.
Metrics. Prevalence: the share of views that land on violating content, estimated by random sampling and human labelling. Precision of enforcement (appeal overturn rate), recall on the sampled set, time to action weighted by views, reviewer workload and exposure. Report per category and language.
Data and labels. Reviewer decisions with quality control (golden items, double review, agreement tracking), user reports (noisy and skewed toward visible content), appeals, and random samples for unbiased measurement. Policy changes require relabelling; version labels by policy.
Architecture.

Hash matching against known illegal or previously removed media, before publication.
Fast per-modality classifiers at upload (text, sampled frames, audio transcript) with category scores.
A heavier multimodal model for uncertain or high-reach items; an LLM reading the policy text handles new or nuanced policies and produces labels to distil into the fast tier.
Decision: automatic action above a high-precision threshold per category, a human queue for the uncertain band, no action below.
Review queues ordered by severity, predicted reach and uncertainty; specialised queues by language and category.
Enforcement options: remove, restrict distribution, age-gate, label; appeals feed back as labels.
Re-scoring when an item gains reach or reports.

Serving. Review capacity fixes the thresholds: 2,000 reviewers at 600 items per day is 1.2M per day, 0.24% of volume. If 0.5% of uploads violate (2.5M per day), automation must take most clear cases. Video cost: 100M videos x 30 sampled frames is 3B frames per day, 35k per second; at an assumed 1,000 frames per second per GPU the fast tier needs about 35 GPUs on average and about 100 at peak. A model 100 times heavier on everything would need thousands, so the cascade sends it only a few percent.
Evaluation and launch. Per-category precision and recall on fresh random samples, shadow mode for new models, staged thresholds, measurement by language and dialect.
Failure modes and iteration. Adversarial evasion (obfuscated text, altered media), drift with news events, disparate error rates across dialects and languages, context-dependent content (news, satire, counter-speech), reviewer inconsistency, over-enforcement that silences legitimate users.
What a senior answer adds. Prevalence as the goal metric, thresholds derived from review capacity and severity, a path for new policies in days, and reviewer wellbeing and appeals treated as parts of the system.



How do you measure recall when you cannot label everything?
A new policy takes effect next week and there are no labels. What do you do?
How do you handle a live stream as opposed to an upload?




Meta, Machine Learning Engineer, Feb 2026: Image copyright-violation detection (PracHub)
Meta, Machine Learning Engineer, Dec 2025: Detect weapon-selling ads in posts using several modalities (PracHub)
Meta, Machine Learning Engineer, Jan 2026: Weapon-sale ad detection system (PracHub)
Meta, Machine Learning Engineer, Nov 2025: Harmful-content text classifier (PracHub)





Design a distributed training platform for large models on a shared GPU cluster.


Clarify. Assume 10,000 GPUs shared by 50 teams. Workloads: a few pretraining runs on 1,000+ GPUs for weeks, many fine-tuning jobs on 8 to 64 GPUs for hours, and interactive or evaluation jobs on 1 to 8. Goals: high utilisation, predictable access for priority work, fast iteration for small jobs.
Metrics. Allocated and used GPU-hours over capacity, queue wait by job class, preemption rate and work lost, job failure rate by cause, time from submission to first training step, cost attributed per team.
Data and labels. Scheduler events, per-job GPU utilisation and throughput, hardware health telemetry. These feed capacity planning and idle-job detection.
Architecture.

Submission API: container image, resources, priority class, checkpoint policy. The same environment works on 1 GPU and 1,000.
Scheduler: per-team quotas with borrowing of idle capacity; borrowed capacity is preemptible. Gang scheduling so that a multi-node job gets all nodes or none. Topology-aware placement on the same high-speed network fabric. Backfill of small jobs around reservations, and reservations so that large jobs are not starved by fragmentation.
Runtime: launchers for data-parallel and sharded training, health checks, automatic restart from the last checkpoint, node draining on hardware errors.
Storage: datasets on a parallel file system or object store with local NVMe caching; sharded parallel checkpoint writes.
Observability: per-job dashboards, idle-GPU alerts, experiment tracking integration.

Serving. Failures set the checkpoint policy. If a node fails once per 1,000 hours on average (an assumption), a 256-node job sees a failure about every 4 hours. With a 2-minute checkpoint, Young’s approximation gives an interval of \(\sqrt{2\cdot 2\cdot 240}\approx 31\) minutes. A 70B-parameter model with Adam state in fp32 is \(3\cdot70\text{B}\cdot4\) bytes, about 840 GB per checkpoint, so writes must be parallel and retention pruned. At an assumed internal cost of USD 2 per GPU-hour, the cluster costs about USD 175M per year, and each point of idle capacity about USD 1.75M.
Evaluation and launch. Replay historical job traces through scheduler policies in simulation before changing them. Migrate team by team. Track wait-time percentiles per class after each change.
Failure modes and iteration. Fragmentation that blocks large jobs while GPUs sit idle, jobs holding GPUs at low utilisation, preemption storms, a slow data loader starving expensive GPUs, silent data corruption or a faulty GPU producing NaNs, checkpoint corruption, one noisy job saturating shared storage.
What a senior answer adds. Quota and priority policy treated as an organisational decision that the scheduler encodes; fragmentation and preemption cost measured; checkpoint economics derived from failure rates; and efficiency (useful work per GPU-hour) tracked alongside utilisation.



A 2,000-GPU job is waiting while 2,500 GPUs are free. Explain how, and fix it.
How do you decide which job to preempt?
How do you detect and handle a job that has hung without crashing?





Design a feature store and real-time ML platform that many teams use for training and online inference.


Clarify. Assume 500 models, 20,000 features, 500M users and 10M items. The largest consumer is a ranking service at 50k requests per second scoring 500 candidates each, with 10 ms for feature retrieval. Features range from daily batch aggregates to counters fresh within seconds.
Metrics. Online read latency at p99, feature freshness against its target, training-serving skew rate, share of features reused by more than one model, time to ship a new feature, incidents caused by feature changes.
Data and labels. Sources are event streams and warehouse tables. Every feature value carries an entity key and an event timestamp. Labels are joined to features as of the prediction time.
Architecture.

Registry: one definition per feature (source, transformation, entity, owner, freshness target, sensitivity), versioned.
Computation: the same definition compiles to a batch job for backfill and a streaming job for online updates; windowed aggregates handle late events with watermarks.
Offline store: columnar tables with history, and point-in-time joins that return, for each training row, the latest value before its timestamp. This is what prevents label leakage.
Online store: a key-value store holding the latest values per entity, grouped so that one read returns a feature group.
Serving logs: log the feature vectors used at inference and train from those logs where possible, the strongest protection against skew.
Monitoring: null rates, distributions, staleness, and offline-online comparison on sampled keys.
Platform services on top: deployment with shadow and canary, and model monitoring.

Serving. Reading item features one by one would mean 50k x 500 = 25M reads per second. Instead, item features (10M x 1 KB is 10 GB) are replicated into ranking-service memory and refreshed from a stream, and the request makes one or two user-keyed reads. The user store is 500M x 2 KB, 1 TB, 3 TB with three replicas. Hot keys and tail latency are handled with caching and request hedging.
Evaluation and launch. Validate a new feature by backfilling, comparing the online and offline values on sampled keys, and measuring model lift in an A/B test. Migrate models gradually, with dual reads during the transition.
Failure modes and iteration. Stream lag serving stale counters (expose age and default safely past a time-to-live), a definition changed in place breaking downstream models (versions are immutable), backfills that use future data, expensive unused features (track consumers and deprecate), sensitive attributes reaching models that must not use them.
What a senior answer adds. Point-in-time correctness and skew as the central problems; read-path arithmetic driving the storage layout; ownership, versioning and deprecation as product features; and freshness tiers priced so that teams choose real time only when it pays.



How do you implement a point-in-time join efficiently at this scale?
A streaming feature is 20 minutes stale during an incident. What should the model see?
When is logging served features better than recomputing them offline, and when is it not?





Design the data engine for a perception system in autonomous driving: long-tail mining, auto-labelling and closed-loop evaluation.


Clarify. A fleet of 1,000 vehicles with cameras, lidar and radar. Perception already works on common scenes; failures concentrate in rare ones. The engine’s job is to find failures, turn them into labelled data, retrain, and prove the new model is better without regressions.
Metrics. For the loop: days from a discovered failure to a deployed fix, labelled examples per unit cost, auto-label agreement with gold labels. For the model: detection and tracking metrics by class, range and scenario slice; a fixed regression suite; closed-loop safety measures (collisions, near misses, hard braking) in simulation; intervention rate on the road.
Data and labels. If each vehicle logs on the order of 1 TB per driving day, the fleet produces about 1 PB per day, so only selected snippets can be uploaded and kept. Human 3D labelling at about 5 minutes per frame makes 1M frames cost 83,000 hours, about 42 person-years, so humans verify and correct, and machines label.
Architecture.

Triggers on the vehicle and offline: driver interventions, disagreement between the onboard model and a larger offline model, disagreement between sensors, tracking inconsistencies, high uncertainty, rare-class detections.
Mining: embed all retained scenes; given a few failure examples, retrieve similar scenes across the fleet by embedding or text query.
Auto-labelling: a large offline model that uses past and future frames, multi-sweep aggregation and track smoothing, which the onboard model cannot. Human review of a sample and of low-confidence labels; gold sets to measure label quality.
Dataset builder: versioned datasets, balanced so that mined rare cases do not distort priors; splits by drive, location and date to prevent near-duplicate leakage.
Training and evaluation: slice metrics, the regression suite, then simulation.
Deployment: shadow mode on the fleet, comparing outputs without acting, then staged rollout.

Serving. Onboard compute and latency are fixed, so offline models are distilled into the deployed one. Triggers must be cheap enough to run on the vehicle, and upload is limited by depot bandwidth, which sets the retention rate.
Evaluation and launch. Open-loop replay scores perception against labels but other agents do not react to changed behaviour. Closed-loop simulation with reactive agents and realistic sensor input measures downstream driving effect, and is itself validated against road data. Release requires no regression on any safety-critical slice.
Failure modes and iteration. The student inheriting the auto-labeller’s errors, mined data shifting class priors and calibration, evaluation scenes that are near-duplicates of training scenes, improvements on mined slices with regressions elsewhere, a simulation gap that hides real failures.
What a senior answer adds. Loop time as the metric to optimise; label economics driving the automation design; evaluation by scenario slice with leakage-safe splits; and the limits of open-loop metrics and of simulation stated plainly.



How do you find examples of a failure you have seen only three times?
How do you measure auto-label quality without labelling everything by hand?
A new model is better on average and worse on one rare slice. Do you ship it?





Design nearby place recommendations for a mobile app: when a user opens the app, show places around them that they are likely to visit. Follow-up: the same system also decides when to send a notification about a nearby place.


Clarify. Assume 100M places worldwide, 500M daily users, 20k requests per second at peak and a 200 ms budget. The surface is a ranked list of about 20 places with no query. Ask what counts as success (a tap, a save, a visit), whether the user is at home or travelling, and what location precision and consent exist.
Metrics. Online: place actions per session (directions, save, call, booking), confirmed visits where consent allows, hides and “not interested”, and retention as the guardrail. Offline: recall@k for retrieval, NDCG for ranking, calibration of the predicted action rates, all sliced by density (city centre against rural), by home against travel, and by new against established places.
Data and labels. Positives are graded: visit > directions or booking > save > tap. Negatives are impressions without action, corrected for position. A visit label comes from location pings matched to a place footprint, which is noisy in malls and tower blocks, so treat it as a probability and not a fact. Log the candidate set and the user’s location cell at request time, so training sees what serving saw.
Architecture.

Geo retrieval. Index places by a hierarchical cell id (S2 or H3). Take the user’s cell and rings of neighbours, widening until there are about 2,000 candidates: the radius must adapt, because 1 km holds thousands of places in a city centre and none in the countryside. Filter by open-now and by category policy.
Personalised retrieval inside the geo candidate set: a two-tower model scoring user against place embeddings, plus sources for popular-nearby, places similar to ones the user saved, and places friends visited if the product has a graph.
Ranking. A multi-task model that predicts tap, save, directions and visit. Features: distance and estimated travel time, user-category affinity, time of day and day of week, place quality (rating, review count, recency), price level, popularity at this hour, weather, and whether the user is far from their usual area. Distance sensitivity differs by category (people travel further for a restaurant than for a coffee), so let distance interact with category.
Re-ranking for category diversity and for exploration slots given to new places.

Serving. The place index is small enough for memory: 100M places with 200 bytes of metadata and a 64-dimension float embedding (256 bytes) is about 46 GB, sharded by region. Scoring 2,000 candidates with a light first-stage model and 200 with the full model fits the budget. Cache the non-personalised parts by coarse cell and hour.
Notifications. This is a different decision: not which place is best, but whether interrupting now is worth it. Score the incremental value of sending (uplift against not sending), subtract a cost for fatigue, enforce a per-user budget and quiet hours, and trigger on events such as arriving somewhere new at mealtime. The guardrails are the rate of notification opt-outs and uninstalls, measured against a long-term holdout that receives none.
Evaluation and launch. Offline replay, then an A/B test by user, read by slice. A visit lags the impression by hours or days, so fix the attribution window before the test starts.
Failure modes and iteration.

Popularity feedback: shown places get the actions that get them shown. Use exploration and position-debiased training.
New places have no history: use content features (category, photos, menu text) and a boost with a decay.
Stale place data: closed businesses and wrong opening hours do more damage than a weak ranker.
Privacy: location history is sensitive. Coarsen what is stored, limit retention, exclude sensitive categories such as clinics and places of worship from inference and from notifications.

What a senior answer adds. Density-adaptive retrieval instead of a fixed radius; the choice of label and its noise as the main modelling decision; notifications framed as an uplift problem with a budget; and privacy treated as a design constraint from the first minute.



A user lands in a city they have never visited. What changes in retrieval and in ranking?
Visits rise 3% and notification opt-outs rise 10%. Do you launch?
How do you tell a real visit from someone walking past the door?




Meta, Machine Learning Engineer, Jan 2026: Real-time nearby-place and notification ranking (PracHub)
Meta, Machine Learning Engineer, Jan 2026: Location recommendation system (PracHub)
Meta, Machine Learning Engineer, Mar 2026: Place recommendation for a maps or local-discovery product (PracHub)
Meta, Machine Learning Engineer, Sep 2025: Real-time nearby place recommendations for a mobile app (PracHub)





You have 10 billion unlabelled images and a labelled dataset of 50 million. Design a system that finds the images in the large corpus that are novel relative to the labelled set, so they can be labelled and added.


Clarify. Novel for what purpose? Here: content the current dataset does not cover, so that a model trained on it fails there. That makes novelty relative to a reference set and to a model, not an absolute property. Ask about the labelling budget (assume 1M images), and about licences and privacy in the corpus.
Metrics. Precision: the share of mined groups that reviewers accept as new and useful. Recall, by a planted test: remove some known classes from the reference set, run the system, and count how many it recovers. Downstream: accuracy gain on target slices per 1,000 labels, compared with labelling a random sample.
Architecture.

Clean first. Remove corrupt and blank files, then duplicates: exact hash, perceptual hash, then near-duplicates by embedding. Without this, the outliers found are mostly junk and the largest “new clusters” are copies of one image.
Embed every image with a general self-supervised or image-text encoder, and with the task model’s own features. Two views matter, because an encoder maps content unlike its training data onto familiar regions.
Score against the reference. Build an approximate nearest-neighbour index over the 50M labelled embeddings; an image’s score is the distance to its k-th nearest labelled neighbour. Add model signals: low confidence, or disagreement between the task model and a larger model.
Separate new modes from singletons. Take the top few percent by score and cluster them. A point far from the reference with many corpus neighbours is a new mode, which is what you want. A point far from everything is usually noise.
Review by cluster. Show reviewers 20 samples per cluster; they name it and accept or reject it. One decision covers thousands of images, which is what makes a 1M-label budget go far.
Select and iterate. From accepted clusters choose a diverse subset (farthest-point or k-centre selection), label it, add it to the reference, and rerun: what was novel is now covered.

Scale. At 2,000 images per second per GPU, embedding 10B images takes 5M GPU-seconds, about 1,400 GPU-hours, so 60 GPUs finish in a day. Decoding and storage reads usually limit throughput before the GPU does. 512-dimension float16 embeddings take 10 TB; product quantisation to 64 bytes takes 640 GB. The index is over the 50M reference set, not the 10B corpus, so scoring is 10B cheap queries that parallelise by shard.
Evaluation and launch. Run the planted-class test before trusting any ranking. Then pilot on 1% of the corpus, measure reviewer acceptance per cluster, and compare the downstream gain with a random-sample baseline at equal label cost.
Failure modes and iteration.

Novelty that is irrelevant to the task (a new watermark style, a new aspect ratio). Reviewer rejections become negatives for a learned relevance filter.
Cluster granularity: too coarse hides a rare class inside a common one, too fine floods reviewers.
Unsafe or private content surfacing in review, since outliers concentrate it. Run safety filters first and protect reviewers.
Adding many rare images shifts class priors; reweight or keep the evaluation distribution fixed.

What a senior answer adds. Novelty defined relative to the reference and the purpose; duplicates and junk handled before any modelling; the mode-versus-singleton distinction; review economics at cluster level; and a planted-class test that makes recall measurable.



Your encoder was trained on data like the labelled set. Why is that a problem, and what do you do about it?
How do you choose the number of clusters when you do not know how many new concepts exist?
After three rounds the system returns almost nothing new. How do you know whether the corpus is exhausted or the method is blind?




OpenAI, Machine Learning Engineer, Apr 2026: Mine novel images from a massive unlabelled corpus (PracHub)





Design a text-to-video generation service: a user submits a prompt and receives a short video minutes later. The model is given. Cover the request path, the GPU fleet and its scheduling, storage and delivery, safety, and what happens under overload.


Clarify. Assume 1M videos per day, clips of 10 seconds, and 2 GPU-minutes per clip on one GPU. Generation takes minutes, so the product is asynchronous: submit, watch progress, get notified. Ask about tiers (free and paid), maximum length and resolution, and whether a failed job is retried or refunded.
Metrics. Time from submit to first frame and to finished video (p50 and p95, by tier), job success rate, GPU utilisation, cost per video, queue age, share of outputs blocked by safety checks, and user actions on the result (download, regenerate) as a quality proxy.
Capacity. 1M x 2 GPU-minutes is 2M GPU-minutes per day, about 1,400 GPUs running flat out. With a peak of twice the average and a 70% utilisation target, about 4,000. Output at 10 MB per clip is 10 TB per day.
Request path.

API: authenticate, check quota, run the prompt safety check, write a job record (id, user, parameters, state) to a durable store, enqueue, return the job id. An idempotency key makes a client retry safe.
Queue: durable, with one logical queue per priority class. The job record is the source of truth; the queue is a hint.
Workers: each holds the model in GPU memory, leases a job with a visibility timeout, heartbeats, writes progress, uploads the result to object storage and marks the job done. A worker that dies lets the lease expire and the job is picked up again; the output key is derived from the job id, so a duplicate run overwrites and does not double-charge.
Post-processing: encode to streaming renditions, make a thumbnail, run output safety checks on sampled frames, add provenance metadata or a watermark, then publish through a CDN with signed URLs.
Status: the client polls or holds a server-sent event stream; preview frames from intermediate steps make a long wait tolerable.

Scheduling the fleet.

Model load takes minutes, so keep workers warm and scale on queue age and backlog in GPU-minutes, not on GPU utilisation, which is always high.
Priority classes with weighted fair queuing across users, so one user’s 500 jobs do not starve the rest. Paid work can preempt free work at a checkpoint between denoising steps.
Job cost varies by length and resolution. Admit by estimated GPU-minutes, and pack short jobs into batches where the model allows it.
Buy the base load reserved, the peak on demand, and run the free tier on preemptible capacity with resumable jobs.

Overload. Decide in advance: reject at admission with a clear wait estimate, degrade (shorter clip, lower resolution, fewer steps) for the free tier first, and never accept work that cannot finish within its promise. A queue with no bound converts overload into timeouts for everyone.
Safety. Check the prompt before spending GPU time and the output before release; treat likenesses of real people and minors as separate policies; rate-limit by account and device; keep an audit trail linking output to request.
Failure modes and iteration. Poison jobs that crash every worker (cap retries, quarantine), a new model version changing the output for a retried job (pin the version in the job record), stuck jobs with live heartbeats (a deadline per job), hot-spotting when every worker reloads weights at once, and storage growth (retention by tier).
What a senior answer adds. The arithmetic from demand to GPUs; idempotent, resumable jobs; autoscaling on backlog measured in work, not requests; and an explicit overload policy by tier.



A deploy of new weights must not drop in-flight jobs. How do you roll it out?
GPU utilisation is 95% and p95 completion time doubled. What do you look at first?
How would the design change if generation took 5 seconds instead of 2 minutes?




OpenAI, Software Engineer, May 2026: Text-to-video generation system (PracHub)
OpenAI, Software Engineer, Jul 2026: Asynchronous video generation service with GPU fleet scheduling (PracHub)
OpenAI, Software Engineer, Jun 2026: Text-to-video platform around a large model (PracHub)

title: Preparation plan
text: The plan follows two facts from the report: the three tracks ask for different skills, and interview loops test a narrower set than postings list. Pick the track you are applying to, work the areas in its order, and let the review app decide what to revisit.

title: Preparation plan
text:
The daily loop

Review, 30 to 40 minutes. Open Review, set your track, and clear what is due plus the day’s new cards. Answer out loud before revealing. Grade honestly: “Good” only if you would have said it in an interview.
One design case every second day. Take a case from Design cases, give yourself 35 minutes on paper, then compare with the answer and its follow-ups.
Coding, 45 minutes. Two problems in the patterns listed in Software engineering, or one ML-coding problem from Deep learning written from a blank file.
One story a day in the last two weeks. Write one behavioural story against the prompts in Senior scope and say it in under three minutes.

The Progress tab of the review app shows a readiness figure per track: the share of cards you know, weighted by how often that track’s postings name each skill. It also lists the highest-demand skills you have not yet covered, with a button to drill each one. Use that list, not this page, once you have started.

title: Positional Encoding
text:
Self-attention alone is permutation-equivariant: permuting the input tokens permutes the outputs in the same way. The attention score \(q_i^T k_j\) contains content similarity, but it does not inherently say whether token \(j\) comes before or after token \(i\), or how far apart they are.
This statement needs one qualification: a causal mask is itself tied to sequence order. Although it does not attach an explicit coordinate to a token, it gives different positions different visible prefixes. This asymmetry is what makes NoPE possible in decoder-only Transformers.
Position information can be introduced by:

adding a position-dependent vector to each token representation
modifying attention scores with a position-dependent bias
transforming queries and keys as a function of their positions


Learning prompt: Precisely distinguish permutation equivariance from permutation invariance. Which one describes self-attention?

title: Positional Encoding
text:
NoPE: No Explicit Positional Encoding
NoPE removes the explicit positional mechanism entirely:
\[
x_i=E_{\text{token}}[w_i],
\qquad
S_{ij}=\frac{q_i^T k_j}{\sqrt{d_h}}.
\]
There is no additive position embedding, relative-position bias, or RoPE rotation. A decoder still applies its causal mask:
\[
\widetilde S_{ij}
=
\begin{cases}
S_{ij}, & j\le i,\\
-\infty, & j>i.
\end{cases}
\]
Thus the visible set at position \(i\) is the prefix \(\{1,\ldots,i\}\). Position is not supplied as a feature; it can emerge from the structure of the computation.

How can order emerge from only a causal mask?
At layer \(\ell\), position \(i\) aggregates representations only from its prefix:
\[
h_i^{(\ell+1)}
=
F\!\left(
h_i^{(\ell)},
\left\{h_j^{(\ell)}:j\le i\right\}
\right).
\]
Each earlier representation already summarizes a different nested prefix. Consequently, a multi-layer model can distinguish orders that one content-only attention layer cannot.
Consider A B C and B A C. At C, a first layer sees the same multiset {A, B, C} in either sequence, so its direct content aggregation can be the same. But the earlier states differ:
A B C:  h_A sees {A};    h_B sees {A, B}
B A C:  h_B sees {B};    h_A sees {B, A}
At the next layer, C attends to these already contextualized states and can distinguish the two orders. This is why the depth qualification matters: causal connectivity can carry order through the network even though the token embeddings contain no position.
The model may also infer approximate absolute position from signals correlated with prefix length, such as its number of predecessors, special anchor tokens, or changes in attention-output statistics. Probing experiments find recoverable absolute-position information in trained NoPE models. However, the causal mask does not hand the model an exact integer \(i\); learning a useful coordinate is an emergent behavior, not a guaranteed primitive.


What the causal mask does and does not provide







Property
Causal NoPE




Which tokens are in the past?
supplied by the triangular connectivity pattern


Exact absolute index \(i\)
not supplied explicitly; may be inferred


Exact distance \(i-j\)
not supplied explicitly; may be represented by deeper computation


Order sensitivity
possible in multi-layer autoregressive Transformers


Bidirectional encoder order
not recovered from a full, symmetric attention mask alone


Extra position parameters or rotations
none



So the answer to “does causal masking fully encode position?” is no. It breaks permutation symmetry and exposes an ordered prefix structure from which the model can learn position. That is weaker and less direct than providing an absolute or relative coordinate.


Minimal implementation
NoPE is implemented mostly by omission: do not add a position table and do not transform \(Q\) or \(K\).
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F


def nope_attention(q: torch.Tensor,
                   k: torch.Tensor,
                   v: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
    """Causal NoPE attention for q, k, v shaped (B, H, T, D)."""
    return F.scaled_dot_product_attention(
        q, k, v,
        attn_mask=None,
        is_causal=True,
    )
KV caching still works. Cached keys need no position-dependent rotation, but the harness or attention kernel must still know which cached tokens precede the new query so it can enforce causality.


Why use or avoid NoPE?







Potential advantage
Potential limitation




no position parameters or rotation cost
weaker positional inductive bias


no learned position table with a fixed maximum index
training must discover useful order and distance features


no RoPE frequencies that move out of their training regime
exact position-sensitive tasks may be harder


strong length generalization on some reasoning tasks
results are architecture- and task-dependent


especially natural for causal decoders
not a direct solution for bidirectional attention



Haviv et al. (2022) found that causal language models without explicit positional encodings can be competitive and develop probe-decodable absolute position. In controlled reasoning experiments, Kazemnejad et al. (2023) found that NoPE generalized to longer sequences better than several explicit alternatives. These findings establish possibility, not a universal claim that NoPE always beats RoPE or relative bias.


Recent update: frontier models use hybrid NoPE
The important production shift is not that frontier models have universally removed positional encoding from every layer. The clearer 2025–2026 trend is to give different layer types different positional roles. One important form interleaves RoPE and NoPE layers:
\[
\operatorname{Attn}_{\ell}
=
\begin{cases}
\operatorname{LocalAttn}(R_iq_i,R_jk_j,V),
& \ell\notin\mathcal L_{\text{NoPE}},\\
\operatorname{GlobalAttn}(Q,K,V),
& \ell\in\mathcal L_{\text{NoPE}}.
\end{cases}
\]
This is a division of labor:

local RoPE layers provide a strong inductive bias for nearby order and relative distance
global NoPE layers communicate across the full context without applying a position-dependent rotation outside its familiar training regime
depth lets the global layer operate on token states that have already acquired local order information from earlier RoPE layers

A second form replaces the local RoPE layers with an ordered recurrent or linear-attention mechanism. The recurrence itself is position-sensitive, so global full-attention layers can use NoPE without making the entire network permutation-invariant. Kimi K3 is the frontier-scale example below.






flowchart LR
    X[Token states] --> R1[Local RoPE]
    R1 --> R2[Local RoPE]
    R2 --> R3[Local RoPE]
    R3 --> N[Global NoPE]
    N --> Y[Repeat the block]






This hybrid is easier to understand as two communication scales than as a vote over which positional encoding is universally best. RoPE answers “where is this token relative to nearby tokens?” Global NoPE answers “which content anywhere in the prefix is relevant?”

Llama 4: iRoPE
Meta calls Llama 4’s design iRoPE, for interleaved RoPE and NoPE. Meta states that most layers retain RoPE while some attention layers omit positional embeddings to improve length generalization. The released reference implementation marks every fourth layer as NoPE; those layers use global causal attention, while the intervening RoPE layers use chunked attention.
For an interval \(r=4\),
\[
\mathcal L_{\text{NoPE}}
=
\{\ell:(\ell+1)\bmod 4=0\}.
\]
Thus “Llama 4 uses NoPE” does not mean all of its attention is position-free: the repeating pattern is three RoPE layers followed by one NoPE layer. See Meta’s Llama 4 architecture announcement and its is_nope_layer implementation.


Apple foundation models
Apple’s 2025 foundation models also interleave sliding-window local attention with RoPE and global attention without positional embeddings. Apple reports this choice as improving length generalization while maintaining long-context model quality. See the Apple Intelligence Foundation Language Models report.
This is stronger evidence of an architectural pattern than one isolated model: two frontier-scale model families independently assign explicit position to local communication and NoPE to global communication.


Kimi K3: NoPE global attention after recurrent position mixing
Kimi K3 makes the more substantial switch that motivates much of the recent NoPE discussion. Kimi K2 and K2.5 used MLA with RoPE, whereas Kimi K3 applies NoPE to every global Gated MLA layer. Its repeating block contains three Kimi Delta Attention (KDA) layers followed by one global Gated MLA layer:
\[
\underbrace{\operatorname{KDA}
\rightarrow \operatorname{KDA}
\rightarrow \operatorname{KDA}}_{\text{ordered recurrent mixing}}
\rightarrow
\underbrace{\operatorname{GatedMLA}_{\text{NoPE}}}_{\text{global content routing}}.
\]
This does not mean that Kimi K3 has no notion of position. KDA updates a recurrent state in token order and uses learned, channel-wise decay, making its mixing both position-sensitive and recency-aware. The later NoPE MLA layer can therefore globally retrieve representations that already contain order. No RoPE frequency needs to be retuned when the context is extended.
This is a useful generalization of the Llama 4 pattern:







Local or recurrent path
Global path




Llama 4: local attention with explicit RoPE
full attention with NoPE


Kimi K3: KDA recurrence with implicit, learned positional dynamics
Gated MLA with NoPE



See the Kimi K3 technical report, especially Sections 2.1 and 3.4.


SmolLM3: an open, reproducible example
Hugging Face’s 3B SmolLM3 is not frontier-scale, but it provides unusually open ablation evidence and a practical implementation. It removes RoPE from every fourth layer and reports improved long-context behavior without hurting short-context results. Its remaining RoPE layers still use YaRN and adjusted RoPE frequencies for context extension. Therefore the model is another hybrid RoPE–NoPE design, not a pure NoPE model. See the SmolLM3 training report.


Model map: NoPE is a trend, not a universal switch








Model family
Position design
Correct interpretation




Llama 4
local/chunked RoPE; periodic global NoPE
hybrid RoPE–NoPE


Apple foundation models (2025)
sliding-window RoPE; global NoPE
hybrid RoPE–NoPE


Kimi K3
three KDA layers; every global Gated MLA layer uses NoPE
recurrent-position + global-NoPE hybrid


SmolLM3
every fourth layer removes RoPE; other layers retain RoPE/YaRN
open small-scale hybrid


Qwen3

not NoPE


DeepSeek-V3
MLA with a decoupled query/key component carrying RoPE
not NoPE



The last two rows are important counterexamples. Qwen3 explicitly retains RoPE and raises its base frequency during long-context training; DeepSeek-V3’s MLA compresses content keys and values but keeps a separate RoPE-bearing component. MLA therefore does not imply NoPE. See the Qwen3 technical report and DeepSeek-V3 technical report.



Minimal hybrid implementation
The layer schedule can be implemented by conditionally applying RoPE:
def hybrid_attention(q, k, v, layer_idx, apply_rope, nope_interval=4):
    """Sketch of a 3-RoPE : 1-NoPE schedule."""
    is_nope_layer = (layer_idx + 1) % nope_interval == 0

    if not is_nope_layer:
        q, k = apply_rope(q, k)

    return F.scaled_dot_product_attention(
        q, k, v,
        is_causal=True,
    )
This sketch changes only the positional transform. Llama 4 additionally changes the attention span: RoPE layers are local/chunked and NoPE layers are global. Kimi K3 instead replaces the RoPE branch with an ordered KDA recurrence. A real implementation must construct the appropriate mask or recurrent state for each layer and handle cached positions consistently.


What changed in our understanding?







Earlier interpretation
More recent interpretation




choose one PE for the entire model
positional strategy can vary by layer


NoPE is mainly a surprising ablation
NoPE can be a global-routing component in a production LLM


every layer must directly encode distance
local layers can encode order for later global layers


context extension is only a RoPE-rescaling problem
architecture can provide a position-free global path


NoPE has zero positional signal
it has no explicit PE but still inherits causal and contextual order



Recent theory also sharpens the role of depth. Work on the counting power of NoPE Transformers finds a large expressivity gap between one and multiple attention layers in a formal hard-attention setting. This supports the nested-prefix intuition above, although a theorem about an idealized hard-attention model is not direct evidence about optimization or quality in a finite-precision frontier LLM.
The practical conclusion is:
\[
\boxed{
\text{modern NoPE trend}
\approx
\text{position-aware local or recurrent mixing}
+
\text{position-free global routing}
}.
\]

title: Positional Encoding
text:
Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE)
RoPE applies a position-dependent rotation to pairs of query and key dimensions:
\[
q_t' = R_t q_t,
\qquad
k_s' = R_s k_s.
\]
Because rotation matrices are orthogonal,
\[
(q_t')^T k_s'
=
q_t^T R_t^T R_s k_s
=
q_t^T R_{s-t}k_s.
\]
Thus the attention score depends on the relative displacement \(s-t\), even though each query and key is rotated using its absolute position.

Interview Questions

Does the causal mask by itself fully encode token positions?

title: Tokenization Across Modalities
text:
Tokenization converts a large or structured input into a sequence of units that a model can process:
\[
x
\xrightarrow{\text{segment}}
(u_1,\ldots,u_T)
\xrightarrow{\text{encode}}
(z_1,\ldots,z_T).
\]
Depending on the method, \(z_t\) may be either:

a discrete ID looked up in an embedding table, or
a continuous vector produced by a linear layer or neural encoder.

This distinction is important. A ViT image patch is commonly called a token, but it is usually projected directly into a continuous vector rather than assigned a discrete vocabulary ID.


A neural network does not directly consume a word, photograph, sound, video, or catalog item. Its kernels consume finite tensors with known dimensions. The raw domains, however, have very different structure:

text is variable-length and drawn from an effectively open symbol space
images are dense two-dimensional arrays with millions of correlated values
audio and video are high-rate signals that would produce enormous sequences
recommendation catalogs contain millions or billions of sparse categorical IDs with little inherent geometry

Tokenization is the interface that reconciles this mismatch. In its broadest sense, it compiles a domain object into a bounded sequence of model-facing units:
\[
\tau(x)
=
\big((z_1,p_1,m_1),\ldots,(z_T,p_T,m_T)\big),
\]
where \(z_t\) is a discrete ID or continuous feature, \(p_t\) describes position or structure, and \(m_t\) can identify the modality or token type. A general sequence model then operates on this interface rather than on the original representation.






flowchart LR
    L[Text] --> TL[Subwords or bytes]
    I[Images] --> TI[Patches or VQ codes]
    A[Audio] --> TA[Frames or codec codes]
    V[Video] --> TV[Tubelets or video codes]
    R[Catalog items] --> TR[Atomic or semantic IDs]

    TL --> E[Token embeddings + structure]
    TI --> E
    TA --> E
    TV --> E
    TR --> E

    E --> M[General sequence model]
    M --> O[Prediction, retrieval, generation, or control]






This is why tokenization is not intrinsically an LLM component. It is an abstraction boundary between domain-specific perception or identity and a model that expects a sequence of vectors. The same Transformer can process different fields once their tokenizers produce compatible shapes and attach the right positional and modality information.



The tokenizer does more than change a data type. It makes several modeling decisions before the backbone sees the input:








Decision
Question
Consequence




Units
What should count as one token?
determines the primitive patterns the model can combine


Compression
How much raw information enters each token?
trades sequence length and compute against lost detail


Parameter sharing
Which observations reuse an ID, code, or encoder?
determines how statistical strength transfers between examples


Structure
How are space, time, hierarchy, and modality represented?
supplies ordering and neighborhood information absent from token values


Reversibility
Must the original input be reconstructed?
separates semantic representations from generation-quality codecs



The token sequence is therefore an information and compute budget. For dense attention with \(T\) tokens, the attention-score matrix costs \(O(T^2)\). Reducing image patch size, audio hop size, or video tubelet size may preserve more detail, but can make the backbone dramatically more expensive.
Tokenization also defines inductive bias. Subwords encourage reuse across related words; image patches encode locality; codec tokens favor reconstructability; semantic item IDs encourage related items to share code embeddings. A downstream model cannot reliably recover information that its tokenizer discarded.



An atomic recommendation ID is already a discrete token, but it is an arbitrary name. With \(N\) items and embedding dimension \(d\), a direct item table requires \(O(Nd)\) parameters, and two similar items share no representation unless the training data teaches their embeddings to be similar.
A semantic tokenizer can replace one huge categorical space with a composition of \(M\) codes drawn from codebooks of size \(K\):
\[
i
\longrightarrow
(c_1,\ldots,c_M),
\qquad c_m\in\{1,\ldots,K\}.
\]
The code embeddings require roughly \(O(MKd)\) parameters while the code tuples can represent up to \(K^M\) combinations. More importantly, rare or new items can reuse codes learned by related items. This is analogous to representing a rare word with reusable subwords, although recommendation systems must additionally preserve exact item identity and prevent invalid or colliding code sequences.



Tokenization is most valuable for inputs that are variable-sized, high-dimensional, high-rate, sparse categorical, or intended to share a sequence backbone. A small, fixed-length dense feature vector can usually be fed directly to an MLP; calling every numeric feature a token adds no inherent value.
The useful first-principles question is therefore not “How do I tokenize this modality?” but:

What representation exposes the task-relevant structure at a token rate and parameter cost the model can afford?













Modality
Common unit
Discrete or continuous?
Typical sequence axis




Text
byte, character, or subword
Discrete
reading order


Image
patch, region, or VQ code
Either
flattened 2D grid


Audio
frame, spectrogram patch, or codec code
Either
time, sometimes time \(\times\) codebook


Video
frame patch, tubelet, or VQ code
Either
time \(\times\) 2D grid


Recommendation
item ID or semantic-ID codes
Discrete
user-event order, then code depth









NoteTokenization is an information bottleneck



Smaller units preserve fine detail but create longer sequences. Larger units shorten the sequence but compress more information into each token. The choice affects model compute, vocabulary size, reconstruction quality, robustness, and what invariances the model must learn.
