    TA --> E
    TV --> E
    TR --> E

    E --> M[General sequence model]
    M --> O[Prediction, retrieval, generation, or control]






This is why tokenization is not intrinsically an LLM component. It is an abstraction boundary between domain-specific perception or identity and a model that expects a sequence of vectors. The same Transformer can process different fields once their tokenizers produce compatible shapes and attach the right positional and modality information.



The tokenizer does more than change a data type. It makes several modeling decisions before the backbone sees the input:








Decision
Question
Consequence




Units
What should count as one token?
determines the primitive patterns the model can combine


Compression
How much raw information enters each token?
trades sequence length and compute against lost detail


Parameter sharing
Which observations reuse an ID, code, or encoder?
determines how statistical strength transfers between examples


Structure
How are space, time, hierarchy, and modality represented?
supplies ordering and neighborhood information absent from token values


Reversibility
Must the original input be reconstructed?
separates semantic representations from generation-quality codecs



The token sequence is therefore an information and compute budget. For dense attention with \(T\) tokens, the attention-score matrix costs \(O(T^2)\). Reducing image patch size, audio hop size, or video tubelet size may preserve more detail, but can make the backbone dramatically more expensive.
Tokenization also defines inductive bias. Subwords encourage reuse across related words; image patches encode locality; codec tokens favor reconstructability; semantic item IDs encourage related items to share code embeddings. A downstream model cannot reliably recover information that its tokenizer discarded.



An atomic recommendation ID is already a discrete token, but it is an arbitrary name. With \(N\) items and embedding dimension \(d\), a direct item table requires \(O(Nd)\) parameters, and two similar items share no representation unless the training data teaches their embeddings to be similar.
A semantic tokenizer can replace one huge categorical space with a composition of \(M\) codes drawn from codebooks of size \(K\):
\[
i
\longrightarrow
(c_1,\ldots,c_M),
\qquad c_m\in\{1,\ldots,K\}.
\]
The code embeddings require roughly \(O(MKd)\) parameters while the code tuples can represent up to \(K^M\) combinations. More importantly, rare or new items can reuse codes learned by related items. This is analogous to representing a rare word with reusable subwords, although recommendation systems must additionally preserve exact item identity and prevent invalid or colliding code sequences.



Tokenization is most valuable for inputs that are variable-sized, high-dimensional, high-rate, sparse categorical, or intended to share a sequence backbone. A small, fixed-length dense feature vector can usually be fed directly to an MLP; calling every numeric feature a token adds no inherent value.
The useful first-principles question is therefore not “How do I tokenize this modality?” but:

What representation exposes the task-relevant structure at a token rate and parameter cost the model can afford?













Modality
Common unit
Discrete or continuous?
Typical sequence axis




Text
byte, character, or subword
Discrete
reading order


Image
patch, region, or VQ code
Either
flattened 2D grid


Audio
frame, spectrogram patch, or codec code
Either
time, sometimes time \(\times\) codebook


Video
frame patch, tubelet, or VQ code
Either
time \(\times\) 2D grid


Recommendation
item ID or semantic-ID codes
Discrete
user-event order, then code depth









NoteTokenization is an information bottleneck



Smaller units preserve fine detail but create longer sequences. Larger units shorten the sequence but compress more information into each token. The choice affects model compute, vocabulary size, reconstruction quality, robustness, and what invariances the model must learn.

title: Tokenization Across Modalities
text:
Text Tokenization

Common methods









Method
Unit
Strength
Weakness




Word
whole word
short, interpretable sequences
huge vocabulary and out-of-vocabulary words


Character
Unicode character
open vocabulary
long sequences; characters are not equally meaningful across languages


Byte
UTF-8 byte
fixed vocabulary of 256 and no unknown input bytes
longer sequences, especially for some scripts


BPE
frequent pair merges
simple and efficient subwords
greedy merge history is not a probabilistic model


WordPiece
subwords chosen to improve a language-model objective
useful compromise between words and characters
training details differ across implementations


Unigram LM
selects a segmentation from a probabilistic subword vocabulary
supports multiple candidate segmentations and subword regularization
requires vocabulary pruning and segmentation search



BPE repeatedly merges frequent adjacent symbols. SentencePiece can learn BPE or a unigram tokenizer directly from raw text without requiring language-specific pre-tokenization.


Typical pipeline
raw text
   ↓
Unicode normalization
   ↓
optional pre-tokenization
   ↓
subword or byte segmentation
   ↓
special tokens + token IDs
Important design choices:

vocabulary size
byte fallback and unknown-token behavior
whitespace representation
Unicode normalization
special tokens such as BOS, EOS, PAD, and modality separators
whether segmentation is deterministic or sampled during training



BPE from first principles
Byte-pair encoding learns a vocabulary between the two extremes of characters and whole words. It begins with small symbols and repeatedly creates a new symbol for the most frequent adjacent pair. Frequent fragments become single tokens, while rare words remain compositions of smaller reusable tokens.
Suppose a pre-tokenized corpus contains word types \(w\) with counts \(c(w)\), and the current segmentation of each word is \(s(w)\). At each training step, count every adjacent pair and select
\[
(a^*,b^*)
=
\arg\max_{(a,b)}
\sum_w c(w)
\sum_i
\mathbf{1}
\left[
(s_i(w),s_{i+1}(w))=(a,b)
\right].
\]
Then replace every non-overlapping occurrence of \((a^*,b^*)\) with the new symbol \(a^*b^*\). For example,
l o w e r
    merge (l, o)
lo w e r
    merge (lo, w)
low e r
The algorithm has two distinct phases:

Training: repeatedly count pairs on the training corpus and store the selected merges in order.
Encoding: start a new input from the base symbols and apply only those learned merges, respecting their learned priority. Pair frequencies are not relearned from the input being encoded.

The ordered merge list is therefore the tokenizer’s learned model. If merge \((a,b)\) was learned before merge \((ab,c)\), the first merge must create ab before the second can create abc.

Minimal BPE with incremental training
A useful middle ground keeps the optimization that matters at corpus scale without reproducing a production tokenizer’s internal data structures.
The trainer maintains:



State
Purpose




pair counts
current corpus-wide frequency of each adjacent pair


pair-to-word index
word types affected by a selected merge


max-heap
retrieve the next pair without scanning every candidate



There is one full pair-counting pass. After that, a merge revisits only word types containing the selected pair and updates their pair-count deltas. Stale heap entries are discarded lazily. This avoids rescanning the entire corpus for every learned token while leaving the BPE recurrence visible.

from collections import Counter, defaultdict
import heapq


def byte_symbols(text):
    return tuple(bytes([value]) for value in text.encode("utf-8"))


def count_pairs(symbols):
    return Counter(zip(symbols, symbols[1:]))


def merge_pair(symbols, target):
    """Merge non-overlapping occurrences of target from left to right."""
    output = []
    index = 0

    while index < len(symbols):
        if (
            index + 1 < len(symbols)
            and (symbols[index], symbols[index + 1]) == target
        ):
            output.append(symbols[index] + symbols[index + 1])
            index += 2
        else:
            output.append(symbols[index])
            index += 1

    return tuple(output)


class MinimalBPE:
    def __init__(self, num_merges, min_frequency=2):
        self.num_merges = num_merges
        self.min_frequency = min_frequency

    def fit(self, texts):
        word_counts = Counter(
            word
            for text in texts
            for word in text.split()
        )
        words = [byte_symbols(word) for word in word_counts]
        frequencies = list(word_counts.values())

        pair_counts = Counter()
        pair_to_words = defaultdict(set)

        # The only full pass over the corpus vocabulary.
        for word_id, (symbols, frequency) in enumerate(zip(words, frequencies)):
            for pair, occurrences in count_pairs(symbols).items():
                pair_counts[pair] += occurrences * frequency
                pair_to_words[pair].add(word_id)

        # Python implements a min-heap, so counts are negated.
        heap = [(-count, pair) for pair, count in pair_counts.items()]
        heapq.heapify(heap)
        self.merges = []

        for _ in range(self.num_merges):
            # Pair counts change over time. Ignore stale heap entries.
            while heap:
                negative_count, best_pair = heapq.heappop(heap)
                if -negative_count == pair_counts.get(best_pair, 0):
                    break
            else:
                break

            if pair_counts[best_pair] < self.min_frequency:
                break

            self.merges.append(best_pair)
            changed_pairs = set()

            # Only these word types can change under this merge.
            for word_id in tuple(pair_to_words[best_pair]):
                before = count_pairs(words[word_id])
                words[word_id] = merge_pair(words[word_id], best_pair)
                after = count_pairs(words[word_id])
                frequency = frequencies[word_id]

                for pair in before.keys() | after.keys():
                    pair_counts[pair] += (
                        after[pair] - before[pair]
                    ) * frequency
                    changed_pairs.add(pair)

                    if after[pair]:
                        pair_to_words[pair].add(word_id)
                    else:
                        pair_to_words[pair].discard(word_id)

            for pair in changed_pairs:
                if pair_counts[pair] > 0:
                    heapq.heappush(heap, (-pair_counts[pair], pair))

        self.merge_ranks = {
            pair: rank for rank, pair in enumerate(self.merges)
        }

        # Byte IDs 0...255 are fixed; learned tokens follow merge order.
        vocabulary = [bytes([value]) for value in range(256)]
        self.token_to_id = {
            token: token_id for token_id, token in enumerate(vocabulary)
        }
        for left, right in self.merges:
            token = left + right
            if token not in self.token_to_id:
                self.token_to_id[token] = len(vocabulary)
                vocabulary.append(token)
        self.id_to_token = dict(enumerate(vocabulary))
        return self

    def encode_piece(self, piece):
        symbols = byte_symbols(piece)

        # At most len(symbols) - 1 merges can happen. Crucially, this searches
        # only adjacent pairs in the piece, not every rule in the vocabulary.
        while len(symbols) > 1:
            candidates = [
                (self.merge_ranks[pair], pair)
                for pair in zip(symbols, symbols[1:])
                if pair in self.merge_ranks
            ]
            if not candidates:
                break
            _, best_pair = min(candidates)
            symbols = merge_pair(symbols, best_pair)

        return list(symbols)

    def encode_tokens(self, text):
        tokens = []
        for word_index, word in enumerate(text.split()):
            if word_index:
                tokens.append(b" ")
            tokens.extend(self.encode_piece(word))
        return tokens

    def encode(self, text):
        return [self.token_to_id[token] for token in self.encode_tokens(text)]

    def decode(self, token_ids):
        return b"".join(self.id_to_token[i] for i in token_ids).decode("utf-8")


corpus = [
    "low lower lowest",
    "low lower",
    "newer wider",
]

bpe = MinimalBPE(num_merges=8, min_frequency=1).fit(corpus)
tokens = bpe.encode_tokens("lowest newer")
token_ids = bpe.encode("lowest newer")

assert bpe.decode(token_ids) == "lowest newer"
print("merges:", bpe.merges)
print("tokens:", [token.decode("utf-8") for token in tokens])
print("ids:", token_ids)

merges: [(b'l', b'o'), (b'lo', b'w'), (b'e', b'r'), (b'low', b'er'), (b'd', b'er'), (b'e', b's'), (b'e', b'w'), (b'es', b't')]
tokens: ['low', 'est', ' ', 'n', 'ew', 'er']
ids: [257, 263, 32, 110, 262, 258]


Let \(C\) be the initial number of symbols across distinct pre-tokenized word types, and let \(A_k\) be the total length of word types affected by merge \(k\). Training costs approximately
\[
O\left(
C + \sum_{k=1}^{M} A_k + H
\right),
\]
where \(H\) is heap overhead. This is substantially better than the naïve \(O(MC)\) full rescan when most pairs occur in only a small part of the vocabulary.
The compact encoder repeatedly finds the learned pair with the best rank among the current adjacent pairs. It is \(O(n^2)\) in the worst case for a piece of \(n\) bytes, but it does not scan all \(M\) learned rules and pre-tokenized pieces are usually short. A production encoder replaces the list rescans with linked neighbors and a candidate heap, approaching \(O(n\log n)\), and adds caching and native parallelism.
This implementation still simplifies pre-tokenization: split() collapses whitespace, and it omits normalization and special-token handling. For production, use native libraries such as Hugging Face Tokenizers or OpenAI tiktoken.






NoteThe key BPE distinction



BPE training is a greedy corpus-compression procedure. BPE encoding is a deterministic replay of the learned merge priorities. Choosing the most frequent pair in each new input would define a different tokenizer and would not produce the token IDs the model was trained on.





Minimal byte tokenizer
This is lossless for valid UTF-8 text and has no learned vocabulary. It is educational rather than a complete production tokenizer.

class ByteTokenizer:
    vocab_size = 256

    def encode(self, text):
        return list(text.encode("utf-8"))

    def decode(self, token_ids):
        return bytes(token_ids).decode("utf-8")


byte_tokenizer = ByteTokenizer()
text = "Minimal ML 🤖"
text_ids = byte_tokenizer.encode(text)
assert byte_tokenizer.decode(text_ids) == text
text_ids

[77, 105, 110, 105, 109, 97, 108, 32, 77, 76, 32, 240, 159, 164, 150]




Questions to fill in

Why does increasing vocabulary size usually reduce sequence length?
What is the difference between BPE, WordPiece, and unigram tokenization?
Why can tokenization make arithmetic, spelling, and multilingual modeling difficult?
What happens when the tokenizer used at inference differs from training?
Why might byte fallback be preferable to an unknown token?

title: Tokenization Across Modalities
text:
Image Tokenization

Patch tokens
Given an image
\[
X \in \mathbb{R}^{C \times H \times W},
\]
split it into non-overlapping \(P\times P\) patches. The token count is
\[
T = \frac{H}{P}\frac{W}{P},
\]
and each flattened patch has dimension \(CP^2\). A learned projection maps it to \(d_{\text{model}}\). This is the continuous-token approach used by Vision Transformer.

import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F


def patchify(images, patch_size):
    """Convert (B, C, H, W) images to (B, num_patches, patch_dim)."""
    batch_size, channels, height, width = images.shape
    if height % patch_size or width % patch_size:
        raise ValueError("height and width must be divisible by patch_size")

    patches = F.unfold(
        images, kernel_size=patch_size, stride=patch_size
    )
    return patches.transpose(1, 2)


images = torch.randn(2, 3, 32, 32)
image_tokens = patchify(images, patch_size=8)
assert image_tokens.shape == (2, 16, 3 * 8 * 8)
image_tokens.shape

torch.Size([2, 16, 192])




Discrete visual tokens
An encoder can first produce a spatial latent grid and then quantize every latent vector to its nearest codebook entry:
\[
z_e(x)_{ij}
\longrightarrow
k_{ij}
=
\arg\min_k \left\|z_e(x)_{ij}-e_k\right\|_2^2.
\]
The grid of codebook indices \((k_{ij})\) is a sequence of discrete image tokens. A decoder reconstructs pixels from the selected code vectors. This is the key idea behind VQ-VAE.
Common image units:

pixels: maximum granularity, extremely long sequence
fixed patches: simple continuous tokens for understanding tasks
learned VQ codes: discrete tokens useful for generation
region or object tokens: adaptive units intended to capture semantic objects


Learning prompt: Why might an image tokenizer optimized only for pixel reconstruction preserve texture better than semantic identity?

title: Tokenization Across Modalities
text:
Audio Tokenization
Audio is a one-dimensional signal with a high sampling rate, so treating every sample as a token produces very long sequences.

Common methods

Waveform chunks: group raw samples into fixed-length frames and project them.
Spectrogram patches: transform the waveform into time-frequency features, then patch them like an image.
Neural codec tokens: encode audio into a lower-rate latent sequence and quantize it with one or more codebooks.
Semantic speech tokens: cluster hidden representations from a pretrained speech encoder; these emphasize linguistic content more than exact waveform reconstruction.

For sample rate \(f_s\), frame size \(W\), and hop size \(H_s\), the approximate number of frames in an \(L\)-sample waveform is
\[
T = 1 + \left\lfloor\frac{L-W}{H_s}\right\rfloor.
\]

def frame_audio(waveforms, frame_size, hop_size):
    """Convert (B, samples) waveforms to (B, frames, frame_size)."""
    if waveforms.shape[-1] < frame_size:
        raise ValueError("waveform is shorter than one frame")
    return waveforms.unfold(-1, frame_size, hop_size)


waveforms = torch.randn(2, 16_000)  # one second at 16 kHz
audio_frames = frame_audio(waveforms, frame_size=400, hop_size=160)
assert audio_frames.shape == (2, 98, 400)
audio_frames.shape

torch.Size([2, 98, 400])


Neural codecs such as SoundStream use residual vector quantization: multiple codebooks progressively encode the residual error. At each time step, this creates several parallel discrete codes.
If the codec emits \(n_q\) codebook IDs per frame at frame rate \(f\), its token rate is
\[
n_q f \quad \text{tokens per second}.
\]
Important tradeoffs:

semantic content versus acoustic detail
bitrate versus reconstruction quality
causal/streamable encoding versus bidirectional encoding
robustness to speakers, noise, and recording conditions

title: Tokenization Across Modalities
text:
Video Tokenization
A video introduces a temporal dimension:
\[
X \in \mathbb{R}^{C \times T \times H \times W}.
\]

Common methods

Frame tokens: encode each frame into one vector; cheap but discards spatial detail.
Per-frame patches: patchify every frame; preserves detail but creates long sequences.
Tubelets: split a video into 3D blocks spanning time and space.
Discrete video codes: quantize a learned spatiotemporal latent grid.
Adaptive tokens: pool tracks, objects, or events into content-dependent units.

For tubelet size \(P_t\times P_h\times P_w\), the number of tokens is
\[
N
=
\frac{T}{P_t}
\frac{H}{P_h}
\frac{W}{P_w}.
\]

import torch.nn as nn


class TubeletTokenizer(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, in_channels, d_model, tubelet_size, patch_size):
        super().__init__()
        kernel = (tubelet_size, patch_size, patch_size)
        self.projection = nn.Conv3d(
            in_channels,
            d_model,
            kernel_size=kernel,
            stride=kernel,
        )

    def forward(self, videos):
        # (B, C, T, H, W) -> (B, D, T', H', W')
        tokens = self.projection(videos)
        # Preserve a conventional time-major raster order.
        return tokens.flatten(2).transpose(1, 2)


videos = torch.randn(2, 3, 8, 32, 32)
video_tokenizer = TubeletTokenizer(
    in_channels=3, d_model=64, tubelet_size=2, patch_size=8
)
video_tokens = video_tokenizer(videos)
assert video_tokens.shape == (2, 4 * 4 * 4, 64)
video_tokens.shape

torch.Size([2, 64, 64])


Video sequence length grows across three axes. Tokenization therefore controls not only information loss but also the quadratic cost of dense attention.


Questions to fill in

What temporal information is lost when every frame is tokenized independently?
How does tubelet size affect motion resolution and sequence length?
When should spatial and temporal attention be factorized?
How should variable frame rates and video durations be handled?

title: Tokenization Across Modalities
text:
Semantic IDs in Recommendation Systems
Traditional recommenders often assign every item an arbitrary atomic ID:
\[
\text{item} \longrightarrow i.
\]
The ID uniquely identifies the item but says nothing about its content or its relationship to other items. A semantic ID instead maps an item embedding to a short sequence of learned discrete codes:
\[
\text{item}
\xrightarrow{\text{encoder}}
z
\xrightarrow{\text{quantizer}}
(c_1,c_2,\ldots,c_M).
\]
Generative recommenders can then predict the next item’s semantic ID autoregressively. TIGER is a representative example using residual-quantized semantic IDs for generative retrieval.

Residual quantization
Starting with item embedding \(z\) and residual \(r_0=z\), codebook level \(m\) selects
\[
c_m
=
\arg\min_k
\left\|r_{m-1}-e_k^{(m)}\right\|_2^2,
\]
then updates
\[
r_m = r_{m-1}-e_{c_m}^{(m)}.
\]
The quantized approximation is
\[
\widehat z
=
\sum_{m=1}^{M}e_{c_m}^{(m)}.
\]
Early codes capture coarse structure; later codes refine the residual. Shared prefixes may therefore reflect semantic similarity, although this is an optimization outcome rather than an unconditional guarantee.


Minimal residual quantizer

def residual_quantize(vectors, codebooks):
    """
    Args:
        vectors: (N, D)
        codebooks: (M, K, D), one K-entry codebook per level

    Returns:
        semantic_ids: (N, M)
        quantized: (N, D)
    """
    residual = vectors
    quantized = torch.zeros_like(vectors)
    all_ids = []

    for codebook in codebooks:
        distances = torch.cdist(residual.float(), codebook.float())
        code_ids = distances.argmin(dim=-1)
        selected = codebook[code_ids]

        all_ids.append(code_ids)
        quantized = quantized + selected
        residual = residual - selected

    return torch.stack(all_ids, dim=-1), quantized


torch.manual_seed(0)
item_embeddings = torch.randn(6, 8)
codebooks = torch.randn(3, 16, 8)
semantic_ids, reconstructed = residual_quantize(
    item_embeddings, codebooks
)
assert semantic_ids.shape == (6, 3)
semantic_ids

tensor([[ 8,  6,  9],
        [14,  7,  9],
        [ 8, 11,  0],
        [10,  5,  9],
        [ 4,  2,  0],
        [12,  6,  9]])


This function performs only nearest-code assignment. Training an RQ-VAE also requires an encoder, decoder, reconstruction objective, codebook/commitment losses, and a strategy for updating codebooks.


Why semantic IDs can help

replace a massive item embedding table with shared code embeddings
expose similarity through shared codes or prefixes
let a sequence model generate and retrieve items token by token
transfer information to rare or new items when their content embeddings can be encoded



What can go wrong

Collisions: multiple items may receive the same complete semantic ID.
Invalid generations: a predicted code sequence may not correspond to any catalog item.
Quantization loss: nearby or distinct item embeddings may be distorted by codebook boundaries.
Catalog drift: new items and changing item semantics can require re-tokenization.
Popularity leakage: content-derived similarity may not capture collaborative preference signals.
Longer decoding: one recommendation now requires predicting several tokens.

Practical systems may add a disambiguation token for collisions and use a catalog trie or constrained beam search so every generated prefix can lead to a valid item.


Atomic IDs versus semantic IDs








Property
Atomic item ID
Semantic ID




Tokens per item
1
\(M\)


Meaning of token
arbitrary identity
learned code or cluster


Similar items share parameters
indirectly
explicitly through codes


Collision-free
yes by construction
requires handling


New-item support
requires a new embedding
can encode item features, subject to model design


Generative retrieval
one huge vocabulary
smaller vocabulary over multiple decoding steps





Interview questions

How are semantic IDs different from hashing item IDs?
Why use multiple residual codebooks rather than one enormous codebook?
Do shared semantic-ID prefixes guarantee similar user preference?
How would you prevent the decoder from generating nonexistent items?
How do collisions affect training targets and retrieval?
When should the item encoder use content, collaborative signals, or both?
How do codebook size and depth affect capacity and decoding latency?

title: Tokenization Across Modalities
text:
One Framework for All Modalities
Many learned tokenizers can be summarized as
\[
x
\xrightarrow{E}
z_{1:T}
\xrightarrow{Q}
c_{1:T}
\xrightarrow{D}
\widehat x,
\]
where:

\(E\) segments and encodes the input,
\(Q\) optionally quantizes continuous latents into discrete IDs,
a sequence model processes or predicts the tokens,
\(D\) is needed when reconstructing the original modality.








Goal
Tokenizer should preserve




Classification/retrieval
task-relevant semantics


Autoregressive generation
enough detail for faithful reconstruction


Streaming
causal, low-latency state


Multimodal modeling
manageable token rate and alignment across modalities


Recommendation
item identity, useful similarity, and valid catalog structure

title: RNNs and LSTMs
text:
An ordinary feed-forward network maps each input independently:
\[
y_t=f(x_t).
\]
A recurrent neural network maintains a hidden state that summarizes the prefix:
\[
h_t=f(x_t,h_{t-1}),
\qquad
y_t=g(h_t).
\]
The same parameters are reused at every time step. This gives an RNN:

a variable-length input interface
parameter sharing across positions
an inductive bias toward sequential processing
a fixed-size state through which past information must flow

\qquad
y_t=g(h_t).

a variable-length input interface

title: RNNs and LSTMs
text:
Vanilla RNN
The standard tanh RNN is
\[
a_t=W_{xh}x_t+W_{hh}h_{t-1}+b_h,
\]
\[
h_t=\tanh(a_t),
\]
\[
y_t=W_{hy}h_t+b_y.
\]
The initial state \(h_0\) may be zero, learned, or provided by another encoder.

Model structure






flowchart LR
    X1[Input x₁] --> C1[RNN cell]
    H0[Initial state h₀] --> C1
    C1 --> H1[Hidden state h₁]
    H1 --> C2[RNN cell]
    X2[Input x₂] --> C2
    C2 --> H2[Hidden state h₂]
    H2 --> C3[RNN cell]
    X3[Input x₃] --> C3
    C3 --> H3[Hidden state h₃]

    H1 --> Y1[Output y₁]
    H2 --> Y2[Output y₂]
    H3 --> Y3[Output y₃]

    classDef state fill:#e8f0fe,stroke:#4c78a8,color:#222;
    classDef cell fill:#f3e8ff,stroke:#8b5cf6,color:#222;
    classDef input fill:#e8f8ee,stroke:#3a8f5c,color:#222;
    class H0,H1,H2,H3 state;
    class C1,C2,C3 cell;
    class X1,X2,X3 input;






The three cells above are copies of the same computation with shared parameters, not three independently learned layers. Drawing the recurrence across time is called unrolling the RNN.


Tensor shapes
For batch size \(B\), sequence length \(T\), input size \(d_x\), hidden size \(d_h\), and output size \(d_y\):



Tensor
Shape




Input sequence \(X\)
\((B,T,d_x)\)


Hidden state \(h_t\)
\((B,d_h)\)


Input weight \(W_{xh}\)
\((d_h,d_x)\)


Recurrent weight \(W_{hh}\)
\((d_h,d_h)\)


Output sequence \(Y\)
\((B,T,d_y)\)





Minimal PyTorch implementation

import torch
import torch.nn as nn


class SimpleRNNCell(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, input_size, hidden_size):
        super().__init__()
        self.hidden_size = hidden_size
        self.input_proj = nn.Linear(input_size, hidden_size, bias=True)
        self.hidden_proj = nn.Linear(hidden_size, hidden_size, bias=False)

    def forward(self, x_t, h_previous):
        return torch.tanh(
            self.input_proj(x_t) + self.hidden_proj(h_previous)
        )


class SimpleRNN(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, input_size, hidden_size):
        super().__init__()
        self.hidden_size = hidden_size
        self.cell = SimpleRNNCell(input_size, hidden_size)

    def forward(self, inputs, initial_state=None):
        batch_size, _, _ = inputs.shape
        if initial_state is None:
            hidden = inputs.new_zeros(batch_size, self.hidden_size)
        else:
            hidden = initial_state

        outputs = []
        for x_t in inputs.unbind(dim=1):
            hidden = self.cell(x_t, hidden)
            outputs.append(hidden)

        return torch.stack(outputs, dim=1), hidden


torch.manual_seed(0)
sequence = torch.randn(2, 5, 3)
rnn = SimpleRNN(input_size=3, hidden_size=7)
all_hidden_states, final_hidden_state = rnn(sequence)

assert all_hidden_states.shape == (2, 5, 7)
assert final_hidden_state.shape == (2, 7)

title: RNNs and LSTMs
text:
Backpropagation Through Time
Unrolling converts recurrence into a deep computation graph whose depth grows with sequence length. Training differentiates through this graph, which is called backpropagation through time (BPTT).
For the vanilla RNN,
\[
\frac{\partial h_t}{\partial h_{t-1}}
=
\operatorname{diag}\left(1-\tanh^2(a_t)\right)W_{hh}.
\]
A gradient traveling from time \(T\) to time \(t\) contains a product of Jacobians:
\[
\frac{\partial h_T}{\partial h_t}
=
\prod_{k=t+1}^{T}
\frac{\partial h_k}{\partial h_{k-1}}.
\]
Repeated multiplication causes:

vanishing gradients when the relevant singular values are mostly below 1
exploding gradients when they are mostly above 1

Tanh saturation further shrinks gradients because \(1-\tanh^2(a_t)\approx0\) for large \(|a_t|\).

Practical mitigations

gradient clipping for exploding gradients
orthogonal or carefully scaled recurrent initialization
truncated BPTT to limit graph length and memory
gated cells such as LSTMs and GRUs
skip connections and normalization in recurrent architectures

Truncated BPTT bounds training cost, but it also prevents gradients from directly assigning credit across truncation boundaries.

title: RNNs and LSTMs
text:
Long Short-Term Memory
An LSTM introduces a cell state \(c_t\) with an additive update path. Three gates control what to forget, write, and expose.
For concatenated input
\[
z_t=[x_t;h_{t-1}],
\]
the gates and candidate memory are
\[
f_t=\sigma(W_fz_t+b_f)
\qquad\text{forget gate},
\]
\[
i_t=\sigma(W_iz_t+b_i)
\qquad\text{input gate},
\]
\[
o_t=\sigma(W_oz_t+b_o)
\qquad\text{output gate},
\]
\[
\widetilde c_t=\tanh(W_cz_t+b_c)
\qquad\text{candidate memory}.
\]
The cell and hidden states update as
\[
\boxed{c_t=f_t\odot c_{t-1}+i_t\odot\widetilde c_t},
\]
\[
\boxed{h_t=o_t\odot\tanh(c_t)}.
\]

LSTM cell structure






flowchart LR
    C0[Previous cell cₜ₋₁] --> MULF((×))
    XH[Input xₜ and hidden hₜ₋₁] --> F[Forget gate fₜ = sigmoid]
    XH --> I[Input gate iₜ = sigmoid]
    XH --> G[Candidate c̃ₜ = tanh]
    XH --> O[Output gate oₜ = sigmoid]

    F --> MULF
    I --> MULI((×))
    G --> MULI
    MULF --> ADD((+))
    MULI --> ADD
    ADD --> C1[New cell state cₜ]

    C1 --> TANH[tanh]
    TANH --> MULO((×))
    O --> MULO
    MULO --> H1[New hidden state hₜ]

    classDef state fill:#e8f0fe,stroke:#4c78a8,color:#222;
    classDef gate fill:#fff2cc,stroke:#c49a00,color:#222;
    classDef candidate fill:#e8f8ee,stroke:#3a8f5c,color:#222;
    classDef op fill:#f3e8ff,stroke:#8b5cf6,color:#222;
    class C0,C1,H1 state;
    class F,I,O gate;
    class G,TANH candidate;
    class MULF,MULI,MULO,ADD op;






The upper cell-state path is the key difference from a vanilla RNN. It combines old memory and new content additively, while sigmoid gates provide element-wise control.


Why the LSTM helps gradient flow
Holding the gates fixed for intuition,
\[
\frac{\partial c_t}{\partial c_{t-1}}=f_t.
\]
Across several steps,
\[
\frac{\partial c_T}{\partial c_t}
\approx
\prod_{k=t+1}^{T} f_k.
\]
When forget gates remain near one, the cell provides a nearly linear path for information and gradients. This avoids repeatedly passing the main memory through a saturating tanh transformation at every time step.
LSTMs mitigate vanishing gradients; they do not eliminate them. Products of forget gates below one still decay, and the full gradient includes additional paths through gate dependencies.

title: RNNs and LSTMs
text:
Minimal LSTM Implementation
Efficient implementations fuse all four affine transformations into one matrix multiplication:
\[
[f_t,i_t,\widetilde c_t,o_t]
=
W[x_t;h_{t-1}]+b.
\]

class MinimalLSTMCell(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, input_size, hidden_size):
        super().__init__()
        self.hidden_size = hidden_size
        self.gates = nn.Linear(input_size + hidden_size, 4 * hidden_size)

    def forward(self, x_t, state):
        hidden_previous, cell_previous = state
        combined = torch.cat([x_t, hidden_previous], dim=-1)
        forget_raw, input_raw, candidate_raw, output_raw = self.gates(
            combined
        ).chunk(4, dim=-1)

        forget_gate = torch.sigmoid(forget_raw)
        input_gate = torch.sigmoid(input_raw)
        candidate = torch.tanh(candidate_raw)
        output_gate = torch.sigmoid(output_raw)

        cell = forget_gate * cell_previous + input_gate * candidate
        hidden = output_gate * torch.tanh(cell)
        return hidden, cell


class MinimalLSTM(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, input_size, hidden_size):
        super().__init__()
        self.hidden_size = hidden_size
        self.cell = MinimalLSTMCell(input_size, hidden_size)

    def forward(self, inputs, initial_state=None):
        batch_size, _, _ = inputs.shape
        if initial_state is None:
            hidden = inputs.new_zeros(batch_size, self.hidden_size)
            cell = inputs.new_zeros(batch_size, self.hidden_size)
        else:
            hidden, cell = initial_state

        outputs = []
        for x_t in inputs.unbind(dim=1):
            hidden, cell = self.cell(x_t, (hidden, cell))
            outputs.append(hidden)

        return torch.stack(outputs, dim=1), (hidden, cell)


lstm = MinimalLSTM(input_size=3, hidden_size=7)
lstm_outputs, (final_hidden, final_cell) = lstm(sequence)

assert lstm_outputs.shape == (2, 5, 7)
assert final_hidden.shape == (2, 7)
assert final_cell.shape == (2, 7)


Parameter count
For input size \(d_x\) and hidden size \(d_h\), the fused LSTM affine layer has
\[
4d_h(d_x+d_h)+4d_h
\]
parameters. A comparable vanilla RNN has
\[
d_h(d_x+d_h)+d_h.
\]
An LSTM cell therefore has roughly four times the recurrent-cell parameters and affine compute of a vanilla RNN with the same dimensions.

text:
Understanding the Gates









Gate
Range
Multiplies
Interpretation




Forget \(f_t\)
\((0,1)\)
old cell \(c_{t-1}\)

Input \(i_t\)
\((0,1)\)

\((0,1)\)

The cell state is not constrained to \((-1,1)\) because it is an additive accumulator. The hidden state is bounded by the output gate and tanh.

Connection to SwiGLU
Both LSTMs and SwiGLU use multiplicative, input-dependent modulation:
\[
\text{content}\odot\text{gate}.
\]
But their roles differ:







SwiGLU

gates state flow across time

maintains \(c_t\) across sequence positions

sigmoid gates remain between zero and one


increases feature interactions
controls remembering, writing, and reading



See Activation Functions for the SwiGLU derivation.

title: RNNs and LSTMs
text:
Common Variants

Bidirectional RNN/LSTM: runs separate recurrences forward and backward; useful when the entire sequence is available, but not causal.
Stacked RNN/LSTM: feeds one recurrent layer’s sequence into another.
GRU: combines LSTM-style control into reset and update gates with no separate cell state.
Peephole LSTM: gates also inspect the cell state.
Encoder-decoder recurrence: encodes one sequence and autoregressively generates another, often with attention.

title: Prediction and Decision Losses
text:
A loss is the interface between:

statistical knowledge: what uncertainty generated the target?
problem abstraction: must the model estimate a probability, value, boundary, order, or representation?
optimization: what differentiable signal is aligned with the real metric?

Let \((X,Y)\sim p^*\), let \(a_\theta(X)\) be a prediction, and let \(C(a,Y)\) be the real cost. The ideal Bayes decision is
\[
a^*(x)
=
\arg\min_a
\mathbb E_{Y\sim p^*(\cdot\mid x)}[C(a,Y)].
\]
Training replaces the unknown population expectation with empirical risk and usually replaces the real cost with a tractable surrogate:
\[
\widehat R(\theta)
=
\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^{N}
\ell(a_\theta(x_i),y_i).
\]
The first-principles question is:

Which surrogate has an optimum and gradient geometry aligned with the decision we actually care about?

For the complete taxonomy, see Losses from First Principles. For objectives that learn a high-dimensional data distribution, see Distribution Learning Losses.


Before choosing a formula, ask:

What is the target: categorical, binary, continuous, count, ordinal, or a pairwise preference?
Do calibrated probabilities matter, or only the final boundary/ranking?
What support and noise model should predictions respect?
Are examples genuinely unequal in cost, or merely unequal in frequency?
What is the evaluation metric, and is the loss a consistent surrogate?
What sampling and reduction define the effective training population?







ImportantLoss and metric are different



Accuracy, F1, recall, and ranking metrics can be nondifferentiable or nondecomposable. A loss is a surrogate. Lower loss matters only insofar as it improves the target decision or gives useful probability estimates.

title: Prediction and Decision Losses
section: 2. Likelihood Turns Statistical Assumptions into Losses
text:
2. Likelihood Turns Statistical Assumptions into Losses
If the model defines \(p_\theta(y\mid x)\), maximum likelihood minimizes
\[
\mathcal L_{\mathrm{NLL}}
=
-\mathbb E_{(x,y)\sim p^*}
\log p_\theta(y\mid x).
\]
For fixed \(x\),
\[
\mathbb E_{y\sim p^*}[-\log p_\theta(y\mid x)]
=
H(p^*)+\mathrm{KL}(p^*\|p_\theta).
\]
The entropy term is constant in \(\theta\), so the population optimum is the true conditional distribution. Log loss is therefore a proper scoring rule.
Many standard losses are simply NLL under different observation models:








Assumption for \(Y\mid X\)
Output
NLL, ignoring constants




Categorical
class logits
cross-entropy


Bernoulli
one logit
binary cross-entropy


Gaussian, fixed variance
mean
squared error


Gaussian, learned variance
mean and log variance
scaled MSE + log variance


Laplace
location
absolute error


Poisson count
log-rate
\(e^\eta-y\eta\)



The clever step is not memorizing the last column. It is choosing a distribution whose support, sufficient statistics, and noise assumptions fit the task.

title: Prediction and Decision Losses
text:
3. Classification as Probability Estimation

3.1 Multiclass cross-entropy
For one of \(C\) mutually exclusive classes with logits \(z\),
\[
p_j=\frac{e^{z_j}}{\sum_k e^{z_k}},
\qquad
\mathcal L_{\mathrm{CE}}
=
-\log p_y
=
-z_y+\log\sum_k e^{z_k}.
\]
Its logit gradient is especially interpretable:
\[
\frac{\partial\mathcal L_{\mathrm{CE}}}{\partial z_j}
=
p_j-\mathbb 1[j=y].
\]
The target logit rises; competing logits fall in proportion to their predicted probability.

Minimal stable implementation

import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F


def cross_entropy_from_logits(logits, targets, reduction="mean"):
    log_normalizer = torch.logsumexp(logits, dim=-1)
    target_logits = logits.gather(
        -1, targets.unsqueeze(-1)
    ).squeeze(-1)
    losses = log_normalizer - target_logits

    if reduction == "none":
        return losses
    if reduction == "sum":
        return losses.sum()
    if reduction == "mean":
        return losses.mean()
    raise ValueError(f"unknown reduction: {reduction}")


logits = torch.tensor([[1000.0, 1001.0, 999.0], [-2.0, 0.5, 3.0]])
targets = torch.tensor([1, 2])
torch.testing.assert_close(
    cross_entropy_from_logits(logits, targets),
    F.cross_entropy(logits, targets),
)




3.2 Logistic regression and binary cross-entropy
Logistic regression specifies a linear log-odds model:
\[
z_\theta(x)=w^Tx+b,
\qquad
p_\theta(y=1\mid x)=\sigma(z_\theta(x)).
\]
Because
\[
\log\frac{p_\theta(y=1\mid x)}
{p_\theta(y=0\mid x)}
=
z_\theta(x),
\]
each coefficient is an additive effect on the log odds. Combining the Bernoulli observation model with this linear logit gives the per-example negative log-likelihood
\[
\mathcal L_{\text{logistic}}(w,b;x,y)
=
-y\log\sigma(z)
-(1-y)\log[1-\sigma(z)],
\qquad z=w^Tx+b.
\]
Thus binary cross-entropy is the logistic-regression loss when its logit is linear in the features. A neural binary classifier uses the same loss with a nonlinear logit \(z=f_\theta(x)\).
For labels \(\widetilde y\in\{-1,+1\}\), the same objective has the compact form
\[
\mathcal L_{\text{logistic}}
=
\log\left(1+e^{-\widetilde y z}\right).
\]
The gradients expose the probabilistic residual:
\[
\frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial z}
=
\sigma(z)-y,
\qquad
\nabla_w\mathcal L
=
[\sigma(z)-y]x.
\]
For a linear logit, its Hessian is
\[
\nabla_w^2\mathcal L
=
\sigma(z)[1-\sigma(z)]xx^T
\succeq 0.
\]
Therefore unregularized logistic NLL is convex in \((w,b)\), although it need not have a finite minimizer on perfectly separable data. L2 regularization makes the problem strongly convex when the design has the appropriate coverage.

Stable BCE form
For \(y\in\{0,1\}\) and \(p=\sigma(z)\),
\[
\mathcal L_{\mathrm{BCE}}
=
-y\log p-(1-y)\log(1-p).
\]
The stable logits form is
\[
\mathcal L_{\mathrm{BCE}}(z,y)
=
\max(z,0)-yz+\log(1+e^{-|z|}),
\]
with derivative \(\sigma(z)-y\).

def binary_cross_entropy_with_logits(logits, targets, reduction="mean"):
    targets = targets.to(logits.dtype)
    losses = torch.logaddexp(torch.zeros_like(logits), logits) - targets * logits

    if reduction == "none":
        return losses
    if reduction == "sum":
        return losses.sum()
    if reduction == "mean":
        return losses.mean()
    raise ValueError(f"unknown reduction: {reduction}")


binary_logits = torch.tensor([-1000.0, -2.0, 0.0, 2.0, 1000.0])
binary_targets = torch.tensor([0.0, 1.0, 1.0, 0.0, 1.0])
torch.testing.assert_close(
    binary_cross_entropy_with_logits(binary_logits, binary_targets),
    F.binary_cross_entropy_with_logits(binary_logits, binary_targets),
)

Use independent BCE logits for multilabel outcomes. Use softmax CE when exactly one class must occur. Independent BCE does not enforce probabilities summing to one.



3.3 Label smoothing
Replace a one-hot target by
\[
q_j
=
(1-\varepsilon)\mathbb 1[j=y]+\frac{\varepsilon}{C}
\]
and minimize \(-\sum_jq_j\log p_j\). This regularizes extreme confidence but also changes the population target. It is a prior about target uncertainty, not a universal fix for mislabeled data.

title: Prediction and Decision Losses
section: 4. Class Imbalance, Cost, and Focal Loss
text:
4. Class Imbalance, Cost, and Focal Loss
Three problems are often conflated:







Problem
Appropriate intervention




unequal real-world error costs
cost-sensitive loss or decision threshold


minority examples rarely sampled
resampling or importance weighting


easy examples dominate total gradient
hard-example mining or focal modulation



Weighted BCE, for example,
\[
\mathcal L
=
-w_+y\log p-w_-(1-y)\log(1-p),
\]
changes the risk being optimized. If the deployment population is unchanged, the resulting probabilities may need recalibration.
Focal loss starts from cross-entropy and downweights already-correct examples. Define
\[
p_t=
\begin{cases}
p,&y=1,\\
1-p,&y=0,
\end{cases}
\]
then
\[
\mathcal L_{\mathrm{focal}}
=
-\alpha_t(1-p_t)^\gamma\log p_t.
\]
At \(\gamma=0\) it becomes weighted CE. For \(\gamma>0\), the vast population of easy examples contributes less gradient. This helped dense detection where easy background anchors overwhelmed rare foreground examples. It can hurt probability calibration, so use it for gradient allocation—not merely because a dataset is imbalanced.

def binary_focal_loss(logits, targets, gamma=2.0, alpha=None):
    targets = targets.to(logits.dtype)
    bce = F.binary_cross_entropy_with_logits(logits, targets, reduction="none")
    p_t = torch.exp(-bce)
    weights = (1.0 - p_t).pow(gamma)

    if alpha is not None:
        alpha_t = alpha * targets + (1.0 - alpha) * (1.0 - targets)
        weights = weights * alpha_t

    return (weights * bce).mean()

title: Prediction and Decision Losses
section: 5. Margin Losses: Learn a Boundary, Not a Distribution
text:
5. Margin Losses: Learn a Boundary, Not a Distribution
If only the decision boundary matters, calibrated probabilities may be excess structure. For \(y\in\{-1,+1\}\) and score \(f_\theta(x)\), hinge loss is
\[
\mathcal L_{\mathrm{hinge}}
=
\max(0,1-yf_\theta(x)).
\]
Correct examples receive a gradient until they lie beyond margin one, then contribute zero. Cross-entropy continues increasing confidence. This is a choice between separation geometry and probability estimation.
For multiclass scores, one structured hinge form is
\[
\mathcal L
=
\max_{j\ne y}
\left[0,m+z_j-z_y\right].
\]
The margin \(m\) defines how much score separation counts as sufficient; score scale and regularization determine what that statement means geometrically.

title: Prediction and Decision Losses
text:
6. Contrastive, Metric, and Ranking Losses
Classification assigns examples to a fixed output vocabulary. Representation learning often needs a different abstraction: specify which observations should be close and which should be distinguishable. See Representation Learning from First Principles for the broader design problem.
“Contrastive loss” is not one unique formula. It is a family of objectives built from positive relations and negative relations.

6.1 Classical pairwise contrastive loss
Let \(r=1\) indicate that a pair \((x_i,x_j)\) is semantically similar, let \(r=0\) indicate a dissimilar pair, and define embedding distance
\[
D_{ij}
=
\lVert f_\theta(x_i)-f_\theta(x_j)\rVert_2.
\]
The classical pairwise contrastive loss is
\[
\mathcal L_{\mathrm{contrastive}}
=
rD_{ij}^2
+(1-r)\left[\max(0,m-D_{ij})\right]^2.
\]
Positive pairs are pulled together. Negative pairs are pushed apart only until they reach margin \(m\); spending capacity separating them further does not help this objective.






NoteCheck the label convention



Some sources use \(y=0\) for similar pairs and \(y=1\) for dissimilar pairs. The formula changes appearance but not meaning. Always define which value denotes a positive pair.



def pairwise_contrastive_loss(
    left_embeddings,
    right_embeddings,
    is_positive,
    margin=1.0,
):
    """Classical contrastive loss; 1 means a semantically matching pair."""
    distances = torch.linalg.vector_norm(
        left_embeddings - right_embeddings,
        dim=-1,
    )
    is_positive = is_positive.to(distances.dtype)
    positive_loss = is_positive * distances.square()
    negative_loss = (1.0 - is_positive) * F.relu(
        margin - distances
    ).square()
    return (positive_loss + negative_loss).mean()


left = torch.tensor([[0.0, 0.0], [0.0, 0.0]])
well_arranged = torch.tensor([[0.1, 0.0], [2.0, 0.0]])
badly_arranged = torch.tensor([[2.0, 0.0], [0.1, 0.0]])
pair_types = torch.tensor([1.0, 0.0])

assert pairwise_contrastive_loss(
    left, well_arranged, pair_types
) < pairwise_contrastive_loss(left, badly_arranged, pair_types)



6.2 Triplet loss
A triplet directly compares a positive and negative relative to the same anchor:
\[
\mathcal L_{\mathrm{triplet}}
=
\max\left(
0,
d(e_a,e_p)-d(e_a,e_n)+m
\right).
\]
It asks for a ranking constraint,
\[
d(e_a,e_p)+m\le d(e_a,e_n),
\]
rather than an absolute target distance. Pairwise contrastive loss considers one relation at a time; triplet loss compares two relations in the same example.


6.3 InfoNCE: classify the positive among candidates
For an anchor \(z_i\), positive \(z_i^+\), similarity function \(\operatorname{sim}\), and temperature \(\tau\), InfoNCE uses
\[
\mathcal L_i
=
-\log
\frac{
\exp[\operatorname{sim}(z_i,z_i^+)/\tau]
}{
\sum_{j=1}^{B}
\exp[\operatorname{sim}(z_i,z_j^+)/\tau]
}.
\]
This is ordinary cross-entropy over a dynamically constructed classification problem: candidate \(i\) is the target class and the other batch elements provide negatives. Temperature controls how strongly the loss focuses on the largest similarities.

def info_nce_loss(anchors, positives, temperature=0.1):
    anchors = F.normalize(anchors, dim=-1)
    positives = F.normalize(positives, dim=-1)
    logits = anchors @ positives.T / temperature
    targets = torch.arange(logits.shape[0], device=logits.device)
    return F.cross_entropy(logits, targets)


torch.manual_seed(0)
anchors = torch.randn(16, 32)
matching_positives = anchors + 0.01 * torch.randn_like(anchors)
wrong_positives = matching_positives.roll(shifts=1, dims=0)

assert info_nce_loss(
    anchors, matching_positives
) < info_nce_loss(anchors, wrong_positives)

The formula assumes that nonmatching batch items are valid negatives. Larger batches provide more comparisons, but also increase the chance of false negatives—different observations that share the same semantics.


6.4 Supervised contrastive loss
If labels reveal multiple positives for anchor \(i\), define
\[
P(i)=\{p\ne i:y_p=y_i\}.
\]
Supervised contrastive loss averages the log probability assigned to every positive:
\[
\mathcal L_i^{\mathrm{sup}}
=
-\frac{1}{|P(i)|}
\sum_{p\in P(i)}
\log
\frac{
\exp[\operatorname{sim}(z_i,z_p)/\tau]
}{
\sum_{a\ne i}
\exp[\operatorname{sim}(z_i,z_a)/\tau]
}.
\]
Unlike ordinary class cross-entropy, it directly shapes within-batch embedding geometry. Its notion of equivalence is still only as good as the labels: same-class examples may contain meaningful substructure that the loss encourages the model to ignore.


6.5 Ranking losses
When supervision says “item \(i\) should rank above item \(j\),” predicting absolute labels solves a harder and possibly ill-posed problem. Use a pairwise abstraction:
\[
\mathcal L_{\mathrm{pairwise\ hinge}}
=
\max(0,m-s_i+s_j),
\]
or the smooth BPR/logistic loss
\[
\mathcal L_{\mathrm{BPR}}
=
-\log\sigma(s_i-s_j).
\]


Sampling is part of the loss
Contrastive and ranking objectives are expectations over constructed tuples, not merely over individual observations. Therefore the positive- and negative-sampling distributions help define the population objective.

easy negatives may provide almost no gradient
false negatives teach an incorrect geometry
extremely hard negatives may be mislabeled or unstable
in-batch negatives couple the effective objective to batch composition

Sampling should reflect which confusions matter at retrieval time. Report it as part of the loss definition rather than as an implementation detail.

title: Prediction and Decision Losses
text:
7. Regression Losses from Noise Models

7.1 MSE and the conditional mean
If
\[
Y\mid X=x\sim\mathcal N(\mu_\theta(x),\sigma^2)
\]
with fixed variance, NLL reduces to scaled squared error. More generally,
\[
\arg\min_f\mathbb E[(Y-f(X))^2\mid X=x]
=
\mathbb E[Y\mid X=x].
\]
MSE targets the conditional mean. Its residual gradient grows linearly, so outliers can dominate.


7.2 MAE and the conditional median
A Laplace likelihood produces
\[
\mathcal L_{\mathrm{MAE}}=|y-\widehat y|.
\]
MAE targets a conditional median and has bounded residual-gradient magnitude. It is robust to large errors but nonsmooth at zero.


7.3 Huber loss
For residual \(r=y-\widehat y\),
\[
\mathcal L_\delta(r)
=
\begin{cases}
\frac12r^2,&|r|\le\delta,\\
\delta\left(|r|-\frac12\delta\right),&|r|>\delta.
\end{cases}
\]
Huber is quadratic for small residuals and linear in the tails. The threshold \(\delta\) states what residual scale counts as an outlier, so it must be chosen relative to target normalization.


7.4 Heteroscedastic uncertainty
If noise varies with \(x\), predict mean \(\mu_\theta(x)\) and log variance \(s_\theta(x)=\log\sigma_\theta^2(x)\):
\[
\mathcal L
=
\frac12
\left[
e^{-s_\theta(x)}(y-\mu_\theta(x))^2+s_\theta(x)
\right].
\]
The first term discounts uncertain examples; the second prevents infinite variance. A seemingly clever learned weight follows directly from a normalized Gaussian likelihood.


7.5 Quantiles and counts
Conditional quantile \(q_\tau(x)\) is elicited by pinball loss
\[
\rho_\tau(r)
=
\begin{cases}
\tau r,&r\ge0,\\
(\tau-1)r,&r<0,
\end{cases}
\qquad r=y-q_\tau(x).
\]
For nonnegative counts, a Poisson model with log-rate \(\eta\) gives
\[
\mathcal L_{\mathrm{Poisson}}
=
e^\eta-y\eta+\log(y!).
\]
Unlike Gaussian regression, the likelihood respects count support and ties variance to the mean. If real counts are overdispersed, a negative-binomial model may be more appropriate.

title: Prediction and Decision Losses
text:
8. Numerical Stability and Reduction
Pass raw logits to CrossEntropyLoss and BCEWithLogitsLoss. Do not materialize softmax/sigmoid probabilities and then take logs.
For CE, use
\[
\log\sum_k e^{z_k}
=
m+\log\sum_k e^{z_k-m},
\qquad m=\max_k z_k.
\]
Also inspect the reduction:

mean over examples versus sum
mean over valid labels versus all padded positions
mean per group versus mean over a population with unequal group size
interaction between sample weights and the denominator

The denominator silently defines which population receives equal importance.

title: Prediction and Decision Losses
text:
9. Design Examples

Rare-event classification
Start with Bernoulli NLL. If false negatives have higher decision cost, adjust the loss or threshold using that cost. If easy negatives dominate gradient compute, consider focal loss. If probabilities drive downstream decisions, measure and repair calibration.


Regression with corrupt targets
Inspect residual tails. MSE is efficient for clean, light-tailed noise; Huber or Laplace NLL is more robust. If uncertainty varies by example, predict a distribution rather than only a robust point.


Retrieval
If evaluation depends only on order, a pairwise or contrastive abstraction is more direct than absolute regression. Design negative sampling around realistic retrieval confusions and audit for false negatives.

title: Prediction and Decision Losses
text:
10. Common Failure Modes







Failure
Diagnostic question




optimizing the wrong population
What sampling and weights define this expectation?


surrogate mismatch
Is this loss calibrated/consistent for the target decision?


shortcut learning
Can an unintended feature satisfy the target?


gradient domination
Which class, task, or group supplies most gradient norm?


bad noise model
Does the likelihood have the right support and tail behavior?


reduction bug
What exactly is divided by what?


numerical failure
Can the objective be computed directly in logits or log space?

title: Losses from First Principles
text:
Let \(Z\sim p^*\) denote an observation and let \(a_\theta\) be the model output. Training minimizes an empirical approximation to a population objective:
\[
R(\theta)
=
\mathbb E_{Z\sim \mu}
\left[\ell(a_\theta,Z)\right].
\]
This compact expression hides four independent design choices:

Statistical object: a distribution, mean, quantile, boundary, representation, ranking, or policy.
Source of supervision: observed outcomes, pairs, latent variables, synthetic corruption, rewards, or a teacher model.
Discrepancy: a proper score, surrogate risk, divergence, variational bound, learned critic, or utility objective.
Expectation distribution \(\mu\): data examples, constructed pairs, noise levels, teacher trajectories, or student-generated states.

The first-principles question is therefore not merely “which formula should I use?” It is:

What should the optimum recover, from which information, over which population, and with what tractable learning signal?

title: Losses from First Principles
section: The Goal Is Not Always to Learn a Full Distribution
text:
The Goal Is Not Always to Learn a Full Distribution
Some losses estimate a full probability distribution. Others deliberately estimate less structure because that is all the decision requires.








Desired object
Example objective
Population optimum or interpretation




conditional distribution
log loss / cross-entropy
\(p^*(y\mid x)\) when the model is well specified


conditional mean
squared error
\(\mathbb E[Y\mid X=x]\)


conditional median
absolute error
a median of \(Y\mid X=x\)


conditional quantile
pinball loss
\(q_\tau(Y\mid X=x)\)


decision boundary
hinge loss
a margin-separated classifier


ordering
pairwise ranking loss
relative preferences between candidates


representation geometry
contrastive or metric loss
invariances and separations defined by pairs


behavior
policy objective
actions that maximize expected utility



Learning a calibrated distribution is valuable when downstream users need probabilities, uncertainty, simulation, or many different decisions. It can be unnecessary excess structure when only one boundary or ranking matters.

title: Losses from First Principles
section: “Assuming a Distribution” Is Not a Binary Property
text:
“Assuming a Distribution” Is Not a Binary Property
The same formula can have both a likelihood derivation and a weaker decision-theoretic interpretation.
For example, if
\[
Y\mid X=x\sim\mathcal N(f_\theta(x),\sigma^2),
\]
then Gaussian negative log-likelihood reduces to scaled MSE. This is an explicit observation-model assumption. But independently,
\[
\arg\min_a\mathbb E[(Y-a)^2\mid X=x]
=
\mathbb E[Y\mid X=x],
\]
whenever the expectation exists. MSE therefore elicits the conditional mean even when the residuals are not Gaussian. Similarly, MAE is Laplace NLL under one model but elicits a conditional median much more generally.
Ask two separate questions:

Likelihood question: under which probabilistic model is this loss an NLL or divergence?
Elicitation question: which statistic or decision does its population minimizer recover without that model being literally true?

Every objective still contains assumptions—about support, noise, costs, invariances, sampling, or teacher reliability—even when it does not specify a normalized density.

title: Losses from First Principles
section: Why Discriminative versus Generative Is Secondary
text:
Why Discriminative versus Generative Is Secondary
“Discriminative” and “generative” describe model factorization more naturally than they describe loss functions:
\[
\text{discriminative: }p_\theta(y\mid x),
\qquad
\text{generative: }p_\theta(x)\text{ or }p_\theta(x,y).
\]
Cross-entropy demonstrates the limitation of using this as the primary loss taxonomy:








Use of cross-entropy
Target distribution
Role




image classification
labels conditioned on an image
discriminative prediction


next-token prediction
next tokens conditioned on a prefix
generative density modeling


knowledge distillation
teacher outputs conditioned on an input or state
teacher-supervised transfer



The algebra is nearly identical. What changes is the target, the sampled state, and the meaning of a successful optimum.

title: Losses from First Principles
section: A Better Map of the Loss Notes
text:
A Better Map of the Loss Notes

Prediction and decision objectives
Use Prediction and Decision Losses when the goal is a label, point estimate, boundary, margin, or ranking. It covers:

proper scoring rules and calibrated classification
logistic regression, CE, BCE, label smoothing, and focal loss
margin and ranking surrogates
mean, median, robust, heteroscedastic, quantile, and count regression



Distribution-learning objectives
Use Distribution Learning Losses when the model must represent or sample from a high-dimensional distribution and direct likelihood is exact, latent, or unavailable. It covers:

exact autoregressive likelihood and next-token prediction
KL geometry
variational likelihood and the VAE ELBO
sample-based adversarial discrepancies
diffusion denoising and score-learning abstractions



Representation objectives
Use Representation Learning from First Principles for contrastive, metric, reconstruction, redundancy-reduction, and predictive objectives. These losses specify which information and invariances a representation should preserve rather than directly specifying a final decision.


Teacher-supervised objectives
Use Distillation: Learning from a Teacher when supervision comes from another model. Distillation can train a classifier, generator, representation, or policy, so it is a cross-cutting supervision mechanism—not a subtype of generative modeling.
The Cursor continual-training case study shows all four axes changing together: production supplies states, the current policy supplies actions, users and tools supply reward, and a reference policy or feedback-conditioned teacher supplies KL anchors.

title: Losses from First Principles
text:
A Loss-Design Procedure
Given a new problem:

Write the real decision, generation, or representation goal.
Decide whether you need a full distribution or only a functional/decision.
State what observations and supervisory signals are actually available.
Choose a proper score, surrogate, divergence, bound, critic, or utility whose optimum is aligned with that target.
Write the expectation distribution and reduction explicitly.
Check support, calibration, robustness, and train–deployment mismatch.
Only then choose a numerically stable parameterization and implementation.

Two objectives may have the same optimum yet very different gradients. A statistically correct objective can also fail when its estimator has high variance, its sampling distribution misses important states, or its parameterization makes optimization difficult.

text:

title: Distillation: Learning from a Teacher
text:
Let \(q\) denote a teacher and \(p_\theta\) a student. Distillation transfers information exposed by the teacher that is not contained in a single hard label:

uncertainty across classes or tokens
similarities between alternatives
intermediate representations
generated solutions or trajectories
behavior on states selected by either teacher or student

The defining property is not one particular formula. It is that the training target comes from another model. A distilled student may be discriminative, generative, representational, or policy-like.
Three choices define a distillation objective:

What is matched? Outputs, logits, features, relations, sequences, or behavior.
Where is it matched? Data inputs, teacher-generated inputs, or student-generated/on-policy states.
How is it matched? Forward KL, reverse KL, MSE, cosine distance, sequence NLL, or an RL-style objective.

title: Distillation: Learning from a Teacher
text:
Let \(q\) denote a teacher and \(p_\theta\) a student. Distillation transfers information exposed by the teacher that is not contained in a single hard label:

uncertainty across classes or tokens
similarities between alternatives
intermediate representations
generated solutions or trajectories
behavior on states selected by either teacher or student

The defining property is not one particular formula. It is that the training target comes from another model. A distilled student may be discriminative, generative, representational, or policy-like.
Three choices define a distillation objective:

What is matched? Outputs, logits, features, relations, sequences, or behavior.
Where is it matched? Data inputs, teacher-generated inputs, or student-generated/on-policy states.
How is it matched? Forward KL, reverse KL, MSE, cosine distance, sequence NLL, or an RL-style objective.

title: Distillation: Learning from a Teacher
text:
Output Distillation: Soft Targets
For class or token logits \(z^T\) and \(z^S\), temperature \(\tau\) defines
\[
q_\tau(i\mid x)
=
\operatorname{softmax}\left(\frac{z_i^T}{\tau}\right),
\qquad
p_{\theta,\tau}(i\mid x)
=
\operatorname{softmax}\left(\frac{z_i^S}{\tau}\right).
\]
Classical output distillation minimizes forward KL:
\[
\mathcal L_{\mathrm{KD}}
=
\tau^2
\operatorname{KL}
\left(q_\tau(\cdot\mid x)\|p_{\theta,\tau}(\cdot\mid x)\right).
\]
The teacher supplies the expectation, so missing a teacher-supported class is costly. The entropy of \(q_\tau\) is constant with respect to the student; therefore this is equivalent to soft-label cross-entropy up to a constant.






NoteOne-hot targets: CE = forward KL = NLL



If the target is one-hot at the observed class \(y\), then \(q(i\mid x)=\mathbf{1}[i=y]\) and its entropy is zero: \(H(q)=0\). Thus the losses are exactly equal:
\[
\operatorname{CE}(q,p_\theta)
= \operatorname{KL}(q\|p_\theta) + H(q)
= \operatorname{KL}(q\|p_\theta)
= -\log p_\theta(y\mid x)
= \operatorname{NLL}(y,p_\theta).
\]
This equality uses forward KL, from target to student, with the same predicted distribution and loss scaling. For soft targets, CE and forward KL differ by the target entropy, but still have the same student gradients when the target is fixed.
To see why, expand the identity for a soft target:
\[
\underbrace{-\sum_i q_i\log p_{\theta,i}}_{\operatorname{CE}(q,p_\theta)}
= \underbrace{\sum_i q_i\log\frac{q_i}{p_{\theta,i}}}_{\operatorname{KL}(q\|p_\theta)}
+ \underbrace{\left(-\sum_i q_i\log q_i\right)}_{H(q)}.
\]
When the teacher target \(q\) is fixed, \(H(q)\) does not depend on the student parameters \(\theta\), so its gradient is zero:
\[
\nabla_\theta\operatorname{CE}(q,p_\theta)
= \nabla_\theta\operatorname{KL}(q\|p_\theta).
\]
The loss values differ, but they produce the same student updates under the same scaling and optimizer. For example, if \(q=(0.5,0.5)\), then \(H(q)=\log 2\approx0.693\) (using natural logarithms). CE is always KL plus \(0.693\), regardless of the student prediction. When \(p_\theta=q\), KL is zero while CE is \(0.693\). For a one-hot target, \(H(q)=0\), so even the loss values are identical.


Larger \(\tau\) reveals relative preferences among non-maximum classes. Dividing logits by \(\tau\) also shrinks their gradients, so the conventional \(\tau^2\) factor approximately preserves gradient scale when comparing temperatures.
A common supervised mixture is
\[
\mathcal L
=
(1-\lambda)\operatorname{CE}(y,p_{\theta,1})
+
\lambda\tau^2
\operatorname{KL}(q_\tau\|p_{\theta,\tau}).
\]
The hard label anchors the student to observed outcomes; the soft target transfers the teacher’s richer geometry. A teacher can also be wrong, biased, or miscalibrated, so the mixture is not automatically better than either term.

Minimal implementation

import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F


def forward_kl_distillation(student_logits, teacher_logits, temperature=2.0):
    """Teacher-to-student KL, averaged over the batch."""
    log_p_student = F.log_softmax(student_logits / temperature, dim=-1)
    p_teacher = F.softmax(teacher_logits / temperature, dim=-1)
    return (
        F.kl_div(
            log_p_student,
            p_teacher,
            reduction="batchmean",
        )
        * temperature**2
    )


torch.manual_seed(0)
teacher_logits = torch.randn(8, 10)
close_student = teacher_logits + 0.01 * torch.randn_like(teacher_logits)
far_student = torch.randn_like(teacher_logits)
assert forward_kl_distillation(
    close_student, teacher_logits
) < forward_kl_distillation(far_student, teacher_logits)

Detach teacher outputs unless the teacher is intentionally co-trained. Otherwise the objective may change the target while the student chases it.

title: Distillation: Learning from a Teacher
section: KL Direction and State Distribution Are Independent
text:
KL Direction and State Distribution Are Independent
Two design axes are often conflated.

Divergence direction
Forward KL uses teacher probability as its local weighting:
\[
\operatorname{KL}(q\|p_\theta)
=
\mathbb E_{a\sim q}
\left[\log q(a)-\log p_\theta(a)\right].
\]
It encourages the student to cover alternatives supported by the teacher. Reverse KL uses student probability as its local weighting:
\[
\operatorname{KL}(p_\theta\|q)
=
\mathbb E_{a\sim p_\theta}
\left[\log p_\theta(a)-\log q(a)\right].
\]
It strongly discourages choices the student makes that the teacher considers unlikely, but can be mode-seeking. These are tendencies; capacity, support, temperature, and optimization also matter.


State or input distribution
The context \(h\) at which the distributions are compared can come from:








State source
What it teaches
Main risk




observed/data inputs
behavior near the training distribution
misses student-induced errors


teacher trajectories
states a strong policy visits
student may not reach them


student trajectories
recovery on deployment-like states
teacher may be unreliable off distribution


mixture or replay
broader coverage
weighting becomes another design choice



One can use forward or reverse KL under any of these state distributions. “Use reverse KL” does not by itself make an objective on-policy.

title: Distillation: Learning from a Teacher
text:
On-Policy Distillation for Autoregressive Models
Teacher forcing trains on data prefixes, whereas generation visits prefixes created by the student. On-policy distillation lets the student generate a prefix \(h_t\) and asks the teacher to evaluate that encountered state.
A common local objective is
\[
\mathcal L_{\mathrm{OPD}}(h_t)
=
\operatorname{KL}
\left(
p_\theta(\cdot\mid h_t)
\middle\|
q(\cdot\mid h_t)
\right).
\]
For a sampled action \(a_t\sim p_\theta(\cdot\mid h_t)\),
\[
r_t
=
\log q(a_t\mid h_t)
-
\log p_\theta(a_t\mid h_t)
\]
can act as a dense token-level reward. Full-vocabulary KL is available when teacher logits can be queried; sampled implementations require care because the sampling distribution itself depends on \(\theta\).
On-policy training addresses state-distribution mismatch. Reverse KL chooses the local discrepancy geometry. They solve different problems.
Potential failures include:

the student reaches prefixes outside the teacher’s reliable region
reverse KL removes useful diversity
teacher querying dominates training cost
sampled gradient estimates have high variance
locally imitating next-token probabilities does not preserve sequence-level behavior

On-Policy Distillation develops the state- distribution view. MiniLLM studies reverse-KL distillation for generative language models. More recent trust-region methods such as TrOPD restrict unreliable updates and can mix forward-KL guidance into uncertain regions.
For a production case, Composer 2.5 constructs a local teacher by inserting textual corrective feedback at a problematic turn, then adds an on-policy KL loss while retaining the trajectory-level RL objective. See Cursor’s Continual Training Loop.

title: Distillation: Learning from a Teacher
text:
Sequence Distillation
When teacher logits are unavailable or expensive to store, generate teacher outputs \(\widetilde y\sim q(\cdot\mid x)\) and train by ordinary NLL:
\[
\mathcal L_{\mathrm{seq}}
=
-\log p_\theta(\widetilde y\mid x).
\]
This converts the teacher into a data generator. It is simple and works across different APIs or vocabularies, but a sampled sequence exposes far less information than the full teacher distribution. Decoding also changes the target: greedy outputs reduce diversity, while sampled outputs introduce variance and possible errors.
For reasoning models, a teacher can supply final answers, rationales, tool-use traces, or verified trajectories. These are different supervisory objects. Imitating a rationale’s tokens does not prove that the student has learned the same internal algorithm, and incorrect rationales can transfer persuasive failure modes.

title: Distillation: Learning from a Teacher
text:
Feature and Relational Distillation
Output matching is not the only transfer channel.

Feature matching
Given teacher and student representations \(h^T(x)\) and \(h^S(x)\),
\[
\mathcal L_{\mathrm{feature}}
=
\left\|P_\phi(h^S(x))-h^T(x)\right\|_2^2,
\]
where \(P_\phi\) aligns dimensions. Cosine distance or attention-map matching may be used instead. Layer alignment is an architectural hypothesis, not a neutral implementation detail: a smaller student may organize computation differently.


Relational matching
Rather than matching coordinates, match relations within a batch:
\[
\mathcal L_{\mathrm{relation}}
=
\sum_{i,j}
\left(
\operatorname{sim}(h_i^S,h_j^S)
-
\operatorname{sim}(h_i^T,h_j^T)
\right)^2.
\]
This preserves teacher geometry while allowing rotations or different feature bases. It connects distillation to Representation Learning.
Self-distillation methods such as BYOL- and DINO-style training use a momentum or stop-gradient teacher to create a stable target. Their main challenge is not compression but preventing representational collapse.

title: Distillation: Learning from a Teacher
text:
Learning from an Unreliable Teacher
The strongest practical evidence here supports checking teacher-generated supervision against external feedback, rather than assuming that confidence or agreement makes a target correct. The following are documented practices and findings, not a universal recipe for arbitrary teacher noise.

Filter generated solutions using correctness signals. DeepSeek-R1 samples multiple reasoning responses, retains those judged correct, and applies readability filters. Its smaller Qwen/Llama students receive SFT on the resulting curated dataset. Some judgments use a model supplied with ground truth, so the pipeline is not entirely rule-verified. See DeepSeek-R1 (2025), §§2.3.3–2.4.
For coding, execute the proposed solution and validate tool use. Qwen3-Coder-Next filters unsuccessful trajectories and malformed tool calls, and verifies SFT responses using compiler, runtime, and environment feedback. This is a concrete alternative to trusting the generator’s self-assessment. See Qwen3-Coder-Next (2026), §§3.1.2 and 4.1.
Do not equate confidence with correctness. Guo et al. show that modern networks can be miscalibrated and study temperature scaling on held-out data. Calibration can improve probability estimates; a positive scalar temperature preserves class ranking and cannot fix a wrong top prediction. See On Calibration of Modern Neural Networks (ICML 2017). For fitting methods and calibration-oriented training, see Model Calibration: From CTR/CVR to Calibrated Decisions.
Select by student task performance, not teacher imitation alone. Stanton et al. find that closer teacher matching does not always improve generalization. This supports evaluating downstream quality separately from distillation loss. See Does Knowledge Distillation Really Work? (NeurIPS 2021).

A practical synthesis is to retain trusted supervision, filter teacher outputs where meaningful verification is available, and compare against a student trained without distillation on held-out tasks. Tune the teacher contribution on validation data; use a separate test set for the final comparison. These are evaluation recommendations drawn from the evidence above, not an established optimal weighting rule. Passing tests does not prove every reasoning step correct, and shared teacher errors can survive consensus.

title: Distillation: Learning from a Teacher
text:
Multi-Teacher Distillation and MoE
Multiple teachers can provide complementary supervision: for example, one specializes in repository repair, another in web development, and another in single-turn code questions. There are distinct ways to combine them.

Combining distributions or selecting a teacher
For teachers \(q_1,\ldots,q_K\) over the same output space, a generic probability mixture is
\[
\bar q(\cdot\mid x)=\sum_{k=1}^K a_k(x)q_k(\cdot\mid x),
\qquad a_k(x)\geq0,\quad\sum_k a_k(x)=1.
\]
At a fixed input and temperature, with fixed weights and teachers,
\[
\sum_k a_k\operatorname{KL}(q_k\|p_\theta)
=\operatorname{KL}(\bar q\|p_\theta)
+\sum_k a_k\operatorname{KL}(q_k\|\bar q).
\]
The last term is independent of the student, so weighted forward KL to individual teachers has the same student gradient as forward KL to their probability mixture. This is an algebraic identity, not a claim about the implementation of the reports below. It does not extend unchanged to reverse KL or averaging raw logits.
Alternatively, select a specialist \(k=d(x)\) for each task, or collect and verify generated solutions from several teachers for sequence-level SFT. Direct token-distribution matching requires compatible token spaces or an explicit alignment; text-based distillation can cross tokenizer boundaries.


Recent coding and agentic model examples
Qwen3-Coder-Next (2026). The report describes specialists for Web Development, User Experience, Single-turn RL, and Software Engineering, trained from a shared starting model and distilled back into the SFT model. The deployed model is an MoE with 80B total and 3B active parameters. Section 4.2.5 documents consolidation but does not specify the distillation loss, teacher weights, or whether rollouts are on-policy; those details should not be inferred. See the technical report, §§1 and 4.2.5.
MiMo-V2-Flash (2026). This 309B-total/15B-active MoE uses Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation (MOPD). A teacher is selected by prompt domain; the student generates the trajectories. Its token-level signal is based on
\[
\log q_{d(x)}(y_t\mid h_t)-\log p_\theta(y_t\mid h_t),
\]
corresponding to reverse-KL distillation. The training surrogate combines this signal with outcome-reward advantages and corrects training/inference policy mismatch. Thus MOPD here means domain-specialist supervision on student rollouts, not averaging every teacher on every token. See the technical report, §4.4.


How this combines with MoE








Concept
What is selected or transferred?
Where it operates




Multi-teacher supervision
A full teacher model or a mixture of teacher targets
Training supervision


Sparse MoE routing
Internal expert subnetworks for each token
Forward passes during training and inference


Distillation into one deployed model
Behaviors from teachers transferred into student parameters
Removes the need to serve the teacher ensemble



A domain teacher is a complete model; it is not necessarily one internal MoE expert. Distilling several teachers into an MoE student does not imply a one-to-one mapping between teachers and expert subnetworks. The student can retain internal MoE routing while deployment uses only that single model.
MoE also introduces a concrete on-policy training concern: MiMo reports replaying the expert routes recorded during rollout to reduce routing mismatch between inference and training. See MiMo-V2-Flash, §4.6.1. Conversely, an MoE teacher can supervise a dense student: DeepSeek-R1 distills into dense Qwen and Llama models through curated outputs, without copying its internal routing. See DeepSeek-R1, §2.4.
For an experiment, compare each single teacher with the multi-teacher setup under a matched student-training budget, and report results by domain as well as in aggregate. This is a suggested evaluation design: the reports establish working systems, not that every additional teacher or MoE architecture improves distillation.
