title: Model Calibration: From CTR/CVR to Calibrated Decisions
text:
Calibration asks whether predicted probabilities agree with observed frequencies. A model assigning 0.02 to many ad impressions should see clicks on about 2% of them. A model reporting 0.8 probability that its answer is correct should be right on about 80% of comparable predictions.
This note covers post-hoc calibration, advertising-specific data problems, and calibration-oriented language-model training. The recent-work discussion was checked on October 5, 2026. Jev’s RLCD is treated as a publicly stated objective; its undisclosed implementation is not reconstructed from related papers.

title: Model Calibration: From CTR/CVR to Calibrated Decisions
section: Define the Probability Before Calibrating It
text:
Define the Probability Before Calibrating It
For a binary outcome \(Y\) and prediction \(p(X)\), population calibration means
\[
\mathbb E[Y\mid p(X)=s]=s.
\]
In finite data, estimate this using groups of nearby predictions. Calibration is a property of a predictor on a distribution, not a certificate that an individual prediction is correct.








Setting
Probability being estimated
Relevant evaluation population




CTR
\(P(C=1\mid X)\)
Served impressions


Post-click CVR
\(P(V_H=1\mid C=1,X)\)
Clicked impressions, with conversion horizon \(H\)


Click-through conversion rate
\(P(C=1,V_H=1\mid X)\)
Served impressions


Multiclass prediction
\(P(Y=k\mid X)\) for each class
Labeled examples from the target population


Answer confidence
\(P(\text{answer is correct}\mid X,\text{answer},\text{available evidence})\)
Answers generated by the deployed model and decoding procedure



A constant predictor equal to the population base rate can be calibrated but useless for ranking. Conversely, a strictly increasing transformation can preserve ranking while damaging probabilities. Calibration, discrimination, and decision quality therefore need separate evaluation.
For multiclass models, top-label calibration checks confidence in the selected class. Classwise calibration checks each class probability. Neither should be silently substituted for calibration of the entire probability vector.

title: Model Calibration: From CTR/CVR to Calibrated Decisions
section: Proper Scoring Rules: Why CE and Brier Are Natural Baselines
text:
Proper Scoring Rules: Why CE and Brier Are Natural Baselines
A loss is strictly proper if its expected value is uniquely minimized by the true outcome distribution. Two binary examples are
\[
\ell_{\log}(p,y)=-y\log p-(1-y)\log(1-p),
\qquad
\ell_{\mathrm{Brier}}(p,y)=(p-y)^2.
\]
If \(Y\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(q)\), then
\[
\mathbb E[(p-Y)^2]=(p-q)^2+q(1-q),
\]
so the optimum is \(p=q\). For log loss, the excess expected loss above the optimum is \(\operatorname{KL}(\operatorname{Bern}(q)\|\operatorname{Bern}(p))\). This connects calibration to cross-entropy and distillation. See Gneiting and Raftery (2007), Strictly Proper Scoring Rules.
Training with CE already has the right population target. Finite data, restricted model capacity, regularization, optimization, and train/serve mismatch can still produce miscalibration. A proper objective is an incentive, not a finite-sample guarantee. Brier and NLL also measure predictive quality beyond calibration, so neither is a pure calibration-error metric.

title: Model Calibration: From CTR/CVR to Calibrated Decisions
text:
Classical Post-Hoc Methods
Freeze the base predictor. Fit a small mapping on a separate calibration set, then evaluate it on untouched test data. Here \(z\) is a raw binary score or logit, \(p\) is an existing probability, and \(\sigma\) is the sigmoid.








Method
Mapping or fit
Useful regime and limitation




Intercept correction
\(\sigma(z+b)\)
Correct a probability-level offset under an appropriate shift model; cannot fix arbitrary shape errors


Platt/logistic scaling
\(\sigma(az+b)\)
Low-variance baseline; \(a>0\) preserves ranking, but a sigmoid may be too restrictive


Temperature scaling
\(\operatorname{softmax}(z/T)\), \(T>0\)
One parameter for multiclass logits; preserves the selected class, cannot correct class-specific biases


Histogram binning
Replace each bin by its empirical positive rate
Simple diagnostic and baseline; sensitive to bins and sparse counts, not necessarily monotone


Isotonic regression
Fit a nondecreasing map minimizing squared error
Flexible scalar correction; needs sufficient data and introduces ties


Beta calibration
\(\sigma(a\log p-b\log(1-p)+c)\)
Flexible correction for asymmetric probability distortion; \(a,b\geq0\) ensure monotonicity



Platt scaling and isotonic regression are compared in Niculescu-Mizil and Caruana (ICML 2005). Fit their parameters using held-out predictions, not the predictions on which the base model was trained.
Guo et al. (ICML 2017) find temperature scaling effective on their neural-network benchmarks. It fits \(T\) by minimizing calibration-set NLL. For a binary logit this becomes \(\sigma(z/T)\); the missing intercept matters when the problem is a changed base rate rather than excessive sharpness.
Beta calibration (AISTATS 2017) includes the identity mapping at \(a=b=1,c=0\). This distinguishes it from fitting \(\sigma(ap+b)\) directly to probabilities. Clip inputs away from 0 and 1 for numerical stability. A multiclass extension is Dirichlet calibration (NeurIPS 2019), which transforms log probabilities with a learned linear map followed by softmax; its extra parameters require regularization and more calibration data.

title: Model Calibration: From CTR/CVR to Calibrated Decisions
section: CTR/CVR: Correct the Data-Generating Problem First
text:
CTR/CVR: Correct the Data-Generating Problem First

Negative downsampling and weighted BCE
Suppose all positive examples are kept, while negatives are retained with probability \(s\). Let \(p_s\) be the posterior in the sampled population. Bayes’ rule gives the production posterior
\[
p=\frac{s p_s}{1-p_s+s p_s},
\qquad
\operatorname{logit}(p)=\operatorname{logit}(p_s)+\log s.
\]
For \(s=0.1\) and \(p_s=0.2\), the corrected probability is about \(0.0244\), not \(0.02\): multiplying by \(s\) is only a small-probability approximation. He et al., Practical Lessons from Predicting Clicks on Ads at Facebook (ADKDD 2014), §6.3 describes this recalibration after negative downsampling.
The formula assumes class-dependent sampling with the stated retention rates and an accurate sampled posterior. Feature-dependent sampling requires the corresponding conditional rates. Do not apply the correction twice if loss weights or an existing calibrator already restore the target population.
A related derivation: weighted BCE with positive and negative weights \(w_1,w_0\) has pointwise optimum
\[
p_w=\frac{w_1q}{w_1q+w_0(1-q)},
\qquad
\operatorname{logit}(q)=\operatorname{logit}(p_w)-\log\frac{w_1}{w_0}.
\]
Thus class weighting changes what the raw output estimates. Record sampling and weighting choices before interpreting a score as CTR or CVR.


Delayed conversions and label maturity
Define conversion within a particular horizon \(H\). A click from one hour ago with no conversion is not yet a known negative for seven-day conversion. Fitting a calibrator on such provisional zeros calibrates toward the wrong observed target.
Use fully matured labels for the chosen horizon, or explicitly model delay and censoring when freshness requires partially observed data. Chapelle, Modeling Delayed Feedback in Display Advertising (KDD 2014) models both conversion probability and conversion delay. A downstream sigmoid cannot by itself repair incorrect labels.


CVR selection and the probability product
For click-attributed conversions,
\[
P(C=1,V_H=1\mid X)
=P(C=1\mid X)P(V_H=1\mid C=1,X).
\]
ESMM (SIGIR 2018) uses this structure to jointly learn CTR and click-through conversion on the impression space, addressing clicked-only training and sparse conversion data. It is a modeling approach, not a post-hoc calibration guarantee.
Evaluate CVR on the relevant clicked population and the joint probability on impressions. Even if two component scores each pass marginal reliability checks, their product need not be calibrated: those checks do not establish that both scores equal the required conditional probabilities. Avoid treating logged CVR as a causal conversion probability under an arbitrary new serving policy.


Field-aware calibration
Overall bias can hide opposite errors across campaigns, placements, devices, or countries. For a slice \(g\), a useful aggregate diagnostic is
\[
\mathrm{P/O}_g=\frac{\sum_{i\in g}p_i}{\sum_{i\in g}y_i}.
\]
Here values above one mean overprediction. This ratio is undefined with no observed positives and unstable with very few; report counts and uncertainty. A ratio near one does not imply calibration within the slice’s score bins.
Pan et al., Field-aware Calibration (WWW 2020) introduces field-level calibration metrics and a neural calibrator of the form
\[
p_{\mathrm{cal}}(x)=\sigma\big(\eta(z(x))+g(x)\big),
\]
combining a scalar logit transformation with a feature-dependent correction, fitted by log loss on development data. Because features affect the mapping, it can change ranking across examples. Check both ranking and calibration; regularize sparse fields instead of fitting an unconstrained map per tiny segment.

title: Model Calibration: From CTR/CVR to Calibrated Decisions
section: Evaluation and a Practical Fitting Workflow
text:
Evaluation and a Practical Fitting Workflow
For bins \(B_b\), binary expected calibration error is commonly estimated as
\[
\widehat{\mathrm{ECE}}
=\sum_b\frac{|B_b|}{n}\left|
\frac{1}{|B_b|}\sum_{i\in B_b}p_i
-\frac{1}{|B_b|}\sum_{i\in B_b}y_i
\right|.
\]
For top-label ECE, replace \(p_i\) with maximum class probability and \(y_i\) with the indicator that the selected class is correct. State which definition you use. Bin choices and whether all classes are evaluated can change conclusions; see Nixon et al., Measuring Calibration in Deep Learning (2019).
Report reliability plots with bin counts, NLL, Brier score, ranking quality, and domain-specific aggregate bias together. For rare events, a small absolute ECE can conceal a large relative error; inspect the low-probability region and important slices. Bootstrap by the relevant independent unit, such as user or time block, when observations are correlated.
A recommended workflow, synthesizing the methods above:

Define the event, horizon, population, and any selection or weighting.
Train the predictor; collect predictions on a later calibration window with mature labels. Reserve a still-later test window. Keep tuning separate from final evaluation, using additional splits or cross-validation.
Compare uncalibrated outputs with a simple logistic/temperature baseline, then isotonic or beta calibration. Add feature-aware calibration only when slice-level evidence and sample size justify it.
Select using probability quality and the downstream decision objective, not one ECE number. Check rare slices and distribution shifts.
Version the predictor and calibrator together. Monitor fresh outcomes and refit when their relationship changes; a calibrator fitted before a model update need not remain valid afterwards.

For binary actions with false-positive cost \(c_{FP}\) and false-negative cost \(c_{FN}\), and zero cost for correct decisions, expected-cost minimization acts positive when
\[
p>\frac{c_{FP}}{c_{FP}+c_{FN}}.
\]
This explains why calibrated probabilities matter beyond AUC. For selective answering, also measure risk–coverage: error rate among accepted answers versus fraction accepted. Choose an acceptance threshold on validation data, then report test performance at that fixed threshold. Finding the best threshold after observing test labels is not a deployment guarantee.

title: Model Calibration: From CTR/CVR to Calibrated Decisions
section: Language Models: What Exactly Is Being Calibrated?
text:
Language Models: What Exactly Is Being Calibrated?
Token likelihood is the probability of a particular string under the language model. It is not automatically the probability that the string’s claim is true. Multiple equivalent answers, prompt format, length, and decoding all complicate that interpretation.



Approach
Confidence signal
Relevant work




Train explicit confidence expression
A generated numeric or verbal estimate
Lin, Hilton, and Evans (2022) show supervised learning of verbalized uncertainty


Ask the model to assess an answer
Probability of a correctness judgment, such as \(P(\mathrm{True})\)
Kadavath et al. (2022) study self-evaluation and knowledge prediction


Calibrate a fixed score
Map an answer score to empirical correctness
Apply held-out logistic/isotonic calibration to the deployed answer-generation pipeline


Change training incentives
Reward both answering and honest probability reporting
Rewarding Doubt, RLCR, and newer methods below



Keep the answer generator, prompt, tools, and sampling procedure fixed when fitting a post-hoc confidence model. Otherwise the correctness event being predicted changes. A monotone binary calibrator adjusts the numeric scale; it cannot turn an uninformative ordering of confidence into a useful ranking of correct versus incorrect answers.

title: Model Calibration: From CTR/CVR to Calibrated Decisions
section: Jev and RLCD: Public Objective Versus Disclosed Methods
text:
Jev and RLCD: Public Objective Versus Disclosed Methods
TypeSafe introduced Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions (RLCD) as the training approach behind Jev in its September 15, 2026 launch post. The public material describes typed probabilistic decisions but does not provide a reproducible reward, optimizer, or complete training recipe. Its workflow comparisons use reference-model probabilities; agreement with those references is different from calibration against observed outcomes.
The product’s confidence field also deserves care: TypeSafe’s documentation defines it as a statistic derived from the returned distribution, with zero at a uniform distribution and one at complete concentration. It is not itself automatically the probability that the chosen answer is correct. Evaluate the relevant returned probabilities against labels, and validate any routing threshold on your own target tasks.






NoteDo not infer Jev’s algorithm from its name



The proper-score objectives below are published related methods, not a claim about Jev’s internal implementation. Also, the earlier RLCD: Reinforcement Learning from Contrastive Distillation (2023) is a different method with the same acronym.



Rewarding Doubt: a proper score for reported confidence
Rewarding Doubt (2025) trains a model to express confidence alongside its answer using a logarithmic reward. Let \(Z\in\{0,1\}\) indicate whether that answer is correct and let \(c\) be the reported probability:
\[
R_{\log}(c,Z)=Z\log c+(1-Z)\log(1-c).
\]
For a fixed answer whose correctness probability is \(q\), expected reward is maximized at \(c=q\). This supplies a direct incentive for honest confidence. It does not imply that arbitrary joint optimization of answers and confidence will also maximize accuracy: changing the answer changes the event being scored. Population optimality and empirical calibration must be distinguished.


RLCR: reward correctness and calibration together
Beyond Binary Rewards: Training LMs to Reason about Their Uncertainty (2025; ICLR 2026) proposes RLCR, with
\[
R_{\mathrm{RLCR}}(c,Z)=Z-(c-Z)^2.
\]
The first term rewards a correct answer, while the second scores its reported confidence. Under the paper’s idealized model, for an answer with success probability \(q\),
\[
\mathbb E[R]=q-(c-q)^2-q(1-q).
\]
The best report is \(c=q\), and the resulting reward is \(q^2\), increasing with answer quality. This makes the two incentives explicit. The theorem concerns ideal optima; finite-capacity RL with imperfect correctness judgments still needs held-out evaluation. The reported scalar confidence is different from a full categorical distribution over all possible answers.


Recent related work and evidence limits



Work
Contribution relevant to calibration
How to interpret the evidence




Calibrating LLMs with Semantic-level Reward (May 2026)
CSR scores semantic answer distributions rather than requiring verbalized confidence
A research preprint; semantic grouping and correctness evaluation are part of the measurement pipeline


Scaling with Confidence (July 2026)
C3RL combines correctness, confidence calibration, and reference-accuracy rewards; uses confidence for adaptive test-time compute
A proposed alternative reward design, not evidence of Jev’s recipe


OpenJev-RLCD (September 30, 2026)
Independent implementation: calibrate the answer distribution after a sampled rationale, then reinforce reasoning with a proper-score reward and a KL anchor
Qwen3-1.7B experiments on two reasoning tasks plus an annotator-disagreement setting; a very recent preprint, not an official Jev reproduction



OpenJev-RLCD separates scoring each rationale’s answer distribution from scoring an average across rationales. For negative Brier score, averaging distributions adds a variance term relative to averaging their scores, so the objectives differ. Its reported selective-prediction improvements are limited to the studied setup; they do not establish universal superiority over supervised CE plus calibration. See OpenJev-RLCD, §§3–5.
Independent studies such as Just Ask Jev (September 2026) and JevAdvBench (September 2026) evaluate Jev’s behavior and robustness. They are useful application evidence, not disclosures of its training algorithm or guarantees of target-domain calibration.

title: Model Calibration: From CTR/CVR to Calibrated Decisions
text:
When Is RL Actually Needed?
For a fixed labeled classification problem with a differentiable probability head, CE or Brier can be optimized directly. Calling negative Brier a reward does not make policy-gradient training necessary. The classical calibration baselines should remain part of the comparison.
RL becomes relevant when training must change sampled reasoning, tool use, or sequential decisions that influence the eventual prediction or observed outcome. Proper scores can supply a calibration incentive, but the choice of what is scored matters: a full outcome distribution, the correctness of a selected answer, and success after taking an action are different targets.
For action-dependent outcomes, specify the action and policy in the target probability. Passive labels collected under an old policy may not identify success under a new one. For annotator disagreement, decide whether to predict a majority label or the distribution of judgments; additional reasoning cannot be assumed to remove disagreement inherent in that target.

title: Model Calibration: From CTR/CVR to Calibrated Decisions
text:
Interview Questions and Exercises

Why can a base-rate predictor be calibrated but unhelpful?
Derive negative-downsampling correction and the weighted-BCE optimum.
Why might temperature scaling fail to correct a shifted CTR base rate?
Why do calibrated CTR and CVR scores not guarantee a calibrated product?
How do you evaluate seven-day CVR without treating pending events as negatives?
Why does a proper score incentivize honest probabilities? What assumptions separate that statement from a production guarantee?
Derive the optimal confidence and answer-quality incentive under RLCR.
Compare event probability, answer correctness, token likelihood, and Jev’s distribution-derived confidence statistic.
Fit logistic, isotonic, and beta calibrators on a chronological split; compare NLL, Brier, reliability plots, P/O, and slice-level results.
Compare CE plus post-hoc calibration with a calibration-reward method using the same data and a reported compute budget; evaluate fixed-threshold risk–coverage on untouched tasks.

title: Agent Harness
text:
A foundation model maps context to tokens or structured actions. By itself, it does not own a durable workspace, execute tools, preserve state across context windows, enforce permissions, recover from failures, or decide when external work is complete.
An agent harness is the software system surrounding the model that supplies those capabilities. It determines how the model:

receives goals, rules, context, and observations
selects and invokes tools
iterates through a workflow
stores state and artifacts
delegates or monitors background work
verifies progress and completion
interacts with users at permission or clarification boundaries

Lilian Weng describes the harness as the deployment layer that orchestrates how the model thinks and plans, acts through tools, perceives and manages context, stores artifacts, and evaluates results. Her Harness Engineering for Self-Improvement is the main reference for this note.
A useful decomposition is
\[
\boxed{
\text{agent system}
=
\text{model}
+
\text{harness}
+
\text{environment}
}.
\]
The model supplies learned reasoning and generation. The harness supplies the runtime contract. The environment supplies files, applications, APIs, people, and consequences.

text:

An agent harness is the software system surrounding the model that supplies those capabilities. It determines how the model:

Lilian Weng describes the harness as the deployment layer that orchestrates how the model thinks and plans, acts through tools, perceives and manages context, stores artifacts, and evaluates results. Her Harness Engineering for Self-Improvement is the main reference for this note.
A useful decomposition is
\[
\boxed{
\text{agent system}
=
\text{model}
+
\text{harness}
+
\text{environment}
}.
\]
The model supplies learned reasoning and generation. The harness supplies the runtime contract. The environment supplies files, applications, APIs, people, and consequences.

title: Agent Harness
text:
2. What a Harness Is Not







Concept
Role




Foundation model
predicts text, decisions, or tool calls from context


Agent harness
turns model decisions into a controlled, stateful execution process


Agent framework
library used to build harnesses; it is not the configured system itself


Workflow
one control policy or graph implemented by the harness


Tool
a bounded capability exposed through the harness


Evaluation harness
runs tasks and computes measurements about a system



An evaluation harness measures behavior. An agent harness produces and controls behavior. An agent harness may call verifiers during execution, but that does not make it merely an evaluation framework.
The word “scaffold” is sometimes used similarly. “Harness” emphasizes the whole runtime boundary: execution, context, memory, permissions, observability, and workflow—not just a prompt template.

title: Agent Harness
text:
3. The First-Principles Problem
The harness exists because a model call is stateless and probabilistic, while a real task is stateful and governed by constraints.
Let \(M\) be a model, \(H\) a harness, \(e\) an environment, and \(x\) a task. We care about system behavior
\[
\tau\sim P(\tau\mid M,H,e,x),
\]
where trajectory \(\tau\) contains model decisions, tool calls, observations, state changes, and the final result. Harness design seeks to maximize expected utility:
\[
H^*
=
\arg\max_H
\mathbb E_{\tau}
\left[
R_{\text{task}}(\tau)
-\lambda_c C(\tau)
-\lambda_t T(\tau)
-\lambda_r R_{\text{risk}}(\tau)
\right].
\]
This framing yields several important insights:

Model quality and harness quality are confounded in end-to-end results.
More autonomy is not inherently better; it is useful only where adaptive decisions outperform deterministic code.
Reliability must come from system invariants, not from hoping the model remembers every rule on every turn.
The harness should make success observable and failure recoverable.


From predictor to closed-loop decision system
A model call is an open-loop predictor: it maps its current context to a proposed continuation or action. A harness turns repeated calls into feedback control:
\[
s_t
\xrightarrow{\text{predict and decide}}
a_t
\xrightarrow{\text{environment}}
o_{t+1}
\xrightarrow{\text{compare}}
\delta_t
\xrightarrow{\text{update}}
s_{t+1},
\]
where \(s_t\) is the harness’s current state estimate, \(o_{t+1}\) is an external observation, and \(\delta_t\) is the mismatch between expected and observed consequences. This is more precise than simply saying that an LLM “becomes an agent”:
\[
\boxed{\text{open-loop predictor}\rightarrow\text{closed-loop decision system}}.
\]
Most harness mechanisms can be located within this loop:








Decision-loop problem
Harness mechanism
Control role




What is currently true?
context, retrieval, memory, task state
state estimation


What might happen?
reasoning, planning, candidate generation
consequence prediction


What should happen next?
controller, routing, skills
action selection and abstraction


How can the system intervene or learn?
tools
actuation and sensing


Did reality disagree?
tests, verifiers, critics
surprise generation


Which assumption failed?
diagnosis and reflection
error attribution


What must survive?
artifacts, checkpoints, persistent memory
state update


Where may the agent go?
permissions and guardrails
reachable-state constraints


How does the system improve?
traces, evaluations, failure analysis
outer-loop learning



This view asks what information closes the loop. Adding more internal reasoning cannot correct a false belief as reliably as an environmental observation that distinguishes competing hypotheses.

title: Agent Harness
text:
4. The Basic Agent Loop






flowchart TD
    G[Goal and constraints] --> C[Compile current context]
    C --> M[Model decision]
    M --> D{Decision type}
    D -- Tool call --> P[Validate permissions and arguments]
    P --> X[Execute tool]
    X --> O[Normalize and record observation]
    O --> S[Update state and artifacts]
    S --> V[Check progress, limits, and failures]
    V -- Continue --> C
    D -- Candidate answer --> F[Verify completion conditions]
    F -- Incomplete --> S
    F -- Complete --> A[Return result]
    V -- Needs authority or clarification --> U[Ask user]
    U --> S






The model does not call the operating system or an API directly. It proposes an action; the harness validates, authorizes, executes, records, and returns a bounded observation. That indirection is the key control boundary.
OpenAI’s open-source Codex runtime is a concrete implementation of this loop. See Codex: Anatomy of an Open-Source Coding Agent for a source-level analysis of its turn loop, typed tool router, event protocol, persistence, and sandbox boundary.

Model decisions versus code decisions
Use the model when the choice requires semantic judgment under ambiguity. Use ordinary code when the rule is known:







Better handled by the model
Better handled by the harness




choosing a promising hypothesis
enforcing a maximum tool-call count


deciding what evidence is missing
validating JSON against a schema


interpreting an unfamiliar error
applying timeouts and retry limits


proposing a plan revision
checking an exit code


synthesizing several observations
requiring approval for a destructive action



Encoding deterministic invariants as prose wastes model capacity and makes them probabilistic.

title: Agent Harness
text:
5. Harness Components

5.1 Context compiler
The context compiler decides what the model sees on the next turn. It assembles:

immutable system and safety rules
task contract and user instructions
available tool interfaces
active plan and working state
relevant persistent memory and artifacts
recent observations and errors

It must resolve ordering, priority, truncation, compaction, and provenance. Simply appending every prior token eventually produces an expensive, noisy, and contradictory context.
Context layout also affects inference cost. A stable prompt prefix can reuse cached transformer computation, whereas reordering tools or rewriting old messages can invalidate that cache. Codex consequently treats model-visible history as append-oriented state, orders dynamic inputs deterministically, and represents environment or permission changes as new context items when possible. This suggests a further invariant:

Keep stable context stable. Compile semantic changes without gratuitously perturbing the reusable prefix.

In control terms, context and memory perform state estimation. From the full history
\[
h_t=(o_1,a_1,\ldots,o_t),
\]
the harness constructs a compact state \(s_t=\phi(h_t)\) that should preserve the information needed for future decisions:
\[
p(o_{t+1}\mid h_t,a)
\approx
p(o_{t+1}\mid s_t,a).
\]
The goal is not maximum context. It is the smallest state for which additional history would not materially change the next good action.


5.2 Tool registry and executor
Each tool needs a contract:







Field
Purpose




Name and description
help the model select the correct capability


Input schema
constrain arguments and enable validation


Output schema
make observations predictable


Side-effect class
distinguish reads, reversible writes, and irreversible actions


Timeout and limits
bound resource use


Retry semantics
prevent accidental repeated side effects


Permission policy
determine whether execution is allowed or needs approval



Good tool descriptions say what the tool does, when to use it, and what it does not do. Overlapping tools create selection ambiguity. Huge, raw outputs consume context and should be normalized or stored as artifacts.
Tools are both actuators and sensors. An edit, deployment, or message changes the environment; a search, test, schema inspection, or diagnostic read primarily reduces uncertainty. A useful epistemic action may have little direct task reward but high information value:
\[
a^*
=
\arg\max_a
\left[
\mathbb E[V(a)]
+\beta I(o_{t+1};z\mid s_t,a)
\right],
\]
where \(z\) is an unknown fact relevant to the decision. This explains why running a cheap test often beats spending many more tokens predicting whether the code will work.


5.3 State and memory
At least four kinds of state should be distinguished:

event log: append-only record of decisions, calls, observations, and errors
working state: current plan, completed steps, open questions, and budgets
artifacts: files, patches, reports, datasets, logs, and generated outputs
long-term memory: durable knowledge intended for reuse across tasks

Weng highlights the filesystem as an effective persistent-memory substrate for long-horizon work. Models already understand files, paths, diffs, and shell operations from pretraining; artifacts remain inspectable outside the context window and survive interruptions.
Do not confuse persistence with relevance. A file can preserve everything, but the context compiler must still select what matters now.
For recovery, make the event log replayable, not merely readable. Codex persists append-only JSONL rollouts and reconstructs thread history from stored items and lifecycle markers. Derived UI state can then be rebuilt after a disconnect instead of becoming a second, inconsistent source of truth.


5.4 Workflow controller
The controller determines the shape of execution:
\[
\text{plan}
\rightarrow
\text{act}
\rightarrow
\text{observe}
\rightarrow
\text{verify}
\rightarrow
\text{revise}.
\]
It owns:

iteration and termination conditions
token, time, monetary, and tool-call budgets
clarification and approval transitions
retries, fallback tools, and escalation
background-job and subagent lifecycles
recovery after interruption

The workflow may be a general loop, a deterministic DAG, or a hybrid in which code fixes the outer stages and the model makes local decisions.
Name the controller’s timescales explicitly. Codex separates a durable conversation thread, a user-facing turn, and each model sampling step within that turn. Budgets, cancellation, caches, and persistence may belong to different levels; a generic “agent step” obscures who owns what.
For uncertain environments, prefer a receding-horizon pattern:
\[
\text{plan}
\rightarrow
\text{act briefly}
\rightarrow
\text{observe}
\rightarrow
\text{replan}.
\]
This resembles model predictive control. A long fixed plan assumes that distant future states are predictable; short execution bursts allow observations to correct the plan. The controller should also allocate compute between internal simulation and acting. When an action is cheap, reversible, and informative, act-and-observe is often preferable to extended reasoning.


5.5 Verifiers
A verifier converts “I think I am done” into observable completion evidence. Examples include:

unit tests and static checks for code
schema validation for structured outputs
source-entailment checks for research
row counts and invariants for data pipelines
screenshots or DOM checks for interfaces
explicit user confirmation for subjective decisions

Verification should test the artifact or environment state, not merely ask the same model whether its answer looks correct.
More generally, verifiers perform surprise engineering:
\[
\delta_t
=
\operatorname{Compare}
(\text{expected consequence},\text{observed consequence}).
\]
A good environment makes wrong beliefs produce cheap, specific, actionable observations. Coding agents benefit from unusually dense signals—compiler errors, test failures, types, linters, and diffs—while research and open-ended work require more deliberate verifiers for coverage and correctness.


5.6 Permission layer
Permissions belong outside the model’s editable reasoning loop. The harness should apply least privilege and classify actions by consequence:

read-only inspection
reversible local mutation
external communication or publication
financial, destructive, privileged, or difficult-to-reverse action

High-impact actions may require user approval even when the model is confident. Retrieved documents and tool outputs are untrusted data, not instructions that can modify the permission policy.
Security is normally a composition rather than one switch. Codex combines OS sandboxing, approval policy, command rules, managed network policy, and agent-native telemetry. These controls cover different failure modes. Also note that sandboxing a built-in shell does not automatically sandbox an external MCP tool; every capability needs an explicit trust and policy boundary.
Formally, the permission layer enforces
\[
a_t\in\mathcal A_{\text{allowed}}(s_t).
\]
This constrains the states the system can reach. Strong boundaries can enable greater autonomy inside the safe action set because catastrophic trajectories are excluded by code rather than discouraged only through prompting.


5.7 Observability
A production harness should make trajectories explainable after the fact:

model and prompt versions
compiled context metadata
model decisions and tool calls
validated arguments and normalized results
state transitions and artifact versions
retries, timeouts, approvals, and failures
token use, latency, and monetary cost
verifier outcomes and final termination reason

Observability is not only for dashboards. Without it, harness optimization cannot distinguish a bad model decision from a bad tool description, stale state, parser bug, permission denial, or verifier failure.
Tracing creates an outer feedback loop around the agent’s inner loop:
\[
\underbrace{s_t\rightarrow a_t\rightarrow o_{t+1}\rightarrow s_{t+1}}
_{\text{agent loop}},
\qquad
\underbrace{\text{trajectories}\rightarrow\text{failure analysis}
\rightarrow\text{harness change}\rightarrow\text{new trajectories}}
_{\text{development loop}}.
\]
A final success score says whether a run failed, but the trajectory is needed to attribute why it failed.
Prefer typed lifecycle events over scraping rendered text. Codex app-server exposes thread, turn, item, approval, interruption, and completion events so different clients can project the same core state. This separation makes reconnection, testing, and protocol compatibility tractable.

title: Agent Harness
text:
6. Context Engineering
Context is the model’s working memory and control surface. Treat it as a compiled view of state, not a transcript dump.
A rough selection objective is
\[
\max_{c\subseteq\mathcal I}
\frac{
\operatorname{relevance}(c)
\cdot
\operatorname{reliability}(c)
}{
\operatorname{tokens}(c)
}
\]
subject to mandatory instructions and a context budget.

Practical hierarchy
Keep these layers distinguishable:

rules: stable and authoritative
task: goal, constraints, and definition of done
state: plan, progress, budgets, and open failures
evidence: selected observations needed for the next decision
history: recent interactions useful for local coherence



Compaction
When context grows:

keep full artifacts and logs outside the prompt
summarize completed phases into structured state
preserve unresolved errors and user constraints verbatim
retain pointers from summaries to raw evidence
discard duplicated tool output and obsolete plans
test whether the compacted state supports resuming after interruption

Lossy compaction is dangerous when it silently drops a constraint, failed attempt, or source attribution.

title: Agent Harness
text:
7. Workflow Design Patterns
Weng identifies three recurring patterns.

Pattern 1: workflow automation
Define an environment in which the model can execute, test, inspect results, and iterate. The feedback loop matters more than a single elaborate prompt.
For coding:
inspect repository -> edit -> run tests -> diagnose -> revise -> verify diff
For agentic search:
decompose -> search -> read -> update evidence gaps -> search again -> verify


Pattern 2: filesystem as persistent memory
Store rich state and artifacts in files while keeping only a compact index in context. This supports long-running tasks, auditability, recovery, and handoff.
Useful artifacts include:

plan.md for mutable strategy
machine-readable task state
experiment configurations and results
patches and source files
background-job logs
evidence ledgers and research summaries
a concise resumption checkpoint

The names are conventions, not requirements. Avoid creating ceremonial files that no component actually reads.


Pattern 3: subagents and background jobs
Parallel work helps when subtasks are independent and expensive enough to justify coordination. The harness needs process-management operations:

start with bounded scope and inputs
assign identifiers and resource budgets
inspect status and logs
interrupt or cancel stalled work
persist outputs as shared artifacts
merge results and resolve conflicts

Subagents should not exist merely to imitate an organization chart. Every delegation adds context duplication, synchronization, and error-propagation cost.
Mechanistically, multi-agent execution is conditional computation, context partitioning, and sometimes parallel search. It helps when specialists can work with mostly independent state. If their subtasks depend on heavily shared hidden context, decomposition can discard information and cost more than one coherent trajectory.

title: Agent Harness
Agent Harness
text:
9. Failure Handling and Recovery
Long-horizon agents should expect partial failure.







Failure
Harness response




malformed tool arguments
reject before execution and return a compact schema error


transient network error
bounded retry with backoff and idempotency protection


deterministic tool error
expose diagnostic output; do not repeat unchanged calls forever


context overflow
compact state and preserve raw artifacts externally


repeated action loop
detect repeated call signatures and force replanning or stop


background job stalls
poll logs, enforce timeout, then interrupt or escalate


verifier fails
attach exact failed condition and resume work


authority missing
stop and ask the user rather than inventing permission


process interruption
reload durable state and resume from the last consistent checkpoint



Retries are especially dangerous for non-idempotent tools. Repeating a timed-out payment, message, or deployment may duplicate the side effect even when the first response was lost.

Reflection should follow evidence
Asking the same model to “reflect” without a new observation may provide useful extra inference, but it does not change the evidence. The stronger loop is
\[
a_t
\rightarrow
o_{t+1}
\rightarrow
\delta_t
\rightarrow
\text{root-cause attribution}
\rightarrow
s_{t+1}.
\]
Reflection should identify which assumption, plan step, tool interpretation, or completion criterion the observation falsified. Without this attribution, an agent may respond to a failed test by making unrelated changes or repeating the same action in different words.

title: Agent Harness
section: 10. Designing the Right Amount of Harness
text:
10. Designing the Right Amount of Harness
There is a spectrum:








Style
Strength
Weakness




Minimal general loop
adapts broadly and benefits directly from stronger models
may wander or miss domain invariants


Prompt-heavy scaffold
fast to prototype
brittle, opaque, and difficult to test


Deterministic workflow
predictable and easy to observe
inflexible when the path depends on new evidence


Hybrid harness
code enforces stages and invariants; model handles judgment
requires careful interface design


Multi-agent organization
parallelism and specialized contexts
high coordination and duplication cost



Prefer the simplest harness that exposes the necessary environment, feedback, and invariants. Overengineering often compensates for one model’s weakness with rules that become harmful or redundant as models improve.

title: Agent Harness
text:
11. Harness Optimization
Harness changes should be treated like changes to any other learned-system pipeline:

collect complete trajectories and verifier outcomes
cluster failures by causal mechanism
map each failure to a harness component
propose the smallest targeted change
predict both improvements and possible regressions
evaluate on held-in and held-out tasks
accept only evidence-supported changes

Useful failure labels follow the closed-loop decomposition: state-estimation, prediction, planning, tool, verification, permission, and state-update failure. This provides better credit assignment than treating every unsuccessful trajectory as a generic model failure.
Possible optimization targets include:

system instructions and tool descriptions
tool schemas and implementations
context selection and compaction
workflow topology and stopping rules
memory read/write policies
subagent configuration
recovery and verification logic

Always compare against simple baselines. A more elaborate harness may consume more test-time compute rather than make better decisions.
Harness configuration can also be part of the model’s training distribution. For example, Kimi K3 varies tools, system prompts, context strategies, skills, memory, and subagent configurations during agentic RL instead of optimizing for one fixed scaffold. This teaches robustness across runtimes, but does not remove the need for task-specific environments and verifiers. See How SOTA systems train deep research for the relationship between harness variation, specialist policies, and a consolidated research/coding/general-agent model.
Cursor closes this loop from the other direction: it trains Composer in a simulation of the production harness, then uses real interactions and product outcomes to update the deployed policy every few hours. The case exposes why harness instrumentation, reward construction, regression gates, and rollback are parts of the learning algorithm rather than only serving infrastructure. See Cursor’s Continual Training Loop.

Self-improving harnesses
A model can propose edits to its own harness, forming a loop:
\[
h_t
\xrightarrow{\text{run}}
\text{trajectories}
\xrightarrow{\text{diagnose}}
\Delta h
\xrightarrow{\text{evaluate}}
h_{t+1}.
\]
This expands the optimization surface beyond prompts to executable workflows, tools, memory, and middleware. It also creates a Goodhart problem: an optimizer may improve the measured score by weakening the verifier, increasing the budget, leaking test answers, or changing the task.
Keep these surfaces outside the editable loop:

evaluator and held-out tasks
permission and security policy
model identity and resource budget
audit log and experiment runner
acceptance and rollback mechanism

Every accepted harness edit should be attributable to evidence from failures and expressed as a falsifiable prediction.

title: Agent Harness
text:
12. Harness Versus Core Intelligence
Some behavior currently implemented in harness code may eventually become a native model capability. Stronger models need fewer prompt tricks and recover from tool errors more naturally.
But several responsibilities remain external by nature:

connecting to the current environment
enforcing organizational permissions
owning durable artifacts and state
applying resource limits
validating external side effects
observing and auditing execution

The boundary will move, but it will not disappear. Better models reduce the need for brittle scaffolding; they do not eliminate the runtime contract.

title: Agent Harness
text:
13. Core Insights

A harness converts model capability into system capability. End-to-end performance cannot be attributed to model weights alone.
Context should be compiled from state, not accumulated as a transcript.
Use models for judgment and code for invariants.
Artifacts outlive context. Files and logs make long-horizon work durable, inspectable, and resumable.
Verification closes the loop. A generated answer is only a candidate completion.
Permissions must live outside self-modification. The agent cannot grant itself authority.
Observability enables improvement. If failure cannot be localized, a harness edit is guesswork.
The simplest sufficient harness usually generalizes best. Add structure in response to measured failure, not aesthetic preference.
Tools are sensors as well as actuators. Information-gathering actions can be more valuable than premature execution.
Useful reflection begins with surprise. New external evidence enables belief revision; repeated introspection alone does not.
Planning should remain feedback-sensitive. Plan, act briefly, observe, and replan when the environment is uncertain.
Stable context is a performance feature. Preserve cacheable prefixes and order dynamic inputs deterministically.
Protocols should expose lifecycle, not presentation. Typed events make clients replaceable and state recoverable.
Concurrency belongs in tool metadata. Parallelize calls only when their declared effects can safely overlap.

title: Agent Harness
text:
Interview Questions

What is the difference between a model, an agent harness, and an agent framework?
Which decisions should be delegated to a model, and which should remain code?
How would you design an idempotent tool interface?
What should be stored in context, working state, artifacts, and long-term memory?
Why does a pre-norm-like “always append history” strategy fail for agents?
What makes a verifier independent enough to be useful?
When do subagents improve performance rather than add coordination overhead?
How should a harness recover after a process interruption?
Which components must remain immutable in a self-improving harness?
How would you determine whether a gain came from the harness or additional test-time compute?
Why are tools both actuators and sensors? Give an example of an epistemic tool action.
What makes a verifier produce useful surprise rather than merely another model opinion?
When is receding-horizon planning preferable to committing to a complete plan?
Why is reflection after a failed test more useful than reflection with no new evidence?
Why can two semantically equivalent prompts have different inference costs?
Why should thread, turn, and sampling-step state be distinguished?
Why does sandboxing the shell not automatically sandbox every external tool?

title: Agent Harness
text:
Exercises

Implement the minimal loop with one read-only tool and a step budget.
Add schema validation, timeouts, and repeated-call detection.
Persist event logs and resumable state to files.
Design a context compiler that retains unresolved errors while compacting completed work.
Add a verifier whose result cannot be overwritten by the agent.
Classify tools by side-effect risk and design approval policies.
Compare a minimal loop with a deterministic workflow on the same tasks.
Cluster failed trajectories and propose one falsifiable harness change.

title: Agent Harness
text:
Further Reading

Harness Engineering for Self-Improvement — Lilian Weng

Codex: Anatomy of an Open-Source Coding Agent

title: Codex: Anatomy of an Open-Source Coding Agent
text:
Scope. Codex CLI has been open-source since April 2025. This note studies the current agent runtime at OpenAI’s openai/codex repository, pinned for this analysis at commit aec653d. The repository exposes the local harness, protocol, sandboxing, SDKs, and supporting services. It does not open-source the Codex model weights or imply that every hosted service and product interface is present.
Codex is valuable to study because it turns the abstract components in Agent Harness into a production system. The main lesson is not a particular prompt. It is how probabilistic model decisions are embedded inside deterministic state, execution, security, and protocol boundaries.

title: Codex: Anatomy of an Open-Source Coding Agent
section: 1. Start from the Actual System Boundary
text:
1. Start from the Actual System Boundary
A coding model proposes tokens and structured actions. A coding agent must also own a workspace, execute processes, preserve history, constrain side effects, stream progress, accept interruptions, and recover across sessions.
Write the end-to-end system as
\[
\boxed{
\text{Codex system}
=
\text{coding model}
+
\text{Codex harness}
+
\text{execution environment}
+
\text{client or orchestrator}
}.
\]
These parts have different jobs:








Layer
Responsibility
Learned?




Model
interpret intent, reason about code, choose actions, synthesize results
mostly


Harness
compile context, run the loop, route tools, persist state, enforce policy
mostly not


Environment
files, Git state, processes, network, APIs, tests, external consequences
no


Client
interaction, review, steering, approval, and presentation
no


Orchestrator
assign tasks, isolate workspaces, supervise many agent sessions
possibly hybrid



The open-source repository is primarily the second layer plus interfaces into the third and fourth. A model can be replaced behind a compatible Responses API endpoint, while a client can communicate with the harness through the app-server protocol. This is an intentional separation of intelligence, mechanism, and product surface.

title: Codex: Anatomy of an Open-Source Coding Agent
text:
2. Architecture: One Core, Several Surfaces






flowchart LR
    U[User or orchestrator]
    C[CLI / TUI / IDE / client]
    A[App-server protocol]
    H[Codex core harness]
    M[Responses-compatible model]
    X[Tool router]
    P[Policy and approvals]
    E[Execution environment]
    R[Rollout and state stores]

    U <--> C
    C <--> A
    A <--> H
    H <--> M
    H <--> X
    X --> P
    P --> E
    E --> X
    H <--> R
    H -. events .-> A






The diagram is conceptual, not a complete crate dependency graph. The source is large, but a few regions reveal the design:



Source area
Architectural role




codex-rs/core
session, turn, context, model, tool, permission, and agent logic


core/src/session/turn.rs
the model–tool feedback loop


core/src/tools
tool specifications, routing, handlers, hooks, and concurrency


app-server and app-server-protocol
UI-independent thread, turn, item, approval, and event API


rollout and state
durable histories, reconstruction, indexing, and metadata


sandboxing and execpolicy
OS isolation and command policy


skills, plugins, and rmcp-client
reusable instructions and external capabilities



The important design choice is that the harness core is not fused to one UI. The app-server exposes a typed lifecycle that multiple clients can project into different experiences.

title: Codex: Anatomy of an Open-Source Coding Agent
text:
3. Three Nested Timescales
“Agent step” is too ambiguous. Codex distinguishes at least three timescales:









Unit
Begins with
May contain
Ends with




Thread
starting or resuming a conversation
many turns
archive, delete, or abandonment


Turn
new user input
many model samples and tool calls
final assistant message, error, or interruption


Sampling step
one model request
streamed items and possibly several tool calls
response completion or retryable failure



This distinction matters for state ownership:

model-client routing and some caches can be turn-scoped
conversation history is thread-scoped
a tool call belongs to the exact step context that advertised it
cancellation can stop an in-flight turn without destroying the thread
steering can append user input while a regular turn is running

The app-server API makes these boundaries explicit through operations such as thread/start, thread/resume, turn/start, turn/steer, and turn/interrupt.

title: Codex: Anatomy of an Open-Source Coding Agent
text:
4. The Core Loop
At a high level, Codex runs
record user input and context changes
repeat:
    construct the current model-visible history and tool list
    stream a response from a Responses-compatible endpoint
    record response items and emit client events
    if the response contains tool calls:
        validate, authorize, dispatch, and observe them
        append bounded tool outputs to history
    otherwise:
        finish the turn with the assistant message
until interrupted, failed, or complete






flowchart TD
    I[User input] --> W[Capture a consistent step context]
    W --> B[Build prompt: history + instructions + tools]
    B --> S[Stream model response]
    S --> T{Tool call?}
    T -- no --> F[Record final assistant message]
    T -- yes --> V[Parse and route typed call]
    V --> G[Hooks, policy, sandbox, approval]
    G --> E[Execute tool]
    E --> O[Record result and emit events]
    O --> K{Context limit or new input?}
    K -- compact / merge --> B
    K -- continue --> B






The real run_turn is more complex because production loops must handle streaming, retries, compaction, hooks, dynamic tools, pending user input, cancellation, telemetry, and partial failures. But its invariant remains simple:
\[
\text{model proposal}
\ne
\text{environmental side effect}.
\]
The proposal becomes a side effect only after harness-controlled parsing, routing, authorization, and execution.

title: Codex: Anatomy of an Open-Source Coding Agent
section: 5. Context Is Compiled State, Not Just Chat History
text:
5. Context Is Compiled State, Not Just Chat History
Codex’s initial model input combines several sources with distinct authority:

model-specific base instructions
sandbox and approval instructions
managed or user developer instructions
hierarchical repository instructions such as AGENTS.md
skill and plugin metadata
environment state such as working directory and shell
conversation items and the current user request

Repository instructions are discovered from the project root toward the working directory, so broad rules can be refined by more local ones. This makes context composition resemble lexical scoping: the effective behavior at a file depends on the instructions along its path. See OpenAI’s AGENTS.md guide and the source implementation in agents_md.rs.

Context also has a systems cost
For transformer inference, a stable prompt prefix can reuse cached computation. Consequently, semantically equivalent context layouts need not have equivalent cost. Codex tries to avoid rewriting earlier history, maintains deterministic tool ordering, and appends changes to permissions or environment as new items.
A better context objective therefore includes both relevance and prefix stability:
\[
c_t^*
=
\arg\max_{c_t}
\left[
U(c_t)
-\lambda |c_t|
+\gamma\,\operatorname{ReusablePrefix}(c_{t-1},c_t)
\right].
\]
This produces a general harness principle:

Treat the prompt prefix like a cache-sensitive interface. Keep stable facts stable, order dynamic collections deterministically, and append state changes when possible.



Compaction is state estimation
Conversation history grows until it competes with future reasoning and output tokens. Codex can replace a long history with a compact representation and then continue the same thread. Compaction is not mere compression; it estimates the smallest state sufficient for future decisions:
\[
p(o_{t+1}\mid h_t,a_t)
\approx
p(o_{t+1}\mid \phi(h_t),a_t).
\]
The failure mode is not only losing prose. A bad summary can discard an unresolved error, user constraint, permission boundary, or the reason an earlier approach failed. Durable rollouts and external artifacts keep raw evidence available even when model-visible history is compacted.

title: Codex: Anatomy of an Open-Source Coding Agent
text:
6. Tools Are Typed Capabilities
The model receives schemas, but the harness owns implementations. Codex’s tool path separates:

specification: what the model is allowed to request
routing: which implementation owns the call
lifecycle: start, stream, finish, abort, and telemetry events
policy: whether the action may execute
execution: how it runs and how output is bounded
observation: the normalized result returned to the model

The ToolRouter maps response items into namespaced typed calls. The registry can combine built-ins, hosted tools, MCP tools, plugins, and dynamically exposed tools.

Concurrency is a tool property
Codex does not assume that all tool calls are safe to parallelize. In parallel.rs, parallel-safe calls share a read lock, while a non-parallel call takes the write lock and excludes the others.
This is a compact concurrency contract:
\[
\text{parallelize}(a_i,a_j)
\iff
\text{their declared effects commute safely}.
\]
The model should decide which operations are useful; deterministic runtime metadata should decide whether their executions may overlap.


Errors are observations unless they break the runtime
A malformed argument, command failure, or unavailable tool is often useful feedback for replanning. Codex can turn an ordinary tool failure into a tool result the model can inspect. A fatal invariant violation instead terminates the sampling path. This distinction prevents both extremes: crashing on every tool error and hiding genuine harness corruption inside natural-language feedback.


Hooks are middleware, not policy by prompt
Pre-tool hooks can block or transform a request; post-tool hooks can attach feedback or additional context. They provide deterministic extension points around the side-effect boundary. Importantly, a post-tool hook cannot undo an already executed side effect, so precondition checks belong before execution.

title: Codex: Anatomy of an Open-Source Coding Agent
section: 7. Security Is the Intersection of Controls
text:
7. Security Is the Intersection of Controls
No single “safe mode” is enough. Codex composes several mechanisms:







Mechanism
Question answered




OS sandbox
What files, processes, and network resources are technically reachable?


Approval policy
When must authority return to a human or reviewer?


Execution rules
Which known command patterns may run, prompt, or be blocked?


Managed network policy
Which destinations are allowed or require review?


Tool-specific policy
What constraints apply to MCP or other external capabilities?


Telemetry
What happened, under whose request, and with what decision?



The effective action set is the intersection
\[
\mathcal A_{\text{effective}}
=
\mathcal A_{\text{sandbox}}
\cap
\mathcal A_{\text{approval}}
\cap
\mathcal A_{\text{rules}}
\cap
\mathcal A_{\text{tool}}.
\]
This separation matters because prompting only influences model behavior; it does not create a hard resource boundary. Conversely, a sandbox alone cannot decide whether sending a message or changing a production record is authorized.
One subtle but general lesson from the agent-loop description is that Codex’s local shell sandbox does not automatically wrap arbitrary MCP tools. Each external tool provider must enforce its own constraints. A harness should never advertise “the agent is sandboxed” without naming which capability is actually inside which boundary.
OpenAI’s deployment guidance adds two production practices: avoid open-ended outbound network access, and combine endpoint security alerts with agent-native logs that preserve the surrounding user intent, tool activity, approvals, and network decisions. See Running Codex safely at OpenAI.

title: Codex: Anatomy of an Open-Source Coding Agent
text:
8. Event-Driven State Makes Clients Replaceable
Codex app-server uses requests for commands and notifications for lifecycle changes. The client does not need to infer hidden state from terminal text; it can observe explicit thread, turn, item, approval, and completion events.
This yields a useful split:
command:      "start this turn" or "approve this action"
event:        "turn started", "item completed", or "turn interrupted"
projection:   what a TUI, IDE, app, or orchestrator displays
Durable rollout records are written as JSONL and can be replayed or inspected. The state layer also indexes thread metadata for listing and resumption. This is event-sourcing-like without requiring every derived UI state to be written into the model conversation.
Why this matters:

clients can disconnect and rehydrate state
CLI, IDE, and app surfaces can share a core runtime
tests can assert lifecycle events rather than scrape prose
interruption and partial completion become explicit states
protocol evolution becomes a compatibility problem that can be tested

The source repository’s own review guidance treats app-server APIs, raw response events, configuration, CLI parameters, and rollout resumption as external compatibility surfaces. That is a strong harness-engineering principle: the protocol is part of the product, not incidental glue.

title: Codex: Anatomy of an Open-Source Coding Agent
text:
9. Persistence, Resumption, and Steering
Long-running work should expect process death, client disconnection, user course-correction, and context replacement. Codex supports these cases with:

append-only rollout records
thread resume and fork operations
history reconstruction
explicit interruption markers
in-flight steering for regular turns
background process handles and cancellation tokens
separate stored artifacts in the workspace

A robust turn is therefore not a blocking function call. It is a resumable state machine:
\[
z_{t+1}
=
F(z_t,\text{command},\text{event}),
\]
where \(z_t\) includes the active turn, history position, running tools, permission state, and client-visible lifecycle.
The practical lesson is to design interruption semantics early. “Cancel” must define what happens to the model stream, in-flight tool, already completed side effects, stored history, and next resumption. Killing a process is not a full cancellation design.

title: Codex: Anatomy of an Open-Source Coding Agent
text:
10. Skills, Plugins, MCP, and Subagents
These mechanisms operate at different abstraction levels:








Mechanism
Adds
Main risk




Instruction file
repository-local constraints and conventions
stale or conflicting context


Skill
reusable procedure plus selected resources
loading too much context


Plugin
packaged skills, hooks, tools, or integrations
dependency and permission expansion


MCP server
external tool/resource interface
trust boundary and side effects


Subagent
another model trajectory with separate context
coordination and duplicated work



The architectural insight is progressive capability disclosure. A small stable description can tell the model what exists; detailed instructions and heavy resources are loaded only when selected. This saves tokens and reduces irrelevant instruction interference.
Subagents are implemented as managed child threads rather than magical extra reasoning. Their benefit comes from parallel compute and context isolation; their cost comes from communication, synchronization, and merge conflicts. They are most useful when work can be partitioned with explicit inputs and inspectable outputs.

title: Codex: Anatomy of an Open-Source Coding Agent
section: 11. What Codex Adds to the Generic Harness Picture
text:
11. What Codex Adds to the Generic Harness Picture
The generic Agent Harness note explains the components. Codex adds several concrete engineering lessons:








Generic principle
Codex realization
Broader lesson




Compile context
layered instructions plus per-step world-state diffs
context has authority, provenance, and cache cost


Route tools
typed, namespaced router and registry
separate model-visible schemas from runtimes


Control side effects
sandbox, approvals, rules, hooks, network policy
safety is an intersection of controls


Preserve state
JSONL rollouts plus indexed thread state
make histories replayable and derived views rebuildable

streaming events, tool results, steering, cancellation

Serve many clients

Manage cost

The most important synthesis is:
\[
\boxed{
\text{reliable autonomy}
=
\text{semantic flexibility inside deterministic boundaries}
}.
\]

title: Codex: Anatomy of an Open-Source Coding Agent
section: 12. What the Source Does Not Prove
text:
12. What the Source Does Not Prove
Reading the harness cannot answer every question about Codex performance:

It does not reveal the proprietary model’s training data or complete post-training recipe.
Code presence does not show which feature is enabled in every product or account.
A configurable mechanism does not establish its production configuration.
End-to-end benchmark gains cannot be assigned to the model or harness without controlled ablations.
A large mature codebase contains compatibility layers and experiments; not every module is a timeless design recommendation.

Separate three kinds of claims when reading an agent repository:

mechanism: the source can do this
configuration: a deployment enables it this way
effect: enabling it causally improves quality, cost, or safety

Source inspection is strongest for the first and needs documentation, telemetry, or experiments for the other two.

title: From Graph Algorithms to Reinforcement Learning
From Graph Algorithms to Reinforcement Learning
text:
1. Graphs as deterministic state-transition systems
Consider a weighted directed graph.
A node corresponds to a state:
\[
s \in \mathcal S.
\]
An outgoing edge corresponds to a possible transition:
\[
s \to s'.
\]
If we can choose among outgoing edges, we can reinterpret each edge as an action:
\[
s \xrightarrow{a} s'.
\]
The edge weight becomes a transition cost:
\[
c(s,a).
\]
A shortest-path problem is therefore already a simple deterministic decision problem.
If \(V(s)\) denotes the minimum remaining cost from \(s\) to the goal, then
\[
V(s)
=
\min_a
\left[
c(s,a) + V(s')
\right].
\]
This is a Bellman equation.

title: From Graph Algorithms to Reinforcement Learning
section: 2. From shortest path to the RL Bellman equation
text:
2. From shortest path to the RL Bellman equation
In an MDP, taking action \(a\) does not necessarily determine the next state.
Instead,
\[
s' \sim P(\cdot \mid s,a).
\]
We also usually express the objective using reward rather than cost.
The optimal value becomes
\[
V^*(s)
=
\max_a
\mathbb E_{s' \sim P(\cdot \mid s,a)}
\left[
r(s,a,s') + \gamma V^*(s')
\right].
\]
The shortest-path recurrence
\[
d[v]
=
\min_{u\to v}
\left(
d[u]+w(u,v)
\right)
\]
and the RL Bellman equation are therefore structurally the same idea:

The value of a state is determined by immediate transition value plus the value of future states.

The main problem becomes:

How do we resolve these recursive value dependencies?

title: From Graph Algorithms to Reinforcement Learning
section: 3. DAG DP: dependencies already have an order
text:
3. DAG DP: dependencies already have an order
Suppose the state-dependency graph is a DAG.
Then we can evaluate states in topological order.
For example,
\[
V(s)
=
\min_{s'\in \operatorname{Next}(s)}
\left[
c(s,s') + V(s')
\right].
\]
If every successor \(V(s')\) is already known when we evaluate \(s\), each state only needs to be solved once.
Thus classical DP can often be understood as
\[
\boxed{
\text{Bellman recurrence}
+
\text{acyclic dependency graph}
+
\text{topological evaluation}
}
\]
Bottom-up DP explicitly chooses this order.
Memoized DFS discovers it lazily by recursively evaluating dependencies first.

title: From Graph Algorithms to Reinforcement Learning
text:
4. Cycles create the interesting problem
If the state graph contains cycles, values may depend recursively on one another:
\[
V(A) \to V(B) \to V(C) \to V(A).
\]
There is no topological order.
Different graph algorithms succeed because they exploit additional structure to resolve these cyclic dependencies.
This gives a useful perspective on shortest-path algorithms.



Algorithm
How Bellman dependencies are resolved




DAG shortest path
known topological order


BFS
increasing hop distance


0–1 BFS
deque maintains distance order


Dijkstra
greedy finalization by minimum distance


Bellman–Ford
repeated relaxation


Floyd–Warshall
introduce an extra DP dimension



The recurrence can remain almost identical.
What changes is the dependency-resolution strategy.

title: From Graph Algorithms to Reinforcement Learning
section: 5. BFS, 0–1 BFS, and Dijkstra as increasingly general schedulers
text:
5. BFS, 0–1 BFS, and Dijkstra as increasingly general schedulers
For shortest paths with unit edge weights, BFS processes states in increasing distance:
\[
0,1,2,3,\ldots
\]
A FIFO queue is enough.
With weights in
\[
\{0,1\},
\]
relaxing a node at distance \(d\) can only produce nodes at distance
\[
d
\quad\text{or}\quad
d+1.
\]
A deque is therefore enough to preserve distance ordering.
For arbitrary nonnegative weights, Dijkstra needs a min-heap:
\[
u
=
\arg\min_{v\in\text{frontier}}d[v].
\]
Therefore:
\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
w=1
&\Rightarrow \text{queue} \\
w\in\{0,1\}
&\Rightarrow \text{deque} \\
w\ge 0
&\Rightarrow \text{min-heap}.
\end{aligned}
}
\]
All three algorithms can be understood as enforcing the same principle:

Process states in an order that allows their shortest-path values to become final.

title: From Graph Algorithms to Reinforcement Learning
text:
6. Dijkstra as greedy value finalization
Dijkstra exploits nonnegative edge weights.
When it extracts
\[
u=\arg\min d[u],
\]
no future path through an unprocessed state can produce a cheaper path to \(u\).
Therefore \(d[u]\) can be permanently finalized.
This is much stronger than what is generally possible in RL.
Dijkstra effectively discovers a valid value-evaluation order dynamically:
\[
\boxed{
\text{Bellman backup}
+
\text{greedy finalization order}
}
\]
The heap is therefore not just an implementation detail.
It implements the algorithm’s value scheduling rule.

title: From Graph Algorithms to Reinforcement Learning
text:
7. Bellman–Ford as deterministic value iteration
Bellman–Ford does not know a safe finalization order.
Instead, it repeatedly applies Bellman relaxations:
\[
d[v]
\leftarrow
\min
\left(
d[v],
d[u]+w(u,v)
\right).
\]
Another interpretation introduces the state
\[
dp[k][v]
=
\text{shortest path to }v
\text{ using at most }k\text{ edges}.
\]
Then
\[
dp[k][v]
=
\min
\left(
dp[k-1][v],
\min_{u\to v}
\left[
dp[k-1][u]+w(u,v)
\right]
\right).
\]
The original cyclic graph has now become a layered dependency DAG:
\[
(k-1,u)\to(k,v).
\]
This is closely related to value iteration in RL:
\[
V_{k+1}(s)
=
\max_a
\mathbb E
\left[
r+\gamma V_k(s')
\right].
\]
Conceptually,
\[
\boxed{
\text{Bellman--Ford}
\approx
\text{deterministic shortest-path value iteration}
}
\]
Both repeatedly apply a Bellman operator rather than finding a one-pass dependency order.

title: From Graph Algorithms to Reinforcement Learning
section: 8. A* introduces an approximate value function
text:
8. A* introduces an approximate value function
Dijkstra prioritizes states using cost already incurred:
\[
f(s)=g(s).
\]
A* instead uses
\[
f(s)=g(s)+h(s),
\]
where

\(g(s)\) is cost from the start to \(s\),
\(h(s)\) estimates the remaining cost to the goal.

The heuristic is therefore an approximate cost-to-go function:
\[
h(s)\approx V^*_{\text{cost}}(s).
\]
This gives a direct connection to RL:
\[
\boxed{
\text{A*}
=
\text{search}
+
\text{approximate value function}
}
\]
If
\[
h(s)=0,
\]
A* becomes Dijkstra.
If \(h(s)\) were a perfect value function, search could focus almost entirely on optimal trajectories.
This is conceptually similar to using a critic to guide decision making.

title: From Graph Algorithms to Reinforcement Learning
text:
9. Planning versus reinforcement learning
At this point the transition from graph algorithms to RL is mostly about what information is available.

Graph algorithms
The graph and transition costs are explicitly known.
\[
(s,a)\to(s',c)
\]
can be queried directly.
The problem is primarily computational:

Given the complete world model, solve for optimal values or paths.



MDP planning
The transition model and rewards are known:
\[
P(s'|s,a), \qquad R(s,a).
\]
But transitions may be stochastic.
We solve for
\[
V^*,\qquad Q^*,\qquad \pi^*.
\]
Algorithms include:

value iteration,
policy iteration,
dynamic programming.



Reinforcement learning
The model may not be known.
Instead, the agent observes samples such as
\[
(s,a,r,s').
\]
Now the agent must estimate values, policies, and sometimes the dynamics themselves from interaction.
Thus:
$$ $$

title: From Graph Algorithms to Reinforcement Learning
section: 10. Bellman backup as the common primitive
text:
10. Bellman backup as the common primitive
Across all of these algorithms, the fundamental operation is some form of value backup.
Shortest path:
\[
d[v]
\leftarrow
\min
\left(
d[v],
d[u]+w(u,v)
\right).
\]
MDP value iteration:
\[
V(s)
\leftarrow
\max_a
\mathbb E
\left[
r+\gamma V(s')
\right].
\]
Q-learning:
\[
Q(s,a)
\leftarrow
Q(s,a)
+
\alpha
\left[
r+\gamma\max_{a'}Q(s',a')
-
Q(s,a)
\right].
\]
The latter differs because we only observe a sampled transition and use a stochastic update.
But the target still comes from the same recursive structure:
\[
\boxed{
\text{current value}
\leftarrow
\text{immediate outcome}
+
\text{future value}
}
\]

title: From Graph Algorithms to Reinforcement Learning
section: 11. Scheduling is a hidden dimension of RL
text:
11. Scheduling is a hidden dimension of RL
Graph algorithms make the scheduling problem very visible.

BFS: FIFO queue
DFS: stack
0–1 BFS: deque
Dijkstra: min-heap
A*: priority by \(g+h\)

RL has analogous scheduling questions.
There are actually two:

Which state should I visit next?
Which state’s value should I update next?

These correspond roughly to:
\[
\text{exploration}
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\text{backup scheduling}.
\]
Standard synchronous value iteration updates every state.
Asynchronous value iteration updates selected states.
Prioritized sweeping prefers states whose values are likely to change significantly.
This is strikingly similar to changing the frontier data structure in graph algorithms.
Thus a more general decomposition is
\[
\boxed{
\text{value update rule}
+
\text{update scheduling policy}
}
\]
and RL adds another dimension:
\[
\boxed{
\text{exploration policy}
}
\]
because the agent may not even know which transitions exist until it experiences them.

title: From Graph Algorithms to Reinforcement Learning
text:
12. Tree search versus graph search
Algorithms such as A* are often drawn as trees, but the underlying environment may be a graph.
Suppose
\[
A\to B\to D
\]
and
\[
A\to C\to D.
\]
A tree-search representation contains two copies of \(D\):
       A
      / \
     B   C
     |   |
     D   D
Graph search recognizes that they represent the same state:
       A
      / \
     B   C
      \ /
       D
This distinction becomes important in AI.
Search algorithms often construct a search tree over trajectories, even when the underlying state space is a graph.
The same idea appears in RL and planning:

a state may be reachable through many trajectories,
value functions merge those trajectories into a common state representation,
trajectory-based search may temporarily treat them separately.

title: From Graph Algorithms to Reinforcement Learning
text:
13. A useful conceptual ladder
The progression from graph algorithms to RL can be organized as:
\[
\boxed{
\text{DAG DP}
\rightarrow
\text{shortest-path algorithms}
\rightarrow
\text{MDP planning}
\rightarrow
\text{RL}
}
\]

DAG DP
Dependencies are acyclic.
Solve once in topological order.


Dijkstra / BFS / 0–1 BFS
The graph may be cyclic, but structural assumptions allow a safe dynamic finalization order.


Bellman–Ford / value iteration
No one-pass order is available.
Repeatedly propagate values until the Bellman equations are satisfied.


MDP planning
Transitions become stochastic:
\[
V(s)
=
\max_a
\mathbb E[
r+\gamma V(s')
].
\]


RL
The transition model or rewards are not fully known.
Bellman updates must be estimated from experience.







TipThe unifying view



Graph algorithms, dynamic programming, planning, and reinforcement learning are all forms of value propagation over a state-transition system.
A useful decomposition is
\[
\boxed{
\text{state representation}
+
\text{transition structure}
+
\text{Bellman/value equation}
+
\text{update scheduling}
+
\text{exploration}
}
\]
Different algorithms become possible because they assume different amounts of structure.

DAG DP gets an explicit dependency order.
BFS / Dijkstra exploit transition-cost structure to discover a safe order.
Bellman–Ford uses repeated relaxation when no such order is available.
A* adds an approximate future-value function to guide search.
RL learns values or policies from sampled interaction when the model itself is not fully available.

The progression is therefore not a set of unrelated algorithms, but increasingly general ways of solving recursive decision problems.
