title: Probabilistic Modeling Practice: 20 Worked Problems
text:
2 Balls into buckets

2.1 Question
You throw n balls independently and uniformly into m buckets.

What is the expected number of colliding pairs?
What is the expected number of occupied buckets?
What is the probability of at least one collision?
Approximate the collision probability when n\ll m.

Concepts: indicators, linearity of expectation, birthday paradox, and Poisson approximation.


2.2 Solution
Throw n balls independently and uniformly into m buckets. Let B_i be the bucket selected by ball i.


2.3 Expected number of colliding pairs
For each pair i<j, define

I_{ij}=\mathbf 1\{B_i=B_j\}.

The collision-pair count is C=\sum_{i<j}I_{ij}. Since P(B_i=B_j)=1/m,

\boxed{E[C]=\binom n2\frac1m=\frac{n(n-1)}{2m}}.

The indicators need not be mutually independent; linearity of expectation does not require independence.


2.4 Expected number of occupied buckets
Let J_k indicate that bucket k is occupied. It is empty only if every ball avoids it:

P(J_k=0)=\left(1-\frac1m\right)^n.

Therefore

\boxed{E[O]=m\left[1-\left(1-\frac1m\right)^n\right]}
\approx m(1-e^{-n/m}).



2.5 Probability of at least one collision
For n\le m,

P(C=0)=\prod_{k=0}^{n-1}\left(1-\frac{k}{m}\right),

so

\boxed{P(C\ge1)=1-\prod_{k=0}^{n-1}\left(1-\frac{k}{m}\right)}.

If n>m, the probability is 1 by the pigeonhole principle.
When n\ll m, use \log(1-x)\approx-x:

P(C\ge1)
\approx 1-\exp\left[-\frac{n(n-1)}{2m}\right].

For rare collisions, C is approximately Poisson with

\lambda=\frac{n(n-1)}{2m}.

If \lambda\ll1, then P(C\ge1)\approx\lambda.

title: Probabilistic Modeling Practice: 20 Worked Problems
text:
3 Length-biased sampling

3.1 Question
Documents have random lengths L with distribution P(L=\ell). Select one token uniformly from all tokens in the corpus and inspect the document containing it.

What is the distribution of that document’s length?
Show that P(L=\ell\mid\text{random token})\propto \ell P(L=\ell).
What is the expected length of the selected token’s document, and how does it compare with the document-level average E[L]?

Concepts: size-biased distributions, conditional probability, and the inspection paradox.


3.2 Solution
Let document length L have document-level distribution P(L=\ell)=p_\ell. Select one token uniformly from the entire corpus and inspect its document.
A document of length \ell contributes \ell possible sampled tokens, so it is \ell times as likely to be encountered as a unit-length document. Normalizing gives

\boxed{
P_{\text{token}}(L=\ell)
=\frac{\ell p_\ell}{E[L]}
}.

Its expected length is

E_{\text{token}}[L]
=\sum_\ell \ell\frac{\ell p_\ell}{E[L]}
=\boxed{\frac{E[L^2]}{E[L]}}.

Using E[L^2]=\operatorname{Var}(L)+E[L]^2,

\boxed{
E_{\text{token}}[L]
=E[L]+\frac{\operatorname{Var}(L)}{E[L]}
\ge E[L]
}.

Equality holds only when all documents have the same length. This is the inspection paradox / size-bias effect.

title: Probabilistic Modeling Practice: 20 Worked Problems
section: 4 Medical test and the base-rate effect
text:
4 Medical test and the base-rate effect

4.1 Question
A disease occurs in 1\% of people. A test satisfies

P(+\mid D)=0.95,
\qquad
P(+\mid\neg D)=0.05.


Given a positive result, compute P(D\mid +).
Recompute it if disease prevalence falls to 0.1\%.
Explain why high sensitivity does not necessarily imply high precision.

Concepts: Bayes’ rule, the law of total probability, and base-rate effects.


4.2 Solution
Suppose

P(D)=0.01,\qquad P(+\mid D)=0.95,\qquad P(+\mid \neg D)=0.05.

Because D and \neg D partition the population,

P(+)=P(+\mid D)P(D)+P(+\mid\neg D)P(\neg D).

Bayes’ rule gives

P(D\mid+)
=\frac{0.95(0.01)}{0.95(0.01)+0.05(0.99)}
=\boxed{0.1610}.

With prevalence P(D)=0.001,

P(D\mid+)
=\frac{0.95(0.001)}{0.95(0.001)+0.05(0.999)}
=\boxed{0.0187}.

The sensitivity P(+\mid D) and the precision P(D\mid+) reverse the conditioning and can be very different.






NoteWhat must sum to one?



P(+\mid D)+P(-\mid D)=1 because the outcomes share the same conditioning event. In general, P(+\mid D)+P(+\mid\neg D) need not equal 1; it happens to do so for the supplied numbers.

title: Probabilistic Modeling Practice: 20 Worked Problems
text:
5 Mixture of coins

5.1 Question
Choose one of two coins. Let Z\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(0.3), where Z=1 selects coin 1. Coin 1 has P(H)=0.8 and coin 2 has P(H)=0.4. You observe H,H,T,H.

Compute P(Z=1\mid H,H,T,H).
Compute the posterior predictive probability that the next toss is heads.

Concepts: latent variables, conditional independence, posterior inference, and posterior prediction.


5.2 Solution
Let Z=1 select coin 1 and Z=0 select coin 2:

P(Z=1)=0.3,\qquad P(H\mid Z=1)=0.8,\qquad P(H\mid Z=0)=0.4.

For X=(H,H,T,H), conditional independence of tosses gives

P(X\mid Z=1)=0.8^3(0.2)=0.1024,


P(X\mid Z=0)=0.4^3(0.6)=0.0384.

The unnormalized posterior weights are

w_1=0.3(0.1024)=0.03072,
\qquad
w_0=0.7(0.0384)=0.02688.

Thus

\boxed{P(Z=1\mid X)=\frac{w_1}{w_1+w_0}=0.5333}.

For the next toss, marginalize the uncertain coin identity:

\begin{aligned}
P(H_{\text{next}}\mid X)
&=\sum_zP(H_{\text{next}}\mid Z=z)P(Z=z\mid X)\\
&=0.8(0.5333)+0.4(0.4667)\\
&=\boxed{0.6133}.
\end{aligned}

title: Probabilistic Modeling Practice: 20 Worked Problems
text:
6 Beta–Bernoulli model

6.1 Question
Suppose

p\sim\operatorname{Beta}(\alpha,\beta),
\qquad
X_i\mid p\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p).

After observing h heads and t tails:

Derive the posterior distribution of p.
Compute E[p\mid D].
Compute the probability that the next toss is heads.

Concepts: conjugate priors, Bayesian updating, and posterior prediction.


6.2 Solution
Let

p\sim\operatorname{Beta}(\alpha,\beta),
\qquad
X_i\mid p\overset{iid}{\sim}\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p).

After h heads and t tails, the likelihood is proportional to p^h(1-p)^t. Multiplying by the prior,

p(p\mid D)
\propto p^{\alpha+h-1}(1-p)^{\beta+t-1}.

Therefore

\boxed{p\mid D\sim\operatorname{Beta}(\alpha+h,\beta+t)}.

The posterior mean is

\boxed{E[p\mid D]=\frac{\alpha+h}{\alpha+\beta+h+t}}.

The next-toss probability is the posterior predictive:

\begin{aligned}
P(X_{n+1}=1\mid D)
&=\int P(X_{n+1}=1\mid p)p(p\mid D)\,dp\\
&=\int p\,p(p\mid D)\,dp\\
&=\boxed{\frac{\alpha+h}{\alpha+\beta+h+t}}.
\end{aligned}

The prior acts like \alpha pseudo-heads and \beta pseudo-tails.

title: Probabilistic Modeling Practice: 20 Worked Problems
text:
7 Dirichlet–categorical model

7.1 Question
A user’s clicks belong to K categories:

\theta\sim\operatorname{Dirichlet}(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_K),
\qquad
X_i\mid\theta\sim\operatorname{Categorical}(\theta).

After observing counts n_1,\ldots,n_K:

Derive the posterior distribution of \theta.
Derive the posterior predictive probability of category j.

Concepts: conjugacy, categorical models, and Bayesian smoothing.


7.2 Solution
Let

\theta\sim\operatorname{Dirichlet}(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_K),
\qquad X_i\mid\theta\sim\operatorname{Categorical}(\theta).

Given counts n_1,\ldots,n_K, the likelihood is proportional to \prod_k\theta_k^{n_k}. Hence

\boxed{
\theta\mid D
\sim\operatorname{Dirichlet}(\alpha_1+n_1,\ldots,\alpha_K+n_K)
}.

Writing \alpha_0=\sum_k\alpha_k and n=\sum_kn_k, the predictive probability for category j is

\boxed{
P(X_{n+1}=j\mid D)
=E[\theta_j\mid D]
=\frac{\alpha_j+n_j}{\alpha_0+n}
}.

This is Bayesian additive smoothing: unseen categories retain nonzero probability when \alpha_j>0.

title: Probabilistic Modeling Practice: 20 Worked Problems
Probabilistic Modeling Practice: 20 Worked Problems
text:
9 Poisson arrivals

9.1 Question
Requests arrive independently according to a Poisson process at rate \lambda=5 per minute. Find:

the probability of exactly three requests in one minute;
the probability of no requests for 30 seconds;
the distribution of the time until the next request;
the distribution and expected value of the waiting time until the tenth request.

Concepts: Poisson processes, exponential waiting times, and Gamma distributions.


9.2 Solution
Requests follow a Poisson process with rate \lambda=5 per minute.


9.3 Exactly three requests in one minute

\boxed{
P(N(1)=3)=e^{-5}\frac{5^3}{3!}\approx0.1404
}.



9.4 No requests for 30 seconds
Thirty seconds is 0.5 minute, so the expected count is 2.5:

\boxed{P(N(0.5)=0)=e^{-2.5}\approx0.0821}.



9.5 Time until the next request

\boxed{T_1\sim\operatorname{Exponential}(5)},
\qquad E[T_1]=\frac15\text{ minute}=12\text{ seconds}.



9.6 Time until the tenth request
It is the sum of ten independent exponential waiting times:

\boxed{T_{10}\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(\text{shape}=10,\text{rate}=5)},


\boxed{E[T_{10}]=\frac{10}{5}=2\text{ minutes}}.

title: Probabilistic Modeling Practice: 20 Worked Problems
text:
10 A/B testing

10.1 Question
Variant A receives 80 clicks from 1000 impressions, while variant B receives 100 clicks from 1000 impressions.

Estimate the CTR difference p_B-p_A.
Derive its estimated variance and a 95\% confidence interval.
Test H_0:p_A=p_B against a two-sided alternative.
With independent Beta priors, formulate and estimate P(p_B>p_A\mid D).

Concepts: binomial modeling, hypothesis testing, uncertainty, and frequentist versus Bayesian inference.


10.2 Solution
Variant A has 80/1000 clicks and B has 100/1000.


10.3 Point estimate and uncertainty

\hat p_A=0.08,\qquad \hat p_B=0.10,


\boxed{\widehat{p_B-p_A}=0.02}.

The unpooled estimated variance is

\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\hat p_B-\hat p_A)
=\frac{\hat p_A(1-\hat p_A)}{n_A}
+\frac{\hat p_B(1-\hat p_B)}{n_B}.

Numerically, SE\approx0.01279, giving the approximate 95\% confidence interval

0.02\pm1.96(0.01279)
=\boxed{[-0.0051,\ 0.0451]}.



10.4 Two-sided test of equal CTR
Under H_0:p_A=p_B, the pooled estimate is

\hat p=\frac{80+100}{2000}=0.09.

Then

SE_0=\sqrt{\hat p(1-\hat p)\left(\frac1{n_A}+\frac1{n_B}\right)}
\approx0.01280,


z=\frac{0.10-0.08}{0.01280}\approx1.56.

The two-sided p-value is about 0.118, so this experiment does not reject equality at the 5\% level.


10.5 Bayesian comparison
With independent \operatorname{Beta}(1,1) priors,

p_A\mid D\sim\operatorname{Beta}(81,921),


p_B\mid D\sim\operatorname{Beta}(101,901).

The exact probability is

P(p_B>p_A\mid D)
=\int_0^1 f_B(b)F_A(b)\,db,

which is approximately 0.94 here. This is not contradictory to the frequentist result: P(p_B>p_A\mid D) is not a p-value, and neither statement says the improvement is large enough to matter practically.

title: Probabilistic Modeling Practice: 20 Worked Problems
text:
11 Simpson’s paradox

11.1 Question
Consider the following A/B results:



Segment
A
B




New users
10/100
90/1000


Existing users
810/900
80/100




Which variant is better within each segment?
Which variant is better overall?
Do these data actually exhibit Simpson’s paradox? Explain how a reversal could arise.

Concepts: conditioning, confounding, aggregation, and weighted averages.


11.2 Solution
The supplied table is:



Segment
A
B




New users
10/100=10\%
90/1000=9\%


Existing users
810/900=90\%
80/100=80\%



Within both segments, A has the higher rate. Overall,

\hat p_A=\frac{820}{1000}=82\%,


\hat p_B=\frac{170}{1100}\approx15.45\%.

So A also wins overall.






WarningThe given numbers are not Simpson’s paradox



There is no reversal in this table. It demonstrates how dramatically different segment mixtures can affect aggregate rates, but both conditional and aggregate comparisons favor A.


In general, each aggregate is a weighted average:

P(Y=1\mid T=t)
=\sum_sP(Y=1\mid T=t,S=s)P(S=s\mid T=t).

Simpson’s paradox occurs when A can have a higher rate within every segment, yet B has a higher aggregate rate because P(S\mid T=A) and P(S\mid T=B) differ sharply. Segment S is associated with both treatment assignment and outcome difficulty. The remedy is not blindly choosing segmented results; it is specifying the causal estimand and adjusting for genuine pre-treatment confounders.

title: Probabilistic Modeling Practice: 20 Worked Problems
text:
12 Missing observations and selection bias

12.1 Question
Suppose user engagement Y is observed only if the user clicks:

C\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(e(X)),

and Y is visible only when C=1.

Can E[Y\mid C=1] estimate overall engagement E[Y]?
Under what assumptions is recovery possible?
Derive an inverse-propensity-weighted estimator.
What changes if selection depends on unobserved outcomes?

Concepts: selection bias, missingness, exchangeability, positivity, and inverse propensity weighting.


12.2 Solution
Suppose engagement Y is observed only when C=1, with

C\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(e(X)),
\qquad e(X)=P(C=1\mid X).

In general,

E[Y\mid C=1]\ne E[Y],

because clicking selects a nonrepresentative population.


12.3 When is the clicked mean valid?
It is valid if observation is completely random with respect to outcome:

Y\perp C,

or under stronger designs that make the observed group representative. Usually this is implausible.


12.4 Adjustment using observed covariates
Assume:

Conditional exchangeability / missing at random: Y\perp C\mid X.
Positivity: e(X)>0 wherever the target population has mass.
The propensity e(X) is known or consistently estimated.
Relevant outcomes and covariates are measured consistently.

Then inverse-propensity weighting recovers the population mean:

\boxed{
E[Y]
=E\left[\frac{CY}{e(X)}\right]
}.

Indeed,

E\left[\frac{CY}{e(X)}\mid X,Y\right]
=\frac{Y}{e(X)}E[C\mid X,Y]
=Y.

If selection still depends on unobserved Y after conditioning on X—missing not at random—the overall mean is generally unidentified without extra assumptions, instruments, experiments, or sensitivity analysis.

title: Probabilistic Modeling Practice: 20 Worked Problems
text:
13 Position bias in ranking

13.1 Question
A document has intrinsic binary relevance R, but clicks depend on both relevance and examination:

C=E\cdot R.

Suppose

P(E=1\mid\text{position}=k)=e_k.


Given logged clicks, how can you estimate relevance?
Why is inverse propensity weighting appropriate?
What goes wrong if clicks are used directly as relevance labels?

Concepts: latent examination, position bias, propensity correction, and counterfactual learning.


13.2 Solution
Under the examination model,

C=E\cdot R,

where E indicates examination and R intrinsic relevance. At position k,

P(E=1\mid k)=e_k.

Assuming examination and relevance are conditionally independent given the displayed context,

P(C=1\mid k,x)=e_kP(R=1\mid x).

Thus an observed click at position k receives inverse-propensity weight 1/e_k. For a fixed item shown at positions k_i, an IPS-style relevance estimate is

\boxed{
\hat r
=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\frac{C_i}{e_{k_i}}
},

with clipping or self-normalization often used to control variance.
Training directly on clicks treats unexamined relevant results as negatives. It therefore learns the old ranker’s exposure policy and position effects along with relevance. Propensities may be estimated through randomized swaps/interleaving or an examination model; purely observational estimation requires additional identifiability assumptions.

title: Probabilistic Modeling Practice: 20 Worked Problems
text:
14 Gaussian parameter estimation

14.1 Question
Suppose

X_i\overset{iid}{\sim}\mathcal N(\mu,\sigma^2).


Derive the MLEs of \mu and \sigma^2.
Why does the variance MLE use 1/n while the unbiased sample variance uses 1/(n-1)?

Concepts: likelihood, optimization, estimator bias, and degrees of freedom.


14.2 Solution
Let X_i\overset{iid}{\sim}\mathcal N(\mu,\sigma^2). The log-likelihood is

\ell(\mu,\sigma^2)
=-\frac n2\log(2\pi)-\frac n2\log\sigma^2
-\frac1{2\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\mu)^2.

Differentiating with respect to \mu,

\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial\mu}
=\frac1{\sigma^2}\sum_i(x_i-\mu)=0,

so

\boxed{\hat\mu_{\text{MLE}}=\bar x}.

Substituting \bar x and differentiating with respect to \sigma^2 gives

\boxed{
\hat\sigma^2_{\text{MLE}}
=\frac1n\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2
}.

Why is this biased? Estimating \mu from the same data imposes

\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)=0,

leaving only n-1 independent residual degrees of freedom. In fact,

E\left[\sum_i(X_i-\bar X)^2\right]=(n-1)\sigma^2.

Therefore the unbiased estimator is

\boxed{s^2=\frac1{n-1}\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2}.

MLE optimizes likelihood; it is not defined by unbiasedness.

title: Probabilistic Modeling Practice: 20 Worked Problems
text:
15 Gaussian mixture model and EM

15.1 Question
Data come from

p(x)=\pi\mathcal N(x;\mu_1,\sigma_1^2)
+(1-\pi)\mathcal N(x;\mu_2,\sigma_2^2),

where component assignment Z_i is unobserved.

Derive P(Z_i=1\mid x_i).
Derive the E-step and M-step updates for EM.
State important limitations of EM for Gaussian mixtures.

Concepts: latent-variable inference, marginalization, responsibilities, and EM.


15.2 Solution
Let

p(x)=\pi\mathcal N(x;\mu_1,\sigma_1^2)
+(1-\pi)\mathcal N(x;\mu_2,\sigma_2^2),

with latent assignment Z_i\in\{0,1\}.


15.3 Posterior responsibility
Bayes’ rule gives

\boxed{
\gamma_i
:=P(Z_i=1\mid x_i)
=\frac{\pi\mathcal N(x_i;\mu_1,\sigma_1^2)}
{\pi\mathcal N(x_i;\mu_1,\sigma_1^2)
+(1-\pi)\mathcal N(x_i;\mu_2,\sigma_2^2)}
}.



15.4 EM algorithm
E-step: compute \gamma_i using the current parameters.
M-step: maximize the expected complete-data log-likelihood:

N_1=\sum_i\gamma_i,\qquad N_2=\sum_i(1-\gamma_i),


\pi^{\text{new}}=\frac{N_1}{n},


\mu_1^{\text{new}}=\frac{\sum_i\gamma_ix_i}{N_1},
\qquad
\mu_2^{\text{new}}=\frac{\sum_i(1-\gamma_i)x_i}{N_2},


(\sigma_1^2)^{\text{new}}
=\frac{\sum_i\gamma_i(x_i-\mu_1^{\text{new}})^2}{N_1},


(\sigma_2^2)^{\text{new}}
=\frac{\sum_i(1-\gamma_i)(x_i-\mu_2^{\text{new}})^2}{N_2}.

Repeat until the observed-data log-likelihood stops improving materially. EM monotonically increases—or leaves unchanged—the likelihood but may converge to a local optimum. Mixtures also have label-switching symmetry and can have singular likelihoods when a component variance collapses toward zero.

title: Probabilistic Modeling Practice: 20 Worked Problems
text:
16 Hidden Markov model

16.1 Question
A user has an unobserved intent state

Z_t\in\{\text{shopping},\text{research},\text{navigation}\},

with transition model P(Z_t\mid Z_{t-1}) and observation model P(X_t\mid Z_t). Given X_{1:T}:

How do you compute P(Z_t\mid X_{1:T})?
How do you find the most likely complete state sequence?
Why are these different inference problems?

Concepts: forward–backward, Viterbi, marginal MAP, joint MAP, and dynamic programming.


16.2 Solution
For latent intent states Z_{1:T} and observed queries X_{1:T},

p(z_{1:T},x_{1:T})
=p(z_1)p(x_1\mid z_1)
\prod_{t=2}^Tp(z_t\mid z_{t-1})p(x_t\mid z_t).



16.3 Filtering and smoothing: forward–backward
Define the forward message

\alpha_t(j)=P(X_{1:t},Z_t=j).

Its recurrence is

\alpha_t(j)
=P(X_t\mid Z_t=j)\sum_i\alpha_{t-1}(i)P(Z_t=j\mid Z_{t-1}=i).

Define the backward message

\beta_t(j)=P(X_{t+1:T}\mid Z_t=j),

with recurrence

\beta_t(i)
=\sum_jP(Z_{t+1}=j\mid Z_t=i)
P(X_{t+1}\mid Z_{t+1}=j)\beta_{t+1}(j).

Then the smoothed marginal is

\boxed{
P(Z_t=j\mid X_{1:T})
=\frac{\alpha_t(j)\beta_t(j)}{\sum_k\alpha_t(k)\beta_t(k)}
}.



16.4 Most likely complete path: Viterbi
Define

\delta_t(j)=\max_{z_{1:t-1}}P(z_{1:t-1},Z_t=j,X_{1:t}).

Then

\delta_t(j)
=P(X_t\mid Z_t=j)
\max_i\left[\delta_{t-1}(i)P(Z_t=j\mid Z_{t-1}=i)\right].

Store each maximizing predecessor and backtrack at T.
Forward–backward computes a separate marginal MAP state at each time; Viterbi computes one joint MAP sequence. The individually most probable states need not form the most probable—or even structurally plausible—joint path.

title: Probabilistic Modeling Practice: 20 Worked Problems
text:
17 Bayesian ranking and exploration

17.1 Question
For each item i,

p_i\sim\operatorname{Beta}(\alpha,\beta),

and you observe c_i clicks from n_i impressions. Compare ranking items by:

empirical CTR c_i/n_i;
posterior mean E[p_i\mid D];
a posterior sample \tilde p_i\sim P(p_i\mid D).

When should each score be used, and how do uncertainty and exposure bias affect the choice?
Concepts: Bayesian smoothing, uncertainty, exploration–exploitation, and Thompson sampling.


17.2 Solution
For item i,

p_i\sim\operatorname{Beta}(\alpha,\beta),

with c_i clicks in n_i impressions. Then

p_i\mid D_i
\sim\operatorname{Beta}(\alpha+c_i,\beta+n_i-c_i).










Ranking score
Formula
Behavior
Best use




Empirical CTR
c_i/n_i
No shrinkage; unstable for small n_i
Large, comparable sample sizes; descriptive ranking


Posterior mean
(\alpha+c_i)/(\alpha+\beta+n_i)
Shrinks uncertain items toward prior mean
Stable exploitation and cold-start smoothing


Thompson sample
\tilde p_i\sim p(p_i\mid D_i)
Uncertain items sometimes rank high
Online exploration–exploitation



Ranking by posterior mean maximizes immediate expected clicks under the model. Thompson sampling may sacrifice immediate reward to acquire information and can improve cumulative reward. If poor recommendations are costly, a conservative lower credible bound may be preferable.






NoteImportant logging issue



In a recommender, impressions are policy-dependent and affected by position. Beta–Bernoulli updating alone does not correct exposure bias; the observation model or experimental design must address it.

title: Probabilistic Modeling Practice: 20 Worked Problems
text:
18 Coupon collector

18.1 Question
There are n equally likely categories. You repeatedly draw one category independently.

What is the expected number of draws required to observe every category?
Derive


E[T]=n\left(1+\frac12+\cdots+\frac1n\right).


Give its large-n approximation.

Concepts: decomposition of expectations, geometric waiting times, and harmonic numbers.


18.2 Solution
There are n equally likely categories. After observing k distinct categories, the probability that the next draw is new is

\frac{n-k}{n}.

Let W_k be the additional draws needed to move from k to k+1 observed categories. Then

W_k\sim\operatorname{Geometric}\left(\frac{n-k}{n}\right),

so

E[W_k]=\frac{n}{n-k}.

Because T=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}W_k,

\begin{aligned}
E[T]
&=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\frac{n}{n-k}\\
&=n\sum_{j=1}^n\frac1j\\
&=\boxed{nH_n}.
\end{aligned}

Since H_n=\log n+\gamma+o(1),

\boxed{E[T]\approx n\log n+\gamma n}.

The last few unseen categories dominate the waiting time.

title: Probabilistic Modeling Practice: 20 Worked Problems
section: 19 Maximum and minimum of uniform variables
text:
19 Maximum and minimum of uniform variables

19.1 Question
Let

X_1,\ldots,X_n\overset{iid}{\sim}\operatorname{Uniform}(0,1).

For M=\max_iX_i:

derive its CDF and PDF;
compute E[M].

Then derive the corresponding CDF, PDF, and expectation for m=\min_iX_i.
Concepts: order statistics, independence, and the CDF method.


19.2 Solution
Let X_1,\ldots,X_n\overset{iid}{\sim}\operatorname{Uniform}(0,1).


19.3 Maximum
For M=\max_iX_i and 0\le x\le1,

P(M\le x)
=P(X_1\le x,\ldots,X_n\le x)
=x^n.

Thus

\boxed{F_M(x)=x^n},
\qquad
\boxed{f_M(x)=nx^{n-1}}.

The expectation is

\boxed{E[M]=\int_0^1x\,nx^{n-1}dx=\frac{n}{n+1}}.



19.4 Minimum
For m=\min_iX_i,

P(m>x)=P(X_1>x,\ldots,X_n>x)=(1-x)^n.

Therefore

\boxed{F_m(x)=1-(1-x)^n},


\boxed{f_m(x)=n(1-x)^{n-1}},


\boxed{E[m]=\frac1{n+1}}.

The key trick is to derive the CDF from an event involving all independent variables.

title: Probabilistic Modeling Practice: 20 Worked Problems
text:
20 Random walk and gambler’s ruin

20.1 Question
A particle begins at X_0 and moves independently at each step:

X_{t+1}=
\begin{cases}
X_t+1, & \text{with probability }p,\\
X_t-1, & \text{with probability }1-p.
\end{cases}


Compute E[X_t] and \operatorname{Var}(X_t).
Starting at i\in\{1,\ldots,N-1\}, compute the probability of hitting N before 0.
Compute the expected time to hit either boundary.

Concepts: random walks, Markov chains, first-step recurrences, and gambler’s ruin.


20.2 Solution
Let increments Y_s\in\{+1,-1\} satisfy

P(Y_s=1)=p,\qquad P(Y_s=-1)=q=1-p,

and X_t=X_0+\sum_{s=1}^tY_s.


20.3 Mean and variance
Since E[Y_s]=p-q=2p-1 and \operatorname{Var}(Y_s)=4pq,

\boxed{E[X_t]=X_0+t(2p-1)},


\boxed{\operatorname{Var}(X_t)=4tpq}.



20.4 Probability of hitting N before 0
Let

h_i=P_i(\tau_N<\tau_0).

First-step analysis gives

h_i=ph_{i+1}+qh_{i-1},
\qquad h_0=0,\quad h_N=1.

Solving,

\boxed{
h_i=
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{1-(q/p)^i}{1-(q/p)^N}, & p\ne q,\\[8pt]
\dfrac{i}{N}, & p=q=1/2.
\end{cases}
}



20.5 Expected time to hit either boundary
Let e_i=E_i[\tau_{\{0,N\}}]. Then

e_i=1+pe_{i+1}+qe_{i-1},
\qquad e_0=e_N=0.

The solution is

\boxed{
e_i=
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{Nh_i-i}{p-q}, & p\ne q,\\[8pt]
i(N-i), & p=q=1/2.
\end{cases}
}

For the unbiased walk, the expected position does not drift, yet absorption still occurs and can take O(N^2) time from the middle.

title: Probabilistic Modeling Practice: 20 Worked Problems
text:
21 Probabilistic graphical-model reasoning

21.1 Question
Consider the common-cause graph

X\leftarrow Z\rightarrow Y.


Are X and Y independent marginally?
Are they independent conditioned on Z?

Now consider the collider

X\rightarrow Z\leftarrow Y.


Are X and Y independent marginally?
What happens after conditioning on Z?

Concepts: factorization, conditional independence, d-separation, common causes, colliders, and explaining away.


21.2 Solution


21.3 Common cause: X\leftarrow Z\rightarrow Y
The joint factorizes as

p(x,y,z)=p(z)p(x\mid z)p(y\mid z).

Therefore

\boxed{X\perp Y\mid Z}.

Marginally,

p(x,y)=\sum_zp(z)p(x\mid z)p(y\mid z),

which generally does not equal p(x)p(y). Thus X and Y are usually dependent because observing one provides information about their common cause.


21.4 Collider: X\rightarrow Z\leftarrow Y
The joint factorizes as

p(x,y,z)=p(x)p(y)p(z\mid x,y).

Assuming no other path connects them,

\boxed{X\perp Y}

marginally. But conditioning on Z gives

p(x,y\mid z)\propto p(x)p(y)p(z\mid x,y),

which generally does not factorize. Therefore

\boxed{X\not\!\perp Y\mid Z}.

This is collider bias or explaining away. If admission depends on either high grades or athletic ability, then among admitted students, learning that one student has weaker grades raises the probability that they have strong athletic ability—even if the traits were independent in the applicant population.

title: Probabilistic Modeling Practice: 20 Worked Problems
text:
22 Final synthesis
These problems fall into a small number of reusable modeling patterns:








Pattern
Problems
Core move




Indicator decomposition
Buckets, coupon collector
Convert a global count into local random variables


Reweighting by observation process
Length bias, missingness, position bias
Model why an observation entered the data


Bayes and marginalization
Medical test, coin mixture, conjugate models
Posterior \propto likelihood \times prior


Likelihood-based estimation
Capture–recapture, Gaussian MLE, GMM
Write the data-generating distribution first


Aggregation and confounding
A/B testing, Simpson’s paradox
Separate estimand, uncertainty, and assignment mechanism


Sequential dynamic programming
HMM, random walk
Condition on the next/previous state


Uncertainty-aware decisions
Bayesian ranking
Distinguish inference from action selection









ImportantSenior MLE / Research Engineer takeaway



The unifying question is not “which formula applies?” It is “what observation process generated this dataset?” Most production failures—selection bias, position bias, confounding, feedback loops, and overconfident ranking—come from modeling outcomes while ignoring that process.

title: Linear Attention
text:
Standard attention for one head is
\[
\operatorname{Attention}(Q,K,V)
=
\operatorname{softmax}(QK^T)V.
\]
For sequence length \(T\), forming the score matrix requires \(O(T^2)\) pairwise interactions and \(O(T^2)\) attention storage in a straightforward implementation. FlashAttention avoids materializing this matrix in high-bandwidth memory, but it does not change the quadratic arithmetic of dense attention.
Linear attention changes the attention function so computation can be reassociated. Its cost becomes linear in sequence length when the feature dimension is treated as fixed.

title: Linear Attention
text:
Standard attention for one head is
\[
\operatorname{Attention}(Q,K,V)
=
\operatorname{softmax}(QK^T)V.
\]
For sequence length \(T\), forming the score matrix requires \(O(T^2)\) pairwise interactions and \(O(T^2)\) attention storage in a straightforward implementation. FlashAttention avoids materializing this matrix in high-bandwidth memory, but it does not change the quadratic arithmetic of dense attention.
Linear attention changes the attention function so computation can be reassociated. Its cost becomes linear in sequence length when the feature dimension is treated as fixed.

title: Linear Attention
section: Why Softmax Attention Cannot Simply Be Reordered
text:
Why Softmax Attention Cannot Simply Be Reordered
Matrix multiplication is associative:
\[
(QK^T)V=Q(K^TV).
\]
But row-wise softmax sits between the two products:
\[
\operatorname{softmax}(QK^T)V
\neq
Q\operatorname{softmax}(K^TV).
\]
The softmax normalization for query \(q_i\) depends on all of its scores against the keys. Moving parentheses alone therefore does not produce linear softmax attention.

title: Linear Attention
text:
Kernel Factorization
Generalized attention can use a non-negative similarity function:
\[
o_i
=
\frac{
\sum_{j=1}^{T}\operatorname{sim}(q_i,k_j)v_j
}{
\sum_{j=1}^{T}\operatorname{sim}(q_i,k_j)
}.
\]
Suppose the similarity factorizes through a feature map \(\phi:\mathbb R^{d_h}\rightarrow\mathbb R^r\):
\[
\operatorname{sim}(q,k)=\phi(q)^T\phi(k).
\]
Then the numerator can be reassociated:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_j \left[\phi(q_i)^T\phi(k_j)\right]v_j
&=
\phi(q_i)^T
\left(\sum_j\phi(k_j)v_j^T\right).
\end{aligned}
\]
Define the sequence summaries
\[
S=\sum_j\phi(k_j)v_j^T
\in\mathbb R^{r\times d_v},
\qquad
z=\sum_j\phi(k_j)
\in\mathbb R^r.
\]
The output is
\[
\boxed{
o_i
=
\frac{\phi(q_i)^TS}{\phi(q_i)^Tz}
}.
\]
No \(T\times T\) matrix is required.

title: Linear Attention
section: Causal Linear Attention as a Recurrence
text:
Causal Linear Attention as a Recurrence
For causal attention, query position \(i\) may use only keys and values at \(j\leq i\). Replace the full summaries with prefix states:
\[
S_i=S_{i-1}+\phi(k_i)v_i^T,
\]
\[
z_i=z_{i-1}+\phi(k_i),
\]
\[
o_i
=
\frac{\phi(q_i)^TS_i}{\phi(q_i)^Tz_i+\varepsilon}.
\]
The causal mask is enforced by the update order, not by constructing a mask matrix. During autoregressive decoding, \((S_i,z_i)\) is a fixed-size recurrent state. This makes the connection to an RNN explicit: the sequence history is compressed into state rather than retained as a growing KV cache.






NoteInclusive versus exclusive recurrence



The equations update the state with \((k_i,v_i)\) before reading it, so token \(i\) can attend to itself. Reading before updating would implement a strictly previous-token convention.

title: Linear Attention
text:
Complexity
Let query/key feature width be \(r\) and value width be \(d_v\).








Method
Sequence work per head
Attention state




Dense softmax attention
\(O(T^2(d_h+d_v))\)
\(O(T^2)\) naïvely; tiled by FlashAttention


Linear attention
\(O(Trd_v)\)
\(O(rd_v+r)\)



Linear dependence on \(T\) is not automatically faster. If \(r d_v\) is large, sequences are short, or the implementation uses a slow sequential loop, dense attention with optimized kernels may win in wall-clock time.

title: Linear Attention
text:
Minimal Causal Implementation
The positive feature map
\[
\phi(x)=\operatorname{ELU}(x)+1
\]
makes every kernel score non-negative. This is a pedagogical kernel attention implementation, not an approximation of ordinary softmax attention.

import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F


def positive_feature_map(x):
    return F.elu(x) + 1.0


def causal_linear_attention(q, k, v, eps=1e-6):
    """
    q, k: [batch, heads, time, feature_dim]
    v:    [batch, heads, time, value_dim]
    """
    q_features = positive_feature_map(q)
    k_features = positive_feature_map(k)

    batch, heads, time, feature_dim = q_features.shape
    value_dim = v.shape[-1]
    state = q.new_zeros(batch, heads, feature_dim, value_dim)
    normalizer_state = q.new_zeros(batch, heads, feature_dim)
    outputs = []

    for index in range(time):
        k_t = k_features[:, :, index]
        v_t = v[:, :, index]
        q_t = q_features[:, :, index]

        state = state + torch.einsum("bhr,bhd->bhrd", k_t, v_t)
        normalizer_state = normalizer_state + k_t

        numerator = torch.einsum("bhr,bhrd->bhd", q_t, state)
        denominator = torch.einsum(
            "bhr,bhr->bh", q_t, normalizer_state
        ).unsqueeze(-1)
        outputs.append(numerator / denominator.clamp_min(eps))

    return torch.stack(outputs, dim=2)

Verify the recurrence against a quadratic implementation of the same kernel, not against softmax attention:

torch.manual_seed(0)
q = torch.randn(2, 3, 5, 4)
k = torch.randn(2, 3, 5, 4)
v = torch.randn(2, 3, 5, 6)

q_features = positive_feature_map(q)
k_features = positive_feature_map(k)
scores = torch.einsum("bhir,bhjr->bhij", q_features, k_features)
causal = torch.ones(5, 5, dtype=torch.bool).tril()
scores = scores.masked_fill(~causal, 0.0)

expected = torch.einsum("bhij,bhjd->bhid", scores, v)
expected = expected / scores.sum(dim=-1, keepdim=True).clamp_min(1e-6)
actual = causal_linear_attention(q, k, v)
torch.testing.assert_close(actual, expected)

The Python loop makes the recurrence easy to see but prevents efficient parallel training. Production implementations use chunking, prefix scans, or specialized recurrent kernels.

title: Linear Attention
text:
Choosing the Feature Map
The feature map defines the attention kernel.

Simple positive maps such as ELU(x) + 1 are cheap but define a different similarity from softmax.
Random-feature methods approximate the exponential softmax kernel. Increasing feature width can improve the approximation but increases compute and state.
Learned features can adapt the kernel but add parameters and training dynamics.
Gated or decayed variants control how old information contributes to the fixed-size state.

The denominator matters. Omitting it produces unnormalized aggregation whose magnitude can grow with sequence length. Non-negative features make the normalizer interpretable and reduce the risk of cancellation near zero.

title: Linear Attention
text:
What Is Gained and Lost?

Advantages

linear sequence scaling for fixed \(r\) and \(d_v\)
constant-size decoding state instead of a KV cache that grows with context
natural recurrent, streaming interpretation
causal masking is implicit in the state update



Limitations

most feature maps do not reproduce exact softmax attention
a fixed-size state can overwrite or entangle information from many tokens
prefix sums can accumulate numerical error over long sequences
efficient parallel training needs more than the simple recurrent loop
positional information, locality, forgetting, and state capacity require explicit architectural choices

FlashAttention and linear attention therefore solve different problems: FlashAttention computes ordinary dense attention with better memory movement; linear attention changes the operator to avoid quadratic pairwise computation.
From Test-Time Training to Continual Intelligence develops the related view that learned fast-weight updates can implement a linear-attention-like recurrent state rather than literal key-value regression.

title: Linear Attention
text:
Interview Questions

Why can \((QK^T)V\) be reassociated while \(\operatorname{softmax}(QK^T)V\) cannot?
Derive the \(S_i\) and \(z_i\) causal recurrences.
In what sense is causal linear attention an RNN?
Why must a quadratic reference use the same kernel for a correctness test?
How does feature width trade approximation quality for state and compute?
Compare the decoding state of softmax attention, linear attention, and an RNN.
Why might FlashAttention outperform linear attention at moderate lengths?

title: Linear Attention
text:
Exercises

Implement the non-causal vectorized form without a Python loop.
Change the code to read state before updating it and explain the mask.
Compare outputs from the ELU kernel and softmax attention.
Add an exponential decay to the recurrent state.
Measure runtime and memory as sequence length grows.

title: From Test-Time Training to Continual Intelligence
text:
NoteCompare the two versions



This is the original, shorter version of the argument.
Read the expanded version, which extends the framework to representation compilation, latent reasoning, auxiliary supervision, and compute routing.

title: From Test-Time Training to Continual Intelligence
text:
Thesis
Test-time training (TTT) is usually introduced as a technique: update some model parameters during inference using a self-supervised loss. But the recent evolution of TTT suggests a more interesting interpretation.
The real question is not:

Can a model update its weights at test time?

Of course it can.
The harder question is:

Can we construct a learning system whose local updates are useful, whose update trajectory remains stable, and whose experiences are routed into the right kind of internal state?

Once phrased this way, TTT stops looking like a niche long-context mechanism. It becomes one instance of a much broader problem: continual intelligence.
A continually learning system does not have one homogeneous memory. It has multiple kinds of state, changing at different timescales:
\[
\boxed{
\text{working state}
\rightarrow
\text{episodic memory}
\rightarrow
\text{semantic knowledge}
\rightarrow
\text{procedural skills}
\rightarrow
\text{meta-learning policy}
}
\]
The central architectural question is therefore not merely what loss should we optimize? It is also:

What should be the substrate of each level of learning?

Should an experience become an activation, a prompt, an external memory, a skill, a harness rule, an adapter, or a permanent weight update?
My working hypothesis is that future continually learning agents will use heterogeneous substrates and progressively compile useful structure downward:
\[
\boxed{
\text{explicit + plastic}
\quad\longrightarrow\quad
\text{implicit + efficient}
}
\]
That gives a possible unifying framework for test-time training, long-context memory, skill libraries, agent harnesses, meta-learning, and eventually online RL.
This note connects three other parts of the site:

Linear Attention for the algebraic view of fast-weight memory
Optimization for SGD, Muon, and optimizer dynamics
Agent Harness for explicit state, skills, verification, and meta-level control

title: From Test-Time Training to Continual Intelligence
section: 1. TTT started as adaptation, not memory
text:
1. TTT started as adaptation, not memory
The original formulation of Test-Time Training was motivated by distribution shift.
A model is trained on one distribution but deployed on another:
\[
p_{\text{train}}(x) \neq p_{\text{test}}(x).
\]
At test time, labels are unavailable, so the model constructs a self-supervised task on the incoming example and updates some of its parameters before making the downstream prediction.
Schematically,
\[
\theta'
=
\theta-\eta\nabla_\theta L_{\text{self-supervised}}(x),
\]
followed by
\[
\hat y = f_{\theta'}(x).
\]
The key intuition was that an auxiliary objective such as rotation prediction could provide a gradient that moved the feature extractor toward a representation more suitable for the current test distribution.
This already contained the seed of the central TTT problem:
\[
\boxed{
\nabla L_{\text{aux}}
\text{ must somehow correlate with }
\nabla L_{\text{task}}
}
\]
even though the true task loss is unavailable.
This is an indirect form of control. We do not optimize the thing we actually care about. We invent a locally observable objective and hope that its optimization changes the model in a useful direction.
That is a very strong assumption.

title: From Test-Time Training to Continual Intelligence
section: 2. TTT then changed meaning: weights became recurrent state
text:
2. TTT then changed meaning: weights became recurrent state
The newer sequence-modeling line of TTT repurposed the same mechanism for a different goal.
Instead of asking:

How do I adapt a model to a shifted distribution?

it asks:

Can parameter updates themselves act as a memory state?

Consider a recurrent model:
\[
h_t = F(h_{t-1}, x_t).
\]
A TTT layer replaces the ordinary hidden state with mutable parameters:
\[
W_t
=
U(W_{t-1},x_t).
\]
The update operator (U) is typically implemented as an optimization step:
\[
W_t
=
W_{t-1}
-
\eta\nabla_W L_{\text{TTT}}(W_{t-1};x_t).
\]
Now the weights are not simply “the trained model.” They are also the evolving state of the sequence processor.
This creates a striking reinterpretation:
\[
\boxed{
\text{optimizer dynamics}
\equiv
\text{recurrent dynamics}
}
\]
and
\[
\boxed{
\text{fast weights}
\equiv
\text{memory state}.
}
\]
This is the conceptual bridge from classical TTT to long-context TTT.

title: From Test-Time Training to Continual Intelligence
section: 3. Why did TTT use KV-binding auxiliary losses?
text:
3. Why did TTT use KV-binding auxiliary losses?
A common long-context TTT construction uses a key-value binding objective:
\[
L_{\text{KVB}}
=
\|f_W(k)-v\|^2.
\]
At first glance this is confusing.
Standard attention computes
\[
o(q)
=
\sum_i
\operatorname{softmax}(q^\top k_i)v_i.
\]
There is no requirement that
\[
k_i \approx v_i,
\]
and no function (f) in ordinary attention that is supposed to map a key directly onto its value.
The intended abstraction is different.
An attention KV cache can be viewed as an explicit associative table:
\[
\mathcal M
=
\{k_i \mapsto v_i\}.
\]
TTT asks whether this explicit table can instead be compressed into a parameterized function:
\[
f_W(k_i)\approx v_i.
\]
Then retrieval is performed by evaluating
\[
f_W(q).
\]
Under this interpretation, the auxiliary loss is a memory-writing rule. It is not derived from the original attention equation. It is chosen because SGD on this objective is hoped to encode useful associations into (W).
That difference matters.
The KVB objective does not follow inevitably from the task. It is an architectural hypothesis about how gradients should implement memory.

title: From Test-Time Training to Continual Intelligence
section: 4. The KVB story may be more accidental than it first appeared
text:
4. The KVB story may be more accidental than it first appeared
Recent analysis complicates the literal “SGD memorizes key-value pairs” explanation.
For a simplified linear fast-weight model
\[
f_W(x)=Wx,
\]
consider a loss whose gradient gives an outer-product update:
\[
L = -f_W(k)^\top v.
\]
Then
\[
\nabla_W L = -vk^\top,
\]
and SGD produces
\[
W_t
=
W_{t-1}
+
\eta v_t k_t^\top.
\]
Starting from zero,
\[
W_t
=
\eta
\sum_{i\le t}
v_i k_i^\top.
\]
Querying the state gives
\[
W_tq
=
\eta
\sum_i
v_i(k_i^\top q).
\]
This is immediately recognizable as an attention-like computation:
\[
\boxed{
W_tq
=
\sum_i
\underbrace{(q^\top k_i)}_{\text{routing weight}}
v_i
}
\]
without explicit KV storage.
The important object is therefore not necessarily the semantic statement
\[
f(k)\approx v.
\]
It may instead be the algebra induced by the gradient:
\[
\nabla_W L
\rightarrow
vk^\top.
\]
That makes the auxiliary objective look less like literal memory regression and more like a way to engineer a desired state-transition operator.
The 2026 paper Test-Time Training with KV Binding Is Secretly Linear Attention pushes this view further, arguing that a broad class of KV-binding TTT architectures can be rewritten as learned linear-attention operators. See Linear Attention for the underlying recurrent-state derivation.
This is an important warning.






NoteA useful way to reinterpret auxiliary-loss TTT



TTT is not necessarily “finding a loss that is intrinsically meaningful.”
It may instead be:
\[
\boxed{
\text{choose a loss whose gradient implements a useful low-level computation}
}
\]
That means success depends on our understanding of the geometry and dynamics induced by the optimizer.


And our understanding of those dynamics is still limited.

title: From Test-Time Training to Continual Intelligence
section: 5. Why not use the actual next-token-prediction loss?
text:
5. Why not use the actual next-token-prediction loss?
For an autoregressive language model, we have an unusually convenient test-time learning signal.
After reading a sequence,
\[
x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_T,
\]
every observed token is also a label for the previous prefix:
\[
L_t(\theta)
=
-\log p_\theta(x_t\mid x_{<t}).
\]
So why invent
\[
L_{\text{KVB}}
\]
at all?
Why not simply use
\[
L_{\text{NTP}}?
\]
There are two answers.

5.1 Systems cost
A local auxiliary objective can update a small fast-weight module without backpropagating through the whole language model.
Next-token prediction originates at the logits.
If we update a parameter (W_l) in a lower layer,
\[
\nabla_{W_l}L_{\text{NTP}}
\]
requires gradients to flow through the layers above it.
Inference now inherits some of the costs of training:

backward kernels,
activation storage or recomputation,
mutable request-specific parameters,
optimizer computation,
synchronization and batching challenges.

This is a real cost.
But it is probably not the deepest obstacle.


5.2 The trajectory problem
Suppose we perform online SGD:
\[
\theta_{t+1}
=
\theta_t-\eta g_t,
\qquad
g_t=\nabla_\theta L_t(\theta_t).
\]
A local update may improve the loss on the current sample:
\[
L_t(\theta_{t+1})
<
L_t(\theta_t),
\]
but this does not imply that the resulting model is better on future data.
The update may:

overfit a transient pattern,
damage pretrained capabilities,
distort future gradients,
reinforce an incorrect local interpretation,
accumulate interference over a long stream.

Worse, the process is recursive:
\[
\theta_0
\rightarrow
\theta_1
\rightarrow
\theta_2
\rightarrow
\cdots
\]
with
\[
g_{t+1}
=
\nabla L_{t+1}(\theta_t).
\]
A bad update does not merely create an additive error. It changes the model that computes the next gradient.
So continual test-time learning is a dynamical-system problem:
\[
\boxed{
\theta_{t+1}
=
F(\theta_t,x_t)
}
\]
and local correctness does not guarantee global trajectory stability.

title: From Test-Time Training to Continual Intelligence
section: 6. “TTT Done Right” fixes a different problem
text:
6. “TTT Done Right” fixes a different problem
Earlier TTT sequence models often updated fast weights every few tokens:
\[
B\approx16\text{--}64.
\]
This gives fine-grained causal updates but poor GPU utilization.
For a 128K-token sequence, a 16-token update means
\[
\frac{128K}{16}
=
8192
\]
small optimizer steps.
Those operations are poorly shaped for modern accelerators.
Test-Time Training Done Right introduces Large Chunk TTT (LaCT), increasing update chunks from tens of tokens to thousands or even much larger blocks depending on the modality.
Instead of
\[
x_{1:16}
\rightarrow W_1,
\quad
x_{17:32}
\rightarrow W_2,
\]
we may have
\[
x_{1:2048}
\rightarrow W_1,
\quad
x_{2049:4096}
\rightarrow W_2.
\]
The trick is to combine the slowly updated TTT state with local/window attention:
\[
\boxed{
\text{local attention}
+
\text{long-timescale fast weights}
}
\]
so attention handles interactions within a chunk, while the fast-weight state carries information across chunks.
LaCT therefore primarily attacks:
\[
\boxed{
\text{temporal resolution}
\leftrightarrow
\text{hardware efficiency}
}
\]
rather than replacing the fundamental auxiliary-loss paradigm.
This distinction is useful because it separates two research questions:

What update dynamics should the model use?
How can those dynamics execute efficiently?

LaCT makes major progress on the second.

title: From Test-Time Training to Continual Intelligence
section: 7. In-Place TTT: move the adaptive state into the existing model
text:
7. In-Place TTT: move the adaptive state into the existing model
Another step is to question why TTT needs a specialized fast-weight memory module at all.
In-Place Test-Time Training repurposes existing MLP parameters—in particular the final projection matrix of MLP blocks—as fast weights.
That changes the architecture from something like
\[
\text{Transformer}
+
\text{special TTT memory layer}
\]
toward
\[
\text{ordinary Transformer whose own parameters become adaptive}.
\]
It also replaces the generic reconstruction target with a language-model-aligned local objective designed around next-token prediction.
The significance is not that it simply performs naive full-model NTP SGD. It does not.
The important conceptual steps are:

reuse the existing model as the memory substrate,
update only selected parameters,
align the test-time objective more directly with language modeling,
preserve chunk-wise efficiency.

In-Place TTT therefore weakens two assumptions of classical TTT:

that a special memory architecture is necessary;
that generic reconstruction is the right update objective.

But it still carefully engineers the adaptation rule.

title: From Test-Time Training to Continual Intelligence
section: 8. TTT-E2E: train the model for its own future learning trajectory
text:
8. TTT-E2E: train the model for its own future learning trajectory
End-to-End TTT goes one level deeper.
Instead of pretraining a static model and later applying some test-time updates, it asks:

What initialization should we learn if we already know the model will continue learning during inference?

Ordinary pretraining solves something like
\[
\theta^*
=
\arg\min_\theta
\mathbb E[L(\theta)].
\]
That objective says:

Find a parameter vector that is directly good at prediction.

But if inference will execute an update operator (U),
\[
\theta_1=U(\theta_0,x_1),
\]
\[
\theta_2=U(\theta_1,x_2),
\]
and so on, then the actual deployed object is not (_0).
It is the entire trajectory
\[
\theta_0,\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_T.
\]
So the outer objective should optimize through those updates:
\[
\theta_0^*
=
\arg\min_{\theta_0}
\mathbb E
\left[
L\left(
U_T(
\cdots
U_2(
U_1(\theta_0)
)
)
\right)
\right].
\]
In practice, online language modeling needs good predictions throughout the sequence, so the more revealing objective is conceptually
\[
L_{\text{meta}}
=
\sum_t
L_t(\theta_{t-1}).
\]
Now every intermediate model matters.
This gives a much stronger interpretation of meta-learning:
\[
\boxed{
\text{do not merely learn a good initialization;}
\quad
\text{learn a region of parameter space in which the update trajectory stays useful}
}
\]
or, more suggestively,
\[
\boxed{
\text{learn a stable manifold of online adaptation}.
}
\]

title: From Test-Time Training to Continual Intelligence
section: 9. TTT-E2E is really learning gradient geometry
text:
9. TTT-E2E is really learning gradient geometry
This reframes the role of training.
Suppose the model has some conceptual decomposition
\[
\theta
=
\theta_{\text{stable}}
+
\theta_{\text{plastic}}.
\]
We want gradients from the current context to mostly change the plastic state:
\[
g_t
=
g_t^{\text{context}}
+
\epsilon_t^{\text{knowledge}},
\]
with
\[
\|\epsilon_t^{\text{knowledge}}\|
\ll
\|g_t^{\text{context}}\|.
\]
Meta-training can shape the representation such that ordinary NTP gradients naturally act like memory-writing operations while avoiding destructive directions.
So TTT-E2E is not only learning parameters.
It is learning:
\[
\boxed{
\text{what SGD means inside this representation}.
}
\]
That is a much more interesting objective.
Ordinary pretraining learns a function.
Meta-trained TTT additionally learns a local learning geometry around that function.
This is closely related to the idea of optimizer programming:
\[
\boxed{
\text{representation learning}
+
\text{optimizer dynamics}
=
\text{learned recurrent transition}.
}
\]

title: From Test-Time Training to Continual Intelligence
section: 10. But long-context memory is only one layer of continual learning
text:
10. But long-context memory is only one layer of continual learning
At this point it becomes natural to compare TTT with human continual learning.
A two-way split between
\[
\text{pretrained knowledge}
\]
and
\[
\text{test-time context}
\]
is useful, but incomplete.
A more interesting hierarchy is:
\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
M &: \text{episodic / contextual state} \\
K &: \text{semantic knowledge} \\
P &: \text{procedural / reasoning skills} \\
A &: \text{meta-policy for reasoning and learning}
\end{aligned}
}
\]
These are not merely different amounts of memory.
They encode fundamentally different things.

title: From Test-Time Training to Continual Intelligence
section: 11. Level I: episodic state — what just happened?
text:
11. Level I: episodic state — what just happened?
Examples:

a definition introduced 30K tokens ago,
a repository-specific convention,
an earlier failed attempt,
a user’s temporary constraint,
a fact relevant only to the current task.

This state needs:
\[
\text{high plasticity}
\qquad
\text{low commitment}.
\]
The best substrates are likely:

activations,
attention/KV state,
recurrent state,
external scratch memory,
request-specific fast weights.

TTT is especially interesting here because it provides a compressed alternative to explicitly retaining all previous activations.
The ideal behavior is:
\[
\text{experience}
\rightarrow
M_{\text{episode}},
\]
not immediately
\[
\text{experience}
\rightarrow
\Delta\theta_{\text{global}}.
\]
Most experiences should be cheap to forget.

title: From Test-Time Training to Continual Intelligence
section: 12. Level II: semantic knowledge — what has become stably true?
text:
12. Level II: semantic knowledge — what has become stably true?
Suppose the system repeatedly encounters evidence supporting a fact or abstraction.
At some point it becomes inefficient to retrieve the original episodes every time.
The information should be consolidated into a slower representation:
\[
M_{\text{episode}}
\rightarrow
K_{\text{semantic}}.
\]
Dense model weights are good at this because they provide:

compression,
abstraction,
broad generalization,
constant-cost implicit retrieval.

But weights are poor at:

provenance,
very recent information,
precise rare facts,
reversible correction.

So semantic knowledge probably wants a hybrid substrate:
\[
\boxed{
K
=
\text{slow weights}
+
\text{retrieval store}.
}
\]
The retrieval store handles the fresh, rare, precise, and attributable long tail.
Weights absorb stable patterns that repeatedly prove useful.
This resembles consolidation:
\[
\text{episodes}
\rightarrow
\text{selection}
\rightarrow
\text{compression}
\rightarrow
\text{slow weights}.
\]

title: From Test-Time Training to Continual Intelligence
section: 13. Level III: procedural knowledge — how should I solve this kind of problem?
text:
13. Level III: procedural knowledge — how should I solve this kind of problem?
This is where a simple “memory” framing breaks down.
Suppose an agent repeatedly solves a new family of problems.
Initially it may reason laboriously:
\[
\text{try A}
\rightarrow
\text{fail}
\rightarrow
\text{try B}
\rightarrow
\text{notice invariant}
\rightarrow
\text{solve}.
\]
Eventually it should learn something like:

When this structure appears, search for invariant (X), transform with (Y), then recurse.

This is not a fact.
It is a reusable procedure.
Let the reasoning policy be
\[
\pi_\phi(a_t\mid s_t).
\]
Procedural learning changes
\[
\phi,
\]
not simply the world model.
This gives an important distinction:
\[
\boxed{\text{knowing that}}
\neq
\boxed{\text{knowing how}}.
\]
Current LLMs contain many reasoning priors in their weights, learned through pretraining and post-training:
\[
\text{decompose}
\rightarrow
\text{solve}
\rightarrow
\text{verify}
\rightarrow
\text{backtrack}.
\]
At inference time those priors generate reasoning traces.
But the traces usually do not permanently improve the procedure that generated them.
A model can rediscover the same strategy many times without proceduralizing it.

title: From Test-Time Training to Continual Intelligence
section: 14. Why NTP is much weaker for procedural learning
text:
14. Why NTP is much weaker for procedural learning
For contextual memory, NTP is beautifully aligned.
If the context says

Alice’s secret number is 73,

then predicting future tokens can reward storing that information.
But imagine a model solves a proof using a terrible 50-step reasoning process and still reaches the correct answer.
Training on its trace using NTP may teach:
\[
\text{produce the same bad reasoning more confidently}.
\]
If the reasoning is wrong, naive self-training can reinforce the error.
So procedural learning needs a signal closer to
\[
\text{reason}
\rightarrow
\text{act}
\rightarrow
\text{observe}
\rightarrow
R
\rightarrow
\Delta\pi.
\]
The relevant feedback may include:

verifier results,
execution outcomes,
environment reward,
counterexamples,
efficiency,
downstream task success.

This is closer to RL and decision learning than to pure prediction.
Cursor Tab and Composer provide a concrete product-scale example: frequent on-policy RL improves action utility, but KL anchoring, task breadth, and regression gates—not RL by itself—provide partial protection against policy regression. See Cursor’s Continual Training Loop.
It also makes the trajectory-stability problem harder.
A corrupted episodic memory can damage one task.
A corrupted reasoning policy can systematically damage every later task.

title: From Test-Time Training to Continual Intelligence
section: 15. Level IV: meta-learning — how should I decide how to think?
text:
15. Level IV: meta-learning — how should I decide how to think?
There is an even higher layer.
A reasoning strategy might say:

Solve this family of problems by backward induction.

A meta-strategy says:

When direct search branches exponentially and the target state is constrained, consider switching to backward reasoning.

And above that:

If several attempts fail in structurally similar ways, stop sampling variants and infer the shared assumption behind the failures.

These are policies over computation itself.
Let
\[
A(s)
\]
select among actions such as
\[
\{
\text{answer},
\text{retrieve},
\text{search},
\text{simulate},
\text{invoke skill},
\text{verify},
\text{backtrack},
\text{store},
\text{learn}
\}.
\]
This is metacognition in an engineering sense.
It decides:

how much computation to spend,
what reasoning method to use,
when to use tools,
when to seek evidence,
when to stop,
what to remember,
what deserves learning.

This is not naturally represented as one static prompt.
It is a control loop.

title: From Test-Time Training to Continual Intelligence
text:
16. The substrate should be heterogeneous
This leads to the central architectural claim of this note.
Different levels of continual learning require different properties.









Level
Contents
Timescale
Preferred substrate




Working state
intermediate computation
tokens/seconds
activations


Episodic memory
current experience/context
session/hours
context, external memory, fast weights


Semantic knowledge
stable facts and abstractions
long
slow weights + retrieval


Procedural skills
reusable reasoning/tool procedures
many tasks
skill objects, programs, adapters


Meta-policy
how to reason/learn
very long / continual
learned controller inside explicit harness



A single homogeneous parameter tensor is poorly matched to this structure.

title: From Test-Time Training to Continual Intelligence
section: 17. Prompts are useful—but probably as an intermediate representation
text:
17. Prompts are useful—but probably as an intermediate representation
Natural language prompts are currently an excellent way to represent a newly discovered procedure.
For example:

When debugging a latency regression:

separate queueing, compute, and network latency;
identify which percentile changed;
correlate with deploys;
run the cheapest discriminative test first.


This is already a reusable skill.
But prompt text has weaknesses:

token overhead,
brittleness,
weak typing,
no execution guarantees,
repeated parsing on every invocation.

So I would treat prompts as something like skill bytecode.
A skill could begin as natural language:
\[
s_{\text{text}}.
\]
Then become a structured object:
\[
s
=
(
\text{trigger},
\text{procedure},
\text{tools},
\text{verifier},
\text{statistics}
).
\]
Eventually it could be compiled into:

a policy adapter,
a tool DAG,
a controller,
a small program,
or even dense weights.

Thus:
\[
\boxed{
\text{prompt is a convenient early substrate, not necessarily the final one}.
}
\]

title: From Test-Time Training to Continual Intelligence
section: 18. Reasoning skills should often be explicit before they become weights
text:
18. Reasoning skills should often be explicit before they become weights
Consider a reusable debugging strategy.
Instead of immediately modifying billions of model parameters, represent it explicitly:
skill: debug_latency_regression

trigger:
  - latency regression
  - distributed service

procedure:
  - establish which percentile changed
  - decompose queue / compute / network
  - compare traces before and after
  - identify correlated deploys
  - choose the cheapest discriminative test

verifier:
  - proposed cause explains observed metric changes
  - intervention changes the predicted bottleneck
This representation has several advantages over an implicit weight change:

inspectable,
editable,
compositional,
attributable,
easy to test,
easy to revert.

If repeated evidence shows that the skill is robust, it can later be distilled.
That suggests a general compilation hierarchy:
\[
\boxed{
\text{experience}
\rightarrow
\text{verbalized skill}
\rightarrow
\text{structured skill}
\rightarrow
\text{learned controller}
\rightarrow
\text{weight consolidation}
}
\]
Each downward transition trades flexibility for efficiency.

title: From Test-Time Training to Continual Intelligence
section: 19. Meta-reasoning belongs primarily in the harness
text:
19. Meta-reasoning belongs primarily in the harness
Questions such as

Should I search?


Should I think longer?


Should I retrieve a previous skill?


Is the current approach failing?


Should I run code?


Should I ask another model?


Should this experience become permanent knowledge?

are decisions about the allocation and organization of computation.
These are naturally expressed as a loop:
\[
s_t
\rightarrow
a_t
\rightarrow
o_t
\rightarrow
r_t
\rightarrow
s_{t+1}.
\]
An explicit agent harness can maintain state and enforce control boundaries:
observe
  ↓
estimate state
  ↓
select strategy / skill
  ↓
execute model or tool
  ↓
evaluate outcome
  ↓
detect surprise / failure
  ↓
decide whether to
  ├─ continue
  ├─ backtrack
  ├─ retrieve
  ├─ switch strategy
  ├─ store episode
  ├─ update skill
  └─ consolidate learning
This does not mean the harness should remain handcrafted forever.
A better endpoint is:
\[
\boxed{
\text{learned policy inside an explicit execution harness}.
}
\]
The boundary remains explicit, while the controller becomes learned.

title: From Test-Time Training to Continual Intelligence
section: 20. A handcrafted harness has the same weakness as handcrafted TTT losses
text:
20. A handcrafted harness has the same weakness as handcrafted TTT losses
There is an important symmetry here.
Old auxiliary-loss TTT says:

Human researchers will design a low-level loss whose gradient happens to produce good memory dynamics.

A fully handwritten agent harness says:

Human researchers will design a set of rules whose branching logic happens to produce good reasoning dynamics.

Both assume too much human understanding.
For example, hard-coded logic such as
if uncertainty > 0.7:
    search()

if failed_attempts >= 2:
    critique()
is useful for bootstrapping, but unlikely to be the final form.
The harness should generate trajectories, outcomes, and feedback that can train a controller:
\[
\pi_\phi(a\mid s).
\]
The controller can gradually learn:

when search is valuable,
when extra reasoning is worth the latency,
which verifier is informative,
which skill applies,
when an experience is novel enough to store.

So the architectural endpoint is neither “everything in weights” nor “everything in code.”
It is:
\[
\boxed{
\text{learned policies operating over explicit computational primitives}.
}
\]

title: From Test-Time Training to Continual Intelligence
section: 21. The missing component: credit routing across substrates
text:
21. The missing component: credit routing across substrates
Once multiple substrates exist, the most important decision may not be the optimizer step.
It is:

What kind of thing did we just learn?

Suppose the agent encounters a surprising outcome.
The same surprise could imply very different updates.

Case A: task-specific episode

This repository’s test suite must be run from /src.

Store in episodic/project memory.


Case B: stable external fact

A library API has permanently changed.

Store in retrieval, perhaps later consolidate into weights.


Case C: reusable procedure

This failure class is best diagnosed by checking ownership before timing.

Update or create a skill.


Case D: reasoning-policy failure

The agent repeatedly keeps searching even when enough evidence already exists.

Update the meta-controller.


Case E: foundational regularity

A pattern is broadly useful across domains and repeatedly confirmed.

Eventually distill into slow weights.
Thus a continual learner requires a routing operator:
\[
C(e)
\rightarrow
\{
M,
K,
S,
\pi_{\text{meta}},
\theta
\}.
\]
where (e) is an experience.
This is continual credit assignment over internal state types.
I suspect this is more fundamental than choosing Adam versus SGD.

title: From Test-Time Training to Continual Intelligence
section: 22. A candidate architecture for continual intelligence
text:
22. A candidate architecture for continual intelligence
A useful abstraction is:
\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
\theta_{\text{base}}
&: \text{general semantic and procedural priors} \\
h_t
&: \text{current working state} \\
M
&: \text{episodic memory} \\
K
&: \text{retrievable semantic knowledge} \\
S
&: \text{reusable skill library} \\
\pi_{\text{meta}}
&: \text{learned strategy-selection policy} \\
H
&: \text{explicit execution harness}
\end{aligned}
}
\]
The system operates as
\[
(x,h,M,K,S)
\xrightarrow{\pi_{\text{meta}}}
a
\]
where (a) chooses a computation.
The harness executes it:
\[
a
\xrightarrow{H}
o.
\]
The outcome produces prediction error, task reward, verifier feedback, or surprise:
\[
o
\rightarrow
\delta.
\]
Then a credit router decides what to update:
\[
\delta
\xrightarrow{C}
\begin{cases}
\Delta h \\
\Delta M \\
\Delta K \\
\Delta S \\
\Delta\pi_{\text{meta}} \\
\Delta\theta_{\text{base}}.
\end{cases}
\]
This is a much richer picture than
\[
\theta
\leftarrow
\theta-\eta\nabla L.
\]

title: From Test-Time Training to Continual Intelligence
section: 23. The key design principle: progressive compilation
text:
23. The key design principle: progressive compilation
Human skill acquisition gives an intuitive analogy.
When learning to drive a manual transmission, actions may initially be explicit:

clutch in, change gear, slowly release clutch.

With practice they become automatic.
Computationally:
\[
\text{explicit working-memory program}
\rightarrow
\text{procedural representation}
\rightarrow
\text{compiled neural policy}.
\]
The same principle could organize artificial continual learning.

Stage 1: raw episode
A single success is stored as an experience.


Stage 2: verbal abstraction
After repeated successes, the system forms a hypothesis:

Backward reasoning tends to work when the goal state is strongly constrained.



Stage 3: structured skill
The system encodes a reusable procedure:
\[
\text{detect constrained target}
\rightarrow
\text{attempt backward reasoning}.
\]


Stage 4: learned controller
Repeated data trains
\[
\pi_\phi(
\text{backward-reasoning}\mid s
).
\]


Stage 5: weight consolidation
If the strategy becomes universally useful, it may be absorbed into the base model.
This suggests a continuum:
\[
\boxed{
\text{harness}
>
\text{skills}
>
\text{memory}
>
\text{weights}
}
\]
where moving downward means:
\[
\text{less flexible}
\quad
\text{but}
\quad
\text{cheaper, faster, more automatic}.
\]
Moving upward means:
\[
\text{more explicit}
\quad
\text{but}
\quad
\text{more expensive and deliberative}.
\]

title: From Test-Time Training to Continual Intelligence
section: 24. This changes how we should think about “reasoning”
text:
24. This changes how we should think about “reasoning”
The current discussion around reasoning models often treats reasoning as extra tokens:
\[
x
\rightarrow
\tau_{\text{CoT}}
\rightarrow
y.
\]
But this conflates three distinct things:

reasoning execution — the current trajectory ();
reasoning skill — the reusable policy that generates good trajectories;
meta-reasoning — the policy that chooses which reasoning method to invoke.

A continually learning reasoning system should improve all three at different timescales.
An individual chain of thought is working state.
A discovered reusable algorithm is procedural memory.
The rule for deciding when to invoke that algorithm is meta-policy.
This distinction suggests that simply increasing inference compute is not sufficient for continual intelligence.
A system that repeatedly discovers a good strategy but never compiles it has no procedural learning.
It is merely re-solving.

title: From Test-Time Training to Continual Intelligence
section: 25. Long-context TTT may be the easiest instance of a much larger idea
text:
25. Long-context TTT may be the easiest instance of a much larger idea
TTT-E2E currently frames long-context language modeling as continual learning.
That is a powerful conceptual shift:

Attention
\[
\text{remember by retaining activations}.
\]


RNN
\[
\text{remember by updating hidden state}.
\]


TTT
\[
\text{remember by continuing to learn}.
\]
But long-context memory may only be the lowest nontrivial level.
The larger progression is:
\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
\text{prediction error}
&\rightarrow
\text{learn this context} \\
\text{task outcome}
&\rightarrow
\text{learn a procedure} \\
\text{history of outcomes}
&\rightarrow
\text{learn a better learning strategy}.
\end{aligned}
}
\]
The first can plausibly use NTP.
The second requires richer feedback.
The third requires meta-level credit assignment.
This is where TTT reconnects with meta-learning—but in a broader form than the original literature.

title: From Test-Time Training to Continual Intelligence
text:
26. A research agenda
The framework above suggests several concrete research questions.

26.1 Learn the credit router
Given an experience (e), predict:
\[
C(e)
\in
\{
\text{discard},
\text{episode},
\text{knowledge},
\text{skill},
\text{meta-policy},
\text{weights}
\}.
\]
This might be one of the most important learned decisions in a continual agent.
The objective should include not only immediate utility but the future cost of storing incorrect abstractions.



26.2 Train update trajectories, not only endpoints
For any mutable substrate,
\[
z_{t+1}=U(z_t,e_t),
\]
optimize the quality of the whole trajectory:
\[
J
=
\sum_t
R(z_t,e_{t+1:T})
\]
rather than merely the final state.
This is the deeper lesson of TTT-E2E.
Stable continual learning requires intermediate states to remain useful.



26.3 Separate plastic and stable capacities
Rather than updating a homogeneous model, expose different timescales:
\[
\theta
=
\theta_{\text{slow}}
+
\theta_{\text{medium}}
+
\theta_{\text{fast}}.
\]
The system should learn which directions belong to each timescale.
This could involve:

adapters,
low-rank fast weights,
modular experts,
learned parameter masks,
optimizer-specific subspaces.




26.4 Treat skill formation as program synthesis
When multiple successful trajectories share structure, synthesize a compact reusable procedure.
Input:
\[
\tau_1,\tau_2,\ldots,\tau_n.
\]
Output:
\[
s
=
\operatorname{CompressProcedure}
(
\tau_{1:n}
).
\]
Evaluate the skill on held-out tasks before promoting it.
This creates an analogue of consolidation with explicit validation.



26.5 Learn when to compile
Compilation should depend on evidence.
A possible hierarchy:
\[
\text{episode count}
\rightarrow
\text{skill hypothesis}
\rightarrow
\text{held-out validation}
\rightarrow
\text{controller integration}
\rightarrow
\text{weight distillation}.
\]
Promotion should be reversible.
Bad abstractions should remain cheap to delete.



26.6 Optimize the harness as a policy
Represent harness decisions explicitly but train their selection.
\[
\pi_\phi(a\mid s)
\]
could choose:

direct answer,
extended reasoning,
search,
tool invocation,
simulation,
retrieval,
skill execution,
critique,
verification,
learning.

The execution graph remains interpretable while the choice policy becomes learned.



26.7 Distinguish prediction surprise from decision regret
NTP gives a useful signal:
\[
\delta_{\text{pred}}
=
-\log p(x_t\mid x_{<t}).
\]
But a reasoning agent also observes decision-level feedback:
\[
\delta_{\text{decision}}
=
R_{\text{expected}}-R_{\text{actual}}.
\]
These signals should update different substrates.
Prediction surprise is often evidence about the world.
Decision regret is often evidence about the policy.
Conflating them into one generic gradient may be fundamentally inefficient.

title: From Test-Time Training to Continual Intelligence
text:
27. A broader decision-loop interpretation
A static language model is approximately
\[
x_t
\rightarrow
p(x_{t+1}).
\]
A recurrent model is
\[
(h_t,x_t)
\rightarrow
(h_{t+1},p_t).
\]
A TTT-style model adds explicit learning:
\[
(\theta_t,x_t)
\rightarrow
\text{prediction}
\rightarrow
\text{surprise}
\rightarrow
\nabla L_t
\rightarrow
\theta_{t+1}.
\]
A continually intelligent agent needs the more general loop:
\[
\boxed{
\text{observe}
\rightarrow
\text{predict}
\rightarrow
\text{decide}
\rightarrow
\text{act}
\rightarrow
\text{observe surprise/outcome}
\rightarrow
\text{assign credit}
\rightarrow
\text{update the appropriate substrate}.
}
\]
The final step is the critical extension.
Not every surprise should modify the same thing.
A token prediction error may update context memory.
A factual contradiction may update semantic memory.
A failed proof may update a reasoning skill.
Repeated strategy failure may update the meta-controller.
A deeply repeated regularity may eventually update slow weights.
This is a much more structured conception of learning than universal SGD.

title: Essays
text:
Non-technical and non-political thought experiments.









When Productivity Outruns Demand: Can AI Become an Economic Goal in Itself?


From the Great Depression to machine-generated final demand





Aug 18, 2026


Kedi Xu





No matching items

title: When Productivity Outruns Demand: Can AI Become an Economic Goal in Itself?
text:
One of the most revealing features of the Great Depression is that the United States did not suddenly forget how to produce.
The workers were still there. The factories were still there. The technology was still there. The natural resources were still there.
Yet output collapsed.
A useful abstraction is
\[
Y = \min(D,\; Y^*)
\]
where \(D\) is effective demand and \(Y^*\) is potential output.
During much of the Depression,
\[
D \ll Y^*.
\]
The economy was capable of producing far more than it actually produced.
The immediate collapse was amplified by a financial feedback loop:
\[
\text{bank failures}
\rightarrow
\text{credit contraction}
\rightarrow
\text{deflation}
\rightarrow
\text{higher real debt burdens}
\rightarrow
\text{defaults}
\rightarrow
\text{more bank failures}.
\]
Roosevelt’s early policies helped break that loop. Banking stabilization, monetary reflation, and relief programs stopped the downward spiral and initiated a large recovery.
But substantial productive slack remained.
World War II finally forced the economy close to its productive frontier.
The government became a buyer with extraordinarily large demand for ships, aircraft, vehicles, steel, factories, energy, logistics, labor, and research. The macroeconomic constraint changed from something like
\[
D < Y^*
\]
to
\[
D \gtrsim Y^*.
\]
At that point, the visible economic problems changed completely: unemployment gave way to labor shortages, materials shortages, rationing, and inflation.
This is the key lesson:

Productive capacity does not automatically create a reason to use itself.

A civilization can possess labor, capital, knowledge, and technology while leaving a large fraction of them idle because no actor generates enough effective demand for their output.
