title: Case Study: Cursor’s Continual Training Loop
text:
Cursor frequently updates Tab and Composer from production interaction data. This makes them useful case studies for three questions:

How can a deployed model generate its next round of training data?
Why use reinforcement learning instead of only next-token prediction?
Does changing the objective to RL solve catastrophic forgetting?

The short answer to the third question is no. RL improves alignment between training signal and product utility. Retention still depends on the task mixture, replay or anchoring distribution, regularization, and regression evaluation.
This note reconstructs only what Cursor has publicly disclosed. Details such as the complete data mixture, reward weights, replay policy, and all anti-forgetting mechanisms remain private.

title: Case Study: Cursor’s Continual Training Loop
text:
Cursor frequently updates Tab and Composer from production interaction data. This makes them useful case studies for three questions:

How can a deployed model generate its next round of training data?
Why use reinforcement learning instead of only next-token prediction?
Does changing the objective to RL solve catastrophic forgetting?

The short answer to the third question is no. RL improves alignment between training signal and product utility. Retention still depends on the task mixture, replay or anchoring distribution, regularization, and regression evaluation.
This note reconstructs only what Cursor has publicly disclosed. Details such as the complete data mixture, reward weights, replay policy, and all anti-forgetting mechanisms remain private.

title: Case Study: Cursor’s Continual Training Loop
text:
Two Meanings of Continual Learning
Cursor’s public loops implement population-level online model improvement:
\[
\text{deploy checkpoint}
\rightarrow
\text{collect population feedback}
\rightarrow
\text{train next checkpoint}
\rightarrow
\text{evaluate and redeploy}.
\]
This differs from a model updating private weights during one user’s lifetime:








Form
Persistent state
Timescale




Cursor’s real-time training
shared model checkpoint
hours to model releases


within-session adaptation
context, cache, files, or memory
seconds to hours


lifelong personalized learning
user-specific persistent memory or weights
months to years



The distinction matters when connecting this case to continual intelligence. Cursor is closing the outer product-training loop, not claiming to solve every layer of lifelong memory.

title: Case Study: Cursor’s Continual Training Loop
section: Cursor Tab: Learn Whether an Action Is Worth Showing
text:
Cursor Tab: Learn Whether an Action Is Worth Showing
Tab observes a state \(s\) containing the codebase, cursor location, and recent interaction. Its action is not merely a token continuation. It can:

propose an edit
propose a cursor jump or subsequent edit
abstain and show nothing

User acceptance or rejection supplies a reward. Cursor repeatedly deploys a checkpoint, collects fresh actions and outcomes, applies a policy-gradient update, and deploys the next checkpoint:






flowchart LR
    P[Current Tab policy] --> D[Deploy]
    D --> I[User interactions]
    I --> R[Accept / reject / abstain rewards]
    R --> U[Policy-gradient update]
    U --> E[Regression and product evaluation]
    E --> P2[Next policy]







Why abstention makes this a decision problem
Suppose the illustrative rewards are
\[
R(\text{accept})=0.75,
\qquad
R(\text{reject})=-0.25,
\qquad
R(\text{abstain})=0.
\]
If a suggestion has acceptance probability \(p\), showing it has expected reward
\[
0.75p-0.25(1-p)=p-0.25.
\]
The optimal policy therefore shows the suggestion only when \(p>0.25\). Changing the reward changes the implicit threshold. The model learns generation and filtering as one policy rather than relying only on a separately trained acceptance classifier.
Cursor reports collecting a new checkpoint’s on-policy data in roughly 1.5–2 hours. Its disclosed result made fewer suggestions while increasing the acceptance rate. See Improving Cursor Tab with online RL.


Why not train only on the user’s next edit?
NTP or behavior cloning would answer:

Given this context, what action did the user take?

Tab’s product objective is closer to:

Given the action this policy would propose, was showing it useful enough to interrupt the user?

One logged user edit is not the only acceptable continuation. It also does not directly label the counterfactual value of showing a particular model-generated suggestion. Acceptance, rejection, suggestion length, jumps, and abstention are more naturally expressed as action-dependent utility.

title: Case Study: Cursor’s Continual Training Loop
section: Composer: Knowledge First, Agent Policy Second
text:
Composer: Knowledge First, Agent Policy Second
Composer does not replace language-model training with RL. Composer 2 uses a staged pipeline:






flowchart LR
    B[Kimi K2.5 base] --> C[Code-heavy continued pretraining]
    C --> L[Long-context extension]
    L --> S[Targeted SFT]
    S --> R[Asynchronous agentic RL]
    R --> O[Real-time production RL]






The stages solve different problems:







Stage
Primary role




continued pretraining
acquire code knowledge and lower code perplexity


long-context training
operate on larger codebases and histories


targeted SFT
initialize useful instruction and tool behavior


simulated agent RL
optimize multi-step problem solving in a controlled harness


production RL
reduce simulator–user mismatch using real outcomes



Cursor reports that lower continued-pretraining cross-entropy predicts better downstream RL performance. This is evidence against the idea that agentic RL makes NTP obsolete. A knowledgeable base makes a better policy learner. See the Composer 2 technical report.

Simulated agentic RL
Composer receives realistic coding tasks and the same classes of tools used in the deployed agent harness: file reading and editing, terminal commands, grep, semantic search, and web search. Multiple trajectories are sampled, executed in sandboxed environments, and updated according to solution quality.
The disclosed task distribution includes new features, debugging, refactoring, codebase understanding, documentation, testing, review, optimization, DevOps, migration, and deletion. Task breadth is important: a narrow stream of one task type would make specialization and forgetting much harder to distinguish.
Composer 2 updates the full parameter set, operates in a single-epoch regime, uses KL regularization, and tries to keep asynchronous rollouts close to the current policy through frequent weight synchronization and MoE-routing replay.


Real-time RL
Cursor later closes the loop with production use:
\[
\text{billions of interaction tokens}
\rightarrow
\text{derived reward signals}
\rightarrow
\text{full-weight update}
\rightarrow
\text{regression suites}
\rightarrow
\text{deployment}.
\]
Cursor reports that this cycle can produce a candidate checkpoint in about five hours. Before deployment, the model is checked against CursorBench and other evaluation suites. Production monitoring revealed reward hacks such as intentionally invalid tool calls and excessive clarification instead of editing; the reward and data pipeline then had to be corrected. See Improving Composer through real-time RL.
This is best understood as a closed-loop product optimizer. The reward is not a fact about the world; it is an evolving measurement system built from user behavior, environment outcomes, latency, persistence of edits, and product judgment.

title: Case Study: Cursor’s Continual Training Loop
section: Composer 2.5: RL and Distillation Are Composed
text:
Composer 2.5: RL and Distillation Are Composed
Long trajectories make credit assignment difficult: a final reward may reveal that the rollout was poor without identifying the bad turn. Composer 2.5 adds targeted textual feedback:

locate a problematic message or tool decision
insert a short corrective hint into that local context
treat the hint-conditioned model distribution as a teacher
apply an on-policy KL loss from the original-context student toward that teacher
retain the broader trajectory-level RL objective

This combines sparse outcome optimization with dense local supervision:
\[
\mathcal L
=
\mathcal L_{\mathrm{RL}}
+
\lambda
\operatorname{KL}
\left(
\pi_{\text{teacher with hint}}
\middle\|
\pi_{\theta,\text{original context}}
\right).
\]
It is a concrete instance of the distinction in Distillation: Learning from a Teacher: the state distribution, teacher construction, KL direction, and trajectory reward are separate design choices. See Introducing Composer 2.5.

title: Case Study: Cursor’s Continual Training Loop
section: RL and NTP Differ in Credit, Not Memory Safety
text:
RL and NTP Differ in Credit, Not Memory Safety
For a demonstrated action \(a^*\), NTP/SFT applies
\[
\nabla_\theta\mathcal L_{\mathrm{NTP}}
=
-\mathbb E
\left[
\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(a^*\mid s)
\right].
\]
A policy gradient applies
\[
\nabla_\theta J
=
\mathbb E_{s,a\sim\pi_\theta}
\left[
A(s,a)\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(a\mid s)
\right].
\]
Both change log probabilities in the same shared parameters. RL changes which actions receive positive or negative weight and permits sequence-level, action-dependent credit. Nothing in this equation automatically protects an old capability whose states are absent from the new training distribution.
This illustrates the four-axis framework in Losses from First Principles:








Axis
NTP/SFT
Online RL




learned object
conditional next-action distribution
utility-maximizing policy


supervision
observed target action
environment or user reward


discrepancy
log loss
advantage-weighted log probability


state distribution
usually logged/static contexts
current policy’s encountered states

title: Case Study: Cursor’s Continual Training Loop
section: Why RL Does Not Solve Catastrophic Forgetting
text:
Why RL Does Not Solve Catastrophic Forgetting
Catastrophic forgetting occurs when updates that improve the current training distribution damage behavior required on earlier or absent distributions. Both NTP and RL can cause it:
\[
\nabla L_{\text{new}}^T\nabla L_{\text{old}}<0
\]
indicates local gradient interference. RL can make the problem worse when its reward is narrow, noisy, or exploitable: policy entropy can collapse, a single tool strategy can dominate, or measurable behavior can displace unmeasured skills.
A KL penalty can limit behavioral drift:
\[
\max_\theta
\mathbb E_{\tau\sim\pi_\theta}[R(\tau)]
-
\beta
\mathbb E_{s\sim\mu}
\operatorname{KL}
\left(
\pi_\theta(\cdot\mid s)
\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(\cdot\mid s)
\right).
\]
But this protects behavior only on anchor states \(s\sim\mu\). If an old skill is missing from \(\mu\), the KL term does not directly test it. KL is a trust region, not a complete memory system.

title: Case Study: Cursor’s Continual Training Loop
text:
What Actually Provides Retention?
Cursor has not disclosed or claimed a complete solution to catastrophic forgetting. The public recipe exposes several practical defenses:








Mechanism
What it protects
What it cannot guarantee




broad task distribution
coverage across common coding workflows
unrelated or rare skills


KL to a reference policy
local behavioral stability on anchor states
retention off the anchor distribution


small, frequent on-policy cycles
lower policy lag and easier diagnosis
absence of long-run feedback loops


single-epoch RL prompts
less memorization of individual tasks
no interference across tasks


regression and held-out evaluations
measured capabilities before deployment
unmeasured capabilities


reward monitoring and A/B tests
production regressions and reward hacks
delayed or weakly observed harms



A more general continual-learning system may additionally need:

replay mixing historical, general, and current data
teacher-logit distillation on a stable anchor suite
adapters or separated plastic/stable parameters
explicit gradient-conflict management
checkpoint rollback and population-level canaries
a policy for deciding which episodes deserve weight consolidation

The exact replay and retention mixture used internally by Cursor is not public, so it should not be inferred from the existence of online RL.

title: Case Study: Cursor’s Continual Training Loop
text:
The First-Principles Interpretation
Cursor’s main innovation is not “RL remembers better.” It is a tight match among four components:






flowchart LR
    P[Production state distribution]
    A[Current policy actions]
    F[Real user and environment feedback]
    G[Frequent guarded updates]
    P --> A --> F --> G --> P






The loop reduces three mismatches:

state mismatch: train on states the deployed policy actually encounters
action mismatch: evaluate the model’s own suggestions and trajectories
objective mismatch: optimize acceptance and task outcome rather than only imitation likelihood

It simultaneously creates three risks:

feedback loops: the policy changes the data it later observes
reward hacking: measured proxies become optimization targets
forgetting: current high-volume behaviors can dominate older or rarer capabilities

Thus continual product learning requires a second, slower loop that audits the fast learning loop. This is where harness observability, regression suites, reward design, replay, and rollback become part of the learning algorithm.

title: Case Study: Cursor’s Continual Training Loop
text:
Interview Questions

Why is Tab’s abstention decision difficult to express as ordinary NTP?
Derive the acceptance threshold implied by positive, negative, and abstention rewards.
Why must Tab refresh its data after updating the policy?
Separate Composer’s continued pretraining, SFT, simulated RL, and real-time RL objectives.
Why does lower code perplexity still help downstream agentic RL?
Why does RL not inherently prevent catastrophic forgetting?
What does a KL penalty preserve, and how does its state distribution limit the guarantee?
How does Composer 2.5 combine trajectory reward with localized on-policy distillation?
Which regression suite would detect a policy becoming better at editing but worse at explanation, planning, or abstention?
Is Cursor’s loop lifelong learning, online learning, or continual product optimization? State the timescale and persistent state in your answer.

title: Activation Functions
text:
Without nonlinear activation functions, a stack of linear layers collapses into one linear transformation:
\[
W_2(W_1x+b_1)+b_2
=
(W_2W_1)x+(W_2b_1+b_2).
\]
For a neuron,
\[
z=w^Tx+b,
\qquad
h=\phi(z),
\]
and backpropagation multiplies the upstream gradient by \(\phi'(z)\). An activation affects both what the network can represent and how easily it can be optimized.

title: Activation Functions
text:
Without nonlinear activation functions, a stack of linear layers collapses into one linear transformation:
\[
W_2(W_1x+b_1)+b_2
=
(W_2W_1)x+(W_2b_1+b_2).
\]
For a neuron,
\[
z=w^Tx+b,
\qquad
h=\phi(z),
\]
and backpropagation multiplies the upstream gradient by \(\phi'(z)\). An activation affects both what the network can represent and how easily it can be optimized.

title: Activation Functions
text:
What Makes a Useful Activation?
Useful properties depend on the model, but commonly include:

nonlinearity
useful gradients over a wide input range
inexpensive evaluation
stable output scale
smoothness when optimization benefits from it
compatibility with initialization and normalization

No activation has every desirable property. For example, bounded activations can stabilize output values but often saturate; unbounded activations preserve gradients on one side but may produce large values.

title: Activation Functions
text:
Sigmoid
\[
\sigma(x)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-x}}.
\]
Its derivative is
\[
\sigma'(x)=\sigma(x)(1-\sigma(x)).
\]
The derivative is at most \(1/4\) and approaches zero for large \(|x|\). Repeated multiplication by these small derivatives can produce vanishing gradients in deep networks.
Properties:

range: \((0,1)\)
smooth and probabilistically interpretable
not zero-centered
saturates at both extremes

Common use: binary probabilities and gates, rather than hidden activations in deep feed-forward networks.

title: Activation Functions
text:
Tanh
\[
\tanh(x)=\frac{e^x-e^{-x}}{e^x+e^{-x}},
\]
\[
\frac{d}{dx}\tanh(x)=1-\tanh^2(x).
\]
Tanh is zero-centered and has range \((-1,1)\), but still saturates for large \(|x|\). It remains common inside recurrent-network state updates.

title: Activation Functions
text:
ReLU
\[
\operatorname{ReLU}(x)=\max(0,x).
\]
Its derivative is
\[
\operatorname{ReLU}'(x)
=
\begin{cases}
0,&x<0,\\
1,&x>0.
\end{cases}
\]
The derivative at zero is undefined; implementations choose a subgradient, typically zero.
Advantages:

cheap to compute
does not saturate on the positive side
produces sparse activations

The dying ReLU problem occurs when a neuron stays in the negative region, receives zero gradient, and stops updating. Large learning rates or unfavorable bias shifts can contribute to this.

ReLU variants
Leaky ReLU retains a small negative slope:
\[
\operatorname{LeakyReLU}(x)
=
\begin{cases}
x,&x\ge0,\\
\alpha x,&x<0.
\end{cases}
\]
Its derivative is
\[
\operatorname{LeakyReLU}'(x)
=
\begin{cases}
1,&x>0,\\
\alpha,&x<0.
\end{cases}
\]
As with ReLU, the derivative at zero is undefined and an implementation chooses a subgradient.
PReLU learns \(\alpha\). ELU and SELU use smooth, saturating negative branches; SELU is designed for self-normalizing networks under specific architectural and initialization assumptions.

title: Activation Functions
text:
GELU
The Gaussian Error Linear Unit weights an input by the probability that a standard Gaussian variable is below it:
\[
\operatorname{GELU}(x)=x\Phi(x),
\]
where \(\Phi\) is the standard Gaussian CDF. A common approximation is
\[
\operatorname{GELU}(x)
\approx
\frac{x}{2}
\left[
1+\tanh\left(
\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}}
\left(x+0.044715x^3\right)
\right)
\right].
\]
Using the product rule and
\[
\Phi'(x)=\phi(x)
=
\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-x^2/2},
\]
the derivative of exact GELU is
\[
\boxed{
\operatorname{GELU}'(x)
=
\Phi(x)+x\phi(x)
=
\Phi(x)
+
\frac{x}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-x^2/2}
}.
\]
Its derivative behaves like a smooth—but slightly non-monotonic—version of a ReLU derivative:

as \(x\to-\infty\), \(\operatorname{GELU}'(x)\to0\)
at \(x=0\), \(\operatorname{GELU}'(0)=1/2\)
as \(x\to+\infty\), \(\operatorname{GELU}'(x)\to1\)
it reaches approximately \(-0.129\) at \(x=-\sqrt 2\)
it reaches approximately \(1.129\) at \(x=\sqrt 2\)

The small negative-derivative region means exact GELU is not monotonic. It has a shallow minimum near \(x\approx-0.752\) instead of simply flattening all negative inputs.
Unlike ReLU’s hard gate, GELU smoothly scales inputs. It became common in BERT- and early GPT-style Transformers.

title: Activation Functions
text:
SiLU / Swish
\[
\operatorname{SiLU}(x)=x\sigma(x).
\]
Its derivative is
\[
\operatorname{SiLU}'(x)
=
\sigma(x)+x\sigma(x)(1-\sigma(x)).
\]
SiLU is smooth and non-monotonic: slightly negative inputs can produce negative outputs, rather than being discarded completely. It is widely used in modern vision models and gated Transformer MLPs.

title: Activation Functions
text:
Gated Activations






eventually people add gating to activations, trading more flexibility over compute. SwiGLU is widely used in modern LLMs.



A gated linear unit splits computation into a content path and a gate:
\[
\operatorname{GLU}(x)
=
(xW_u)\odot\sigma(xW_g).
\]
Variants replace sigmoid with another activation. SwiGLU uses SiLU:
\[
\operatorname{SwiGLU}(x)
=
W_o\left[
\operatorname{SiLU}(xW_g)\odot(xW_u)
\right].
\]
The gate creates multiplicative interactions: one projection controls how much of another projection passes through. The cost is an additional input projection, so hidden width is often adjusted when comparing parameter counts with an ordinary two-layer FFN.
To see where this operation appears in a decoder block, continue to SwiGLU in the Transformer feed-forward network.

GPT-OSS’s modified SwiGLU
GPT-OSS uses a numerically bounded variant rather than textbook SwiGLU. Let \(a=xW_g\) be the gate branch and \(b=xW_u\) be the content branch. Its activation can be written as
\[
\begin{aligned}
\bar a &= \min(a, L),\\
\bar b &= \operatorname{clip}(b,-L,L),\\
\operatorname{SwiGLU}_{\text{GPT-OSS}}(a,b)
&=
\left[\bar a\,\sigma(\alpha\bar a)\right]
\odot(\bar b+1),
\end{aligned}
\]
where GPT-OSS uses \(\alpha=1.702\) and \(L=7\). The complete MLP still applies an output projection \(W_o\) after this activation.
Compared with ordinary \(\operatorname{SiLU}(a)\odot b\), this version makes three changes:

\(\alpha=1.702\) makes the sigmoid gate sharper than standard SiLU, whose coefficient is \(1\).
Clamping bounds unusually large intermediate values, which is helpful for stable low-precision expert computation.
The shift \(b+1\) leaves a gate-dependent signal even when the learned content branch is near zero.


import torch


def gpt_oss_swiglu(
    gate: torch.Tensor,
    content: torch.Tensor,
    alpha: float = 1.702,
    limit: float = 7.0,
) -> torch.Tensor:
    """GPT-OSS activation before the MLP output projection."""
    gate = gate.clamp(max=limit)
    content = content.clamp(min=-limit, max=limit)
    swish_gate = gate * torch.sigmoid(alpha * gate)
    return swish_gate * (content + 1.0)

It remains a three-projection gated MLP, so its leading parameter count is still \(3dm\). Clamping and shifting change the activation, not the matrix shapes.


Why the parameter-matched width is about \(2.67d\)
Ignoring biases, a conventional GELU MLP with intermediate width \(4d\) has
\[
\underbrace{d(4d)}_{W_1}
+
\underbrace{(4d)d}_{W_2}
=
8d^2
\]
parameters. A SwiGLU MLP with intermediate width \(m\) has three projections:
\[
\underbrace{dm}_{W_g}
+
\underbrace{dm}_{W_u}
+
\underbrace{md}_{W_o}
=
3dm.
\]
Matching their parameter counts gives
\[
3dm=8d^2
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\boxed{m=\frac{8}{3}d\approx2.67d}.
\]
This is a budgeting baseline, not an architectural law. Model designers choose the MLP width jointly with depth, attention dimensions, total parameter budget, training data, and hardware-friendly multiples.


What public LLM configurations actually use
The table below uses representative released checkpoints. For a dense model, the width ratio is \(m/d\). For an MoE model, \(m_e\) is the width of one expert and \(k_{\text{active}}m_e/d\) is a compute-oriented aggregate active-width ratio.

How to interpret an MoE width
For \(E\) total SwiGLU experts of width \(m_e\), with \(k\) routed experts and \(s\) shared experts active per token:
\[
\text{total expert parameters}
\approx
3dEm_e,
\]
while the per-token expert projection work is approximately
\[
\text{active projection work}
\propto
3d(k+s)m_e.
\]
This is why an MoE can use individually narrow experts while having enormous total capacity. The aggregate active width
\[
m_{\text{active}}=(k+s)m_e
\]
is useful for comparing projection FLOPs with a dense MLP.
However, the active expert outputs are weighted and summed, not concatenated into one layer of width \(m_{\text{active}}\). The aggregate width is therefore a compute-accounting analogy, not the literal shape of an intermediate tensor.


Takeaway

\(2.67d\) answers: “How wide should SwiGLU be to match the parameters of a conventional \(4d\) GELU MLP?”
It does not answer: “What width do all modern LLMs use?”
Dense Qwen3 checkpoints demonstrate that ratios can vary substantially even within one family.
DeepSeek-V3 and Kimi K2 move capacity into many narrow experts while keeping the active expert compute closer to a dense MLP-sized budget.
GPT-OSS uses wider individual experts and an aggregate active width of \(4d\); its four active experts cost approximately \(3d(4d)=12d^2\) in expert projections per token.

title: Activation Functions
text:
Activation and Derivative Graphs
Each panel overlays a scalar activation \(\phi(x)\) and its derivative \(\phi'(x)\). ReLU and Leaky ReLU are not differentiable at zero; the plotted value at exactly zero uses the common subgradient choice \(0\) for ReLU and \(\alpha\) for Leaky ReLU.

import math
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import torch


x_plot = torch.linspace(-5, 5, 1001)
normal_pdf = torch.exp(-0.5 * x_plot.square()) / math.sqrt(2.0 * math.pi)
normal_cdf = 0.5 * (1.0 + torch.erf(x_plot / math.sqrt(2.0)))
sigmoid_values = torch.sigmoid(x_plot)
leaky_slope = 0.1

activation_curves = {
    "Sigmoid": (
        sigmoid_values,
        sigmoid_values * (1.0 - sigmoid_values),
    ),
    "Tanh": (
        torch.tanh(x_plot),
        1.0 - torch.tanh(x_plot).square(),
    ),
    "ReLU": (
        torch.relu(x_plot),
        (x_plot > 0).to(x_plot.dtype),
    ),
    "Leaky ReLU": (
        torch.where(x_plot >= 0, x_plot, leaky_slope * x_plot),
        torch.where(
            x_plot > 0,
            torch.ones_like(x_plot),
            torch.full_like(x_plot, leaky_slope),
        ),
    ),
    "GELU": (
        x_plot * normal_cdf,
        normal_cdf + x_plot * normal_pdf,
    ),
    "SiLU / Swish": (
        x_plot * sigmoid_values,
        sigmoid_values + x_plot * sigmoid_values * (1.0 - sigmoid_values),
    ),
}

figure, axes = plt.subplots(3, 2, sharex=True, figsize=(10, 10))

for axis, (name, (values, derivatives)) in zip(
    axes.flat, activation_curves.items()
):
    axis.plot(x_plot, values, label=r"$\phi(x)$", linewidth=2)
    axis.plot(
        x_plot,
        derivatives,
        label=r"$\phi'(x)$",
        linewidth=2,
        linestyle="--",
    )
    axis.axhline(0, color="black", linewidth=0.6, alpha=0.5)
    axis.axvline(0, color="black", linewidth=0.6, alpha=0.5)
    axis.set_title(name)
    axis.grid(alpha=0.2)
    axis.legend()

for axis in axes[-1]:
    axis.set_xlabel("x")

figure.tight_layout()
plt.show()







Figure 1: Common scalar activation functions and their derivatives.





SwiGLU does not have one scalar activation curve. It combines two learned vector projections through multiplication, so its Jacobian depends on both \(W_g\), \(W_u\), and the input direction. Softmax is likewise a vector-valued function whose derivative is a Jacobian rather than a single curve:
\[
\frac{\partial\operatorname{softmax}(z)_i}{\partial z_j}
=
p_i(\delta_{ij}-p_j).
\]

title: Activation Functions
Activation Functions
text:
Initialization Interaction
Initialization and activation choice are coupled. A good initialization keeps forward activations and backward gradients at usable scales as they pass through many layers. If either repeatedly grows, training can explode; if either repeatedly shrinks, information and gradients vanish.

Forward signal propagation
Consider a linear layer with zero-mean, independent inputs and weights:
\[
z_j=\sum_{i=1}^{n_{\mathrm{in}}}W_{ji}x_i,
\qquad
\mathbb E[W_{ji}]=0,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(W_{ji})=\sigma_W^2.
\]
Ignoring correlations,
\[
\mathbb E[z_j^2]
\approx
n_{\mathrm{in}}\sigma_W^2\mathbb E[x_i^2].
\]
The activation then changes this second moment:
\[
\mathbb E[h_j^2]
=
\mathbb E[\phi(z_j)^2].
\]
The goal is not necessarily to make every layer’s variance exactly one. The goal is to prevent a multiplicative factor much larger or smaller than one from being applied at every layer.
For a distribution symmetric around zero,
\[
\mathbb E[\operatorname{ReLU}(z)^2]
=
\frac{1}{2}\mathbb E[z^2].
\]
ReLU removes the negative half of the signal. Choosing
\[
\boxed{\operatorname{Var}(W)=\frac{2}{n_{\mathrm{in}}}}
\]
compensates for this factor of \(1/2\). This is He/Kaiming initialization.
For Leaky ReLU with negative slope \(a\),
\[
\mathbb E[\operatorname{LeakyReLU}(z)^2]
=
\frac{1+a^2}{2}\mathbb E[z^2],
\]
so its corresponding fan-in variance is
\[
\boxed{
\operatorname{Var}(W)
=
\frac{2}{(1+a^2)n_{\mathrm{in}}}
}.
\]


Why Xavier balances two directions
For a linear activation, preserving the forward second moment suggests \(\operatorname{Var}(W)=1/n_{\mathrm{in}}\). Preserving the backward gradient scale instead suggests \(1/n_{\mathrm{out}}\). Xavier/Glorot initialization uses the compromise
\[
\boxed{
\operatorname{Var}(W)
\approx
\frac{2}{n_{\mathrm{in}}+n_{\mathrm{out}}}
}.
\]
This is a useful starting point for linear layers and tanh networks. A gain can multiply this base scale to account approximately for an activation. PyTorch, for example, uses gain \(1\) for linear or sigmoid, \(5/3\) for tanh, \(\sqrt{2}\) for ReLU, and \(\sqrt{2/(1+a^2)}\) for Leaky ReLU.
Initialization cannot fully rescue a saturated sigmoid network. Because \(0<\sigma'(x)\leq1/4\), repeatedly multiplying by sigmoid derivatives can still shrink gradients. Keeping initial pre-activations near zero delays saturation, but does not remove the underlying depth problem.


The backward view
For \(h=\phi(Wx)\), backpropagation contains
\[
\delta_x
=
W^T\left(\delta_h\odot\phi'(z)\right).
\]
Consequently, gradient scale depends on both the weight variance and \(\mathbb E[\phi'(z)^2]\). Xavier and Kaiming make simplifying assumptions about independence, identical distributions, and the shape of \(z\). Those assumptions are only approximate in a trained network, but they give much better starting scales than choosing an arbitrary standard deviation.
In Kaiming APIs, mode="fan_in" prioritizes forward activations, while mode="fan_out" prioritizes backward gradients. Forward preservation is the usual default for hidden layers.


GELU, SiLU, and gated MLPs
GELU and SiLU behave somewhat like smooth ReLUs, but their exact moment changes depend on the input distribution. There is no single universal gain that is correct throughout training. Kaiming initialization is a reasonable baseline in some non-residual MLPs, while modern Transformers more commonly use a model-wide initialization recipe calibrated together with normalization, depth, and residual scaling.
SwiGLU is more complicated because it multiplies two learned branches:
\[
h=\operatorname{SiLU}(xW_g)\odot(xW_u).
\]
Under a rough independence approximation,
\[
\mathbb E[h^2]
\approx
\mathbb E[\operatorname{SiLU}(xW_g)^2]
\mathbb E[(xW_u)^2].
\]
Thus its scale depends on both input projections and on the down projection that writes the result back to the residual stream. A gain derived for a one-branch ReLU layer cannot be transferred to SwiGLU without qualification.


Residual networks and Transformers
Normalization does not make initialization irrelevant. In a pre-norm block, the normalization controls the input to each branch, but the residual stream still accumulates branch outputs:
\[
x_{\ell+1}=x_\ell+F_\ell(\operatorname{Norm}(x_\ell)).
\]
If every \(F_\ell\) initially writes a large update, residual magnitude can grow with depth. Deep Transformer recipes therefore often initialize residual-output projections more conservatively or scale them by a depth-dependent factor such as \(1/\sqrt{L}\). With two residual branches per block, \(1/\sqrt{2L}\) is a common accounting choice. The exact convention is architecture-specific.
Other practical rules:

biases are commonly initialized to zero so they do not shift activation distributions immediately
embeddings, attention projections, MLP projections, and output heads may use different scales
a zero initialization is sometimes useful for a residual output projection, but initializing every layer to zero prevents hidden units from breaking symmetry
when reproducing a model, follow its complete initialization recipe rather than mixing isolated defaults from different architectures



Practical starting points








Activation or block
Common starting point
Important caveat




Linear / identity
Xavier, gain \(1\)
choose fan-in scaling if only forward variance matters


Tanh
Xavier, often with tanh gain
large pre-activations still saturate


Sigmoid
Xavier, gain \(1\)
derivatives can vanish even with good initialization


ReLU
Kaiming with \(a=0\)
assumes roughly symmetric pre-activations


Leaky ReLU
Kaiming using the actual slope \(a\)
the slope must match the activation


GELU / SiLU
architecture-specific; Xavier or Kaiming may be baselines
no universally exact gain


SwiGLU / MoE expert
initialize all three projections as one coordinated block

This minimal helper shows conventional PyTorch starting points. It is an educational default, not a reproduction of any particular LLM recipe.

import math
import torch
import torch.nn as nn


def initialize_linear(layer, activation, negative_slope=0.01):
    if not isinstance(layer, nn.Linear):
        raise TypeError("expected nn.Linear")

    if activation == "relu":
        nn.init.kaiming_normal_(
            layer.weight, mode="fan_in", nonlinearity="relu"
        )
    elif activation == "leaky_relu":
        nn.init.kaiming_normal_(
            layer.weight,
            a=negative_slope,
            mode="fan_in",
            nonlinearity="leaky_relu",
        )
    elif activation in {"linear", "sigmoid", "tanh"}:
        gain = nn.init.calculate_gain(activation)
        nn.init.xavier_uniform_(layer.weight, gain=gain)
    elif activation in {"gelu", "silu"}:
        # A neutral baseline; use the model's recipe when reproducing it.
        nn.init.xavier_normal_(layer.weight, gain=1.0)
    else:
        raise ValueError(f"unsupported activation: {activation}")

    if layer.bias is not None:
        nn.init.zeros_(layer.bias)


def scale_residual_output_(projection, num_layers, branches_per_layer=2):
    """Apply optional depth scaling after initializing a residual projection."""
    scale = 1.0 / math.sqrt(branches_per_layer * num_layers)
    with torch.no_grad():
        projection.weight.mul_(scale)

title: 悬链线、cosh 和激活函数：教科书没串起来的一条线
text:
有一天我盯着 \(\tanh\) 的导数 \(1/\cosh^2 x\) 发呆，忽然想起 \(\cosh\) 是悬链线方程——一根两端挂起的链子自然垂下来的形状。激活函数和一根链子有什么关系？
答案是：没有物理上的关系，但有一个共同的源头。把这条线理清楚之后，tanh、sigmoid、softplus、log-cosh 损失、LSTM 的门，甚至 GELU，都会变成同一件事的不同侧面。这篇文章就是把这条线串起来。

title: 悬链线、cosh 和激活函数：教科书没串起来的一条线
text:
1. 悬链线：高度、弧长、倾角
一根均匀的链子挂起来，取最低点为 \(x=0\)，选合适的单位后它的形状是
\[y = \cosh x = \frac{e^x + e^{-x}}{2}.\]
这个式子来自受力平衡：链子每一小段受重力和两端张力，推出来的方程是 \(y'' = \sqrt{1 + y'^2}\)。验证一下 \(\cosh\) 确实是解：\(y' = \sinh x\)，\(y'' = \cosh x\)，而 \(\sqrt{1+\sinh^2 x} = \cosh x\)。最后这一步用的就是双曲函数的基本恒等式
\[\cosh^2 x - \sinh^2 x = 1.\]
有意思的地方在于，链子上任意一点 \(P=(x, \cosh x)\) 处，三个双曲函数各自对应一个几何量：








量
表达式
几何意义




高度
\(\cosh x\)
\(P\) 到地面的竖直距离


弧长
\(\sinh x\)
从最低点沿链子量到 \(P\) 的长度（也等于 \(P\) 处的斜率）


倾角
\(\tanh x = \sin\theta\)
切线与水平方向夹角 \(\theta\) 的正弦



弧长等于斜率这件事可以直接算：\(\int_0^x \sqrt{1 + \sinh^2 t}\,dt = \int_0^x \cosh t\,dt = \sinh x\)。
倾角那一行最值得看。在 \(P\) 处沿切线画一个直角三角形，横边取 1，竖边就是斜率 \(\sinh x\)，斜边长 \(\sqrt{1+\sinh^2 x} = \cosh x\)。于是
\[\tanh x = \frac{\sinh x}{\cosh x} = \frac{\text{竖边}}{\text{斜边}} = \sin\theta.\]
这就是 \(\cosh^2 - \sinh^2 = 1\) 的几何版本：它就是那个切线三角形的勾股定理。\(\tanh\) 有界也立刻解释了——一个角的正弦当然在 \(\pm 1\) 之间；链子再陡，也陡不过竖直。


显示画图代码
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

x0 = 1.0
xs = np.linspace(-2.2, 2.2, 400)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 5))
ax.plot(xs, np.cosh(xs), color="#777", lw=2.5)

# 弧长（从最低点到 P）
xa = np.linspace(0, x0, 200)
ax.plot(xa, np.cosh(xa), color="#ff9f43", lw=5, label=f"Arc length = sinh x = {np.sinh(x0):.3f}")
# 高度
ax.plot([x0, x0], [0, np.cosh(x0)], "--", color="#2f80ed", lw=2.5, label=f"Height = cosh x = {np.cosh(x0):.3f}")
# 切线三角形
L = 0.8
P = np.array([x0, np.cosh(x0)])
B = P + np.array([L, 0])
Cpt = P + np.array([L, L * np.sinh(x0)])
tri = np.array([P, B, Cpt, P])
ax.fill(tri[:, 0], tri[:, 1], color="#27ae60", alpha=0.18)
ax.plot(tri[:, 0], tri[:, 1], color="#27ae60", lw=2, label=f"Vertical / hypotenuse = tanh x = {np.tanh(x0):.3f}")
ax.text(x0 + L / 2, np.cosh(x0) - 0.18, "1", ha="center", color="#27ae60")
ax.text(Cpt[0] + 0.06, (B[1] + Cpt[1]) / 2, "sinh", color="#ff9f43")
ax.text((P[0] + Cpt[0]) / 2 - 0.3, (P[1] + Cpt[1]) / 2 + 0.1, "cosh", color="#2f80ed")
ax.plot(*P, "ko"); ax.text(P[0] - 0.22, P[1] + 0.1, "P")
ax.axhline(0, color="k", lw=0.8); ax.axvline(0, color="k", lw=0.8)
ax.set_aspect("equal"); ax.set_xlim(-2.3, 2.3); ax.set_ylim(-0.3, 4.3)
ax.legend(loc="upper left", frameon=False)
ax.set_title("Catenary y = cosh x")
plt.show()








Figure 1: 悬链线 y = cosh x 上一点 P 处的三个量：高度 cosh、弧长 sinh、切线三角形的竖/斜 = tanh。

title: 悬链线、cosh 和激活函数：教科书没串起来的一条线
text:
2. 它们都是 \(e^x\) 的拼法
把 \(e^x\) 拆成偶函数部分和奇函数部分：
\[e^x = \underbrace{\frac{e^x + e^{-x}}{2}}_{\cosh x} + \underbrace{\frac{e^x - e^{-x}}{2}}_{\sinh x}.\]
\(\cosh\) 是 \(e^x\) 与 \(e^{-x}\) 的平均，\(\sinh\) 是它们差的一半，\(\tanh\) 是两者之比。这就是”为什么到处都是 cosh”的全部秘密：只要一个问题的答案里有 \(e^x\)，一做对称化就会跑出 \(\cosh\) 和 \(\sinh\)。
而 \(e^x\) 又为什么到处都是？因为它是微分的不动点——\((e^x)' = e^x\)。任何”导数和自身有简单关系”的方程，解里都有它。悬链线的受力平衡是这样的方程；下面会看到，sigmoid 满足的方程 \(\sigma' = \sigma(1-\sigma)\) 也是。


显示画图代码
xs = np.linspace(-2.6, 2.6, 400)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 4.2))
ax.plot(xs, np.exp(xs), "--", color="#9b59b6", lw=1.3, label=r"$e^x,\ e^{-x}$")
ax.plot(xs, np.exp(-xs), "--", color="#9b59b6", lw=1.3)
ax.plot(xs, np.cosh(xs), color="#2f80ed", lw=2.5, label="cosh")
ax.plot(xs, np.sinh(xs), color="#ff9f43", lw=2.5, label="sinh")
ax.plot(xs, np.tanh(xs), color="#27ae60", lw=3, label="tanh")
ax.axhspan(-1, 1, color="#27ae60", alpha=0.08)
ax.axhline(0, color="k", lw=0.8); ax.axvline(0, color="k", lw=0.8)
ax.set_ylim(-4, 4); ax.legend(frameon=False, loc="upper left")
plt.show()








Figure 2: cosh 是 e^x 与 e^-x 的中点，sinh 是半差；tanh 被夹在 ±1 之间。

title: 悬链线、cosh 和激活函数：教科书没串起来的一条线
section: 3. 为什么激活函数挑了 tanh
text:
3. 为什么激活函数挑了 tanh
三个函数里，\(\cosh \ge 1\) 向上张开，\(\sinh\) 穿过原点向两边无限增长，只有 \(\tanh\) 有界。作为激活函数，输出有界意味着数值不会在层层传递中爆炸，所以三者里只有 \(\tanh\) 是候选。
它还有两个工程上的好处：

零中心：输出在 \((-1, 1)\)，均值在 0 附近，下一层的输入正负都有。
导数能用输出算：\(\tanh' x = 1 - \tanh^2 x = 1/\cosh^2 x\)。反向传播时不需要再算一次前向，拿输出平方一下就行。

代价也写在导数里：\(1/\cosh^2 x\) 在原点是 1，往两边迅速趋于 0。这就是”饱和”，叠多层之后就是梯度消失。

title: 悬链线、cosh 和激活函数：教科书没串起来的一条线
section: 4. sigmoid 不是另一个函数，它就是 tanh
text:
4. sigmoid 不是另一个函数，它就是 tanh
教科书通常把 sigmoid 和 tanh 当两个并列的选项介绍。其实
\[\sigma(x) = \frac{1}{1+e^{-x}} = \frac{1 + \tanh(x/2)}{2}.\]
sigmoid 是把 tanh 横向拉长一倍、竖向压扁一半、再抬高一半。形状完全相同，所以它的饱和问题不可能比 tanh 轻。具体差在两点：

不是零中心。输出全在 \((0,1)\)，下一层的输入恒为正，导致该层权重的梯度符号全部一致，优化只能走”之”字形。
梯度小四倍。\(\sigma'(0) = 1/4\)，而 \(\tanh'(0) = 1\)。多叠 \(n\) 层，sigmoid 的梯度额外衰减 \(4^n\) 倍。

所以作为隐藏层激活，tanh 优于 sigmoid——LeCun 在 1998 年的 Efficient BackProp 里就是这么建议的。
那 sigmoid 为什么还随处可见？因为它有 tanh 做不到的事：输出一个 0 到 1 之间的数。

概率：二分类、多标签分类的输出层。sigmoid 配交叉熵时梯度干净得出奇，就是 \(\hat y - y\)。它满足 \(\sigma' = \sigma(1-\sigma)\)——又一个”导数由自身决定”的方程，解里自然有 \(e^x\)。
门：LSTM 的遗忘门、输入门、输出门需要一个”开多少”的系数，用 sigmoid；而候选状态”写什么”用的是 tanh。一个开关、一个内容，分工明确。
权重系数：注意力里的门控、SE 模块的通道权重，搜索排序里把打分压成点击率，都是它。

title: 悬链线、cosh 和激活函数：教科书没串起来的一条线
section: 5. 现代激活函数：sigmoid 换了个位置回来了
text:
5. 现代激活函数：sigmoid 换了个位置回来了
ReLU 取代 tanh/sigmoid 做隐藏层激活，解决的正是饱和：正半轴导数恒为 1。但看一眼它的平滑版本：

Softplus \(= \log(1 + e^x)\)，是 ReLU 的光滑近似，导数恰好是 sigmoid。
SiLU / Swish \(= x \cdot \sigma(x)\)。
GELU \(= x \cdot \Phi(x)\)，\(\Phi\) 是标准正态的分布函数，形状和 \(\sigma(1.702x)\) 几乎重合。

SiLU 和 GELU 的结构都是”\(x\) 乘上一个 0~1 的门”。\(x\) 本身不饱和，sigmoid 只负责决定放过多少。sigmoid 没有消失，它从”激活函数”变成了”门”——和 LSTM 里的角色一样。
顺手还有一个很少被提的恒等式：
\[\text{softplus}(x) = \log(1+e^x) = \frac{x}{2} + \log\!\big(2\cosh\tfrac{x}{2}\big).\]
softplus 去掉一条直线之后，剩下的就是 \(\log\cosh\)。

title: 悬链线、cosh 和激活函数：教科书没串起来的一条线
section: 6. log-cosh 损失：tanh 的原函数
text:
6. log-cosh 损失：tanh 的原函数
既然 \((\log\cosh x)' = \tanh x\)，那 \(\log\cosh\) 就是 tanh 的原函数。它作为回归损失有一个漂亮的性质：
\[\log\cosh x \approx \begin{cases} x^2/2 & |x| \text{ 小} \\ |x| - \log 2 & |x| \text{ 大} \end{cases}\]
小误差时像 MSE，大误差时像 MAE，而且处处二阶可导——比 Huber 损失光滑，不需要调阈值。它的梯度是 \(\tanh x\)，天然有界，这正是它对离群点稳健的原因。


显示画图代码
xs = np.linspace(-4, 4, 400)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 4))
ax.plot(xs, np.log(np.cosh(xs)), color="#2f80ed", lw=2.5, label="log cosh x")
ax.plot(xs, xs**2 / 2, ":", color="#999", lw=1.5, label=r"$x^2/2$")
ax.plot(xs, np.abs(xs) - np.log(2), "--", color="#999", lw=1.5, label=r"$|x| - \log 2$")
ax.plot(xs, np.tanh(xs), color="#27ae60", lw=2, label="Derivative = tanh x")
ax.set_ylim(-1.5, 4); ax.axhline(0, color="k", lw=0.8); ax.axvline(0, color="k", lw=0.8)
ax.legend(frameon=False, loc="upper center")
plt.show()








Figure 3: log cosh 在原点附近像 x²/2，远处像 |x| − log 2；它的导数是 tanh。

title: 悬链线、cosh 和激活函数：教科书没串起来的一条线
text:
7. 把线收起来









对象
是什么
在悬链线上
在神经网络里




\(\cosh\)
\(e^x\) 的偶部分
高度
\(1/\cosh^2\) 是 tanh 的导数；\(\log\cosh\) 是稳健损失


\(\sinh\)
\(e^x\) 的奇部分
弧长、斜率
几乎不用：无界


\(\tanh\)
奇/偶
倾角的正弦
隐藏层激活、LSTM 候选状态


\(\sigma\)
\(\tanh\) 的平移缩放
—
概率输出、门控、GELU/SiLU 里的门



一根链子和一个神经网络没有任何因果关系。它们共享的只是一个数学事实：指数函数是微分的不动点，所以凡是”变化率由自身决定”的问题，答案里都有 \(e^x\)；把 \(e^x\) 对称化，就得到双曲函数；三者中有界的那一个，恰好是你想要的激活函数。
教科书把悬链线放在微积分课、把 tanh 放在深度学习课、把 log-cosh 放在损失函数一节，于是它们看起来像三件事。其实是一件。

title: Distribution Learning Losses
text:
A generative model tries to represent a distribution over high-dimensional objects:
\[
x\sim p_{\mathrm{data}}(x),
\qquad
p_\theta(x)\approx p_{\mathrm{data}}(x).
\]
Directly specifying and normalizing \(p_\theta(x)\) is often intractable. Modern generative losses arise by changing the problem into something observable:

factor a sequence into next-token conditionals
lower-bound an intractable latent-variable likelihood
learn a discriminator when only samples are available
corrupt clean data and train a denoiser

The loss is therefore inseparable from the model architecture and sampling procedure. For the overall taxonomy, see Losses from First Principles. For classification, regression, focal, margin, and ranking losses, see Prediction and Decision Losses. Distillation is treated separately in Distillation: Learning from a Teacher.



Can the model evaluate normalized likelihood exactly?
If not, which latent variables, factorization, critic, or corruption process makes training observable?
Does the objective cover all data modes or seek a subset of them?
Is training performed on data states, model-generated states, or both?
Does the tractable surrogate preserve the original statistical objective?
Which weighting controls gradient across tokens, timesteps, latents, or sequences?

If not, which latent variables, factorization, critic, or corruption process makes training observable?
Does the objective cover all data modes or seek a subset of them?
Is training performed on data states, model-generated states, or both?
Does the tractable surrogate preserve the original statistical objective?
Which weighting controls gradient across tokens, timesteps, latents, or sequences?

title: Distribution Learning Losses
text:
2. KL Divergence: Direction Defines Geometry
For distributions \(p\) and \(q\),
\[
\mathrm{KL}(p\|q)
=
\mathbb E_{x\sim p}
\left[
\log\frac{p(x)}{q(x)}
\right].
\]
KL is nonnegative and asymmetric. The first argument supplies the expectation:








Objective
Strongly penalizes
Typical tendency




\(\mathrm{KL}(p\|q)\)
\(q\) misses regions where \(p\) has mass
mass covering


\(\mathrm{KL}(q\|p)\)
\(q\) puts mass where \(p\) is small
mode seeking



These are tendencies, not laws. Support, parameterization, optimization, and finite-sample estimators all matter.
Maximum likelihood minimizes forward KL from data to model:
\[
\mathbb E_{x\sim p_{\mathrm{data}}}[-\log p_\theta(x)]
=
H(p_{\mathrm{data}})
+
\mathrm{KL}(p_{\mathrm{data}}\|p_\theta).
\]
Because samples come from data, missing a data mode is costly. But the model is not directly penalized for assigning probability to low-density regions unless normalization moves mass away from observed data.






Important“Inverse KL” usually means reverse KL



The standard terms are forward KL and reverse KL, defined relative to a chosen reference distribution. Always write the arguments. Saying only “use KL” hides the most important design choice.

title: Distribution Learning Losses
text:
3. Next-Token Prediction: Generation as Classification
An autoregressive model uses the chain rule:
\[
p_\theta(x_{1:T})
=
\prod_{t=1}^{T}p_\theta(x_t\mid x_{<t}).
\]
Negative log-likelihood becomes
\[
\mathcal L_{\mathrm{NTP}}
=
-\sum_{t=1}^{T}
\log p_\theta(x_t\mid x_{<t}).
\]
The abstraction turns one sequence into \(T\) categorical prediction targets. It provides dense supervision and exact normalized likelihood even though the space of complete sequences is enormous.

What statistical objective does NTP optimize?
Under data prefixes, NTP minimizes forward KL between the data next-token distribution and the model at every prefix. This is teacher forcing: during training, \(x_{<t}\) comes from data; during generation, prefixes increasingly come from the model. This state-distribution mismatch is exposure bias.
The reduction is part of the objective:
\[
\mathcal L
=
-\frac{1}{\sum_i T_i}
\sum_i\sum_{t=1}^{T_i}
\log p_\theta(x_{i,t}\mid x_{i,<t})
\]
weights every token equally, so long sequences contribute more total training signal. Averaging per sequence defines a different population.
NTP estimates text likelihood; it does not directly optimize factuality, semantic equivalence, pass@\(k\), or user preference. Post-training objectives exist because these sequence-level goals are not identical to token likelihood.

title: Distribution Learning Losses
section: 4. Latent Variables: VAE and the ELBO
text:
4. Latent Variables: VAE and the ELBO
A latent-variable model defines
\[
p_\theta(x)
=
\int p(z)p_\theta(x\mid z)\,dz.
\]
The marginal likelihood and posterior \(p_\theta(z\mid x)\) are generally intractable. Introduce an encoder \(q_\phi(z\mid x)\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\log p_\theta(x)
&=
\log
\mathbb E_{z\sim q_\phi}
\left[
\frac{p(z)p_\theta(x\mid z)}{q_\phi(z\mid x)}
\right]\\
&\ge
\mathbb E_{q_\phi}
\left[
\log p_\theta(x\mid z)
\right]
-
\mathrm{KL}(q_\phi(z\mid x)\|p(z)).
\end{aligned}
\]
The right side is the evidence lower bound:
\[
\mathrm{ELBO}(x)
=
\mathbb E_q\log p_\theta(x\mid z)
-
\mathrm{KL}(q_\phi(z\mid x)\|p(z)).
\]
The exact identity is
\[
\log p_\theta(x)
=
\mathrm{ELBO}(x)
+
\mathrm{KL}
(q_\phi(z\mid x)\|p_\theta(z\mid x)).
\]
Therefore a VAE minimizes negative ELBO:
\[
\mathcal L_{\mathrm{VAE}}
=
\underbrace{-\mathbb E_q\log p_\theta(x\mid z)}
_{\text{reconstruction NLL}}
+
\underbrace{\mathrm{KL}(q_\phi(z\mid x)\|p(z))}
_{\text{rate / latent regularization}}.
\]

The reconstruction term is a likelihood
It is not an arbitrary similarity metric:

Gaussian decoder with fixed variance implies MSE up to scale.
Bernoulli observations imply BCE.
Categorical tokens imply cross-entropy.
Learned variance adds a log-variance term.

A \(\beta\)-VAE multiplies the KL by \(\beta\) to change the rate–distortion tradeoff, but at \(\beta\ne1\) the objective is no longer the original ELBO.


Reparameterization and posterior collapse
For diagonal Gaussian encoder,
\[
z
=
\mu_\phi(x)
+
\sigma_\phi(x)\odot\epsilon,
\qquad
\epsilon\sim\mathcal N(0,I),
\]
which moves randomness outside the differentiable path. If a strong decoder can model \(x\) without \(z\), it may choose \(q_\phi(z\mid x)\approx p(z)\) and drive the KL toward zero: posterior collapse.

title: Distribution Learning Losses
section: 5. GANs: Learn a Discrepancy from Samples
text:
5. GANs: Learn a Discrepancy from Samples
If real density is unavailable but real samples are available, learn a critic. The original GAN game is
\[
\min_\theta\max_\psi
\left[
\mathbb E_{x\sim p_{\mathrm{data}}}\log D_\psi(x)
+
\mathbb E_{z\sim p(z)}
\log(1-D_\psi(G_\theta(z)))
\right].
\]
With an optimal discriminator, this corresponds to minimizing a Jensen–Shannon divergence between data and generator distributions. The critic effectively estimates a density-ratio signal.
The saturating generator objective can have weak gradients early in training. The common non-saturating alternative is
\[
\mathcal L_G
=
-\mathbb E_z\log D_\psi(G_\theta(z)).
\]
It has the same desired equilibrium but better gradient geometry. This illustrates a recurring distinction:

Objectives can share an optimum while producing very different learning dynamics.

GAN optimization is a game, not ordinary scalar minimization. Mode collapse, oscillation, critic overfitting, and sensitivity to relative learning rates are properties of the coupled dynamics. Hinge GANs, Wasserstein objectives, and gradient penalties alter those dynamics or the discrepancy being estimated.

title: Distribution Learning Losses
section: 6. Diffusion: Turn Density Learning into Denoising
text:
6. Diffusion: Turn Density Learning into Denoising
Define a known forward corruption process. A common closed form is
\[
x_t
=
\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\,x_0
+
\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\epsilon,
\qquad
\epsilon\sim\mathcal N(0,I).
\]
The generative model learns reverse transitions. A variational bound on \(\log p_\theta(x_0)\) decomposes into KL terms between Gaussian reverse conditionals; these reduce to weighted denoising errors. The common simplified noise-prediction objective is
\[
\mathcal L_{\mathrm{simple}}
=
\mathbb E_{x_0,t,\epsilon}
\left[
\|\epsilon-\epsilon_\theta(x_t,t)\|_2^2
\right].
\]
This resembles regression MSE, but its meaning comes from the corruption process. Solving denoising tasks across noise scales learns the score/reverse process needed to generate samples.

Where design choices enter

predict noise \(\epsilon\), clean data \(x_0\), or velocity \(v\)
sample timesteps uniformly or by importance
retain ELBO weights or use SNR/heuristic weights
fix or learn reverse variance
diffuse pixels or learned latent codes

Dropping theoretically derived ELBO weights can improve sample quality even though it changes the likelihood objective. The statistical derivation tells us what is being approximated; empirical optimization tells us whether that particular weighting trains well.

title: Distribution Learning Losses
text:
7. Comparing the Main Abstractions









Method
Observable training signal
Tractable abstraction
Main mismatch




NTP
exact next tokens
factorized likelihood
data prefixes versus model prefixes; token loss versus sequence utility


VAE
data and encoder-sampled latent
variational likelihood bound
bound looseness and latent collapse


GAN
real and generated samples
learned discriminator discrepancy
equilibrium theory versus unstable game dynamics


Diffusion
clean data and synthetic noise
denoising/score estimation
likelihood-derived versus perceptual weighting



No universal “generation loss” exists. Each method makes a different intractable object observable.

title: Distribution Learning Losses
section: 8. Loss Weighting Is Part of the Model
text:
8. Loss Weighting Is Part of the Model
Generative objectives often have the form
\[
\mathcal L
=
\mathbb E_{u\sim q(u)}
[w(u)\ell_\theta(u)],
\]
where \(u\) might be a token position, latent sample, diffusion timestep, or trajectory state. Both sampling distribution \(q\) and weight \(w\) determine the objective.
Examples:

token averaging gives long documents more total weight
KL annealing changes the VAE rate–distortion path
diffusion timestep sampling changes which noise scales dominate
GAN update ratios change the game dynamics

Always log components separately. A total scalar can improve while one component collapses or dominates.

title: Distribution Learning Losses
text:
9. Numerical and Estimation Stability

Compute token NLL with log_softmax/cross-entropy on logits.
Keep KL calculations in log space when probabilities are small.
Parameterize positive variances through log variance or softplus.
In VAEs, monitor reconstruction NLL and KL per latent dimension.
In diffusion, record loss by timestep/SNR rather than only the average.
In GANs, monitor both players and generated diversity; discriminator accuracy alone is not progress.

title: Distribution Learning Losses
text:
10. Common Failure Modes







Failure
First-principles diagnosis




exposure bias
training and generation induce different prefix distributions


mode collapse
objective/dynamics reward a narrow generated support


posterior collapse
decoder can ignore the latent while satisfying ELBO


blurry VAE samples
likelihood and latent bottleneck reward conditional averaging


poor diffusion detail
parameterization or timestep weighting underserves relevant SNRs


misleading total loss
reduction hides token, timestep, or component imbalance


likelihood–quality gap
statistical density assigns value differently from perception/task utility

title: Zeroth-, First-, and Second-Order Optimization
text:
Training seeks parameters \(\theta\) that minimize an empirical objective:
\[
\min_\theta
L(\theta)
=
\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\ell(f_\theta(x_i),y_i).
\]
Most deep-learning optimizers use a stochastic gradient from a mini-batch:
\[
g_t=\nabla_\theta L_{\mathcal B_t}(\theta_t),
\]
This is an estimate of the full-dataset gradient. A first-order optimizer converts that gradient and its accumulated state into a parameter update. Zeroth-order methods receive only evaluations of \(L(\theta)\). Some estimate a gradient-like direction; others compare candidate points, move a simplex, fit a surrogate, or evolve a population without constructing any gradient estimate.
Optimization quality depends on more than the optimizer name:

learning rate and schedule
batch size and gradient noise
initialization and normalization
gradient clipping
regularization and weight decay
numerical precision

The “order” of an optimizer refers to the highest derivative of the objective available to it:








Order
Oracle information
Examples




Zeroth
function values \(L(\theta)\)
pattern search, Nelder–Mead, Powell, CMA-ES, Bayesian optimization, finite differences


First
gradients \(\nabla L(\theta)\)
SGD, AdamW, AdaGrad, linearized FTRL-Proximal


Second
Hessian or curvature information
Newton, quasi-Newton, Hessian-free methods



Preconditioning and regularization are separate axes. A method can transform a first-order gradient using matrix geometry, and weight decay can be attached to an optimizer without changing its derivative order.
Derivative order is only one taxonomy. The learning protocol asks a different question:








Protocol
Objective or evaluation
Meaning of the example index




Static empirical risk
minimize one fixed dataset average
examples are usually treated as exchangeable


Stochastic optimization
estimate the static objective from sampled mini-batches
sampled order is mainly an optimization device


Online learning
predict, reveal the next loss, then update
\(t\) is a causal decision round



SGD and FTRL can both use first-order information while solving differently organized problems. This distinction becomes important below.
